<meta>This page continues the discussion on the vanity of human existence and the necessity of deep spiritual self-examination, moving from moral philosophy to the internal work of the Holy Spirit.</meta>

the air. We live, we flee, we die, and a tiny speck <note>original: "mote"</note> at the last is the reward of our life's work. <margin>Psalm 62:9</margin> *Every living person is altogether vanity.* <note>original: "Vniuerſa vanitas omnis homo viuens."</note> And as *God* has all good in essence, and all evil in understanding only, so we are quite the opposite: we have all our good in our imagination <note>original: "fansie"</note> and all evil in essence.

<margin>Desires.</margin>
We cannot choose what we should; what we have chosen and obtained does not content us. Present things are loathed; we long <note>original: "bleat"</note> after things absent, unknown, and yet to come.

<margin>Pleasures. *From the very fountain of delights, something bitter rises up.* <note>original: "Medio de fonte leporum, ſurgit amari aliquid." — Lucretius</note></margin>
We cannot enjoy our good things and delight in our pleasures without some mixture of evil and grief.

<margin>Sorrow. *There is a certain pleasure in weeping.* <note>original: "Eſt quædam flere voluptas." — Ovid</note></margin>
We often let our highest pleasure cause a dejection of heart, just as sorrow is also never pure; in sorrowing, there is some pleasure.

<margin>Spiritual consideration of ourselves goes deeper.</margin>
The spiritual consideration of ourselves goes beyond the previous two methods. It searches most deeply: it evaluates <note>original: "ranges"</note> those who are of the best natures, the most civil behavior, and the most respectable profession, as well as those who are endowed with a supernatural decrease of sinfulness and some measure of inward graces. It pierces to the lowest bottom of the best regenerate <term>regenerate</term> <note>Spiritually reborn or restored to a state of grace</note> heart and spies spots in the face of innocence; it shows that despite all that is done well already, *Christ* still has something against them. <margin>Revelation 2:4, 14</margin> It finds blemishes even among the truest streams of grace. We are commanded to make this consideration of ourselves, unless we are reprobates <term>reprobates</term> <note>Those rejected by God or hardened in sin</note>. <margin>2 Corinthians 13:5</margin> *Test yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith; examine yourselves. Do you not know yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you—unless indeed you fail the test?*

<margin>Wrought by the Spirit. Proverbs 16:2; 1 Corinthians 2:10.</margin>
This is accomplished not only by the *Word* of God, but also by the most secret search of the *Holy Spirit*, who *weighs the spirits*. He reveals both the *things of God to us* and our own most secret faults <note>original: "spots"</note> to ourselves.

Here is required great humiliation, frequent meditation, and strict examination, with frequent short, fervent prayers <note>original: "ejaculation" — brief, sudden outbursts of prayer</note> and lifting up...

<margin>The benefit of knowing ourselves.</margin>
O man, why should you wear yourself out trying to know the sea and land, the stars and everything else, and yet not know yourself? It is one of the best parts of wisdom to know yourself. When Demonax <note>A Greek Cynic philosopher.</note> was asked when he began to practice philosophy, he answered, "When I began to know myself."

<margin>It makes us humble.</margin>
It will beat down your pride. Philip of Macedon <note>The father of Alexander the Great.</note>, to restrain and hold down his pride, appointed someone each day to wake him with these words: "Arise, O King, and remember you are a man."

<margin>And wise. To know nature.</margin>
It is great wisdom and great philosophy to know ourselves. It leads us to the true knowledge of our nature. Basil <note>original: "Basilius"; likely Saint Basil the Great.</note> says, "Be mindful of nature, and you shall never be proud. Observe yourself, and you shall be mindful of nature."

<margin>And God. "Man is a model of God in a small image." <note>original Latin: Exemplarqué Dei homo est in imagine parva.</note></margin>
It leads us to the true knowledge of God. The perfect knowledge of yourself shall sufficiently lead you, as if by the hand, to the knowledge of God.

<margin>It prevents judgments. Zephaniah 2:1, 2. 1 Corinthians 11:31. Epictetus's Handbook <note>original: "Epict. Enchir."; the Enchiridion or Manual of the Stoic philosopher Epictetus.</note>.</margin>
It prevents God's judgments. *Examine yourselves, even examine yourselves, O nation not worthy to be loved, before the decree is issued.* <note>Zephaniah 2:1-2</note> *If we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged.* <note>1 Corinthians 11:31</note> If you desire to become good, first believe that you are bad.

<margin>Lamentations 3:40.</margin>
It is the beginning and foundation of grace and repentance. *Let us search and test our ways, and turn again to the Lord.* <note>Lamentations 3:40</note>

<margin>More benefits. Psalm 16:7. Psalm 4:4. 1 Corinthians 11. 2 Corinthians 13:5. 1 Timothy 1:15, 16, 17. Romans 7:24, 25. "Looking to yourself." <note>original Greek: Σκοπῶν σεαυτὸν; a reference to Galatians 6:1.</note></margin>
It is a blessed gift of God for which to give praise; He gives us that counsel, *our inner thoughts also teach us in the night.* <note>original: "reines"; referring to the kidneys or "reins," historically believed to be the seat of emotions and secret thoughts. See Psalm 16:7.</note> It casts out and keeps out sin. It prepares a person properly for Communion. It assures a man that he is no castaway <note>original: "reprobate"; one rejected by God.</note> and makes him thankful to God for that assurance. It preserves him from many temptations (Galatians 6:1). It helps others who fall (likewise).

# CHAPTER III.
# The other blindness of mind, or ignorance of God.

---

> Isaiah 42:19 and 56:10. *Who is blind but my servant?*

---

-> Description <-

<margin>To what extent God is to be known.</margin>
Our knowledge cannot comprehend *God* as He is; yet we ought to understand Him as He has revealed Himself to us: partly through His works, and partly through His Word. *Adam* could have known Him perfectly in this way. But we cannot do so, for our miserable blindness and ignorance of *God*—and of His will and ways in *Christ* for our salvation—is so great and so profound.

<margin>Holy ignorance. Romans 11; Deuteronomy 29:29; Romans 12:3; Unspeakable words <note>original: Αρρητα ρηματα (Arrhēta rhēmata)</note>. 2 Corinthians 12:4.</margin>
Ignorance of *God*, insofar as He has obscured and hidden Himself from us, is no sin. As the scripture asks, *Who knows the mind of the Lord?* Or who knows the exact moment of Christ's second coming? This type of ignorance concerns the secrets of *God* and is a "holy ignorance." Secret things belong to *God*, and revealed things belong to us. It concerns things that are above, meaning that which is *fitting to understand*. An example of this was *Paul's* experience of hearing words that cannot be spoken. We must know all that we need to know and all that we are permitted to know; we should consider ourselves happy if *God* admits us to His court, even if He does not admit us to His private counsel <note>A metaphor: being a member of the royal household (the "court") versus being a member of the inner circle of advisors (the "counsel")</note>.

<margin>Perverse ignorance.</margin>
But the ignorance of *God*—insofar as He has most clearly and carefully revealed Himself through His works and Word—is not a simple *lack of knowledge* <note>original: neſcience</note> or a general want of

<summary>This page defines two types of ignorance regarding God: a "holy ignorance" of things God has intentionally kept secret, and a "perverse ignorance" of what God has clearly revealed through His Word and creation.</summary>

# CHAPTER 3. 2. Blindness of mind.

...of knowledge. It is not a simple privation <note>original: "priuation," meaning an absence or lack</note>, or a mere want of that specific knowledge that we should have had. Instead, it is an ignorance joined with a **perverse disposition**, by which the mind is not only blinded against **God** and godliness, but also plainly rebels against them. There are some notions left since the Fall concerning **God**, good, evil, life, right, wrong, truth, and falsehood; however, they are generally corrupted, maimed, and covered with dross. They are like carved stones in the heap of a ruined palace, serving only to make us inexcusable.

<margin>It is native and acquired.</margin>
This perversely disposed ignorance of **God** (in which we are all born and by which we are corrupted) quickly begins to increase, strengthen, and grow in degrees the further it spreads, like a fire. It becomes a compound blindness, made up of both native and acquired ignorance, and it continues to increase until it passes all bounds.
<margin>It grows.</margin>

<margin>Excusable ignorance.</margin>
The specific types of this ignorance are categorized according to its degrees. One kind is, in part, **excusable**; the rest are more **inexcusable**. **Excusable ignorance** is that which is unwitting <note>original: "witlesse"</note> but not willful; in this state, the will is deceived and errs only because of the mind's blindness.
<margin>1 Timothy 1:13; Philippians 3:15; Acts 17:30; John 9:41.</margin>

Thus **Paul** says: ***God* had mercy on me, because I did it ignorantly.** And, **If any be imperfect in the faith, they should be supported. If you are otherwise minded, *God* will reveal the same to you.** And, **The time of this ignorance, *God* overlooked.** This refers to the Gentiles. Also, **If you were blind, you would have no sin.** But take note: this simple ignorance is not altogether excusable, since it is our duty to know that which we are ignorant of. However, it is excusable in part compared to willful ignorance or sins committed against knowledge. The servant who knows his master’s will shall be beaten with many stripes, but he who does not know it shall be beaten with few.
<margin>It excuses not the whole [guilt], but only a portion. <note>original: *Excusat non a toto, sed a tanto*</note></margin>
<margin>Luke 12:47.</margin>

<margin>Inexcusable and malicious ignorance.</margin>
**Inexcusable ignorance** is malicious and willful. **They say unto *God*, "Depart from us, for we do not desire the knowledge of your ways. Who is the Almighty, that we should serve Him?"** Because of this, **they willfully do not know.** They regard...
<margin>Job 21:14; 2 Peter 3:5; Romans 1:28; Psalm 14:1; John 12:4; Genesis 6:5.</note>

It uses the metaphor of a ruined palace to describe the remaining but corrupted natural knowledge of God in humans.</summary>

The second part is *not to know God*. Many are willingly ignorant so that they may sin more freely. Vanity of mind causes willful blindness to grow until *the foolish heart becomes full of darkness*, and at last becomes *finally a reprobate mind*. This leads to that *spiritual intoxication* <note>original: "ebrietie"</note> and the *power of delusion* <note>original: "efficacie of delusion"</note> that causes people to *believe lies*.

Our natural ignorance of *God*—his godhead, his power, and so on—is less than our ignorance of *Christ* and of the grace found in him. By the greatest light of human reason, the gospel is considered altogether nothing but foolishness.

---

->*Parts affected.*<-

<margin>
The mind.
</margin>
The mind is the faculty chiefly affected here, to a greater or lesser degree, and the rest of the faculties are affected by association. By the light of nature, the *mind* possesses some principles and common notions by which *God* may be known. However, the *mind* is narrow and weak—like the eye of an owl before the *sun's beams*. It can only know him in general terms, but not in specific detail.

<margin>
Common notions <note>original Greek: "Κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι"</note>.
Apprehension <note>original Greek: "Κατάληψις"</note>.
Aristotle in *Metaphysics*.

Acts 14:14.
Acts 17:24.
</margin>
For example, principles such as *there is a God* and *God is to be worshipped* are common, obscure, and imperfect. The men of *Lystra* knew that there was a *God* by their common natural light, but they erred in the specific application because they tried to offer sacrifices to *Paul* and *Barnabas*. Through reason, the blinded *mind* may attain this natural sight of *God*, but only with great difficulty and many helps; it is obtained by few and takes a long time to achieve. Even when it is attained, it is mixed with many errors and the *suppressing of the truth in unrighteousness* <note>original: "withholding of the truth in unrighteousnesse"</note>. Without the supernatural remedies of grace to strengthen and perfect it, the mind must continue to remain in darkness.

### Chap. 3. 2. Blindness of mind.

...to continue and grow in their ignorance. Many things that should be known are unknown, either by negligence to know, or sluggishness to learn, or bashfulness <note>original: "shamefastnesse": being too shy or modest to ask questions</note> to inquire; such ignorance has no excuse.

->Signs and Symptoms.<-

<margin>He is an atheist. Galatians 4:8.</margin>
He who is thus blinded and ignorant of the true **God** either impiously has no **God** or superstitiously has too many gods. His heart is haughty, and the usual word of all his thoughts is, *There is no God*. Or if he acknowledges that there is a **God**, he still denies His providence and presence, and says in his own mind, *God has forgotten, He hides His face, He will not look out, He will never search*. He has toward God no love, no fear, no trust, because he does not know Him. He either (like an atheist) never worships **God**, or else (like the **Athenians**) does it ignorantly <note>original: "Ignoto Deo": To the unknown God</note>. As for godliness, he either denies it, mocks it, or counterfeits it for profit. No man gets a paralyzed <note>original: "palise": palsied</note> hand through a blinded eye. But the blinded mind has a paralyzed heart and is senseless of sin and wrath, and of the silent <note>original: "deafe"</note> strokes of a punishing <note>original: "reuenging"</note> conscience. His conscience always sleeps; or if it stirs, he has enough fleshly songs to sing it back to sleep. From the beginnings <note>original: "preludies"</note> of sins, he comes to a habit of them, so that at last he cannot repent, nor change his dark <note>original: "Morian": Moorish or Ethiopian, referring to Jeremiah 13:23</note> skin, nor cleanse his leopard spots. He is wise to do evil and ignorant to do good.

# Chapter 3. Section 2: Blindness of mind.

<margin>Natural knowledge is a tutor <note>original: "Pedagogue"</note> that leads to the light of grace.</margin>
...by supernatural light, sight, and divine contemplation <note>original: "Theorie"; from the Greek *theoria*, meaning a looking at or contemplation of the divine</note>. By natural light, we are led—as if by a tutor—to know God, his Divinity <note>original: "Godhead"</note>, goodness, wisdom, power, providence, some articles of our faith, and the Ten Commandments. Thus, we are fitly prepared to be taught by supernatural contemplation.

<margin>The knowledge of God is three-fold.</margin>
You must understand that the knowledge of God is either purely *Natural, Scriptural, or Spiritual.*

<margin>Natural knowledge is two-fold: Inborn and acquired.</margin>
Again, natural knowledge is either *inborn or acquired.*
Inborn knowledge is naturally grafted into the minds of all people. Through principles known by nature, they may understand that there is a God.

<margin>Acquired knowledge.</margin>
Acquired knowledge of God is gathered from his works and creatures. These act as many *characters* <note>original: "Characters"; symbols or written signs</note> and footsteps of the *Deity*, imprinted everywhere and in everything, and understood by the things that have been made.

<margin>Romans 1:19-20. "And every blade of grass represents the presence of God" <note>original: "Præsentémque refert quælibet herba Deum"</note>. Psalm 19:1. Job 12:7, 8, 9, and 10.</margin>
Consider God, not by physical sight, but by his works. The heavens sound out the glory of God; their greatness and brightness suggest <note>original: "insinuates"</note> to us the power and glory of the Master-builder <note>original: "Work-master"</note>. Indeed, all creatures resemble the majesty of the Creator. *Ask now the beasts, and they shall teach you; and the birds of the heaven, and they shall tell you; or speak to the earth, and it shall show you; or the fish of the sea, and they shall declare unto you. Who is ignorant of all these, or does not know that the hand of the Lord has made them? In whose hand is the soul of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind.* The creatures are the "Book of Nature," as said *Anthony the Hermit* <note>original: "Antonius Eremita"; Saint Anthony the Great, an early Christian monk</note>. When he was criticized for his lack of books, he answered the philosopher: "My book, O philosopher, is *the nature of things created.*"

<margin>Nicephorus, Book 1, Chapter 43. Dionysius, *On Mystical Theology* <note>original: "l. de myst. Theol."</note>, Chapters 2 and 7.</margin>
There are three ways our minds collect the knowledge of God from the light of nature and from creatures:
1. By the way of *excellence* <note>original: "Via eminentiæ"</note>: when we attribute to God (by a certain similarity) whatever is excellent in creatures. For example, when we count God the most wise, the most just, the most merciful, and so on.
2. By the way of *negation* <note>original: "Via negationis"</note>: when we remove from God whatever is defective or

<margin>The way of excellence. The way of negation.</margin>

# ### Chapter 3, Section 2: Blindness of Mind.

...other. And in Judas, after the betraying of Christ.

<margin>The harmony of the world.</margin>
Behold the order, progress, and end of all causes: the complete harmony of the universe, where there are so many opposites, yet such harmony among them. Everything comes from one, and everything returns to one <note>original Latin: "Omnia ab uno, omnia ad unum"</note>.

<margin>Predictions.</margin>
Behold the prediction of future events; the strange signs and wonders that have occurred, along with their outcomes, which proclaim a higher power.

<margin>This appears through the analogy of a ship.</margin>
If you see a well-equipped ship at sea, coming into its home port and sailing smoothly before the wind, wouldn't you quickly conclude that there is a captain <note>original: "Governor"</note> within it who guides it? In the same way, when you behold this beautiful universe with all its decorations and continuous motions, you may say that there is an internal and supreme Mover behind it.

<margin>A clock.</margin>
If you look into a clock, you see that one wheel is moved by the next wheel; that one is moved by another wheel, and that by yet another, until you reach the weight <note>original: "poize"</note>. And then you must conclude that a craftsman formed it and made everything move, while he himself remains unmoved.

<margin>Yourself.</margin>
If you consider yourself, notice how the veins from your liver provide nourishment. Your nerves from the brain allow for movement. Your arteries from the heart sustain your life; in them, you perceive a spirit, and by that, a pulse which you cannot stop, even to save your life. Observe the wonders of your brain, of your heart, and of your other vital organs <note>original: "noble parts"</note>, and see how wonderfully you are made.

<margin>Psalm 139:14. A tree.</margin>
Does not the tree that your eye sees lead your mind to the root, which is unseen beneath the earth? Does not a river lead your thoughts to its source and its first springs? And should not created things <note>original: "the Creatures"</note> lead your mind to the Creator?

<margin>A cottage in India. Psalm 8:1.</margin>
If you enter into India <note>In this period, "India" often referred generally to any distant, newly explored land, including the Americas.</note> and, in some newly discovered part there, spy a cottage, wouldn't you say, "Here are the footsteps of men"? And who does not see the footsteps of God throughout all the world? *How excellent is his name throughout all the world!*

### Chapter 3, Section 2: Blindness of Mind.

<margin>It is a wrong way to know God through the devil. Plutarch in his treatise, *On the Obsolescence of Oracles* <note>original: "de defec. oracul."</note>.</margin>
It is a fair and seemly thing when a man is drawn to God by the *inward light* of his mind and the *outward sight* of the world. But it is a backwards way to be led forward by the devil's hand. An example of this is that governor <note>original: "president"</note> in Sicily, an atheist, who believed there was a God only because there was a devil, after he asked his *idol* for an answer to a question he had delivered in a sealed envelope.

<margin>The universal consent of all people.</margin>
Go through every corner of the world and search through all ages; behold all kingdoms, and even the very dens and caves of the most barbarous people, wherever mankind has lived. You will find this universal consent among them: that there is a God. This truth is written and read in every climate; it is engraved and deeply ingrained in man. People in newly discovered lands, though they may be without kings, laws, houses, or clothes, are never found to be without some knowledge of the Godhead. It is so natural for man to know the author of life and the cause of nature that all of antiquity agrees with this. <margin>The testimony of antiquity.</margin> The *Indian Brahmins <note>original: "Brachmanes"</note>, the Persian Magi, Pythagoras, and Plato,* as well as all the most ancient poets—*Orpheus, Homer, Hesiod, Pherecydes, Theognis, etc.*—always begin their works with *Jupiter*.

He is that only and universal *Unnamed One* <note>original: "Innominat"</note> who is above every name. # Chapter 3. 2. Blindness of mind.

<margin>Polytheism is atheism <note>original: "πολυθεοτης eſt αθεοτης"</note>.</margin>
...did not in their hearts acknowledge them, but only did so to please the people and the King. To have many gods is to have no God; for the gods of the **Gentiles** <note>In this context, non-Jewish people or pagans.</note> were either noblemen who had died, or devils falsely taking the name of gods upon themselves, or else they were simply stars.

<margin>The Gentiles did not receive this knowledge from the Jews.</margin>
While it might be said that the **Gentiles** received their knowledge of God from the **Hebrews**, the answer is: 1. The **Jews** did not spread the mysteries of their religion among the infidels. 2. The pagans <note>original: "Ethnickes"</note> mocked the Jewish religion.

<margin>God is seen and praised in his works.</margin>
Therefore, say with **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure from antiquity associated with wisdom and the "universal nature."</note>: *Lord, shall I contemplate you in things above, or in things below? You have created all things, and this universal nature is nothing else but your image.* But rather say with **David**: *Bless the Lord, all you his works, and let my soul bless the Lord.*

<margin>Psalm 103:22.</margin>
<margin>The school of nature has three types of students: Epicureans, Philosophers, and Christians.</margin>
The "school of the creatures" <note>The study of God through the natural world.</note> contains three types of students. 
1. Wordly **Epicureans**, wallowing sensually among the creatures; they feed themselves like beasts and are filled with **vanity**. 
2. **Curious heads**, busy with dark and troublesome questions; they are filled with **variety** <note>Likely referring to the fragmented and conflicting opinions of secular philosophy.</note>. 
3. Spiritual **Christians**, using the creatures as if they did not use them, and are filled with **truth** <note>original: "verity"</note>. 

Be you of this third type, who both sees God and enjoys him best through his creatures. You can perceive this more sensibly than the Orator <note>Referring to the Roman statesman Cicero.</note> could declare when he said: *The benefits that we use, the light that we enjoy, and the spirit that we breathe—we see that they are given and shared with us by God.*

<margin>Cicero.</margin>
<margin>Nature teaches only that God exists, but not what he is.</margin>
This natural knowledge of God teaches only in general that there is a God. However, it does not explain who he is or how he should be worshipped. Yet, this kind of knowledge is granted to men to draw them toward a further and better search for God. As **Paul** said: *As I passed by and beheld your devotions <note>Your objects of worship.</note>, I found an Altar where it was written, "Unto the unknown God." Him, whom you then ignorantly worship, I show to you: God who made the world and all things that are in it, etc. That they should seek...*

<margin>Acts 17:23–29.</margin>

<summary>This page argues that while nature reveals the existence of God, it cannot reveal his true identity or the proper way to worship him. It distinguishes between the empty curiosity of pagan philosophers and the spiritual understanding of Christians who see God's hand in creation.</summary>

In his Word, Romans 1:4.
In his Christ. Hebrews 1:3.

Second, he is found in his Word through the enlightenment and revelation of that mystery now made manifest. For although God is proclaimed to us throughout the whole world as God in his creatures, he is not only revealed in that way; he is revealed far more clearly in the Scriptures and declared to be a God in his *Christ, for the salvation of man.*

# Chapter 3. 2. Blindness of mind.

<margin>
John 5:39.
Acts 8:31.
Romans 10:14.
Acts 26:18.
Romans 2:20.
Scriptural knowledge is common to the wicked.
</margin>
...is obtained by searching the *Scriptures* and by the help of a guide or preacher. Its purpose is *to open the blinded eyes* through a form of knowledge that is common even to the wicked. And because there is nothing more in such a person except only *natural and scriptural knowledge*, he may become a shining lamp, but not a burning coal. He may enlighten others but not inflame himself; he may reveal to others their inward slumber, deadness, darkness, and hardness. Yet he himself remains within the depths of his soul, which is darkness itself—darkness in the abstract—and he is one who cannot see far off. This knowledge is only very general; it is merely a pedagogy <note>the method and practice of teaching</note> and a manuduction <note>original: *manuduction*; a leading by the hand or guidance</note> toward a more holy and heavenly knowledge that follows.

<margin>
2 Peter 1:9.
Ephesians 5:8.
2 Peter 1:9.
Spiritual knowledge of God.
Ephesians 1:17.
Colossians 1:9.

1 Thessalonians 4:9.
John 6:45.
Colossians 1:13.
Psalm 4.
2 Corinthians 3:13.
Philippians 1.
Psalm 119:99.

The spiritual knowledge of God is that Spirit of revelation, wisdom, and spiritual understanding. By this, although a person sees no more than what is in the Scriptures, they see those same things more clearly and better than through the Scriptures alone. Their enlightened eyes see supernatural truth more deeply than the simple letter of the Scripture can direct them. This is brought about by the secret illumination of the *Spirit*. And by that *Anointing* which he has received and which dwells in him, the Spirit teaches him of all things; and it is true and not a lie. He is made truly taught of God <note>original: *theodidaktoi*</note> and is truly acquainted with the mysteries of salvation. He also knows the dimensions of it: the breadth, length, depth, and height. He has a glorious and comforting, transforming sight of God's face. His light makes him both a shining lamp and a burning coal: he is at once both enlightened and inflamed. He determines matters of conscience with judgment and sincerity. He does all things with a gracious manner of single-mindedness and sincerity of heart, in all circumstances, for God's glory, his own good, and the good of others. In times of confusion, he has the noblest <note>original: *bravest*</note> resolutions. In afflictions, he makes the right use of the greatest evils.

### CHAPTER IV.
## Madness of Mind.

<margin>Ecclesiastes 9:3</margin>
> **2 Timothy 3:9.** *Their madness shall be evident to all men.*
> **2 Peter 2:16.** *The beast forbade the Prophet's madness.*

### Description.

<margin>
Romans 1:21, etc.
Titus 3:3.
Galatians 3:1.
2 Peter 2:16.
2 Timothy 3:1 and 9.
</margin>
The mind is like a vessel that can never be empty: if it is not filled with the heavenly knowledge of ourselves and of God (the two fountains of true wisdom and happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note>), it is replete with strange, mad imaginations and concepts, from which flow the floods of all wickedness and vice. For there is no evil that can be either thought or performed that must not be ascribed to this disease of madness and folly. Just as these great armies <note>original: "troups"</note> of impieties of the **Gentiles** <note>Non-Jewish people; in this context, the author refers to the pagan nations of antiquity</note> against God and nature sprang from a **mad** and foolish heart, it also stems from this: that men are unwise. The **Galatians'** <note>The people of Galatia, whom the Apostle Paul rebuked for being "foolish" for abandoning his teachings</note> fall flowed from their foolishness. The mute beast <note>Referring to the donkey of the prophet Balaam, which spoke to stop his reckless path</note> forbade the Prophet's madness. And all the wickedness of men in these last days and perilous times begins with their **madness**, and these sins are nothing else but the symptoms of it.

This is not like that madness that proceeds from the body's physical imbalance <note>original: "distemper"</note> and is cured by natural **medicine** <note>original: "physike"</note>; nor is it like the rage of those who are **afflicted by tarantism** <note>original: "Tarantat," referring to a historical dancing mania believed to be caused by the bite of a tarantula</note> and are cured

<summary>This chapter introduces "madness of the mind" as a spiritual disease that fills the soul when it lacks divine knowledge, citing it as the root cause of all historical and biblical sin. The author distinguishes this spiritual madness from physical ailments or specific medical conditions like tarantism.</summary>

<header>CHAPTER 4. Madness of Mind.</header>

<margin>Mark 5:2</margin>
...by music. Nor is it like that **Corybantic** <note>original: "Corybanticke"; referring to the wild, frenzied rituals of the priests of Cybele</note> fury of the Vestal Priests, as if they were in a trance <note>original: "extasie"</note>. Neither is it like the madness of those **demoniacs** <note>Individuals possessed by demons</note> whom Christ cured (Mark 5:2).

<margin>Genesis 6:5 and 8:21. Matthew 15:19.</margin>
But it is that acquired, impure, and immediate calamity of the mind, *whereby, through the inventions* <note>original: "forgery"</note> *and imaginations of man's own heart—which are only evil, and that continually*—he runs headlong into error to his endless ruin. If those who run into fires, waters, depths, and dangers to the risk of their bodies are considered **furious** <term>furious: in this context, meaning insane or dangerously mad</term>, then they are to be considered much more mad who willfully throw themselves into endless dangers by their idle and foolish **conceits** <term>conceits: private opinions or fanciful notions</term>.

<margin>
Vain Opinion.
Galatians 5:8.
Ephesians 4:17.
1 Peter 1:18.
</margin>
The first and immediate work of this madness of mind is an imagined opinion. It proceeds from a mind deluded <note>original: "illuded"</note> by the imagination, which the diseased person thinks to be both true and good, when in itself it is both false and evil—the very vanity of the mind.

<margin>
Opinion is either true or false, good or evil.
True and good.
False and good.
False and evil.
</margin>
Opinion, as it is always weak <note>original: "infirme"</note> and uncertain in its own nature, is either true or false in regard to its **object**, and either good or evil, wise or foolish, in respect to its **effect** and **end**. Even if an opinion were completely false, if it leads to no evil, it is less foolish and less to be concerned about. For a man to consider his swarthy <note>original: "blacke"</note> wife beautiful <note>original: "faire"</note> makes him loving; to consider himself worse than he is makes him humble; to account all things for the best procures peace for himself. His opinion may be false, but it is not very foolish. Such opinions and imaginations are not to be cured. 

But if an opinion is both false and tends toward ill effects and ends—to the offense of himself, of others, or of God—and if they are the imaginations of **wicked enterprises**, then it is foolish and to be cured, if it is possible.
<margin>
An opinion that is false and evil is madness, and it is either... Proverbs 6:18.
</margin>

<margin>
Simple.
2 Peter 2:10.
Hosea 7:11.
Willful.
2 Peter 2:10.
</margin>
Some are simply corrupted by themselves or deceived by others, having soft minds like wax that receive any impression <note>original: "stampe"</note>, being like a foolish dove. Some, again, are full of self-conceit, *wiser in their own conceit than seven* <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "uen" refers to "seven men that can render a reason" from Proverbs 26:16</note>...

He distinguishes between harmless false opinions (like seeing beauty in a spouse) and dangerous ones that lead to sin and ruin.</summary>

There are also <term>schismatics</term> <note>original: "Schismatikes"; those who create divisions or sects within a church</note>, from whose own brains come new, inbred opinions which they most stubbornly hold onto as if they were divine oracles.

Pestilent.

They are so married to their own opinions (acting as absolute and assertive dogmatists) that they would have all the world ruled by their own laws, and they would tyrannically have everyone subject to the authority of their sayings.

| [[margin: **Envy is a wasting disease <note>original: "consumption"</note>.**]] | **I**t is rightly called *the rotting of the bones*, as it is so painful to the mind and harmful to the body. Like a persistent fever <note>original: "feuer hecticke"; a wasting fever often associated with chronic illness</note>, it consumes a person and brings them to their end, just as the rotting of the marrow does within the bones. |
| :--- | :--- |

In this way, the envious person misconceives and sinisterly misinterprets another man’s happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note>. |
| [[margin: **Envy has two targets <note>original: "obiects"</note>.** **Happiness.**]] | It is a complex and confused passion, having two types of targets. The first is the welfare and happiness of another, for which the mind feels sometimes a sadness and discontented grief, sometimes a hatred, and sometimes both. This happens because the good which we dislike in others is either something we lack and desire to have, or we fear some evil will come from it to ourselves or to others whom we love, or we believe the person envied is unworthy of it. |

Envy arises from those things that are nearest to us: "One beggar is miserable that another goes by the same gate." Envy frets most at those who have recently risen in status. But if that rising cost the person much—such as through great suffering in wars or through painful service to kings—envy is then less provoked. However, if glory and greatness come to anyone freely, and by "fortune’s favor" (as they say), envy is stirred up all the more. The envious person makes another's happiness his own torment; but when the best people, in their best state, are envied, it is not their own misery, but the disease of the envious.

[[margin: *Plutarch.*]]

[[margin: *Ecclesiastes 4:4.*]] *Solomon observed all toil <note>original: "trauell"</note> and every perfection of work, and found that this was the envy of a man against his neighbor.*

[[margin: **Self-love.**]] Self-love begets too many needless desires. It is hardly satisfied with its own abundance; it likes the good things of others which it has never tasted better than its own, which it enjoys daily. Because of rich desires, it always makes itself poor. In the midst of wealth, when it sees others have what it lacks, it envies because it feels in want. 

[[margin: **Avarice.** / *Those who envy are in want. Plautus.* <note>original Latin: "Qui invident, egent."</note>]]

[[margin: **Ambition.**]] And if there is also a mind puffed up with ambition, thinking that another’s light is likely to darken their candle, or another’s fire to draw away their heat, or another’s glory to obscure their spark, they fret all the more. These three vices—self-love, avarice, and ambition—crave a fourth to join them: *Hatred*, hating him who has the thing we love. All conspire to beget envy. 

[[margin: **Hatred.** / *Augustine.*]]

We envy superiors because we are not equal to them; we envy inferiors lest they become equal to us; and we envy those who are equal because they have been made equal. So Saul envied David’s happiness; Rachel envied Leah’s fertility; and Cain envied Abel’s piety and grace.

### ->Curation and remedies.<-
---
<margin>Consider closely the occasions for your envy. Plutarch.</margin>
**I**f the occasions for envy were removed, it would soon cease. Take away the fuel, and the fire will cease. But it would be extremely unreasonable for anyone to become unhappy just to cure another's envy. And because the nature of envy does not extend itself toward any man's person simply, or toward any man's happiness without respect to the person, but toward the person as he enjoys and lives in his present happiness.

### CHAPTER 21. ->The Wasting Away of Envy<- | [[page number: 319]]
---
<margin>Points for consideration. Envy feeds on the living; after death it rests. <note>original Latin: Pascitur in vivis livor, post fata quiescit.</note></margin>
For as soon as happiness <note>original: felicity</note> leaves the envied person, or the envied person leaves their happiness through death, envy ceases of its own accord. It is the duty of a virtuous person to make it cease willingly before it ceases out of necessity. Imagine the happiness of others in your mind abstractly, as a temporary circumstance <note>original: separable accident</note> enjoyed only for a short time—like a borrowed loan that perhaps tomorrow must belong to someone else. Consider the happy person again apart from their prosperity: imagine them in your mind as a mortal human, perhaps to be stripped naked tomorrow, running from the very things you envy in them and rushing toward their grave. Their best things are only in their "becoming" <note>original: Fieri; a philosophical term for things in the process of being made or happening</note>. Wait with patience for the conclusion of the comedy or tragedy of their life. And if that person is godly, they are to be crowned with glory when you lie condemned in torment with devils because of your devilish envy.

<margin>Love, and motives for it. 1 Corinthians 13:4; Romans 13:10.</margin>
Diligence must be used to attain or renew our spiritual rebirth <note>original: regeneration</note>, which expresses itself most clearly in love that does not envy: *It is not puffed up, it does not seek its own interests, and it bears all things.* We are all the mutually serving members of one body, united to one Head <note>referring to Christ</note>. The good things of others are for our benefit, if we could only see it. The strength of one serves for the use of another. Resenting <note>original: repining</note> the happiness of another member of the body is nothing but attacking our own welfare. Love your friends in God, and your enemies for God’s sake. If you feel that anyone provokes you to envy, consider it your required duty to pray for them as a Christian. Include them in your secret prayers, and your envy shall cease. 

<margin>Consider carefully the prosperity of others. Psalm 73:3.</margin>
If those who are good, or at least not the worst sort of people, are prosperous, it moves people's minds to fret a little. But if the wicked or unworthy flourish, it increases the passion of envy much more. Their painless <note>original: bondlesse; likely meaning a death without the "bands" or pangs of a long illness</note> death, vigorous <note>original: lusty</note> life, their fat bodies, their abundance exceeding their desires, their lack of restraint, presumption, blasphemy, and daily increase in riches provoke even the godly to impatient 
->fretting.<-

<summary>This page argues that envy is irrational because earthly happiness is temporary and ends at death, urging readers to instead practice Christian love and prayer. It acknowledges the particular difficulty of seeing the wicked prosper, a common spiritual trial.</summary>
<keywords>envy, mortality, spiritual rebirth, Christian charity, prosperity of the wicked, Psalm 73, 1 Corinthians 13</keywords>

### CHAPTER 21. ->The Wasting Power of Envy.<- <note>original: "consumption"</note>

<margin>Points of consideration: God's providence.</margin>
...fretting. The chief remedy is to enter, with *David*, into the Sanctuary and School of God. Learn by His Word and Spirit that He orders all things most wisely and justly: He corrects you with the lack of the good things that others have, and tries others by the benefits that you lack. Consider that expected endless happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note> prepared for the godly, which makes them despise <note>original: "contemne"</note> all earthly vain pomp as unworthy to be envied. Who can charge God with folly for bestowing on anyone more than is appropriate? Who can challenge Him for unrighteousness for giving anyone less than is due? Consider that no one has perfect blessings, pure and free from the mixture of troubles; he who has the fairest outward appearance may have the greatest sorrow. The consideration of the one should keep us from envying the other.

<margin>Walk worthy of the light. Romans 13:11–14.</margin>
Consider the season: that it is now time for us to arise from sleep, and after the darkness of ignorance has passed, it is our special duty that all wicked affections (which are the fruits of darkness) be driven out of us by the saving and sanctifying knowledge of God's truth. We must order all our passions and actions according to that certain and sure rule of all righteousness. For if now our salvation is nearer than when we first believed, the night is past and the day is at hand. It is our duty to cast away the works of darkness, *and let us put on the armor of light. Let us walk honestly, as in the day: not in gluttony and drunkenness, nor in sexual immorality <note>original: "chambering"</note> and wantonness, nor in strife and envying. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to fulfill its lusts.*

<margin>Amend your pride and self-love <note>original: "Philauty"</note>. Strangle the mother, and there will be no daughter. <note>original Latin: "Suffoca matrem, & non erit filia."</note> Augustine, *Sermons on the Words of the Lord*.</margin>
Pride does not have a barren womb; wherever it exists, it brings forth children, of which envy is the most common. Strangle the mother, and there shall be no daughter. Endeavor to be endowed with the contrary quality of humility. <margin>True contentment <note>original: "contentation"</note>, a notable remedy for envy.</margin>
Temporal <note>original: "temporall"; meaning worldly or physical things belonging to time rather than eternity</note> things are but finite; they cannot satisfy everyone, and they are less than what can content any single person. The more they are divided among many, the less they satisfy. From this arises envy, when one person desires to have what another has; the possessor is thought either to frustrate or restrict the seeker from his desires. It is the duty of all to moderate and bridle their delights and desires in temporal things, and to attain to true contentment by despising, in some true measure, those things below, and by converting our appetites to spiritual, heavenly, and eternal things, which are not limited <note>original: "scanted"</note> by the number of owners. The more that they are enjoyed by many, the more they appear to increase. And because they are infinite in

# ->C H A P T E R  XXII.<-
## ->A trembling heart.<-
---
<margin>Deuteronomy 28:65; 1 Samuel 14:15, 16; Psalm 55:4.</margin>
*Deuteronomy 28:65: The Lord shall give you there a trembling heart.* **1 Samuel 14:15, 16.**
*Psalm 55:4: My heart trembles within me.*

---
->### Description.<-
---
<margin>The object of fear.</margin>
**E**xtreme fear forces the heart to tremble because of those imminent evils that the mind unwillingly perceives as being opposed and contrary to our will and well-being. <margin>Fear is a sickness.</margin> Fear is a pitiful disturbance <note>original: "perturbation"</note> and is most unbecoming in a man; for it is a shame for a man to be called fearful, and to be sick with such a foul <note>original: "filthy"</note> sickness.

<margin>The object of fear is some terrible thing. Aristotle, Ethics, Book 3, Chapter 6. Ibid Chapter 7. Luke 21:11.</margin>
The object of fear is some evil, disliked and detested as harmful <note>original: "noisome"</note> and imminent—even if it is so only in appearance and perhaps never actually happens. It is therefore called "the expectation of evil," specifically an evil that is terrible to our perception. Christ calls such evils "fearful things" <note>Luke 21:11</note> which we would gladly avoid <note>original: "eschew"</note>. Those who lay desperate hands on themselves (which is one of the most terrible evils) do not fear death because they have no desire to avoid it; instead, they seek it as if it were some good thing.

<margin>Many sorts of fear, such as natural fear.</margin>
**1.** There are many sorts of fear. **1.** A natural fear, from—

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;2. *A blind or empty <note>original: "vaine"</note> fear*, where there is no cause. This is that *Panic terror* <margin>Blind fear. *Politian's Miscellanies*</margin> (so called from the fictional god *Pan* <margin>*Pausanias*, Book 10</margin>, who was thought to be the author of sudden terrors without cause, driving one out of his wits) which happens to men of all ranks, orders, ages, and professions—the most serious, holy, wise, temperate, and strong. Even beasts are not free from it, such as horses, dogs, etc.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;3. *Carnal and unfaithful fear*, when the physical power <note>original: "fleshly arme"</note> of man is feared more than God. This is that ^a *fear of man that brings a snare* <margin>Carnal fear. ^a Proverbs 29:25</margin>. That forbidden fear: ^b *Do not fear man who is able only to kill the body* <margin>^b Matthew [10:28]</margin>. ^c *This is that fear that should not be feared* <margin>^c 1 Peter 3:14; Isaiah 8:12; Deuteronomy 9:19</margin>: this was in *Abraham* when he denied his wife, but more in *Peter* when he denied his Lord. It was in *Jacob* regarding *Esau*, and in *Samuel* regarding *Saul*.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;4. *Servile fear*, which is like a hired <note>original: "mercenary"</note> servant <margin>Servile fear. 2 Timothy 1:7; Romans 8:15</margin>, fearing punishment for offending, and fearing to offend only for fear of punishment. And like an adulterous woman, fearing to offend, not out of love, but for fear of her husband: His presence is burdensome; if he is absent, she fears his coming. It is like the people of Israel’s fear of the oath <margin>1 Samuel 14:26; 1 Samuel 15:24</margin>, the breaking of which was feared more for the punishment than for the sin. Or as *Saul* feared the people more for the danger to his own person than for love of their persons. Or as the people of Israel feared *God* for his judgments, *and served their own gods* <margin>2 Kings 17:40, 41</margin> out of their own whims <note>original: "phantasie"</note>. This *servile fear of God* is primarily for His judgments and wrath. It is characteristic of the wicked, and is most justly called wicked or miserable because the most wicked and miserable are afflicted <note>original: "diseased"</note> with it <margin>2 Timothy 1:7. *Deilia* from *deido* <note>Greek: "cowardice" from "to dread"</note></margin>.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;5. *Desperate fear* <margin>Desperate fear.</margin> is a kind of servile fear, and the highest degree of it, which was in *Saul* and is in damned devils. 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;6. *Filial fear* <margin>Filial fear. <note>Relating to a son or daughter's respectful duty.</note> Ephesians 5:33; Romans 13:7; Leviticus 19; Numbers 12:8</margin>, which is a loving reverence by which the heart stands in awe of offending anyone. <margin>Psalm 130:4; Romans 8:15</margin> (*With whom there is mercy, so that he may be feared*) For *we have not received the spirit of bondage to fear again, but we have received the spirit of adoption, by which we cry, "Abba, Father."* This is like the fear of a loving child, reverencing his father: it honors him whom it loves <note>original: "affecteth"</note> with a sweet respect. It spares nothing and fears nothing in order to fear him rightly. <margin>Isaiah 66:5</margin> <margin>Genesis 22:12; Ephesians 5:33</margin> **Abraham**, because of his fear of God, did not fear to go and kill his own son. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Blind fear is foolish; *natural fear* is full of pity <note>original: "pittious"</note>. *Carnal, servile, and desperate fears* are impious and faithless. *Filial fear* <note>The fear of a child toward a parent, based on love rather than dread.</note> is godly and faithful.
<margin>All the sorts of fear compared together.</margin>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The *blind and natural fears* are more neutral <note>original: "indifferent"</note>. The *carnal and servile fears* are forbidden; the *filial* is commended and commanded.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;To the ungodly, *servile fear* is a teacher <note>original: "pedagogue"</note> driving them toward desperate fear. But to the *godly*, it is a teacher leading them toward filial fear.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<margin>Psalm 55:19; Isaiah 57:11. The godly and ungodly: how they fear.</margin> The godless may be without any kind of fear because *they experience no changes* <note>This refers to the ungodly living in prosperity without challenges.</note> and because *God holds his tongue for a long time*. But the godly fear always. The ungodly may have all the sorts of fears in their full measure, except only for *filial fear*, of which they can have no part. The godly may be troubled with *blind and natural fear*, ensnared in *carnal fear*, and terrified and prepared by *servile fear*—but they are encouraged and comforted by *filial fear*.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The ungodly begin with no fear and come to *carnal fear*; from the carnal, they proceed to *servile fear*. This often increases until it becomes *desperate*. This, in turn, never ceases until it becomes endless. But in the godly, the *carnal and servile fears* are converted into *filial fear*. The more a person wanders from God, the more his *servile fear* grows; but the nearer he is to God, the less it becomes.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<margin>What fear unsettles the soul.</margin> With all these sorts of fear, the soul is troubled and unsettled <note>original: "diſeaſed"; meaning lacking in peace or ease.</note>

### *The Part Affected*

<margin>The natural emotion of fear.</margin>
There is in man a natural emotion of fear, by which the soul is grieved upon the anticipation of some imminent and impending <note>original: "impendent"</note> evil. The evil is conceived of as something in the future; but the nearer it is, the more it stirs the soul. Whether the evil is real or only apparent, the effect is the same. When the occasion is just and the amount of fear is appropriate, then it is rightly stirred and well accompanied by study, care, and foresight. 

If the evil is a <term>turpitude</term> <note>a shameful or wicked act</note>, it is followed by blushing and <margin>Modesty. Mark 8:38, Rom. 6:21.</margin> modesty <note>original: "shamefastnesse"</note>, even if it is a bygone committed evil. This natural emotion is the immediate seat of this disease when it is forced to be out of balance <note>original: "distempered"</note> and to exceed without just cause. In this state, it is ruled neither by grace nor reason, disturbing both the mind and heart and inordinately disquieting the whole person. 

The heart contracts itself and pulls back, collecting within itself almost all the "spirits" <note>In Early Modern medicine, "spirits" were vital fluids or vapors thought to carry life and sensation through the body</note>. Because of this, the external parts of the body grow pale and cold with a moist sweat. Yet the heart sends some of these spirits out again to provide a little courage and strength to the body. In this <margin>Trembling. Dan. 5:6.</margin> <term>colluctation</term> <note>original: "colluctation"; a struggle or conflict</note> of spirits gathered and scattered, the heart not knowing what to do, there follows a secret trembling of the heart within. If the fear is great, it makes the whole body quake.

<margin>God giving man over to fear. Psalm 14:5, Jer. 20:4.</margin>
Because men do not truly fear God, He justly inflicts upon them this *trembling plague*. And where they think themselves most secure, there they shall be overtaken with fear—even with the terrors of an evil conscience, where...

<margin>*Gellius Book 19, Chapter 1.*</margin>
...almost shipwrecked, he was so afraid that a fearless soldier scorned him because he did not behave himself *philosophically*. But he answered, "You and I do not have the same cause to be affrighted: you are not fearful for the life of a knave <note>original: "knaue"; here meaning a common person or rogue</note>, but I am terrified for the life of a philosopher." Sudden evils so affect the imagination that before a man can gather his wits, he must be somewhat disturbed. This is a fear of weakness, proceeding from the infirmity of human nature. This was seen in <margin>^a Genesis 32:7. ^b 2 Corinthians 7:5. ^c Exodus 2:14. Hebrews 12:21. ^d Luke 7:16. ^e Luke 9:34.</margin> ^a Jacob, who immediately after he was comforted by the Angel, was terrified of his brother Esau. ^b Paul had many of these natural fears. ^c So had Moses. ^d The people were astonished at the restoring of the dead body to life; ^e and the three Apostles at Christ's Transfiguration. This sort of fear is no sin, unless it exceeds its bounds or degenerates into some other kind of fear.

<margin>Corrupt imagination.</margin>
Corruption of judgment makes us so that we do not know what things are terrible, what are not terrible, and what are neutral. Opinion and strong imaginations have the greatest sway over us. <margin>We suffer more often in imagination than in reality. *Seneca, Letter 13.* Blind fear.</margin> There are many things that frighten us more than they actually assault us. It is only our apprehension that makes many things appear evil which are not so in themselves, or in their effect. From this comes that *blind fear*, where there is no true and real occasion; the fault lies only in the corrupt imagination. <margin>*Sigebert of Gembloux.*</margin> For example, in the year 900, when the soldiers in the opposing army followed with great cries a hare that was fleeing toward the city of Rome, the Romans within were so faint with fear at the tumult that they lay in such heaps within the walls that the enemy easily entered and overcame them. Infants are terrified by those who have their faces masked, or at the naming and inventing of ghosts; this proceeds from their natural imagination, which is so strong in conceiving such fears and yet too weak to discern them.

<margin>Plutarch.</margin>
This terror will also arise at the sight or remembrance of those whom we fear most. For instance, when Cassander was made King of Macedonia and Greece, while he was in Delphi, he saw...

It uses historical and biblical examples, such as the Roman army's panic over a hare and the fears of Jacob and Moses, to illustrate how apprehension often exceeds actual danger.</summary>

-> ### *Treatment and remedies.* <-
---

| Fear is treated poorly in many ways, such as when it is merely hidden or slightly altered—as Saul’s fear was with music—or when one forces himself to face terrible dangers despite his fear, either to ambitiously acquire some honor or to avoid <note>original: "eschew"</note> some greater punishment (as those who are desperate do). Sometimes fear is suffocated by anger and fury, by drunkenness, or by the hope of victory. At other times, it is smothered by the encouragement of skill <note>original: "Art"</note> or experience, as seen in soldiers. Ignorance keeps fear down; the hope of gain prevents fear from being felt. Present protection and safety allay it, as when Barak desired the company and protection of Deborah the prophetess. This was the comfort (but not the cure) that David gave to Abiathar: *Stay with me and do not fear, for with me you shall be in safeguard.* Likewise, David wished for the wings of a dove to fly away from his fear. Do not distress your mind with evils before they arrive; they may just as easily never come as come. Fears and hopes deceive us both alike. All things come and go in their own time and by turns. There are millions of unexpected events hidden within the hand of God's providence; the smallest accidents... | <margin>Bad remedies for fear. Be not like the Epicure <note>A follower of the philosophy of Epicurus; here referring to one who believes the soul does not survive death.</note> who fears death because he is terrified of non-existence. Innocence of life and a deep, studied knowledge of the virtues of death give the strongest confidence against the fear of it. Ask of God the lesson to *number your days* <note>Psalm 90:12</note>. -> # CHAPTER XXIII. <-
-> ## The Heaviness of Sorrow. <-
---
**Proverbs 12:25. Heaviness in the heart of man makes it stoop.** <note>original: "doth bring it downe"</note>
**Proverbs 14:10. The heart knows its own bitterness.** <note>original: "knoweth the bitterneſſe of the ſoule"</note>
---

-> ### Description. <-

<margin>What sorrow is.</margin>
**S**orrow is a passion of the heart, arising from the perception <note>original: "apprehenſion"</note> of some present or near-approaching and harmful <note>original: "noyſome"</note> evil. It differs from fear, which perceives evils as they are in the future; sorrow perceives them as they are present. The Jewish people, in their mourning, <margin>It is a sickness, Jer. 10:19.</margin> acknowledged it to be a sickness, saying, *This is my sickness, and I will bear it.*

<margin>Division. 2 Cor. 7:9, 10, 11.</margin>
Sorrow is either godly or worldly.
Godly sorrow is either for sin or for trouble. The <margin>Godly sorrow for sin, and its seven effects. 2 Cor. 7:11.</margin> sorrow for sin is not harmful: it causes repentance leading to salvation, which is not to be regretted. It brings forth all seven effects of true repentance: namely, *care for amendment; clearing ourselves from guilt; indignation against ourselves; fear of offending God; a great desire to approve ourselves to God; zeal for His glory; and revenge <note>In this context, "revenge" refers to self-discipline or the active correction of one's own faults.</note> against our own corruption.* Nothing is so suitable <note>original: "competent"</note> a subject for mourning as sin, which is to the wicked 

<insert>Z 4</insert>

<summary>This page defines sorrow as a psychological and spiritual reaction to present evil, distinguishing it from fear. It specifically highlights the benefits of "godly sorrow" for sin, which leads to repentance through seven distinct spiritual effects.</summary>
<keywords>sorrow, godly sorrow, repentance, sin, Proverbs 12:25, 2 Corinthians 7:11, passions of the heart, spiritual health</keywords>

<margin>Psalm 51:3; 1 Peter 1:5, 6, 8; 2 Corinthians 7:9, 10 and 6:10; Romans 5:2, 3 and 8:26; Proverbs 14:10.</margin>
...wicked, the chief matter of their joy. With their worldly <note>original: "fleshly"</note> joys, they banish all sorrow for both their sins and their sufferings. But the godly—even after their past <note>original: "bigane"</note> sins have been repented for, pardoned, and the tyranny of those sins subdued—keep them in good remembrance. They do this not to condemn themselves any more, but to humble themselves further and to shield <note>original: "hedge"</note> themselves from future sins. 

They sorrow for sin and rejoice in correction. They sow in tears and reap in joy. They rejoice in trembling, and in the midst of heaviness, they have unspeakable and glorious joy. Their sorrow is not something to be regretted <note>original: "not to be sorrowed for"</note>. *The heart knows the bitterness of the soul, and a stranger shall not interfere with its joy* <note>quoting Proverbs 14:10</note>. So the heart may simultaneously have great sorrow for sin and unspeakable joy in God; the sorrow is felt more deeply by themselves than it is known by others.

It is a comforting <note>original: "comfortable"</note> sorrow to mourn for one's own sins, both past and present (Romans 7:22, etc.), and for imminent temptations to sin (1 Peter 1:6). One should also sorrow for the sins of others, just as Lot did (2 Peter 2:8), as did David (Psalm 119:158, 136), Jeremiah (Jeremiah 13:17), Ezra (Ezra 9:3), Christ (Mark 3:5; Luke 9:41), and Paul (Romans 9:2; 2 Corinthians 2:4). Those who do so are blessed (Matthew 5). Their sacrifices and contrite hearts are acceptable (Psalm 51:17). They are marked on the forehead with the letter *Tau* <note>the Hebrew letter used in Ezekiel 9:4 as a mark of protection for those who grieved over the sins of the city</note> (Ezekiel 9:4). God looks upon them (Isaiah 66:1). They do not need to stand mourning <margin>Esther 4:2.</margin> outside the gate of mercy, but may boldly enter in as those most welcome to God. He is the opposite of the *Persian Kings*, who could tolerate no mourners nor mourning clothes in their presence.

<margin>For trouble: Lamentations 3:3; 1 Peter 1:6, 8; Psalm 120:5; Proverbs 18:14; Romans 8:23; Ecclesiastes 7:4; Romans 12:15; 1 Corinthians 12:26; Philippians 2:26.</margin>
Sorrow for trouble among the godly is natural and moderate; it is converted into sorrow for sin and, in the end, into joy. He is sorry for the absence of God and counts it his greatest trouble. He is sometimes subject to the heaviness of a wounded spirit. He sighs within himself while waiting for the redemption of his body. He sympathizes with the trouble of others and of the Church; <insert>he</insert>...

| **CHAP. 23.** | ***The heaviness of Sorrow.*** | **345** |
| :--- | :---: | ---: |
__________________________________________________________________

[[margin: Amos 6:6. [[gloss: Insensibility. <note>original: Αμερσια (likely a variation of "carelessness" or "lack of grief")</note>]]]]
He is sorry for the <term>affliction of Joseph</term><note>A biblical metaphor for the suffering of the people of God or the nation of Israel.</note> and the desolation of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 2:3; Psalm 137:1; Jeremiah 14:17).

[[margin: 2 Corinthians 2:7.]]
If godly sorrow becomes excessive and turns into a "fullness of heaviness," oppressing all the faculties of the soul—or if it becomes an anguish and trouble of conscience where the heart is ready to be swallowed up by too much heaviness—in that case, it must be cured by the remedies for a wounded spirit.

[[margin: Worldly sorrow feigned. Matthew 6:16; Isaiah 58:5.]]
As for worldly sorrow, it is either feigned or real. **Feigned sorrow** is that which has only the outward appearance and show of grief. It is sometimes used in the profession of religion by those who *look sour, and those who afflict their souls for a day, bowing down the head like a <term>bulrush</term>,<note>A plant that bends easily; used here to describe a superficial or performative display of humility.</note> and lying down in sackcloth and ashes.* Sometimes it is used at funerals: some do it by imitation or affectation, some by being hired as professional mourners, and others by command. This ceremony [[margin: Herodotus; Diodorus.]] began with the Egyptians and Chaldeans. The Greeks borrowed this custom from the Egyptians, and the Romans from the Greeks, who concluded their funeral mourning with their *final "hail and farewell"* <note>original: Supremum Salve & vale</note> to the corpse. [[margin: "Hail to you forever, most great Pallas, and forever farewell." <note>original Latin: Salve aeternum mihi maxime Palla, aeternumq; vale, &c. From Virgil, Aeneid, Book 11 (the OCR incorrectly cites Book 3).</note> Jeremiah 9:17.]]

This was also used in Israel (2 Chronicles 35:24). Such lamentation for the dead should not be feigned or immoderate (1 Thessalonians 4:14). Instead, it should be decent, without the ceremonies of the <term>infidels</term><note>Here referring to non-Christian or pagan practices.</note> (Leviticus 19:27 & 21:5; Deuteronomy 14:1). It should be true and moderate (Acts 8:2; 1 Thessalonians 4:14; 1 Samuel 3:31, etc.), and greater for the most worthy people (John 11:33) and less for the unworthy (Jeremiah 22:19; Acts 5:6, 10).

[[margin: Real sorrow. Psalm 42:5; 101:7, 10.]]
**Real worldly sorrow** (which causes the death of both body and soul) is that which is immoderate. It does not humble the heart in a healthy way but instead disquiets, disturbs, and unsettles it. This happens whether the sorrow proceeds from outward evils and losses (which may affect even the best people, such as David and Joshua) or from inward evils, which mostly arise from <term>melancholy humors</term><note>In early modern medicine, "black bile" was one of the four humors thought to govern health; an excess was believed to cause deep depression or "melancholy."</note> and, worst of all, from an evil conscience.

[[margin: It is a sickness.]]
This is a most miserable sickness of the soul.

<insert>It is.</insert> <note>original Greek: ἔστι (esti)</note>

<summary>This page distinguishes between godly sorrow, which can become overwhelming if not managed, and worldly sorrow, which the author categorizes as either feigned (performative and ceremonial) or real (a destructive "sickness of the soul" caused by loss or guilt).</summary>
<keywords>godly sorrow, worldly sorrow, mourning rituals, funerals, melancholy humors, conscience, Egyptian customs, Roman customs</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the psychological and physiological effects of sorrow, specifically how it burdens the heart and depletes the body's vital energies.</meta>

| **346** | **CHAP. 23. *The heaviness of Sorrow.*** |
| :--- | ---: |
__________________________________________________________________

<margin>Menander the comic poet, Antiphanes, Proverbs 12:25</margin>
*Sorrow is a most great evil* <note>original Greek: ἔστιν ἡ λύπη κακόν</note>. *All sorrowful grief is a sickness to a man* <note>original Greek: Ἀπὸ τὸ λυπεῖν ἐστι δυσέρωτον νόσον</note>. And truly says the wisest man, *Heaviness in the heart of a man brings it down.* It brings it down because it wastes the natural, vital, and animal spirits <note>In early modern medicine, "spirits" were believed to be subtle fluids that circulated through the body to maintain life, movement, and thought.</note>. Because sorrow, by troubling and afflicting the heart, consumes it. These spirits are wasted partly by the contraction of the heart, whereby the spirits are choked <margin>2 Corinthians 2:4 <gloss>Anguish of heart.</gloss> <gloss>This [sorrow] comes from dissolving.</gloss></margin> (according to that type of sorrow called *anguish* and *straitness of the heart* <note>term: "straitness" refers to a feeling of tightness or constriction</note>). They are also wasted partly by the dissolution of the spirits (whereby sorrow is called *dissolution*) because it dissolves the spirits and consequently wastes the body, and sometimes resolves it into tears or sweat. It is <margin>Psalm 42:4, Job 39:16</margin> also aptly called *a pouring out of the heart like water.*

---
-> ### Part affected. <-
---

<margin>The natural affection of sorrow. 2 Corinthians 7:11, John 16:20</margin>
**A**s fear regards evil that is future and imminent, the natural emotion of sorrow regards evil as present. At this present evil, a person should be rightly grieved and should be just as careful to shun it. This sorrow should be both moderate and rightly provoked by that which is truly evil. As the evil grows in magnitude, so should the mourning be continuous and increase (if the evil requires it) to the point of lamentation. This is the immediate seat of this perturbation <note>term: "perturbation" refers to a disturbance of the mind or a strong emotion</note> when a person either grieves for that which is not evil in itself, or for something that is not as great an evil as it appears, or when one grieves more or longer than one should; then it creates a sensible dolor <note>original: "dolour"; physical or mental pain</note> and pain in the heart. The heart is the next part affected by this overly stirred passion, and by sympathy, the mind is agitated.

<insert>Causes.</insert>

<summary>This page explains the physical and psychological toll of sorrow, describing how it "wastes the spirits" and constricts the heart, while defining sorrow as a response to present evils.</summary>
<keywords>sorrow, spirits, heart, physiology of emotion, Menander, Antiphanes, anguish, dissolution, grief</keywords>

-> ### Causes. <-

<margin>God. Lamentations 1:12, 13. 1 Samuel 2:33.</margin>
**G**od inflicts heaviness and sorrow of heart, justly punishing the former insolence of those who have provoked him. As Jerusalem confessed: *“Behold and see if there be any sorrow like my sorrow, which is done to me, wherewith the Lord has afflicted me in the day of his fierce wrath. He has made me desolate and daily in heaviness. Again, he has filled me with bitterness and made me drunk with wormwood.”* <note>original: "wormwood"; a proverbially bitter plant used here to symbolize extreme grief or calamity.</note> That is, he has made me lose my senses through great anguish and sorrow. He corrects the hearts of his own people with sorrow to teach <note>original: "learne"</note> them better how to sorrow for sin, and to make them value the joys of his Spirit more highly.

<margin>Satan.</margin>
Satan is ready to be employed as that evil and malicious spirit, directed and permitted by the command of God to execute his will against the wicked. *Just as the evil spirit was sent by the Lord upon Saul and tormented him with sorrow and grievous pangs.*

<margin>External trouble. Genesis 30:1. 1 Kings 21:4, 6.</margin>
External troubles, pains <note>original: "dolours"</note>, disgraces, disappointments, and the loss of friends, parents, wives, children, honors, profits, or pleasures provoke this passion. This is especially true if your mind is infected with self-love or habitual <note>original: "customable"</note> impatience, by which the mind is made weak and is not prepared or armed for both types of fortune <note>referring to both prosperity and adversity</note>. Indeed, it is not only the loss of things we once had that grieves us, but also the lack of things we most desire moves us just as much: *As Rachel, when she saw that she bore Jacob no children, said to him in the anguish of her heart, “Give me children, or else I die.” Ahab’s spirit was sad because he could not get Naboth's vineyard.*

<margin>Melancholic food <note>original: "nutriment"</note>.</margin>
Among external causes, one must also count those things that cause a melancholic imbalance <note>original: "distemper"</note>, and in particular, any melancholic food, such as tainted <note>original: "dannelled"; likely referring to bread contaminated with darnel, a weed known to cause sickness or "drunkenness"</note> bread and drink, too much staying awake <note>original: "watching"</note>, immoderate sexual indulgence <note>term: "venery"</note>, idleness, solitude, or staying too much <insert>in</insert> [solitude].

...in one place (that has gross air), too much crudity <note>original: "cruditie"; indigestion or raw, undigested matter in the stomach</note> and drink without meat, and such things: these are the antecedent causes of the bad humor of melancholy.

<margin>Melancholy, and how it is caused.</margin>
The imagination and fantasy are often, without any external cause, greatly disturbed with the fumes and blackish vapors of atrabillious <note>original: "atrabillious"; relating to "black bile," one of the four humors believed to cause melancholy</note> humors and adust <note>original: "aduſt"; scorched or burnt by heat, thought to make humors more harmful</note> melancholic blood. From this, many strange terrors and implacable sorrows are born. This happens because the brain and its ventricles (the instruments of discretion) are corrupted and darkened by the cloudy, vaporous spirits arising from that boiling blackish puddle, obscuring our native, clear animal spirits <note>original: "animall ſpirits"; in early medicine, these were subtle fluids that carried thought and sensation through the nerves</note>. 

It is not so extreme at first as it becomes over time. This creates not just a simple absence of light, but a substantial and perverse darkness that becomes habitual to the brain over time, corrupting the imagination <note>original: "conceit"</note>. In this way, it always produces fearful and sorrowful passions and the forgery of disguised shapes, causing great anguish. The imagination sends doleful—yet false—reports to the heart. The heart, in turn, responding with the same melancholic affection, turns all joy into discomfort, all hope into fear, and all confidence into despair. 

One might marvel how any <margin>A doubt answered.</margin> gross humor in the body can affect the simple soul? But the answer is easy: the soul is not so much affected as its functions are corrupted and disturbed. That fundamental spirit—the bond and vehicle of the soul <note>original: "vinculum & vehiculum anime"</note>, through which the faculties of the soul work and its functions are practiced—is infected and corrupted by the contagion of the most subtle vaporous spirits of melancholy. And as the spirit is, so are the actions and passions of the soul. Just as if the eye looks through green spectacles, all things appear green according to that medium; even so, when the spirit is corrupted, all the functions of imagination and passion are corrupted.

[[margin: A guilty conscience. 1 Cor. 7. 2 Sam. 11:25. Prov. 14:13.]]
When many sinful pleasures have given birth to a guilty conscience, they are converted into many secret sorrows; even though they think their worst deeds shall never cause trouble, yet at last they feel the sting. *Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful, and the end of that mirth is heaviness.* <note>Proverbs 14:13</note> Among sports and greatest delights, the ungodly have gripings of sorrows and vexations of heart: when their pleasures are ended, their pangs begin. Their mirth was impure and mixed with secret griefs, but their sorrow shall be pure, without any mixing or mingling of comfort or hope to sweeten the bitterness of their terrors. They may be thoroughly sad, but never thoroughly merry: *their rejoicing is short, and the joy of hypocrites is but for a moment; and like the noise of thorns under a pot: their laughter shall be turned to weeping.* <note>Job 20:5; Ecclesiastes 7:6</note> They have always the sting of an ill conscience marring their mirth: *there is no peace to the wicked.* Their guilty conscience is like an arrow-head sticking in their flesh; so that in the midst of their most joyful pleasures, it pains them with private sorrows. It is like a most painful <term>canker</term><note>original: "canker"; a spreading sore or ulcer, often used metaphorically for something that corrupts or consumes from within.</note> that gold, silks, and jewels may cover, but not cure. In regard to their restless conscience, they are like the raging sea that cannot rest. And so much the more for fear of death, they are all their lifetime subject to bondage, knowing (against their wills) *that it is appointed unto men once to die, and after that comes judgment.*
