His pulse is weak and slow <note>original: "creeping"</note>, and his natural humors are corrupted <term>viciate: impaired or made morbid</term>. In his longing for death, his sighing comes before he eats. His face is pale and full of wrinkles, his flesh fades, his skin grows black, and his bones burn with heat. His bowels and milt <term>melt: the spleen, historically believed to be the seat of various emotions, including melancholy</term> swell and boil without rest.

<margin>Special symptoms if it comes from melancholy.</margin>
If it proceeds from melancholy, many of those former symptoms will appear in him. Additionally, his thoughts <note>original: "cogitations"</note> will be empty, and his eyes will occasionally be too fixed. He cannot get his sighs deep enough, nor raise them as high as he would like. He conceives many absurd and ridiculous imaginations about himself. His sorrow has no external cause. He will imagine his least sins to be the greatest, and his minor sins <note>original: "indifferent sins"</note> to be sins against the Holy Spirit <term>sin against the Holy Ghost: often interpreted in this period as the "unforgivable sin," leading the sufferer to believe they were beyond God's mercy</term>. Sometimes he will not be persuaded otherwise but believes that heaven, earth, and hell are all conspiring against him. His sorrows come at intervals, and now and then he experiences involuntary heats and sweats.

<margin>Deuteronomy 28:65. Special symptoms if it comes from an evil conscience.</margin>
If it comes from an evil conscience, his heart trembles and experiences secret terrors. His heart feels a sharp pain <note>original: "gripeth"</note> and is heavy in the midst of his greatest delights. The most horrible sins that he has committed will occasionally stand before his eyes. He finds a worm <term>worme: the "worm of conscience," a traditional metaphor for the persistent gnawing of guilt</term> within him gnawing at the root of his heart. When he looks for the greatest ease, the fury of his evil conscience disquiets him. He thinks God has a legal grievance <term>controuersie: a formal dispute or case brought by God against a sinner</term> against him. While his face is smiling, his conscience is rebuking him. In the midst of all his delights, his inward joy is eclipsed. The evil spirit of terror and bondage vexes him. He tries to be eased by some worldly delight but cannot find any real relief; and no sooner does the entertainment <note>original: "the play"</note> end, but the refreshment vanishes with it, and the grief and torment return.

Time is the physician of all sorrow. Whoever finds no end to his mourning through counsel will find it through time. The reason is that no one can mourn both intensely and for a long time. If sorrow becomes deep-seated <note>original: "inveterate"</note>, it is looked down upon, and not without cause. It is a foolish thing, therefore, to reject so many excellent remedies and, in the meantime, allow time (the consumer of all things, and perhaps of you before your grief) to have more power over you than wisdom and piety. For a wise man, simply becoming weary of mourning is the basest remedy for sorrow. It is far better to stop your sorrow before it stops on its own <note>The author suggests it is better to master grief through wisdom than to simply wait for emotional exhaustion.</note>. <br> It is not always possible to have the cause of sorrow removed (which, if it could be done, would instantly ease the grief). Friends are often found to be "miserable comforters," or else provide no comfort at all. Tears are not always available on command, and they provide little benefit. To rely upon the medicine <note>original: "physicke"</note> of *time* is uncertain, as we do not know whether time will consume us or our grief first. It is therefore most necessary to establish some very excellent remedies to cure sorrow in the heart while the external and prior cause of it remains unremoved. <br> Just as physicians do with agitated humors in the body (which are in violent motion) when they cannot easily purge them or suddenly change them—calling some back to their own source and drawing others aside to a more convenient place—so also are the proper remedies of sorrow categorized as either "revulsion" or "derivation." | ...evils that provoke it to passion: For example, when the mind esteems itself so serene, so high, so excellent, and worthy that it scorns to be affected by any kind of evils. It views them as inferior things—so base, so wicked <note>original: "naughty"</note>, and unworthy of causing a disturbance <note>original: "commotion"</note> or enslaving a divine mind. Furthermore, these evils are considered either not to be evils at all, or else so small and light (no matter how great they truly are) that they are thought unworthy of causing the soul to be molested and pained. The noble <note>original: "royall"</note> mind disdains to complain about them, judging the sorrow for them to be against nature (defacing nature's beauty), against equity (reproaching nature’s law, which has made all things changeable), against piety (murmuring against the providence of God), and against our own usefulness <note>original: "utility"</note>: (killing under a false appearance <note>original: "under colour"</note>). Just as **Jael** killed **Sisera**, covering him with a blanket and driving the nail into his brain all the way to the head <note>See Judges 4:18-21. Jael lured the enemy general Sisera into her tent, offered him hospitality, and then killed him while he slept.</note>. Consider sorrow to be a viper bred in our own bosom: It weakens <note>original: "effeminates"</note> us and covers us with indecent shame. It dries up the bones and eclipses the light of our good fortune. It sours <note>original: "tarteth"</note> the sweetest things that we enjoy, poisoning our best virtues and deeds, and making our whole life bitter. This remedy is rare and excellent, but very difficult <note>original: "difficill"</note>; yet the ancient philosophers taught it, as the **Platonists**, **Stoics**, **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note>, and various others have attained it, as is recorded of **Socrates** at his death. <br> Remedies by *derivation* <note>Redirection or diversion.</note> occur when the heart is diverted from the evil that grieves it toward some other object. By this, the heart may be moved to find more joy in that object than it had sorrow in the evil, or may be made, in a manner and to some measure, to forget the evil. These kinds of remedies are both easier and more common. In physical medicine, hemorrhages, fluxes <note>An excessive discharge of fluid from the body.</note>, inflammations, defluctions <note>A discharge of humors or fluids.</note>, and such things are cured by diversion: turning the flowing stream from a part that is more dangerous to one that is less perilous. <br> This is used in both smaller and greater evils. <br> ->Aa 2<- | [[margin: A disdaining of evils.]] <br> <br> <br> <br> <br> <br> [[margin: A contempt of sorrow.]] <br> <br> <br> <br> <br> <br> <br> [[margin: *Judges* 4. 18, 19.]] <br> <br> <br> <br> <br> <br> <br> <br> <br> <br> <br> <br> <br> <br> <br> <br> <br> <br> [[margin: Remedies by derivation are more easy.]] |

That way, when they come, they may find the heart made firm, and the heart may find them less terrible. Premeditation and the expectation of evil make the mind gather its own forces and make perfect preparation for the tempest. He who exercises himself with the thought <note>original: "conceit"</note> of evils finds the real conflict with them easy. Whatever is long expected falls more lightly, and things, when they come, are half-passed in their violence. It is good for the mind never to be over-confident <note>original: "secure"</note>, lest suddenly surprising evils make it miserable and leave it desperate. Resolution of mind gives the safest advantage in this. <br> <br> If one would object that it is a torment to the mind to think on evil before it comes, the answer is: it is no pain, but a pastime; and the unspeakable comfort in the time of trouble does more than recompense the effort <note>original: "trauell"</note>. ### CHAPTER 23. ->*The Heaviness of Sorrow.*<-

---

...will. There is nothing stable in this world. There is no fixed happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note> in pleasures, pomp, or riches. *Croesus* (that most wealthy King) banished *Solon* from his soil because he reproved him for placing his happiness in his wealth, saying, *“No man is happy before his end.”* But at last, when he was to be put to a cruel death by *Cyrus*, King of Persia, he cried out, *“O Solon, Solon!”* If you lose the goods of fortune, content yourself with the goods of the body; if you lose the goods of the body, content yourself with the goods of the mind. In your losses, look not on the thing that you lack <note>original: "wantest"</note>, but on the things that you have, and enjoy them.

<margin>*Plutarch.* Reason is the ground of all moral comfort.</margin>
Some tart things, a little sweetened, make a pleasant sauce. Lighten all your sorrows with reason. Things which are sad in themselves should be alleviated by reason <note>original: *Res per se tristes ratione sunt allevandæ*</note>. Upon these and similar reasons, all the moral *philosophers* grounded their remedies against sorrow and gave their counsel and precepts accordingly. So it was that *Euphrantes Syrus*, at the death of his wife, quarreled with *Philosophy*. To consider what grief others have suffered more than you—how patiently they have borne their evils and how they had their sorrow cured—affords no small comfort and remedy. This is as seen in the *suffering of the Prophets*, the *patience of Job*, *and what end the Lord brought about*; *knowing that the same afflictions are experienced by your brothers who are in the world.* You must not think evil accidents are a strange thing, but should rather rejoice, inasmuch as we are partakers of Christ's sufferings, so that when His glory shall appear, you may be glad and rejoice. To consider that you have the *Son of God* as a fellow companion in suffering, both with you and for you, is a most powerful <note>original: "forceable"</note> remedy (which none of the *philosophers* ever understood) to bring you comfort in the midst of sorrow and to sweeten all your sores by comparing them with His wounds.

<margin>“O Philosophy, your precepts are tyrannical: you command us to love, but forbid us to grieve.” <note>original: *O Philosophia, tyrannica sunt præcepta tua: amare iubes, dolere prohibes.* Joannes Stobaeus, Sermon 106.</note></margin>

<margin>Consider the examples of others. James 5:10, 11. 1 Peter 5:9. 1 Peter 4:12, 13 <note>The original margin incorrectly cites 1 Peter 12:13.</note></margin>

You can see no one who does not complain of something. <note>Solon (c. 630 – c. 560 BC) was a famous Athenian statesman and one of the Seven Sages of Greece.</note> Solon made one of his mourning friends look down from a high castle at all the houses in the city; he urged him to think to himself how many sorrows and mournings had been there in the past, how many there are presently, and how many are yet to come. He said to him, "Stop mourning for human evils as if they were unique to yourself alone. Have not our betters endured more? And have we not deserved more?" Comparing ourselves with others is a great comfort in misery, and having companions in suffering provides some solace.

<margin>Valerius Maximus, Book 7, Chapter 2.</margin>

<margin>The basis of spiritual comfort is to run to God and to His Word. 2 Corinthians 1:3-4; Psalm 119:50, 76; Romans 15:4.</margin>

But neither can reason (no matter how clear it is), nor examples (no matter how numerous they are) remove sorrow as effectively as running to the God of comfort and to His Word, the true fountain of comfort. For *whatever things were written in the past were written for our instruction, so that we, through patience and the comfort of the Scriptures, might have hope.* <note>Quoting Romans 15:4.</note> It is a futile thing to strive against Him who is greater than man and who gives no account of all His matters. For though God speaks to man through His various judgments, He is not understood until He opens the ears of men, even through the corrections that He had sealed <note>original: "sealed" — meaning God's predetermined or decreed trials.</note> (that is, those He determined to send upon them). He does this so that He might cause man to turn away from an evil undertaking, to beat down the pride of man, and to keep his soul back from the pit <note>original: "the pit" — a common biblical term for the grave or destruction.</note>.

He is also struck with sorrow upon his bed, and the grief in his bones is sore. But if there is a messenger with him—an interpreter, one in a thousand—to declare the righteousness of God to man; and speaking to him of grace, shall (pray to God and) say, "Redeem him (so that he does not go down into the pit) by the reconciliation <note>original: "reconciliation" — here referring to the "ransom" or atonement found in the book of Job.</note> that I have found," then his flesh shall be refreshed more than a child's, and he shall return as in the days of his youth. The meaning of this is that the primary remedy for sorrow during affliction is to be found in God, so that as—

### CHAP. 23.  ->*The Heaviness of Sorrow.*<-

---

Just as He <note>Referring to God</note> inflicts the wound, so He must also provide the healing ointment. The administration of this divine remedy is entrusted to the faithful and exceptional messenger of God. His method must be, first, to declare to the patient the fairness of God in His government, and especially in inflicting that particular cross upon the person. Secondly, he must preach and declare to the patient the grace and mercy of God. Thirdly, he must pray for the patient, so that they may be reconciled to God and obtain mercy. The character of the messenger is also defined: he must be someone who has personally experienced atonement with God and received comfort from Him.

<margin>James 5:14; 2 Corinthians 1:4, 6</margin>

<margin>A consideration of the diversity of trouble: Punishments.</margin>
Consider that all calamities are either *punishments, corrections, trials,* or *martyrdoms.* *Punishments* are either universal—affecting all of mankind equally as common troubles (Genesis 3:17), sicknesses (Psalm 39:10–12), and death (Romans 5:12, Psalm 9:7)—or they are specific, exemplary judgments that befall those who are <term>facinorous</term> <note>original: "facinorous"; meaning extremely wicked or criminal</note> (Luke 23:41, Numbers 25:14, 1 Corinthians 10:11).

<margin>Corrections.</margin>
*Corrections* are fatherly <term>chastisements</term> <note>disciplinary or corrective punishments</note> (Hebrews 12:7, 1 Corinthians 11:23) by which the godly are afflicted and reminded both of their daily weaknesses and flaws (Jeremiah 30:11) and of their more serious sins (Lamentations 1:14). They are warned to be careful of their conduct in the future (Isaiah 38:15, John 5:14).

<margin>Trials.</margin>
<margin>Galatians 4:14</margin>
*Trials* are those calamities that God places upon His own people to test and refine them, just as one would refine metal in the fire (Psalm 66:9, Zechariah 13:9, 1 Peter 1:7). An example of this was the affliction of Job (Job 1:19, James 5:11).

<margin>Martyrdom.</margin>
<margin>John 5:34; Tertullian</margin>
*Martyrdom* is the calamity that falls upon those whom God has chosen to bear witness to His truth even unto death (Hebrews 12:1, Isaiah 34:10). By this "cloud of witnesses," others who are otherwise hard-hearted may be drawn to believe the truth through the indescribable kindness of God. As <note>Tertullian, an early Christian author</note> said, "The blood of martyrs is the <term>seminary</term> <note>original: "Seminary"; here meaning a seedbed or nursery where something grows</note> of the Church."

It is good for you, when you sorrow under calamity,

<margin>*1 Peter 1:3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9*</margin>

And if they are trials, your remedy is to turn your mind away from your trouble and to fix your attention upon your present grace and future glorious state. *You are under the hope of an inheritance that is immortal, undefiled, and that does not wither, reserved in heaven, in which you have cause to rejoice. The trial of faith is much more precious than gold that perishes, and shall be found to result in praise, honor, and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ, in whom you have cause to rejoice with unspeakable and glorious joy.* If when you do well, you suffer wrong and take it patiently, it is praiseworthy: *It is acceptable to God. To this you are called: you should follow Christ's example. You are blessed; the Spirit of glory rests upon you. You should not be ashamed but should glorify God in this regard. You should not think the fiery trial a strange thing, but should rejoice, insofar as you are a partaker of Christ's sufferings, so that when his glory shall appear, you may be glad and rejoice.*

<margin>*1 Peter 2:20, 21. and 3:16, 17, 18*</margin>

<margin>Under Martyrdom.</margin>
If you fall under the calamity of *Martyrdom*; the remedies against all grief within it unspeakably abound. They are so plentifully provided by the divine influence of the secret power and comforts of the Spirit that no tongue can express them, nor pen set them down.

<meta>This page continues a discussion on the nature of despair, specifically focusing on "Violent Desperation" and the distinction between temporal and final hopelessness.</meta>

| ### CHAPTER 24. | ->*Violent Desperation.*<- |
| :--- | :--- |

---

<margin>Final.</margin>
...withdrawal from the thing desired because of an imagined <note>original: "conceited"</note> impossibility. Unholy desperation is either final or temporal. Final desperation is that which is incurable; it happens only to reprobates <note>those the author believes are rejected by God or destined for damnation</note> and to those who die without any hope of comfort. 

<margin>Temporal.</margin>
Temporal desperation is a rejection of hope and comfort to a great degree and in a significant manner, but it is neither full nor final. This may happen even to God's children.

<margin>Desperation strictly defined.</margin>
Desperation, in its most strict sense (as it is commonly <note>original: "vulgarly"</note> used), is a fearful passion and disturbance <note>original: "perturbation"</note> of the soul. Through it, the distressed person thinks he can find no ease or help except in death; thus, he resolves to lay violent hands upon himself, either to be avenged on himself or to be freed from some heavier calamity. He is too sensitive to 

<margin>Two goals.</margin>
his burden and too impatient with his cross <note>a metaphor for life's suffering or divine testing</note>. He desires death either to be a scourge to himself or to be a comfort. 

<margin>Desperate desire for death.</margin>
A scourge, if he is grieved *at* himself; a comfort (though a miserable one) if he is only grieved *in* himself. He does not desire death as the godly do, *who desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.* Nor does he hold his afflicted life in patience while holding death in desire. In his burning sorrow, he does not simply desire death or impatiently crave it from God, as Job did: 

<margin>Job 6:8–9; Job 7:15.</margin>
*And chooses rather to be strangled and to die, than to remain in his body <note>original: "bones"</note>:* But he also goes further; what he chose, he performs with his own hands—acting as his own hangman—most impatiently.

<margin>Sudden, planned, or caused by wrath, hardship, or melancholy.</margin>
Desperation taken this way is either sudden or more long-deliberated. Again, it occurs either under the sense of God's wrath, as Judas was, or under the "cross" (hardship), as many of the Pagans used to do. Or else, it happens under the rage of some furious melancholy <note>a clinical term for severe depression or mental illness at the time</note> or frenzy, as may happen to any man who is out of his wits and does not know what he is doing.

->*Part*<-

---

->### *The Part of the Person Affected.*<-

<margin>Diverse <term>faculties</term><note>The various powers of the soul, such as reason, will, and emotion.</note>.</margin>
**T**his dreadful disturbance <note>original: "perturbation"</note> is a complex affliction, and has its specific place among the various faculties of the soul. It involves a complete deprivation of all joy and hope, as well as a loss of trust and confidence in any present or future good that is loved. In their place, the emotions of sorrow and fear become excessive, making the heart horribly impatient with any present or future evil that it hates, and rendering the person entirely skeptical of relief. The conscience is mortally wounded, and the mind is completely overshadowed by dark fumes arising from a "burning lake" of secret terrors.

->### *Causes.*<-

<margin>Misery.</margin>
**A** misery that is considered beyond remedy—one that seems as though it can only be helped by death—stirs up this passion. Such causes include a troubled life, the fear of a worse death, or the extremity of any fear and danger.

<margin>Jeremiah 8:3; Revelation 9:6; <term>Appian</term><note>A Roman historian known for writing about the Mithridatic Wars.</note>.</margin>
For instance, Mithridates (finding no comfort in his unfortunate circumstances) first attempted to kill himself with poison. When he could not carry this out (because he had always used his own antidotes, still called <term>Mithridate</term><note>A famous complex "universal antidote" used in antiquity and the Middle Ages, named after King Mithridates VI.</note>), he ordered Bitallus, his Captain, to kill him.

<margin>God as a withdrawing cause. 1 Chronicles 10:14.</margin>
Many people (as they justly deserve) are abandoned by God; they have foolishly surrendered themselves to the service of Satan and allowed that "Old Serpent" to lie too long in their hearts <note>original: "bosoms"</note>.

<margin>Satan as an active cause.</margin>
Eventually, he begins to wake them by biting them through the heart, until they can find no rest except in their own foolish destruction. Thus the devil entered into Judas—first to betray his Master, and then to commit suicide <note>original: "put violent hands upon himself"</note>.

<margin>1 Samuel 16:14, 23:13, and 28:8.</margin>
God sent an evil spirit upon King Saul, which first caused him heartache, led him to kill all the priests, and finally drove him to seek counsel from the

B b ->Witch,<-

...witch, and at last killed himself.

<margin>Melancholy.</margin>
<term>Adust melancholy</term> <note>original: "Adust melancholy"; in the medical theory of the four humors, this referred to "burnt" black bile, which was thought to cause intense depression, anxiety, and mania.</note> is the messenger of great despair; its dark vapors make a person’s spirit feel intoxicated. The mind conceives strange, deluding imaginations. Even if a person were entirely free of external misfortune, a corrupt imagination presents thousands of imagined <term>crosses</term> <note>original: "crosses"; trials, afflictions, or burdens to bear.</note> to the heart. They imagine sometimes that they have sinned against the Holy Ghost, that they are cast away from God, or that troops of calamities are coming against them or have already seized them, and other such thoughts. The heart and emotions—always affected by what the mind reports—become so extremely terrified and troubled that they simply wait for the melancholic mind’s decision on what to do. And because the mind’s information was nothing but sorrow and fear, the resolution is nothing other than final despair and a violent death.

<margin>Mental madness defends suicide.</margin>
Many are preoccupied with a madness of the mind and a foolish opinion that desperate <term>self-murder</term> <note>original: "self-murther"; suicide.</note> is lawful. Some think it shows great courage; some see it as an ancient practice of the greatest and most excellent people of every nation. Some think it is a testimony of their love, as did the wives of Seneca, Fulvius, Labio, Scaurus, and Paetus, who died only to follow their husbands into death and to witness their kind affection to the world. Others argue that whatever they may justly desire, they may also justly do when the power is in their own hands. They think a voluntary death is the most noble death; they believe that when they take their own life, they take only what is their own, breaking no laws and offending no other person. They think they can apply to themselves the logic used in medicine:

<margin>Extreme remedies for extreme evils. <note>original: "Extremis malis extrema remedia."</note></margin>
"For extreme diseases, extreme remedies should be used." Such other foolish ideas swarm in their minds, moving them to think one of the greatest sins is actually lawful. Meanwhile, their hearts are filled with cowardice and impatience, cowering from the blows of Fortune within the den of death.

<margin>Blindness.</margin>
When one has been long ignorant of himself, and suddenly, by God’s secret judgment, is revealed to himself, he is so heavily distressed that the more he looks into himself, the more impatient he becomes with himself. His inward face terrifies him, and the sight of himself is an intolerable horror. He thinks himself such an outcast <note>original: "abiect"</note> and a declared enemy to God that he considers it too little revenge to end his own life. Desperation likewise proceeds no less from the ignorance of God.

<margin>Other diseases of the soul not cured.</margin>
Incredulity, hardness of heart, remorseless lack of repentance <term>dedolent impenitency</term>, the spirit of slumber, self-love, hypocrisy, apostasy, impatience, passions, a seared <term>cauterized</term> conscience, and discontentment all strongly work together in bringing on this passion. For those who are thus affected, they either die like blocks <note>Dying without feeling or spiritual awareness.</note>, as Nabal did, or become desperate, as Cain, Saul, Ahithophel, and Judas did.

<margin>A wounded spirit. Matthew 27. Acts 1. 1 Chronicles 10:13.</margin>
But above all, *a wounded spirit* that is not cured in time—and especially in a reprobate <note>In the theology of the time, a person rejected by God and destined for damnation.</note>—makes the most painful provocation for this malady. Examples of this are Judas and Spira <note>Francesco Spira (d. 1548), a lawyer whose deathbed despair and belief that he was beyond God's mercy became a famous cautionary tale.</note>. This is even more likely if any capital crime has been committed by them. For instance, Saul died desperately for the transgression he committed against the Lord—specifically against the Word of the Lord, which he did not keep—and because he sought and asked counsel from a medium <note>original: "familiar spirit"</note>. Here, sorrow and fear always follow.

<margin>Foolish notions of a weak mind defend self-murder.</margin>
Many are the foolish ideas <note>original: "fond conceits"</note> that enter into a man's cowardly mind to provoke him to this rage. Some have died to avoid illnesses, as did Pomponius Atticus, Tullius, and Marcellinus. Cleanthes the philosopher died by willful starvation to free himself from the illnesses that tormented him. Some died because their affairs did not succeed, or because they would not fall into their enemies' hands, as did Cato and the whole town of Saguntum <note>An ancient city in Spain; its citizens famously chose mass suicide over surrender to Hannibal.</note>. <margin>Cares for danger are diverse.</margin>

...lays claim to the wrath of God. Of all disturbances of the mind, despair is the most destructive. The desperate person is like a fish that leaps out of boiling water into a burning fire; he kills both body and soul at once. This is one of the judgments of God, which he uses to plague the persecutors of his Church, as appears in the examples of *Saul, Ahithophel <note>original: Achitophel; a counselor to King David who betrayed him and committed suicide (2 Samuel 17:23)</note>, Judas,* and *Montanus* <note>A 2nd-century heretic who, according to tradition, hanged himself.</note>.

<margin>Ambrose on Luke, book 3. Augustine on Psalm 50.</margin>

<margin>A question of the salvation of the desperate, answered.</margin>
The question may be raised: can any who lay violent hands upon themselves be saved? The answer is short and easy. If their deaths were so sudden that they could not have enough time to wish for mercy in their hearts, then the worst is to be suspected, because they die in sin and without repentance. If their deaths were slightly more lingering—yet still beyond their power to recover after the attempt—allowing them some time in their hearts to cry for mercy, then charity <note>In this context, "charity" refers to a compassionate or favorable Christian judgment.</note> may judge for the best. Several people have been rescued from the very act of hanging or drowning themselves; they have confessed that as soon as they attempted the act, they both repented of the deed and cried for mercy in their hearts at that very instant. If any lay desperate hands on themselves because of a frenzy, physical madness, or melancholy <note>A historical term for severe depression or mental illness.</note>, and if they have previously given testimony of their regeneration <term>the spiritual rebirth or conversion to a Christian state of grace</term>, we must make the best interpretation of it, considering that they did this not so much from the mind as from the body.

**B**uy, through humble prayer, that eye-salve <note>A biblical metaphor from Revelation 3:18 referring to spiritual insight or the ability to see divine truth.</note> of the secret illumination of the Spirit, and anoint your eyes with it, so that you may see and become truly taught by God. Do not neglect the means of searching the Scriptures and holy meditation, until the time you gain *a mind to know him who is true, and to know the love of Christ, which passes...*

<margin>Revelation 3:18. 1 John 2:27. 1 John 5:20. Ephesians 3:19.</margin>

He concludes with spiritual remedies like prayer and scripture to combat despair.</summary>

<margin>Against despair of mercy.</margin>
If you despair of mercy, remember that all the promises of grace are made as amply to you as to any man. Christ's mercy and merits are infinite; do not increase your sins by despairing. There is set before you a harbor for repentance. Let not the multitude of your sins move you to despair. *The Lord knows how to change His sentence, if you know how to amend your fault* <note>original Latin: *Nouit Dominus mutare sententiam, si tu noueris emendare delictum*</note>. Although you have spent all your life in sin until your very end, do not despair. Let your end amend everything. God judges and values everyone not according to their past <note>original: "bigane" (bygone)</note> life, but according to their end. For as death finds us—either repentant or unrepentant—so shall it deliver us up again at the last day, to be saved or condemned. The past life of the penitent thief was not remembered when he said to his Lord, "Remember me when you come into your kingdom." To whom it was readily and sweetly answered, "Today you shall be with me in Paradise." Your sins are far below the mercy of God and the value of Christ's ransom. God cannot receive a greater wrong, nor can we ourselves more greatly injure ourselves, than to despair of forgiveness. Christ raised one who was dead and newly departed <note>the daughter of Jairus</note>; another in a coffin <note>the son of the widow of Nain</note>; and a third, already smelling in the grave <note>Lazarus</note>. This declares that just as there is no degree of death so desperate that it is past help, so there are no sins so desperate (in number or greatness) that they can be past mercy.

<margin>Augustine, Commentary on Psalm 50, Sermon 6.</margin>
<margin>Luke 23:42, 43.</margin>
<margin>Luke 8:54; Luke 7:14; John 11:43.</margin>

<margin>Against despair of a wounded spirit.</margin>
If your despair arises from a wounded spirit <term>wounded spirit: a traditional term for a soul suffering from deep spiritual anxiety, guilt, or the feeling of being abandoned by God</term> under the sense of God's wrath, do not wander in a confused generality regarding your sins. Convict yourself of some of your greatest and personal offenses. Begin repentance, or else renew it. Force yourself into some measure of prayer. Be grieved at sin; at least, be grieved that you are *not* grieved, and that is a great beginning of repentance. Persuade yourself that your sins are pardonable. God's mercy is...

...is infinite. God's promises exclude no penitent <note>one who is repentant</note>. A sense of God's wrath actually furthers, rather than hinders, a person's pardon. Thirst for mercy, and then you shall receive it. Call for grace, and then you will have it.

<margin>A soft heart.</margin>
And because no one can suffer this calamity unless hardness of heart both causes and accompanies it: embalm your heart with the blood of the true <term>Scapegoat</term> <note>original: Scape-Goate; referring to Jesus Christ taking on the sins of humanity</note>. Even if your heart were as hard as a diamond, it shall be softened. The Physician's blood <note>referring to Christ</note> was shed and made into medicine for the <term>frenzied</term> <note>original: phrenetick; one suffering from delirium or madness</note>. Cry out unceasingly for that *ointment and oil of gladness*, and anoint your heart with it, and it shall be quickly softened.

<margin>Leviticus 8:10, 26. Augustine, Book 5, Against Heresies. 1 John 2:27. Hebrews 1:9.</margin>

<margin>Against despair arising from discontentment.</margin>
If any discontent <note>original: discontentment</note> disturbs your heart with this passion, it is because of some perceived misery and present calamity. Consider your burden to be one shared by all; make use of your trials with patience. The <term>cross</term> <note>meaning suffering or affliction</note> drives no one to despair except for fools. Do not be ignorant of the source of these crosses. Do not impatiently oppose yourself against the Author of them <note>God</note>. Run to the one who strikes you, and beg for His mercy. Make a virtue of necessity. Sweeten your cross by healing your conscience. Turn your misery into a medicine, and your dejection into steps toward glory. Endeavor toward a sweet <term>enjoyment</term> <note>original: fruition</note> of God, who alone is a thousand-fold happiness, completely eclipsing all those inferior sparks of misery.

<margin>Moderate passions.</margin>
Moderate your immoderate passions; beware of self-love. Divert your mind to other objects. Always be fully resolved to stop yourself when you should, like a well-bridled horse. <term>Mortify</term> <note>to subdue or put to death through discipline</note> your passions through Christ's suffering. Reverence God's providence and His will in all things. If your <term>servile fear</term> <note>fear of a slave toward a master; fear of punishment</note> is great, let the <term>filial fear</term> <note>the reverent love of a child for a parent</note> of God correct it, and use all the remedies against fear. If your sorrow is extreme, use all the antidotes that are prescribed against it. If it arises from a <term>melancholy humor</term> <note>an imbalance of bodily fluids once thought to cause depression</note>, your body must first be physically cured. Use every means to be freed from the *spirit of slumber* and from a <term>seared conscience</term> <note>original: cauterized conscience; one that has become numb or unfeeling toward sin</note>, lest you fall into the same snare again.

# CHAPTER 25
## *Insatiable Avarice.*

---

Proverbs 30:15: *The horse-leech <note>original: "Horse-leech"; a type of blood-sucking worm, used here as a metaphor for insatiable greed.</note> has two daughters that cry, "Give, give."*

---

-> *Description* <-

<margin>Avarice: what it is (1 Timothy 6:10, Mark 7:22, Proverbs 23:4–5, Ecclesiastes 5:9).</margin>

**A**varice <term>original: "Auarice"; extreme greed for wealth or material gain.</term> is an excessive love of gain, or an excessive desire for having more. He is to be called covetous who loves silver and is not satisfied with silver, and he who loves riches without the fruit <note>Meaning the use or benefit of those riches for good works.</note> of them.

<margin>Kinds of avarice.</margin>
From excessive love proceeds excessive desire, exceeding the bounds of piety, equity, charity, honesty, humanity, or necessity. And it passes the just limits either in acquiring or in retaining. 

<margin>In acquiring (Valerius, Suetonius, 2 Corinthians 7:2 and 12:17–18, 1 Thessalonians 4:6 and 2:5).</margin>
In acquiring, it is done either unjustly—as do thieves, deceivers, and oppressors—or dishonestly—as was the "urinal tribute" of Caligula <note>Roman Emperor (reigned 37–41 AD) known for his decadence and cruelty.</note> and Vespasian <note>Roman Emperor (reigned 69–79 AD) who famously taxed the collection of urine from public toilets; when his son Titus complained, Vespasian reportedly held a gold coin to his nose and said, "Pecunia non olet" (money does not smell).</note>. This may be done openly <term>original: "apertly"</term> or covertly by defrauding, which is called "colored covetousness" <term>Greed disguised as a virtue, such as frugality or business shrewdness.</term>.

<margin>In retaining.</margin>
In retaining, it is done by stinginess <term>original: "niggardnesse"; extreme greed or mean-spiritedness in spending.</term>, when he who should give either does not give

<summary>This page defines avarice as an inordinate desire for gain and categorizes it into two forms: unjust/dishonest acquisition and stingy retention of wealth.</summary>

In itself, gain is indifferent <note>original: "indifferent," meaning neither good nor bad in its own nature</note>; using it is good, abusing it is evil, worrying over it is worse, and obtaining it through foul means <note>original: "conquest" here likely refers to the acquisition of wealth</note> is filthy. <br><br> To be frugal or thrifty is not the same as being covetous. For frugality is a virtue by which gain is obtained lawfully, kept carefully, and spent wisely on necessary and profitable uses. *The thoughts of the diligent surely bring abundance, but whoever is hasty surely comes to poverty. He who loves pleasure shall be a poor man, and he who loves wine and oil shall not be rich. Drink the water of your own cistern, and the running waters from the midst of your own well. Let your fountains flow forth, and the rivers of water in the streets, but let them be yours—yours alone—and not shared with strangers.* From this comes the <term>Questuary Art</term> <note>The "Questuary Art" (from the Latin *quaestus*) refers to the practice or "art" of profit-making and business.</note>. Two extremes are to be avoided: carelessness (a defect) where one makes no provision, which makes a person worse than a heathen; and "carefulness" (an excess) where one distrusts God and distracts the heart with worry. *Agur* desired neither poverty (lest he should steal) nor riches (lest he should deny God), but only the food appropriate for him. *Solomon* pleased God because he did not ask for riches, which are the superfluity of gain. We must neither pray for riches nor against them; instead, while continuing in hard work and piety, we should be thankful if they come, and patient if poverty comes in their place. The sweat of our brows may lawfully be used to earn our living and to eat the fruit of our own labors. Otherwise, we live in an orderly way, like a soldier out of his rank. Men must provide for their families, or else they are worse than infidels. <br><br> To be rich is not the same as being covetous, provided one is rich in God. |

<margin>Philippians 4:11; Hebrews 13:5; Aristotle’s *Rhetoric*, Book 1, Chapter 5. A description.</margin> ...content with his condition, and is inclined not so much to love his riches as to possess them; and not so much to possess them as to use them; and not so much to use them as to distribute them for his own good, the good of others, and above all, for the honor of God.

But the covetous person is like a greedy dog; <margin>**a** Isaiah 56:11</margin> he can never have enough. <margin>**b** Jeremiah 22:17</margin> His eyes and heart are set only on covetousness. <margin>**c** Matthew 6:24</margin> He serves riches <margin>**d** Luke 12:21</margin> and hoards treasure for himself, caring only for himself and trusting in nothing but himself and his own gain. <margin>**e** Colossians 3:5; Ephesians 5:5</margin> He is rightly called an idolater, and his avarice <term>idolatry</term> <note>original: "auarice idolatry"; the author refers to the biblical idea that greed is a form of false worship because it replaces God with money.</note>. <margin>**f** Proverbs 11:28; Jeremiah 48:7</margin> This is because the covetous person prefers gold over God and puts his trust and confidence in it more than in God. <margin>**g** Jeremiah 22:17</margin> His eyes and heart are only for covetousness, <margin>**h** Ezekiel 33:31</margin> and his heart follows after greed <margin>**i** 1 Peter 2:14</margin> and is practiced in it. This is the person who <margin>**k** Habakkuk 2:9</margin> *covets an evil covetousness.*

***

-> ### *The Part Affected.* <-

The part of the person affected by this vice is the primary passion of desire, which stirs up the heart and mind to obtain what it thinks is necessary. If the desire is moderate and lawful, it does not harm the soul; but if it is unlawful or excessive, it becomes a malady of the mind and the *lust of the eyes* <margin>Desire. 1 John 2:16</margin>. All those inferior and secondary "good things" <note>Referring to material wealth and worldly status.</note> cannot fill or fully satisfy the heart's desire. The heart of man is but one syllable, one word, a small substance; yet in its capacity, it is greater than the world. It is so infinite in desire that this entire universe and globe cannot fill the triangle of it <note>This refers to a popular 17th-century mathematical metaphor: the world is a sphere (round) and the heart is a triangle (representing the Trinity). A circle cannot fill the corners of a triangle; therefore, the world cannot satisfy the human heart.</note> until the time that, by virtue and grace, it is settled in true contentment. With worldly things, the heart cannot help but overreach and disquiet itself by seeking more. What is currently possessed feels burdensome and does not bring satisfaction.

---

It is nothing else but that *form of godliness* without its <margin>2 Timothy 3:5</margin> power.

Upon the unavoidable <note>original: "uneschewable"</note> pain of your own damnation, you must take up another course: rouse your soul from your former slumber; pray against <note>original: "deprecate"; here meaning to pray for deliverance from or to earnestly regret</note> your former hypocrisy; cast away everything that presses you down, and <margin>Hebrews 12:1</margin> the sin that clings so fast. With a renewed repentance, run the race that is set before you, so that you may truly be a partaker of the Divine Nature and saving grace. Endeavor by all ordinary and spiritual means to <margin>2 Peter 1:10</margin> make your calling, persuasion, and election sure; in doing so, you shall never fall. And lest you should be ignorant of what the *power of saving grace* consists, you shall be informed as follows.

The *power of godliness and saving grace* consists <margin>Consider the power of godliness and saving grace. It must be universal.</margin> most generally in a *universal sanctification of the whole person*. It is like leaven that leavens the whole lump <note>An allusion to Matthew 13:33; leaven represents a transforming influence that spreads through everything.</note>, being of a spreading and growing nature. It is like the sun in the sky, enlightening the whole world; and just as the vital spirits are begun and fixed in the heart, and from there dispersed through the arteries throughout the whole body and every part of it, so the *power of godliness* and <margin>2 Thessalonians 2:13</margin> that sanctification of the Spirit is seated in the heart and is dispersed through the whole body and soul and their powers. It changes, lightens, softens, purges, awakens, sanctifies, mortifies <note>original: "mortifying"; in a theological sense, this means putting sinful desires to death or subduing the "flesh."</note>, informs, conforms, reforms, comforts, directs, and makes grace communicable to others.

By this universal sanctification, we do not mean <margin>And perfect, not in degrees, but in sincerity and integrity. 1. Its subject must be all parts of our person: body, soul, and faculties.
2. Its object must be *all* the Commandments.
3. It must be respectful toward *all* persons and directed toward **God** in <margin>N 4</margin> holiness,

...and filthy. It makes men fall into fearful sins and precipitates them from there to the ocean of **God's** wrath, <margin>Called falling sickness.</margin> and finally to that endless fire.

   Sometimes men fall from the faith, sometimes from <margin>Specific instances: 1 Timothy 4:1; 2 Samuel 12:4; 1 Kings 11:3. Imputed guilt.</margin> a godly life, and sometimes from both, as *Solomon* did. There are many sorts and degrees of falling. The most general of these is that *imputed defection and guilt* of our first parents, under which everyone lies. For *in Adam we have sinned*, and that which was personal to *Adam* has become natural to us. As soon as we are capable of life, we are capable of this sin and fall, from which we are freed by justification.

   Secondly, that *original inherent proclivity and disposition <margin>Inherent corruption.</margin> toward evil* in which we all lie; this is a potential and habitual infection and defection <note>original: "defection"—here meaning a falling away or desertion from a moral standard</note>, containing not only a simple deprivation of all good, but also a perverse disposition and inclination toward all evil. This is propagated from *Adam* to all his posterity in a most just and secret manner. This should be believed more than inquired into; <margin>Whitaker, book 1, *On Original Sin*, chapter 8; Psalm 51:5.</margin> it may be more easily inquired into than understood, is better understood than expounded, and we are freed from this fall in sanctification.

   Thirdly, that frequent <term>claudication</term> <note>original: "claudication"—meaning limping or lameness</note> and halting of the <margin>Frequent limping: Jeremiah 20:10; Psalm 38:17. *To cholon* <note>Greek: "the lame [limb]," referring to Hebrews 12:13</note>.</margin> regenerate <note>the "regenerate" are those who have been spiritually reborn or converted</note> by sudden, unadvised steps proceeding from their daily lamented infirmities. By these, if they do not make straight steps for their feet, *that which is halting will be turned out of the way, though it should rather be healed*. These three sorts of falls are not what is meant here.

   Fourthly, that falling away and relenting <note>relenting: here meaning slackening or weakening in fervor</note> from the former <margin>Gross omission: 2 Peter 3:17.</margin> degrees of grace and powerful fruits of piety, whether it be in persuasion, devotion, affection, or external action. *As the Church of Ephesus left her first love* and was <margin>Revelation 2:4, 5.</margin> commanded by *Christ* *to remember from where she had fallen*. <margin>Precipitation <note>a sudden fall</note>: Galatians 6:1. *Paraptoma* <note>Greek: a lapse or false step</note>.</margin>

   5. That sudden anticipation <note>anticipation: here meaning being overtaken or caught unawares</note> whereby the weak Christian is overtaken by some occasion of offense and becomes like one who has a dislocated or disjointed leg. Such a person cannot help but fall and lie in his fall until his joint is restored; as...

Just like those who are provoked to envy or wrath, or similar emotions, people can be suddenly moved to do things that they would not have done if they had acted deliberately. ᵃ Noah was suddenly overtaken by drunkenness; ᵇ Lot by incest; ᶜ Abraham with a lie; and ᵈ Peter with the denial of his Master <note>referring to Peter's denial of Jesus during his trial</note>.

6. A staggering and stumbling, which is like a headlong rush immediately before a greater fall. This happens when someone takes offense at the way of truth and allows their heart to rave with errors: *As a drunken man wanders in his own vomit* <note>referring to Isaiah 19:14</note>.

7. A turning out of the way, which occurs when the wicked do not heal their limping <note>original: "haltings"</note> and pay no regard to their stumbling. They "turn back after Satan" and wander away regarding the faith, turning their ears completely away from the truth and toward fables. Combined with this is *astochia* <note>Greek for missing the mark</note>, which is a deviation from the target and a falling away from the original goal. This is like wandering from a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith, and turning instead to "useless chatter" <note>original: "vaine iangling"</note>. Like Hymenaeus and Philetus, who wandered from the truth and "missed the mark."

8. That common and habitual foul type of falling that overtakes all sorts of people. Indeed, it affects even many of the most spiritually renewed <note>original: "regenerate"</note> individuals after their conversion. This comes from ignorance, weakness, terrifying temptations, and similar spiritual infections of the heart, in which the sinner falls most dreadfully: as Solomon fell into idolatry, and David into murder and adultery. Yet, in due time, they are restored by grace.

9. Relapse, which does not refer to when an unrepentant person <note>original: "vnregenerate"</note> falls many times into the exact same sin, or when they fall from one sin into another. Instead, it is when someone who has risen from a sin falls back into that very same sin. He who "rises" hypocritically may, like the sow and the dog, return to the mud puddle and the vomit. However, even someone who has truly risen may undoubtedly fall into the same sin again, though we do not find such an example in the Word of God <note>the Bible</note>. David sinned often, but only once in adultery, and only once...

-> ### *The Part Affected* <-

**Because** this malady is a complex evil and takes different forms—being sometimes a matter of faith and other times a matter of how we live—the soul is affected accordingly. If the apostasy is in religion (doctrine), the **mind** is first affected. If it is in a person's conduct <term>conversation: in this period, "conversation" referred to one's entire way of life and behavior, not just speech</term>, the **heart** and **affections** are first affected. <margin>**Mind.** **Heart.** **Affections.**</margin> When any one part is first affected, it draws in the rest of the soul's faculties through a kind of "sympathy" <note>In early medicine and philosophy, "sympathy" referred to the way one part of the body or soul naturally reacts to a change in another part.</note>. In this state, not one function of the soul remains free; instead, sooner or later, directly or indirectly, they all become infected.

Satan is an efficient cause <note>original: "efficient"; the primary agent that brings something about.</note> of man's fall. By his *transformations, deep deceits, methodical stratagems, and temptations,* he blinds the imagination and corrupts the heart and affections; he makes sin seem small and pleasant. He makes the sinner presume too much upon God’s mercy, Christ’s death, and His gracious promises; he persuades the sinner that he already possesses faith before he sins, and will not lose it when he does; and that he shall have enough time and power to repent well enough once he has sinned. His purpose is to make the heart sin without resistance, drawing it toward Epicurean <note>original: "epicurian"; here meaning a godless pursuit of pleasure or indifference to divine judgment.</note> contempt, final defection <note>Total abandonment of faith.</note>, or hopeless desperation.

# CHAPTER 14. *The Gangrene of Heresy.*

---

| [[margin: Difference between a heretic and one who holds a heresy. Augustine, *The Usefulness of Believing*, Chapter 1.]] | There is a great difference between the *heretic* and the person who believes his heresy. For if, out of simplicity and a gullible heart (deceived by *heretics*), a person yields to an error without being stubborn, and when warned of it, does not argue but instead gives way and repents, he is not to be called a *heretic*. |
| :--- | :--- |
| [[margin: Difference between a heretic and a schismatic.]] | There is also a difference between the *heretic* and the *schismatic*. A *schismatic* separates himself from the unity, peace, and body of the *Church* regarding life, order, or discipline. A *heretic* sins against the truth; the *schismatic* sins against charity <note>original: "charity," meaning Christian love and communal unity</note>. Often, the very same man sins against both, and so is both a *heretic* and a *schismatic*. |
| [[margin: Heresy is a disease. John Chrysostom, *Homily on 1 Corinthians 15*. "Those who cause confusion," etc. 2 Timothy 2:17.]] | *Heresy* is a most deadly and contagious disease, just as it was said of some that they were sick with the *Manichean* <note>The Manicheans were followers of a dualistic religion that was a major rival to early Christianity; the author uses them as a historical example of heretics.</note> heresy. It is most truly called by the *Apostle* <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul.</note> a *gangrene*, which is the death <note>original: "mortification"</note> of the affected body part. It arises from a lack of vital heat and spirit, which is either driven away or kept from the area (by constraints, bruising, or blockage) or else smothered and extinguished (by an excess of humors, inflammations, obstructions, the stopping of natural breathing through the skin, piercing cold, or a poisonous quality). In the same way, the heretic maliciously rejects grace, and God justly withholds it from him. His foolish imaginations, his violent passions, his heart frozen in the dregs of sin, and the venom injected by the Devil, choke and extinguish his inherent common light and ordinary graces. Thus, he becomes entirely gangrenous; in his devilish and malicious opinions against divine truth, he becomes most poisonous and stubborn. |
| [[margin: Why it is called a gangrene. *Gangraina* (Greek). How it "frets" or eats away: *Nomen echei* (Greek: it has a spreading nature). Consuming ulcers. Pliny and Dioscorides. Matthew 16:6, 11; Revelation 8:7 and 9:2; Hebrews 12:15.]] | This gangrene is said to *fret* or *spread* by eating up and consuming the parts around it. Heresy is of a spreading nature and infectious to the whole body of the *Church*, much like poison, leaven <note>leaven: yeast that spreads through dough</note>, or fire and smoke rising out of the bottomless pit, and like a "root of bitterness" springing up. |

| <margin>To test the godly. 1 Corinthians 11:19. Deuteronomy 13:3. Tertullian, *The Prescription Against Heretics*.</margin> | And partly, it is for the trial of His own people: *For there must be heresies even among you, so that those who are approved among you might be recognized. Because of heresy, the Scriptures are searched more diligently. The condemnation of heretics has made it clear what the Church believes and what truth is contained in wholesome doctrine. The falsehood of heresies and the light of the truth (like two opposing contraries) argue against each other. Heresy appears more vile because of the truth <note>original: "verity"</note>, and the truth appears clearer because of the opposing heresy. The one becomes more hated, and the other more loved. |

| (Learning, fretting with envy, and corrupted with covetousness, ambition, and contention) has kindled the first seeds and roots of this gangrene. <note>The author uses "gangrene" as a metaphor for heresy, suggesting it is a disease that rots and spreads through the "body" of the church.</note> | |

| 1. *Reason*, by which they think that everything that agrees with reason is divine truth. They believe whatever does not harmonize with the "light of nature" <note>The "light of nature" refers to human logic and observation without the aid of divine revelation.</note> is mere folly; in this, they are greatly deceived and prove to be great fools. | <margin>Reason. *1 Corinthians 3:14.*</margin> |

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the origins and causes of religious heresy, specifically focusing on how philosophy and personal "revelations" distort Christian doctrine.</meta>

[[page number: 208]]
->**CHAPTER 14. *The Gangrene of Heresy.***<-
---
[[margin:
<note>original: Μεταψυχωσις</note> Transmigration of souls.
What has Athens to do with Jerusalem? etc. <note>original: Quid Athenis cum Hierosolymis</note>
Tertullian, *On the Prescription of Heretics*, Book 1.

1 Corinthians 1:22; 2:4, 5, 6, 7, 8.
1 Corinthians 3:1, 9.

Traditions.

Augustine, *Against Cresconius the Grammarian*, Book 2, chapter 32.

Inspiration.

The blind vanity of man's heart.
2 Timothy 3:5, 6.
]]

The idea that matter is equal to God comes from *Zeno*. The idea of a fiery God comes from *Heraclitus*. The passing of souls from body to body <note>the doctrine of reincarnation</note> comes from *Pythagoras*. What has *Athens* to do with *Jerusalem*? What do the *Academics* <note>followers of Plato’s school of philosophy</note> have to do with the Church? Let those who prefer *Stoic*, *Platonic*, and *Dialectic* <note>logic and philosophical debate</note> reasoning to Christian truth consider this. The heavy mixing of *Philosophy* with *Divinity* caused *Origen* <note>an early Christian scholar</note> to corrupt the Scriptures in many places. 

This led the *Apostle* <note>St. Paul</note> to write so much against the wisdom of the *Greeks*, of the world, and of the princes of the world. In all his preaching, he rejected the *enticing speech of human wisdom*, and always spoke simply of the *wisdom of God in a mystery*. For *the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God*; as it is written: *He catches the wise in their own foolishness*.

3. The traditions of predecessors, praised merely for their antiquity, are a refuge for heretics. They fail to consider that antiquity is only good when it concerns good things (for a sin is not better just because it is ancient). Antiquity should not be so highly commended unless it is *the most ancient* <note>original: Antiquissima</note>. The truth is the most ancient thing of all, existing before every kind of error and heresy. In the antiquity of traditions, nothing should be respected except that which agrees with the Scriptures. As *Augustine* says of *Cyprian*: "I am not bound to *Cyprian’s* authority, because I do not regard his letters as Canonical, but I evaluate them based on the Canonical Scriptures."

4. *Enthusiasms* <note>original: Enthusiasmi; here meaning claims of direct divine inspiration</note>, or secret inspirations and revelations, are another cause. Through these, people deceive themselves and delude others. The heretic *Montanus* was so bewitched by his two companions, *Prisca* and *Maximilla*, that whatever they dreamed, imagined, or thought about the future, he affirmed to be divine revelations. He even preferred these to the written Word of God. 

The natural rebellion, blindness, and vanity of the human heart is the most direct and immediate cause of this "Gangrene," occurring when a person contents himself with the *show*

## ->*Signs and Symptoms.*<-

**H**eresy is like the *Ape*, because it counterfeits the gestures of piety; like the *Fox* in its falseness, the *Dragon* in cruelty, and the *Serpent* in subtlety. A heretic does not love the truth; he is strongly deluded, believes lies, and has pleasure in unrighteousness. He is a mocker of the truth; he speaks lies through hypocrisy and has his conscience <term>cauterized</term> <note>original: "cauterized"; meaning the conscience has been seared or made insensitive to right and wrong, as if by a hot iron</note>. He is given to fables, unstable, presumptuous of mercy, and confident in his own knowledge and opinion. 

He is loaded with a burden of sins, such as pride, covetousness, envy, contention, and the like. He is full of brawlings; he walks after the flesh in the lusts of uncleanness and stands in his own conceit, having a heart exercised with covetousness, loving *Balaam's* wages of unrighteousness <note>Balaam was a biblical figure who attempted to curse Israel for financial gain (Numbers 22-24)</note>. He is a well without water, a cloud carried about with a tempest, speaking swelling words of vanity, promising liberty, while he is himself the servant of corruption.

Heresy is like the *viper*, straining to slay the Mother Church. It is chaff among the good corn; it is a contagious leprosy, a poisonous venom, a desperate shipwreck of one's own faith and the faith of others, and a most turbulent tempest. This heresy **a** eats away like a <term>canker</term><note>original: "Canker"; in Early Modern English, this referred to a spreading sore or gangrene, following the imagery of 2 Timothy 2:17.</note>, **b** deceiving others, and **c** secretly bringing in damnable heresies **d** with fabricated words, selling simple people like cattle at a fair, and **e** speaking perverse things to draw disciples after it. It is like a fierce wolf that does not spare the flock, speaking evil of those in authority and of things which it does not understand, delighting in its own deceptions and beguiling unstable souls.

the heretical gangrene is contrary to the Scriptures and is proven false by the truth. It has <term>contumacy</term><note>stubborn or willful resistance to authority</note> joined to its error and is always bent on propagating itself until it goes out of bounds, both in its subject matter and among people.

*Simon Magus* claimed to be Christ and bewitched the people of *Samaria* through witchcraft, claiming to be some great man. The people paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, "This man is the great power of God." His <term>gangrene</term><note>The author uses this term as a metaphor for the infectious spread of false doctrine.</note> spread among all the Simonians to *Menander*, who professed that he was sent "from the invisible realms" <note>original: *ab invisibilibus*</note> to be a savior to mankind. *Menander's* heresy spread among all the *Menandrians* to *Saturninius*, who was against the Trinity and held that the world was made not by God, but by certain angels. He also held that the true Savior was incorporeal and visible only "in appearance" <note>original: *putative*; a reference to Docetism, the belief that Christ's body was an illusion.</note>. He denied the resurrection of the body.

The gangrene of *Saturninius* spread among all the *Saturninian* heretics and through almost all of Egypt to *Basilides*, who continued to profess his "highest power" <note>original: *Summam virtutem*</note> against the Trinity. He gave this highest power the strange name of *Abraxas*, which in Greek letters amounts to the number 365, claiming there were that many heavens. He denied Christ's Passion and the resurrection—

## ->*Prognostics.*<-

**T**he gangrenous heretic, in the beginning of his malady, has some hope of being cured, especially if he is a chosen child <note>i.e., one of the elect</note>. But if the condition is long-established <note>original: "inveterate"</note>, he is most difficult to help. Heresy does more harm than persecution; and this gangrene kills more than the sword does. It snares many thousand souls into destruction <note>original: "perdition"</note> under the pretense of sanctity and truth, and stirs up great internal rebellion <note>original: "intestine sedition"</note> in the Church, which is worse than war. In this, Satan reaps his harvest: having the doctrine of the person and nature of Christ attacked in the East <note>original: "Orient"</note> as far as the South <note>original: "Meridian"</note> under <term>Islam</term> <note>original: "Mahometisme"</note>, and the doctrine of his merits perverted in the West <note>original: "Occident"</note> under <term>Papism</term> <note>original: "Papisme"; a derogatory term for Roman Catholicism</note>.

*But evil men and deceivers shall grow worse and worse, deceiving and being deceived—those who once were with us and among us. Yet (oh, it is to be lamented!), they went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. But this happens so that it might appear that they are not all of us.*

The visible judgment of God has fearfully fallen upon heretics. *Montanus* <note>A 2nd-century heretic who claimed to be the mouthpiece of the Holy Spirit</note> with his two harlots desperately hanged themselves. *Cerinthus* <note>An early Gnostic opponent of the Apostle John</note> was struck from above <note>meaning by divine intervention</note>, and so was Emperor *Anastasius I* punished. *Arius* <note>The 4th-century priest whose teachings led to the Arian controversy regarding Christ's divinity</note> had all his intestines burst forth while on the toilet <note>original: "stoole"</note>; and the same happened to *Anastasius II*. *Olympius*, who publicly detested the Trinity, was struck by three lightnings, by which his body was completely burned. Emperor *Valens* was burned in a hut; and *Julian the Apostate* (a most violent enemy and Arian heretic), being wounded to death, threw a handful of his blood toward heaven, crying with his last breath: "At last, you have overcome, O Galilean" <note>Referring to Jesus Christ; this is a famous legendary deathbed confession of Julian</note>.

-> ### Curations and remedies. <-

**T**he first thing is to test the gangrene <note>The author uses "gangrene" as a medical metaphor for heresy, suggesting it is a contagious rot that spreads through the "body" of the Church.</note> (according to the counsel of Saint *John*: *Dearly beloved, believe not every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are of God: for many false prophets have gone out into the world.*) There is no fitter way to test it rightly than by the Scriptures. *For all Scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable to teach, to improve, to correct, and to instruct in righteousness.* And although heretics use, or rather abuse, the holy Scripture for their defense—mutilating and distorting <note>original: "detorting"</note> it to suit their bad intentions—yet by that single, sound, constant, and perpetual Scriptural truth, they are most easily convicted and driven from their strongholds.

<margin>Trial. 1 John 4:1, 2 Timothy 3:16.</margin>

Great wisdom must be used here. For first, they must not be received into the house, nor should they be greeted: *for he who greets them is a partner in their evil deeds. Mark them diligently who cause division and offenses, contrary to the doctrine which you have learned, and avoid them*, so that being ashamed of themselves, they may be brought to some consideration of their error. *The deceit and malice of heretics is either to be lamented, as they are men; or to be avoided, as they are heretics; or to be scorned, as they are ignorant and proud* <note>original Latin: "Fraus & malitia hereticorum, vel dolenda est, tanquam hominum; vel cauenda, tanquam haereticorum; vel irridenda, tanquam imperitorum, & superborum."</note>, and no further to acknowledge—

<margin>Shunning. 2 John 10, 11; Romans 16:17. Augustine, *Against Adimantus*. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 4, Chapter 14.</margin>

The censures of the Church must be used, and specifically by those who have authority: *After one or two warnings, the heretic is to be rejected, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment,* as *Paul* did with *Hymenaeus*; *whom he delivered to Satan, so that he might learn not to blaspheme.*

The Magistrate has power over both schismatics (as they are the authors of division) and disturbers of the religious <note>original: "Ecclesiasticke"</note> and political state, to restrain and correct them. He also has power over heretics, especially those who have emerged from the heart of the Church itself. These people are to be punished—not so much because they have been convicted of error or stubbornness <note>original: "contumacy"</note> in defending it, but primarily because they spread their "gangrene" (privately or publicly) to the ruin of others and the disruption of public order.

<margin>The Magistrate’s power.</margin>

The same is seen in the actions of the Emperors *Valentinian*, *Theodosius*, *Marcian*, and *Justinian*.

-> # CHAPTER XV. <-

-> ## The plague of Discontentment. <-

-> **1 Kings 8:38** *When everyone shall know the plague in his own heart.* <-

-> ### Description. <-

[[meta: Large ornamental initial letter T, approximately 5 lines high, decorated with floral motifs.]]

**T**he mind should study to attain to that happy state in which it may freely enjoy itself on all occasions, with sound contentment and peaceful balance. It should be like a pair of scales, whose plates, beam, and needle <note>original: "tongue"</note> keep a very equal and steady course. In times of prosperity, it should not be lifted up too much with pride and lightheartedness, or with self-satisfaction <note>original: "complacency"</note> and excessive joy. Nor should it be too deeply discouraged <note>original: "dejected"</note> when our desires and delights are frustrated. If the mind is slightly disturbed <note>original: "agitate"</note> or suddenly overcome, it should resolutely return to its balance again. Neither should it always strive only for ease, or hope to never have occasion to be shaken; rather, it should endeavor to make itself firm and strong against everything that might assault it, whether by weighing it down or puffing it up. This is one of the essential aspects of the soul’s integrity and health.

<margin>Contentment.</margin>

The opposite of this is the *Plague of Discontentment*. It is a widespread <note>original: "epidemicall"</note> and universal plague. It is a most heavy calamity for everyone; it does not fail to torment the wealthiest and most powerful, and it gnaws at the hearts of the greatest Princes.

<margin>1 Kings 8:38. Discontentment.</margin>

How many thousands does it every day assail, making their lives invisibly miserable? Their death more sudden and cursed, and their souls (which is worst of all) most damned. It is a storm, causing many a person to suffer shipwreck. It is an internal battle <note>original: "intestine battell"</note>, banishing all peace. It is a staggering <term>Titubation: A physical or mental wavering; a state of instability or uncertainty.</term>, a grief, and an offense of the mind; an enemy to that balance <note>original: "euenness"</note> of mind. It is a bitterness of the heart, bitterer than wormwood and gall. It is a vexation of the spirit, and this is that darkness of the heart that is accompanied by much grief, sorrow, and anger: a sickness indeed, tormenting the heart (Ecclesiastes 5:17).

<margin>Judges 13; Psalm 119:53; 1 Samuel 25:31; 1 Samuel 22:2; Ecclesiastes 1:14; Ecclesiastes 5:17.</margin>

-> ### Part affected. <-

The heart (or will) is primarily affected here: either when it is frustrated in achieving an enjoyed or desired good (whether it be good in itself, or only in appearance) or else when it is troubled <note>original: "annoyed"</note> by some present or looming evil (whether it be an evil in itself, or only in appearance). Sometimes the heart will be under an absolute <term>Peremptory: Final and absolute, leaving no room for refusal or delay.</term> discontentment; sometimes again, it is under a state of hesitation and suspense. And because there is a back-and-forth between the heart and the mind (the mind first informing the will, and the will thereafter forcing the mind with anxiety to meditate and deliberate upon the heart's grief), it results that the mind, as well as the heart's affections, are grievously tormented with this plague.

<margin>Heart. Mind. Affections.</margin>

-> ### Causes. <-

The prosperity of the wicked made David fret, as he confesses of himself: "Certainly my heart was vexed, and I was pierced in my kidneys <term>Reins: From the Latin 'renes' (kidneys); historically considered the seat of one's deepest emotions and secret thoughts.</term>: So foolish was I and ignorant, I was like a beast before you." Thus said the Prophet,

<margin>The prosperity of the wicked. Psalm 73:21, 22.</margin>

Why are all those in wealth who rebelliously transgress?* And Job, <margin>Job 24:13 and 21:6, 7</margin> making mention of the insolence of the wicked, complains that God does not charge them with folly <note>original: "folly," here meaning moral or spiritual failure</note>. This grief happens especially to the godly; but it does not continue: for they run to the Word <note>The Bible</note> for instruction and a remedy for this.

<margin>Presumption of too much strength and too rigid designs. Exodus 18:17, 18</margin>
When we presume too much of ourselves and of our gifts, undergoing burdens of affairs that are too heavy for us, with unknown and unconsidered weakness: in the end, we are forced to groan under the weight and utter discontented complaints. And having too many peremptory <term>peremptory: fixed, absolute, or insisting on immediate attention</term> designs, desires, plots, and hopes—never looking to that over-ruling providence which in all events should be respected and reverenced—if anything falls out <margin>Ecclesiastes 4:15, 16; 2 Kings 6:11; Job 7:3, 6</margin> otherwise than we devised or desired, we begin to complain and exclaim at the failing of our unlimited hopes.

<margin>Evils not premeditated.</margin>
When the worst of evils that may befall our best goods are not premeditated <note>planned or thought about beforehand</note>, but the best in everything is foolishly expected, it causes men to be surprised suddenly. Thus, when the storm arises before the mind is made strong to meet with the sorest <note>original: "forest," likely a typesetting error for "sorest," meaning most severe</note> tempest, it breeds many unexpected, tyrannizing griefs of the mind. <margin>Job 30:26; Isaiah 59:9; Jeremiah 8:15</margin> This appeared in Job, who discontentedly complained that when he *looked for good, evil came to him*. And in the people of Israel, who looked for peace when evil came upon them.

<margin>Our minds are set too far on evils and diverted from our present good.</margin>
We make no use of the worst of every accident; we fight more with ourselves than with our evils; we cannot subordinate our lightest evil to our great good, so that the one may eclipse the other. We fix our eyes too much on our evil and too little on our good—like little children, who for the loss of one puppet or little bauble <note>original: "bable," a small trinket or toy</note>, throw all their best things away in a rage. We suffer the occasion of smaller griefs to provide us a raging sea of disquietness and to choke many present blessings, both temporal...

### Causes.

---

<margin>Causes of secret hypocrisy: Satan seducing, God deserting.</margin>
When Satan cannot tempt those who are born again <note>original: "regenerate"</note> into dominant <note>original: "reigning"</note> sins or higher degrees of hypocrisy, he attempts to stain the face of innocence with a false belief <note>original: "conceit"</note> that they have more grace than the heart actually possesses. He causes the remnants <note>original: "reliques"</note> of a person's proud nature to rise up in their own opinion, leading them to think too highly of themselves and the value of their own spiritual gifts. He dazzles their eyes so that for a long time they cannot recognize their own hypocrisy. God withdraws from His own people for a time and permits Satan to test them.

<margin>Spiritual pride. Proverbs 12:26; 2 Peter 1:4.</margin>
<margin>2 Corinthians 12:7.</margin>
When the *godly* person finds himself *more excellent than his neighbor,* and that he is a *partaker of the divine nature,* and sees his own reformed reflection <note>original: "shadow"</note> in a clear fountain of godliness, he is joyfully amazed and admires his own happiness. He begins to think better of himself than he truly is. He becomes proud of his humility, and proud because he believes he is not proud. While other sins spring from poisonous <note>original: "pestilent"</note> roots, this one is drawn from the purest streams of grace; it is unique to God’s children, whereas other sins are common to everyone. The Apostle Paul was overtaken by this, as he says:
> *And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, so that I should not be exalted above measure.*

<margin>Causes of temporizing <term>temporizing: changing one's behavior or beliefs to suit the current time or circumstances, especially for personal gain</term> hypocrisy. Satan's strategy: he bribes them.</margin>
As for temporizing hypocrisy: God allows Satan to bestow worldly trifles upon a person, which act like golden shackles, a sleeping potion, and *Naboth’s* vineyard <note>A biblical reference to something desired and seized unfairly (1 Kings 21)</note>, an honorable servitude, a golden wedge <note>A reference to Achan's sin in Joshua 7</note>, and a glorious misery—their only *Diana* <note>A reference to the idol of the Ephesians in Acts 19:28, representing a person's chief obsession or source of profit</note>. The Devil is wise, willful, and cunning; he reigns and rules in their hearts. If he cannot lead men to open impiety and the rejection of religion, he works to make them subject religion to their own idols, making it subordinate. He also makes him
