## CHAPTER 12. Rotten <note>original: "Putride"</note> Hypocrisy.

<margin>He allows them to have an imaginary persuasion of mercy.</margin>
...to have an imaginary persuasion of mercy, grounded upon outward shows and general, confused motivations <note>original: "motions," referring to internal impulses</note>, like morning dews and clouds of common <note>original: "vulgar"</note> graces, natural light, polite behavior <note>original: "civil carriage"</note>, and external restraint from open sins. He causes the person to think this is sufficient religion.

<margin>Ignorance of oneself.</margin>
He is so busy and delighted with the world that he is loath to see his internal vileness. He never descends into himself to examine the lowest depths of his heart. He can never rightly see or understand <note>original: "take up"</note> his own inherent darkness, deadness, disorder, and spiritual slumber. This does not make his sins better known to himself, but rather makes them more obvious and sinful before God, his damnation more just, and himself more inexcusable.

<margin>By comparing himself with those who are worse, he thinks himself good enough. Luke 18:11; Proverbs 30:12.</margin>
He compares himself with people worse than himself and says, like the Pharisee <note>a Jewish sect often associated in this period with legalism and outward show</note>, *"O God, I thank you that I am not like other men—extortioners, unjust, adulterers—or even like this tax collector <note>original: "Publican"</note>"* (Luke 18:11). He thinks himself to be far superior to adulterers, murderers, and oppressors. He keeps up the external forms of religion and belongs to *"the generation of those who are pure in their own eyes, and yet are not washed from their filthiness"* (Proverbs 30:12). He also observes the deaths of others (who were worse than him) and assumes they were godly and happy because he sees in their deaths some show of repentance and forced, brief prayers <note>original: "urged light ejaculations"</note> for mercy. Thus, he contents himself with his current model of imaginary confidence, believing he has reached a sufficient perfection in grace.

<margin>A misinterpretation of true godliness. Psalm 38:20; Proverbs 28:1; Isaiah 8:18.</margin>
He holds a biased opinion of true godliness and of those who are truly godly. He thinks that the godly have many enemies and are poorly regarded. Their lion-like boldness is labeled as pride; their zeal is dismissed as being overly fussy <note>original: "preciseness," a term often used to mock the strictness of Puritans</note>; their sorrow is judged as melancholy; their austerity is seen as nothing but misery. Their minds are considered weak, their spirits low, and they themselves are viewed as lowly, unfit for the world, and objects of amazement <note>original: "wonders"</note> in Israel. And if he himself were to follow their path, he thinks there is a "lion in the way" <note>Proverbs 26:13; a metaphor for making excuses to avoid a difficult task</note>; the way...

It also explains how such people misinterpret the sincere zeal and trials of truly godly people as personality flaws or misery.</summary>

### Chapter 12. Rotten Hypocrisy <note>original: "putride," meaning decaying or morally corrupt</note>.

<margin>He fears the inconveniences of true godliness. Isaiah 59:15.</margin>
The way is too straight <note>original: "straite," meaning narrow or difficult</note>, too narrow, and full of thorns. He will not fight against his own corruptions, the devil's temptations, and the world's troubles, arguing that *he who turns away from evil makes himself a prey.* <note>original: "maketh himselfe a prey," a reference to Isaiah 59:15, implying that being good makes one a target for the wicked.</note>

For these reasons, he thinks the safest and best course is not to be "precise" <term>precise: a term often used in the 17th century to describe Puritans who were overly strict or scrupulous in religious observance</term> or too stubborn in his piety. Instead, he maintains a middle ground <note>original: "mediocrity," here meaning a moderate or lukewarm path</note> that fits his worldly attitude and the current customs of the day, so as not to trouble his mind any further. Based on this foolish idea, and hoping for the best, he gambles with his soul.

<margin>A misunderstanding of sin, justice, and mercy; and false evidence of them.</margin>
He is full of a foolish misunderstanding of sin, judgment, and mercy. To him, sin is minor and easily forgiven; justice is small and avoidable; and mercy is above all of God’s other works, his truth, and his promises—something to be obtained at the first call. He presumes upon mercy. He thinks that prosperity, outward peace, and an inward, hollow taste of *godliness* are certain signs of mercy. He convinces himself he is holy enough because he is happy and secure enough. He makes no further progress in piety, but contents himself with "common graces" <term>common graces: general blessings such as health or intellect shared by all people, rather than the specific saving grace required for salvation</term>.

<margin>A bad conscience.</margin>
His conscience is too loose and unlimited, strong enough to digest any sin. He favorably downplays, excuses, interprets, and justifies his actions. He has reconciled the accusing and excusing powers of his conscience so that one hardly interferes with the other. He thinks that a little grace can be gained while much sin is committed, as long as there are some "good intentions" or hopes involved. He does not lack theoretical principles of divine truth, but when it comes to practicing them, he has his own reservations, exceptions, and limitations. He follows them only as far as they agree with his worldly well-being; when they interfere with his plans, he stops or turns away from his faith.

<margin>❦ Matthew 13:21.</margin>
Therefore, he is a temporizer <term>temporizer: a person who changes their behavior or opinions to suit the current circumstances or for personal gain</term>. The guides for this broad conscience are social examples, customs, public opinions, worldly wisdom, and basic natural ideas of right and wrong. He will not subject his conscience to the full yoke...

# Chapter 12. Rotten Hypocrisy <note>original: "putride," meaning decaying or morally corrupt</note>.

...yoke of God’s will, nor will walk according to that rule.

<margin>Ignorance of God.</margin>
He may have a natural and scriptural knowledge of God, but he lacks a spiritual and sanctifying knowledge. He is a shining lamp, but not a burning coal; he may enlighten others, but he does not inflame himself. His light shines on the outside, but not within. He is enlightened like the moon (which has a borrowed light to give to others, but darkness within her own body, which makes her spots all the more noticeable); he remains, within his own heart, darkness itself.

<margin>Ephesians 5:8.</margin>
He thinks honey is sweeter than his light, and gold more precious. Pleasure is better, profit is more relevant, and honor is more delightful. He subordinates the light of truth to his wealth, his honor, his pleasures, and the light of nature.

<margin>He harbors some secret "bosom sin" that keeps him back from true piety. <note>original: "bosome sinne," a favorite, habitual sin that an individual nurtures and protects in private.</note></margin>
Although he goes beyond the open atheist and the grand hypocrite, and is more moderate and civil than they are, and though he hates the infamous sins of adultery, drunkenness, heresy, and such things—yet he always lodges within himself some "sweet" secret bosom sin. His mind runs on this sin most often, his best thoughts are spent on it, and all the light and grace within him are resolutely made to serve it.

<margin>Causes of the grossest hypocrisy: Satan, etc. Leaning on ceremonies. Acts 5:3; 1 Timothy 4:1–2; Proverbs 7:14; Romans 2:27, etc.; Isaiah 1:13–15; Jeremiah 7:10, 4, etc.</margin>
As for the grossest hypocrisy, Satan—by God’s special permission—fills the heart "as a spirit of error to make a man speak lies through hypocrisy." He causes him to lean too much on bare knowledge and the ceremonies of religion rather than its substance; he has the form of knowledge but no practice of it. He simultaneously glories in the Law and in breaking the Law. He relies more on the circumcision of the flesh than on the circumcision of the heart. He "will come and stand before the Lord in His House, and say, 'We are delivered,' even though we have done all these abominations" <note>original: "abominations," referencing Jeremiah 7:10.</note>.

<margin>Blindness. Luke 12:56–57.</margin>
He is skilled at discerning the face of heaven and earth, but as Christ says, "And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?" This self-ignorance made the Laodicean

-> ### Chap. 15. *The Plague of Discontentment.* <-

Avoid all impossible, irrelevant <note>original: "impertinent"</note>, and idle tasks; for he who takes too much upon himself gives fortune much power over him. <margin>Psalm 131:1</margin> *Do not concern yourself with great matters or things hidden from you.* Withdraw your mind from too many external things and bring it back to itself; yet, at the same time, avoid a lowly carelessness and do not be lazy in your necessary and honest affairs.

Consider that you are a pilgrim in a dangerous place. <margin>Premeditate evil. Revelation 15:1.</margin> In your sailing upon this glassy sea <note>A metaphor for the precarious and transparent nature of life</note>, remember that you may encounter a storm. Never be so fixed in one state of life as to be impatient with change; on your journey, all kinds of accidents may affect you. Therefore, premeditate the worst in all things: foresee evil and prevent it, or else learn to be strong against it when it arrives. As *Anaxagoras* <note>A Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher (c. 500–428 BC)</note>, when it was told to him that his son was dead, answered contentedly, "*I knew well that he was mortal.*" He who prepares for the worst in such a way shall never say in the end (whatever happens), "*I hadn't thought of that.*"

Remember that we are all prisoners of fortune, either <margin>Count your burden as common to all.</margin> subject to ourselves or to others, and enslaved to a thousand causes of discontent. A person's life is both a warfare and a bondage. All are prisoners: some in golden chains, some in iron chains. Some are slaves to poverty, some to riches, some to honor, and some to lowliness <note>original: "basenesse"</note>. Learn, therefore, to consider even the best things as merely golden chains and burdens held by golden ropes; the bondage is exactly the same as that found in rusty shackles <note>original: "gieues," an archaic spelling of gyves</note>.

Time, necessity, and habit <note>original: "vse"</note> will make you carry your iron <margin>And make use of it with patience.</margin> chains more easily. Patience lessens the grief of greater evils; in every trouble, overlook <note>original: "dissemble"</note> the bad and make use of the good. And since there is no perfect evil, consider that even the worst things offer some comfort. For example, when *Jonah* lay miserable in the whale's belly, he made use of and found comfort in his solitude <note>original: "leasure"</note> and prayed to God for help. *Diogenes* <note>Diogenes of Sinope, a Greek philosopher and founder of Cynicism</note> studied wisdom during his banishment. *Socrates* learned patience from his difficult <note>original: "euill"</note> wife; like a bee, out of the bitterest...

-> ### Chap. 15. *The Plague of Discontentment.* <-
---
[bitter]est herbs draws out some sweet honey. Make your life like someone playing backgammon <note>original: "playing at Tables," a popular board game of the era</note>: be content with your roll of the dice. Be resolved to lose as well as to win, and improve a bad roll with your better skill.

<margin>Choose your close friends.</margin>
Choose your close companions carefully, ensuring they are faithful, gentle, discreet <note>original: "secret"</note>, cheerful, and wise, and free from dominating vices. If you cannot find someone with all these perfections, choose the one who has the fewest flaws. Choose a friend who is a good fit for both your personality and your business, in whose company you may refresh your spirits with a variety of recreations, meals, and all other honest pleasures. Beware of those who are too gloomy, complaining, despairing, suspicious, brooding <note>original: "pensive"</note>, overly sensitive, fearful, and nosy <note>original: "curious"</note>.

<margin>Live with simple truth.</margin>
Live with an honest and simple truth: be free of hypocrisy. Do not waste away by hiding your weaknesses. If you are naturally inclined to be extremely cheerful, do not force yourself to be extremely serious; instead, try to restrain and correct your weaknesses and bring them into a healthy balance.

<margin>Avoid excesses. *The happy ones have held the middle ground.* <note>Latin: "Medium tenuere beati"</note></margin>
Cut off <term>superfluities</term> <note>excessive or unnecessary items</note>, and remove all the pomp and vanity of status, clothing, retinues <note>original: "traines"</note>, and diet. Always keep to the middle ground <term>the mean</term> and focus on what is necessary, rather than what is based on people's opinions and fantasies. Keep your lifestyle as humble as you can without damaging the dignity of your social rank. If you cannot lower your status without failing, manage your authority so that men attribute your stateliness to your office and not to your natural disposition. Remember that thunder and lightning commonly strike the highest places.

<margin>Be ready for both prosperity and adversity.</margin>
Remain steady and balanced <note>original: "indifferent"</note> throughout all the stages of your life, always maintaining the same composure and courage. Like a skilled craftsman, find a way to profit from everything. Like the excellent sculptor *Phidias* <note>A famous ancient Greek sculptor</note>, who could form all kinds of images out of any material with the same focused expression, you should look at the two faces of fortune. Be armed for both types of struggle: with a spur against adversity, to stir up your cou-

-> ### Chap. 15. *The Plague of Discontentment.* <-
---
[[margin: <note>original Greek: ανεχου και απεχου</note> Bear and forbear. *Epictetus*]]
...rage: use a bridle against prosperity, to rule yourself with modesty. Endure and refrain. 

[[margin: Moderate your heart in prosperity, and the motives for doing so.]]
In prosperity, moderate your heart with reason and religion by thinking on your sins, weakness, misery, mortality, and on the fickleness of fortune. Beat down your haughtiness: consider that the greatest happiness that the whole world can afford is not able to fill the unlimited desire of the heart; it is no true happiness. All this material globe is not proportional to the precious soul. The greatest worldly welfare cannot 
[[margin: Dan. 5; Zeph. 1:17, 18; Ezek. 7:19; Obad. 4.]]
secure the conscience, nor prevent judgment. While fortune is smiling on you, your heart may be mourning within. All worldly pleasures are but cold comforts: they cannot stretch to eternity. The world is a fool’s paradise, full of vipers: the obscure mark of unreliable <note>original: "vnsound"</note> joys: a sporting (but doubtful) passage: a dreamed sweetness: and a very ocean of bitterness <note>original: "gall"</note>. All is uncertain and full of vexation: common to the worst people, and cannot better the mind, nor comfort nor content the best. The happiest fortune is but honeyed poison.

Bridle, therefore, your affections, and compose your actions by reason. Prosperity is a slippery path. Walk with fear and doubt; be not carried beyond yourself, and do not always keep yourself in a state of pursuit and acquisition. Settle your rest and sweet contentment once and for all. Frequently remember King Philip’s <note>Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great, who allegedly hired a page to remind him daily of his mortality.</note> ordinary morning reminder: *“You are a man”*; and the Christian’s watchword: *“You are dust, and to dust you shall return.”* Thus, you shall not suffer your mind to wander in the vanities of discontent.

[[margin: Be content with your status and situation, and the reasons for it. Compare yourself not with those in better positions, but with the worse conditions of others.]]
Do not elevate your mind above your status <note>original: "estate"</note>. If your status will not be framed to your mind, labor to frame your mind to your status, as Socrates said. Compare not your status with the better circumstances of other men, but with the worse conditions of even better men, or those as good as yourself. The Ape and the Ass both complain: the one because he has no horns; the other because he lacks...

...lacks a tail. The *Mole* (also called a *Want*) <note>original: "Want" was a common regional name for a mole in Early Modern English</note> answers in this way: "But if you truly considered my miserable blindness, you would not complain so much about your own lack." Cast your gaze down toward those below you; look at others who lack what you have. Many who are now in misery would be content with your current state.

<margin>Do not fix your eye upon your superiors, but on your inferiors. — *Plutarch*</margin>
Do not let the prosperity of others torment you more than your own circumstances are able to comfort you. If you focus only on those in a higher state than yourself, you will always be restless. For prisoners think no one is happy but those with their liberty; those with liberty think no one is happy but the rich; the rich think no one is happy but those in high office; and officials think no one is happy but kings. There is no state of life without its complaints. As that King in *Homer* <note>Likely Agamemnon in the *Iliad*</note> complains: *Great Jupiter has imprisoned me with great cares; oh, how happy are those who live in their little cottages, exempt from these dangers!*

<margin>Keep within your own area of expertise.</margin>
*Hannibal* <note>The famous Carthaginian general</note> said he had known many old fools, but never one quite like the *Philosopher* <note>This refers to the philosopher Phormio, who famously gave a long lecture on the duties of a general to Hannibal; Hannibal was unimpressed since the philosopher had no practical experience</note> who lectured so boldly in the schools about the strategies of war, because he discussed things that are not learned in academies. All things are not appropriate for all people. *Megabyzus* <note>original: "Megabises"</note> of *Persia*, a man of great worth, once went into the workshop of *Apelles* <note>The most renowned painter of ancient Greece</note> and claimed to have skill in painting. *Apelles* answered him: "Before I heard you speak, I thought you were wise; but since you have discussed my art, my apprentices are laughing at you." The poets depict the fictional gods as each being content with their own office and estate: *Mars* with war; *Minerva* with the sciences; *Mercury* with eloquence; *Cupid* with love; *Jupiter* with heaven; and *Pluto* with hell.

*Dionysius* <note>original: "Dionyse," the tyrant of Syracuse</note> thought his own status was incomplete because *Philoxenus* surpassed him in poetry and *Plato* in philosophy. Therefore, he condemned the one to banishment and the other to the plow <note>Dionysius was notoriously sensitive about his amateur poetry and famously feuded with Plato, eventually having him sold into slavery</note>. Every creature must be content with its own state and skill: the ox is for tilling the soil, and the horse is for riding. All the different states of life in the world come together to form the necessary parts of a musical harmony; some...

If you have given no occasion, you have all the more reason to rejoice in your innocence. Think it no marvel to be injured, for wherever we find men, we shall find injuries. If the person who offended you is foolish, why do you complain about a madman? Pay him no mind, and that shall be a grievous revenge to a fool.

It is a weakness of mind not to know how to despise <note>original: "contemne"</note> an offense. If he is a wise man, suspect evil in yourself; he discovers some of your infirmities. Make profit of all injuries, so that you may better manage your...

As for adversity (the common cause of most discontentment) which drives fools to rage and desperation: consider that it is not as evil in itself as it is commonly <note>original: "vulgarly"</note> thought to be. If your burdens are just arriving and falling upon you, have a mind resolved for the worst; by doing so, evils will not come any sooner, but they will be easier to bear. Visualize these evils in your mind <note>original: "conceit"</note> before they happen, and their violence will be half over by the time they actually occur. Learn to fence in the school before you fight in the fields. Use meditation for this purpose, thinking about the worst outcomes and preparing yourself to receive them. A man forewarned is half armed. A good mariner prepares for a storm; a wise captain prepares for war during times of peace. Therefore, see that no evil surprises you. Stand on your guard, foresee what is to come, and be prepared for all possibilities. <margin>Future burdens.</margin> <margin>The blow of a foreseen evil is soft. <note>original: *Præmeditati mali mollis ictus.*</note></margin> <margin>I have prepared the man for human things. <note>original: *Hominem paraui ad humana.*</note> Present burdens.</margin>

# **C H A P T E R  X V I.**
## **The grief of Impatience.**
---

> *Psalm* 42:5, 11. *Why are you cast down, my soul, and disquieted within me?*
> *Psalm* 73:21. *Certainly my heart was vexed, and I was pricked in my reins.* <note>original: "reines" — an archaic term for the kidneys, once considered the seat of deep emotions or the conscience.</note>

### **Description.**

[[margin: What impatience is. Insensibility: natural or Stoic.]] **I**mpatience is an unwilling endurance of any kind of thing that troubles us. The opposite extreme is insensibility: whether it be natural, as in those who are brutish and born like blocks <note>original: "blockes" — referring to inanimate, unfeeling objects</note>; or voluntary, which is a Stoic practice of putting a press on the heart, exempting it from all kinds of grief. The middle virtue is [[margin: Patience.]] patience: which is a willing suffering <note>In this context, "suffering" means "enduring" or "bearing up under."</note> of any trouble.

There is one sort of impatience toward God: when [[margin: Two sorts of impatience.]] we grumble under the crosses <note>original: "crosses" — a metaphor for trials, afflictions, or burdens sent by God.</note> he sends us. This implies a dislike of God or of his dealings toward us, even if in other ways we seem to endure ever so fairly. There is another sort toward men: regarding their persons, status, actions, or injuries as they offend us.

The heart sometimes is agitated like a ship in a tempest [[margin: 3. Degrees of impatience. 2 Thessalonians 2:1, 2. To be shaken <note>Greek: *saleuein*</note>. Agitation. To establish <note>Greek: *sterizein*</note>, alluding to that figure, a solid cube <note>Greek: *stereon schema*</note>.]] and takes no rest, but is rolled up and down like a ball <note>original: "bowle" — likely a reference to the heavy ball used in the game of lawn bowls.</note>. The opposite of this is to establish the heart: so that under all evils it may lie steady, like a four-squared stone <note>A cube, which remains upright no matter which side it is thrown upon.</note>, *James* 5:8.

Other...

-> ### Description. <-

| **H** | **E** is said to be intemperate who is given to enjoy delights and pleasures immoderately. And as the object of impatience is grief; so the object of intemperance is bodily pleasure, nutritive <note>original: nutritiue; relating to food and nourishment</note>, or generative <note>original: generatiue; relating to reproduction</note>: and especially that which concerns the sense of touch. There are some pleasures natural, necessary and common to all, even with the beasts: as in hunger and thirst, the pleasure of meat <note>In this period, "meat" usually referred to food in general.</note> and drink. Some again are neither common, nor natural, but adventitious <note>original: aduentitious; meaning acquired or coming from external sources</note> or acquired, and proper to some, according to custom, and unruliness of the mind. These become, in a manner, natural. In natural pleasures, fewer people are said to be intemperate; but in proper <note>Here meaning "specific to the individual."</note> pleasures, many are: such as those who are given inordinately to particular sorts of meats, drinks, <term>venery</term> <note>original: venery; the pursuit of sexual pleasure</note>, and other special sorts of bodily pleasures, without which they might otherwise live very well. These are things that either they should not enjoy, or not enjoy as much as they do. | <margin>Who are intemperate.</margin> <br><br><br> <margin>The object is bodily pleasure.</margin> <br> <margin>Pleasures are either common, or proper.</margin> <br><br> <margin>According to the nature of the individual, not the species. <note>original: Secundum naturam indiuidui, non speciei.</note></margin> |

-> ### **CHAPTER 17. *The Excess of Intemperance.*** <-

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| <margin>What is true abstinence?</margin> | True abstinence is when anyone, out of the love he has for God and for his own good, bridles himself—not only from unlawful things, but sometimes also from things that are lawful and permitted. If it is associated with the fellow virtues and graces of faith, knowledge, patience, goodness, and so on, it is a confirmation of our calling and election. Otherwise, sobriety is not commendable; for those who abstain from food <note>original: "meate"</note> but still do evil are like devils, who lack food but do not lack sin. Or, if we abstain for selfish <note>original: "sinister"</note> reasons rather than for conscience, it is not true temperance—just as when we abstain more for the sake of health <note>original: "wholesomeness"</note> than for spiritual blessedness. |
| <margin>*2 Peter 1:6*</margin> | |
| <margin>Accustom yourself to temperance. Motives for doing so. *Aristotle, Rhetoric, Book 1, Chapter 9. It is a virtue to have abstained from pleasing goods <note>original Latin: "Est virtus placitis abstinuisse bonis."</note>* </margin> | Accustom yourself to commanding your delights. Rule them by reason rather than by sensuality, and especially by divine law. Keep a sense of proportion <note>original: "measure"</note> even in lawful pleasures, and practice some abstinence; by doing so, you will be better able to abstain from unlawful desires and will find your lawful delights to be even more pleasant. For overindulgence <note>original: "satiety"</note> breeds loathing, and when sweet things are rare, they provide more delight. If anyone exceeds moderation, even the most pleasant things shall become most unpleasant. Reason and moderation have always argued for temperance among the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicks"</note> as a way to command their unbridled lusts. And seeing that of all vices, impatience during trials <note>original: "evils"</note> and intemperance in pleasures are both the most common and the greatest, Epictetus said: "If any man would imprint in his heart these two words, *Sustain* and *Abstain*, they would serve greatly for temperance and tranquility." |
| <margin>*Aulus Gellius, Book 17, Chapter 19.* <gloss>Endure and abstain <note>original Greek: "Ανεχου & απέχου"</note></gloss></margin> | |

# CHAP. 18. -> The Frenzy of Passions. <-

---

### -> *Part affected.* <-

[[margin: Affections.]]
**T**he parts affected are the natural affections <note>original: "affections" refers to emotions, feelings, or passions</note> of the soul, which were once created good, but thereafter lost their holiness and rectitude <note>original: "rectitude" means moral uprightness or righteousness</note>. In respect to the other more noble and principal faculties <note>likely referring to reason and the will</note>, they are considered lowly. They are compared to the "feet" of the soul, which are both paralytic, gouty, and full of many passionate sores that disturb both the head and the heart, and sympathetically affect the conscience, the will, and the mind.

---
### -> *Causes.* <-

[[margin: God as a deficient cause. Romans 1:21, 24, 26, 28.]]
**G**od justly gives many people up to their hearts' lusts of uncleanness, so that out of a conscienceless and remorseless mind, they may do those things that are not proper <note>original: "not convenient" here means morally inappropriate or shameful</note>. This He does, more or less, according to the measure of His anger—inflicting this malady by degrees, as it pleases Him, upon those who are unthankful.

[[margin: Satan as an efficient cause. 1 Chronicles 21:1.]]
Just as it is the temperament and disposition of man to be passionate, either by nature or by current circumstances, so Satan goes along with the flow of their existing inclinations to urge them on and make them stronger in their fury. *The Devil stood up against Israel and provoked King David <note>The original cites 1 Cor 21:1, but 1 Chronicles 21:1 is the correct biblical reference for David numbering Israel.</note> to be more ambitious and to vainly trust in himself by counting the people of Israel.* [[margin: Acts 5:3; Ephesians 2:2.]] *Judas* was driven by his insatiable greed to betray his *Master*. Likewise, *Ananias* and *Sapphira* had *their hearts filled by Satan to lie to the Holy Spirit and keep back part of the price of their property. The prince who rules in the air—the spirit who now works in the children of disobedience*—is at once the fire to kindle, the bellows to blow, and the fuel to feed; he is a diligent agent who brings all disordered passions to the most destructive effects and ends.

Man's nature is most subject to the imitation of evil. The fashion of this world poisons his heart: evil examples stir him up to walk according to the course of this world, in worldly lusts—following the lusts of men and the lusts of the Gentiles in excessive riot. <margin>The course of this world. Ephesians 2:2. Titus 2:12. 1 Peter 4:2, 3.</margin>

Such is the <term>frowardness</term><note>original: "frowardnesse"; meaning perversity, stubbornness, or a tendency to go against what is right.</note> of man’s corruption that the more he is prohibited by the Law, the more sin within him takes the opportunity through the commandment to produce all kinds of <term>concupiscence</term><note>concupiscence: strong sexual desire or lust.</note>. For without the Law, sin is dead. <margin>Rebukes. Romans 7:8.</margin> Many are even more enraged when they are rebuked; they become more set upon their passions when they encounter any obstacles. <margin>We strive for what is forbidden, etc. <note>original: "Nitimur in vetitum, &c." A reference to Ovid: "We always strive for what is forbidden, and desire those things which are denied."</note></margin>

Human emotions are like gunpowder: the slightest fiery spark from the world's inflammatory objects (entering through even the smallest sense) is able to set everything ablaze. *The lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life* are like ready-burning matches, waiting to ignite on any occasion. *David*, when he looked upon *Bathsheba* <note>original: "Bethsabe"</note>, was inflamed with lust. *Holofernes* <note>original: "Olofernes"</note> had his eyes ravished by the *slippers of Judith*, and her beauty took his mind prisoner. *Jacob*, when he saw *Joseph's* garment sprinkled with blood, was struck almost dead with sorrow. *Cato* frightened the Senate of *Rome* when he showed them green *Carthaginian* figs <note>Cato the Elder famously displayed fresh figs from Carthage to the Roman Senate to demonstrate how close and threatening the rival city was, sparking the Third Punic War.</note>. This is common even among beasts: to be incensed by the presence of enticing objects. <margin>Objects. 1 John 2:16. Judith 16:9. Genesis 37.</margin>

The unbalanced constitution of the body (through a certain sympathy) causes disordered disturbances. The <term>humors</term><note>humors: In early medicine, these were the four fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control a person's health and temperament.</note>, whether through their physical substance or their vaporous, volatile spirits, corrupt the organs that carry out the soul's functions. Sometimes the brain is altered, causing it to send a false report to the heart. At other times, the heart is altered, causing it to misunderstand the true report from the brain. Or occasionally, both are altered, so that the brain’s perception and the heart’s emotion are both corrupted together, generating a storm of outrageous passions. People of a *sanguine* <note>original: "Sanguineans"</note> temperament are inclined toward excessive joy and <term>venery</term><note>venery: the pursuit of sexual pleasure.</note>. Those of a *choleric* <note>original: "Cholerians"</note> temperament are prone to anger and revenge. Those of a *phlegmatic* <note>original: "Phlegmaticks"</note> temperament... <margin>The imbalance <note>original: "distemperature"</note> of the body.</margin>

# -> CHAP. 18. The frenzy of Passions. <- | 261

*...the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the hardness of their heart; which, being past feeling, have given themselves over to wantonness, to practice all uncleanness even with greediness.* <note>This is a modernization of Ephesians 4:18-19.</note> Ignorance is strong enough to breed passions, but even more so if it is joined with the vanity and madness of the mind, hardness of heart, and a conscience past feeling. For as the <term>inorganic</term> <note>original: "inorganicke"; here used to mean the non-physical or spiritual faculties of the soul</note> mind and will are in their judgment or choice, so they excite or permit the passions to stir themselves. <margin>Hardness of heart, etc.</margin>

There are many people with weak minds and strong imaginations. Their imagination—which acts as the mind’s deputy, yet is both deceitful and deceived—overrules and captivates reason through inward delusion, the bribery of the senses, and the foolish reports of common judgment. It sets up a foolish opinion to sit on reason's throne and proclaims liberty to all the insolent <term>affections</term> <note>original: "affections"; in this context, it refers to emotions or internal impulses rather than just fondness</note>, moving every passion by the appearance and opinion of what is good or what is ill. <margin>Weakness of wit and strength of imaginations.</margin>

But the most closely linked and inevitable cause is 그 natiue inherent corruption (which is called "the flesh"), through which affections and passions exert force in our <term>members</term> <note>original: "members"; referring to the parts and faculties of the physical body</note>. This is that obedience to the lusts of our mortal body. The passions are the "works of the flesh" and the "lusts of the flesh" in fulfilling the will of the flesh and of the mind. Those in whom such passions reign are unregenerate—natural people who do not have the Spirit. They are mastered by that "old man" who is corrupt through deceitful lusts, and they serve various lusts and pleasures. Every person is tempted when they are drawn away and enticed by their own <term>concupiscence</term> <note>original: "concupiscence"; strong desire or lust, often specifically referring to worldly or carnal desires</note>. Then, when lust has conceived, it brings forth sin; and sin, when it is finished, brings forth death. <margin>Native impurity. Romans 7:5; Romans 6:12; Galatians 5:17, 19; Ephesians 2:3; Jude 19; Ephesians 4:22; Titus 3:3; James 1:14, 15.</margin>

-> S 3 Signs <-

<summary>This page identifies three primary causes for the "frenzy" of human passions: spiritual ignorance, a dominant imagination that overthrows reason, and inherent human corruption or "the flesh." It argues that when reason is bypassed, unruly emotions and sinful desires take control of the individual.</summary>

# CHAP. 18. -> The Frenzy of Passions. <-
---

### -> *Signs and Symptoms.* <-

[[margin: His words. Laertius. Job 32:19.]]
**T**he passionate man's speech is the mirror representing his passions. If any will challenge him with the saying, "Speak, so that I may see you" <note>original: *Loquere ut te videam*; attributed to Socrates by the biographer Diogenes Laertius</note>, his outbursts will carry the scent of his heart. As Elihu said in his zeal, so the passionate man has a belly like wine that has no vent, and is like new bottles that burst <note>Job 32:19</note>. The center of his speech, and the axle upon which his talk mostly turns, is his passion: whether it be brawling, boasting, indecency, bragging, quarreling, or such like.

[[margin: His actions.]]
As with his words, so his actions are the cracks and crevices through which the sparks of his passions flash; they are the leaves and fruits of that tree of bitterness. His troubled fountain yields impure streams. His clothing, his playing, his choice of company, his feasting, drinking, writing, and walking—as well as his sorrow, pain, music, and various occurrences—indicate the pattern of his inward emotions.

[[margin: His will. His wit.]]
He is more stubborn than wise and makes himself a fool at his own expense. Appetite is his master, while reason and piety are his slaves. Passions are his "green spectacles" <note>A metaphor for seeing things through a distorted or biased lens</note>, through which all things appear to him in a false color and according to the mood of his <term>humor</term> <note>In early medicine, the four bodily fluids believed to determine temperament</note>. He will be both judge and interested party in the same cause. All the world are fools in his <term>conceit</term> <note>opinion or imagination</note>. His understanding is corrupted and so overwhelmed by intense perception and false mental representation that he is thoroughly choked and carried away by his agitation. He can neither speak, hear, eat, drink, sleep, think, nor pray. He forces his reason and intelligence to devise all sorts of <term>sophisms</term> <note>clever but false arguments</note> to plead for the "rights" of his passion, and he uses every device to further the tasks of his mood.

[[margin: His rashness. His sensuality. His foolishness.]]
He is reckless, impulsive, and rash, inconstant and fleeting. His will has two natural inclinations: the one toward reason, and the other toward the senses. But he enslaves them both to follow sensuality and bribes his will with the baits of the senses. He is wonderfully metamorphosed

[The person is] alienated from himself, as if by Circe’s potions <note>original: "fed from himselfe... with Circes potions"; referring to the Greek enchantress who transformed men into animals, symbolizing how passion degrades human nature.</note>. His fairest calmness is turned into a storming tempest, and his wisest counsel into frantic foolishness. He is a burden to himself and creates many crosses for himself, both real and imaginary.

<margin>His hopes and desires.</margin>
He feeds himself with vain hopes and is vexed with even vainer wishes. Whatever he thinks will benefit him must be had or done, even if the whole world cannot provide it. Rachel desired children, or else she would die <note>A reference to Genesis 30:1.</note>. Those two drunkards, Philoxenus and Melanthius <note>Classical figures cited by Aristotle and others as examples of gluttony; they wished for long necks to prolong the taste of food and drink.</note>—wishing they might have more pleasure as the drinks descended to their stomachs—wished, one for a swan's throat and the other for a crane's neck. Here, fantasy commands and reason is but a drudge. Time and place are cursed if they do not afford an opportunity to rage. Like the dropsical person <note>original: "Hydropicke"; one suffering from edema, traditionally characterized by an unquenchable thirst.</note>, the more he drinks, the more he thirsts.

<margin>Proverbs 30:15, 16.</margin>
With the horse-leech and her two daughters, he cries, "Give, give!" And like the grave, the barren womb, the earth that cannot be satisfied with water, and the fire, he says, "It is not enough."

<margin>His inconstancy.</margin>
His most peaceful thoughts and bravest resolutions will be suddenly disturbed by a sudden flood of tempestuous appetite. For the sake of a small, passionate trifle <note>original: "toy"</note>, he will reject the enjoyment of all his other sweet contentments. At one moment, he is mounted with pride, fretted with envy, shaken with fear, inflamed with lust, consumed with ire <note>anger</note>, and overflowing with hope; yet immediately <note>original: "incontinent"</note> afterward, he is ebbing with sorrow and despair. Prosperity puffs him up; adversity dejects him. In love, he pines; in hate, he frets; in anger, he rages; in fear, he trembles; in joy, he is unrestrained <note>original: "dissolute"</note>; he faints in hope, and in woe, he is desperate.

<margin>His torment and battle.</margin>
Desires distract him, and his passions are like so many hungry hounds, gaping and gnashing at his mind until they are filled. His inward basilisks <note>Mythical serpents said to suck the life out of victims or kill with a look.</note> suck out his heart. Like Prometheus <note>The Titan punished by Zeus; an eagle was sent to eat his regenerating liver every day.</note>, the eagle of his passions upon the high Caucasus of his own imaginings <note>original: "conceits"</note> corrodes his own breast. He is like Phaeton <note>The son of Apollo who lost control of the sun chariot and scorched the earth.</note>, the sun’s son, overwhelmed

If reason or piety prescribe pain and labor, passion commands sluggishness. When piety bids one to fast, sensuality bids one to feast. When reason pardons, passion seeks revenge. *The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, and these are contrary to one another.*

<margin>Galatians 5:17.</margin>

### -> *Prognostics.* <note>Signs or symptoms that predict the course or outcome of a disease.</note> <-

<margin>A dangerous case.</margin>
Inordinate passion is a most sharp and violent disease: always dangerous and deadly, but so much more so if the mind’s inclination, a graceless heart, a distempered body, habit, and the presence of the tempting <term>baiting</term> object all coincide.

<margin>Ensuring evils to the soul.</margin>
Most of all, the greatest evils spring from the fountain of passion. The soul is disquieted, wit <note>intellect or reasoning ability</note> is defaced, grace is extinguished, and the whole man is made a fool before the world, an enemy to himself and to others, and stands guilty of judgment before God.

<margin>To the body. Proverbs 14:30. Proverbs 17:22.</margin>
Passions distemper the body, loosen the spirits <note>In early medicine, "spirits" were subtle fluids or gases thought to animate the body and carry out its functions</note>, engender humors <note>Bodily fluids like blood and bile believed to control health and temperament</note>, and produce diseases. Although *a sound heart is the life of the body* and *a joyful heart causes good health* (because the heart is then enlarged, the spirits are multiplied and distributed through the body), yet if joyful, enlarging passions are too vehement, they cause great infirmity, dissolving the spirits, weakening the heart, and often bringing on sudden death. Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher who allegedly died of laughter after seeing a donkey eat figs</note> and Zeuxis <note>A Greek painter who reportedly died laughing at a portrait of an old woman he had painted</note> died laughing. Sophocles the Poet and Philippides the Athenian died instantly for joy. If passions that constrict <note>original: "coarct"</note> the heart—such as fear, despair, and sadness—are too vehement, they endanger the body. *A sorrowful mind dries the bones and engenders diseases.*

<margin>Caelius <note>Ludovicus Caelius Rhodiginus (1469–1525), an Italian philologist</note> book 1, chapter 18 & book 3, chapter 15.</margin>

<margin>Proverbs 17:22.</margin>

<margin>Passions</margin>
...all grief) and contrary bad passions are no true remedies for passions: such as using sorrow to amend wantonness, or joy to overthrow anger.

<margin>Bodily remedies for passions</margin>
If the distemper of the body is the chief cause of any passion, it must be physically cured. All the noisome <note>harmful or foul-smelling</note> spirits and humors that deprave the organs and pervert the functions of the soul must be altered, purged, diverted, and corrected.

<margin>Reject common opinions and examples</margin>
Withdraw yourself from common <note>original: "vulgar"</note> opinions that pervert your imaginations and inflame passions. Do not follow the multitude; frequenting common people is contagious. Beware of examples and customs; suspect that which delights everyone, and count it madness to follow the filthy trail of the foolish people's conceit.

<margin>Eschew objects and occasions. (Numbers 16)</margin>
Study to divert evils and avoid all occasions of this frenzy. *Occasiones faciunt latrones* <note>Latin: "Opportunities make thieves"</note>; indeed, even the occasions for such opportunities should be shunned. The *Nazarites* <note>Individuals in the Hebrew Bible who took a vow of abstinence</note>, so that they might abstain from drunkenness, were forbidden wine as the occasion of drunkenness. They were also forbidden to eat raisins, lest they be allured to the wine by them. Beware also of any calling, errand, or exercise for which your nature, gifts, or practice is not suited, or taking on a heavier burden than you are able to bear. Otherwise, you cannot help but be continually troubled by striving against your weak wit, staggering strength, and slender skill.

<margin>Beware of self-love. (Proverbs 3:5)</margin>
Preserve yourself from a foolish doting upon yourself; do not be your own idol, nor your own ultimate goal <note>original: "scope"</note>. In all things, suspect yourself; beware of complacency; never rely on your own opinion. Be humble and affable, and *lean not unto your own wisdom.*

<margin>Press toward the contrary passion. (Aristotle)</margin>
If you perceive yourself inclined to any vehement and extreme passion, study to bow and bend yourself (as far as you can) to the contrary extreme, so that you may more easily reach the *golden mediocrity* <note>The "Golden Mean," Aristotle’s concept that virtue exists as the middle ground between two extremes of excess and deficiency</note>. As the *Philosopher* <note>Aristotle</note> declares by the simile of a crooked staff: to make it stand even, we must bend it far

to the contrary side. But you must be very wise in this, so that you do not stay there too long, nor fix yourself too deeply, nor bend too far, lest you break.

<margin>While fools avoid vices, they fall into the opposite extremes <note>Latin: *Dum vitant stulti vitia, &c.*</note>. Divert your mind from the objects of your passion. Change your passion into a contrary passion, or change the subject of it.</margin>
Divert your heart to some other objects, and transport your attention to some other thing. Give your unwelcome guest <note>original: "ill guest," referring to a disruptive passion or emotion</note> meager entertainment; while your passion looks for your attention, neglect it and be the more diligent in other affairs. Devise some other good passion (contrary to various ones) to exercise your heart. In your greatest delights, pause upon some sorrowful object. In your sadness, think upon your sweetest supreme contentments; in your anger, muse upon some fear. Or else, if you cannot change your passion into one of another and better nature, then alter the subject of it, and give it some other thing to work upon. As for example: turn your sorrow into a sorrow for sin; convert your fear into the fear of God; change your joy into the joy of the Spirit; convert your hatred of the person into the hatred of his vice; and alter your greedy appetites for food, riches, and honor into these holy desires for righteousness, for the bread and water of *Life*, for the riches of grace, and for the privileges <term>prerogatives</term> of the sons of God.

<margin>John 1:12; Hebrews 12:22</margin>

<margin>A powerful resolution.</margin>
Learn in the greatest assaults and tempests of the most vehement temptations to be of the strongest resolution. Just as Joseph was when he was allured by his vile mistress, and Abraham when he was commanded to kill his son, they pulled up their hearts most resolutely. With one nail they drove out another <note>A common early modern proverb meaning to displace one powerful emotion or thought with another of equal force.</note> and took advantage of temptations. Job, at the brink of desperation, most resolutely concluded, saying: *Although God would kill me, I will trust in Him.* This is a most commendable act, practiced only by those who are of gallant spirits and best regenerated by grace: at the brunt of the greatest temptations, and in the midst of the race of the most raging passions, to pull up and hold their hearts fast stayed, like well-bridled horses.

<margin>1 Corinthians 10:11; 2 Corinthians 8:9; Job 13:15</margin>

# CHAPTER 19. The Fury of Anger.

<margin>
*Seneca, Book 2 on Anger, chapter 5.*
</margin>
...[having] slew three hundred men in a day, he walked proudly among the dead and said, "O kingly matter! This was not anger, but savagery." <note>original: *O rem regiam! Non fuit haec ira, sed feritas.*</note>

<margin>
Degrees of anger.
*Anger (Ira). Wrathfulness (Iracundia).*
</margin>
There are degrees in *anger*: Some are angry upon some sudden occasion, and some are accustomed to being angry. There is an anger without a voice, an anger with a voice, and an anger with both words and voice. Again, anger is either hidden and subdued, or hidden and nourished, waiting for the opportunity of revenge. It is also either silent or professed—shown by the face, by speaking, or by doing. 

<margin>
*There are a thousand kinds of manifold evil. Seneca, On Anger, Book 1, chapter 4.*
</margin>
Some are soon angry and soon appeased; some are slowly angry and slowly reconciled. Some are the opposite: soon angry but slowly pleased; and some are slowly angry and soon pleased.

### Anger arises by a battle of two contrary disturbances, assaulting the heart at the same instant. 

<margin>
The essence of anger and its ground.
</margin>
The grief and dislike of the offered and offending injury causes the heart to contract itself and makes the thinnest blood and purest spirits retreat from the nearest and furthest parts. Because of this, the face grows pale and blackish, and great heat is gathered around the heart. This internal flame immediately breaks out again with an enlarging of the heart, driven by the desire and delight of revenge, which immediately appears with another mask <note>original: "visour"</note> on the face. 

<margin>
*Seneca, Book 2 on Anger, chapter 32.*
*It is sweet to return pain.*
*Genesis 27:42.*
*A composite evil.*
*Nazianzen.*
*Acts 5:17.*
*1 Corinthians 13:4.*
*Zeal <note>Greek: ζηλος (zelos)</note>*
*Aristotle, Book 1, chapter 1 on Animals.*
*Anger (Ira) is as if "ura," from burning.*
</margin>
So, with grief at the injury (constricting the heart) and delight to be revenged (enlarging the heart), the intensity of both and the suddenness of this mixed motion—combined with the agitated heat boiling out—kindles anger. If it is vented by any word, deed, or resolution, it is the sooner quenched; but if the flame is in any way forcibly restrained, it makes the agony so fervent that the heart almost bursts. It is a fiery passion, involving a kindling of the blood around the heart. 

<margin>
Who are said to be angry.
*Aristotle, Ethics, Book 4, chapter 5.*
</margin>
Those are most properly called angry who are soon stirred up—both against those they should not be, and for such causes, and more severely and longer than is appropriate—and those who are more slowly reconciled, and then only if revenge follows.

## CHAPTER 19. *The Fury of Anger.*

<margin>
The parts of anger:
1. Sorrow <note>original: "Dolour"</note>.
*Aristotle, Ethics, book 7, chapter 6.*
2. Impatience.
3. Rash judgment.
4. Desire for revenge.
Anger, from desire <note>original: ὀργὴ, ἀπὸ ὀρέξεως; a Greek etymological definition of anger linked to the appetite for retribution</note>.
</margin>

**A**nger has, first, a sorrow <note>original: "dolour"</note> conceived from some injury, whether it be in reality or in appearance and imagination; whether it be past, present, or to come. 2. A felt impatience and weakness, by which it judges the burden of the wrong to be more than can be borne. 3. A seizure of power <note>original: "usurpation"</note>, by which it takes upon itself to be both judge and party, and a decider <note>original: "carver"</note> in its own cause. 4. A desire to be revenged and to repay with pain, encouraged by some hope and power of performance. It desires to punish him who has not deserved it, or to punish more than is deserved; or to punish in an unlawful manner, or to punish not for the right end (which is the preservation of justice or correction of the fault), looking more to the person than to the wrongdoing.

The natural emotion <note>original: "affection"</note> of anger.
*Mark 3:5* and *10:14.*
*2 Corinthians 7:11.*
</margin>

**T**he immediate seat of this fury is that natural emotion of anger, whose moderate function and movement should arise from a just sorrow for evil and a lawful desire for revenge. When it is immoderately moved, then it is not only diseased by a fury, but likewise also the heart and mind (by sympathy) are troubled and agitated.

Actual injuries.
*Proverbs 15:1.*

Suspected injuries.

# CHAPTER 19. The Fury of Anger.

<margin>Augustine to Dioscorus. Seneca, *Of Anger*, Book 2, Chapter 23.</margin> ...sent fuel to this fury. <margin>Aggravating factors of injuries taken from the injurer.</margin> If the one who does the injury is low-born (causing contempt), or powerful (leaving a great impression), or a friend (showing unnatural behavior), or one who is obligated to you (showing unthankfulness), or one who is malicious (showing cruelty), or one often pardoned (showing insolence), anger is stirred all the more.

<margin>The injured.</margin> Or, if the person injured is a great person, or greatly harmed, a special friend, or singled out from the rest.

<margin>The injury.</margin> Or, if the injury itself is great, and prejudices us much in the goods of reputation <note>original: "fame"</note>, fortune, body, or soul—in any one or more of these. If the injury is universal, spreading its pestilent poison to more people. If it was committed knowingly, willingly, maliciously, and for some even greater mischief.

<margin>The manner of injuring.</margin> Or, if the method of the injury was under the color of friendship, and with dissimulation and premeditation. If it was public, disgraceful, or any other of a hundred ways whereby the manner may aggravate the matter. In all those respects, injuries are occasions to kindle anger, considering that injuries are thought to be more than just points of unrighteousness. "Because the will is involved, and every injury is committed by one who is willing—and not against one who is willing" <note>original: "Quia voluntas accedit, & omnis iniuria sit à volente: & non volenti." This refers to the ethical and legal principle that an injury requires intent from the doer and a lack of consent from the victim.</note>. <margin>Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book 5, Chapters 8, 9; Diogenes Laertius, Book 5, Chapter 1.</margin> And as Aristotle’s answer was, "Favor ages quickly, but injury ages slowly" <note>original: "Gratia citò, iniuria tardè senescit." Kindness is soon forgotten, but wrongs are long remembered.</note>. So all memories (however dull they may be in other things) are most sharp in retaining the impression of wrongs: <margin>Proverbs 26:20</margin> *"Without wood, the fire is quenched,"* yet people always judge it a point of special wisdom to seek restitution <note>original: "to be repaired"</note>.

<margin>Education. Examples. Custom.</margin> Bad education, worse examples, and most wicked habits <note>original: "consuetude"</note> (becoming a second, acquired evil nature)...

[The hair] rises, the hair turns <note>original: "turne"; likely meaning it bristles or stands on end</note>, the eyes reel, the color of the face changes, the feet move, the tongue stammers, and bursts forth (like dogs) with secret quarreling. As Shimei did against David (2 Samuel 16:5).

<margin>Democritus, from Antony’s Maxims, sermon on anger: "An angry man speaks nothing but accusations." <note>original: "Iratus nil nisi crimina loquitur"</note> Seneca, in the tragedy *Thyestes*, act 2: "An impatient mind, curses, blasphemy, and insults." "Revenge, strife, and threats are the seven pledges <note>original: "pignora"</note> of anger." Virgil, *Aeneid*, book 2: "Fury and anger drive the mind headlong." Inwardly. Ephesians 4:27. In his mind and other passions. Sallust, in *The Jugurthine War*: "Desire and anger are the worst counselors." <note>original: "Cupido & ira pessimi consultores"</note></margin>
Impatience, cursings, blasphemy, reproach, revenge, scolding, and threats are the seven children of anger. Moderation of speech and decent behavior are choked. It is rightly called anger, from the Latin word *angor* <note>meaning a tightening, strangling, or distress</note>, because it strangles, and sometimes so numbs a person that nothing is left but, like a donkey, to bite and to kick.

The image of God is defiled; a place is given to the devil, wisdom is lost, righteousness is forsaken, friendship is broken, truth is darkened, and the light of nature and grace is ruined.

The angry mind is greatly agitated and is like a fair <note>original: "faire"; a busy marketplace or festival</note> wherein there are great tumults, confusion, meetings of all parties, and people going here and there with shouting and business. It causes the smallest injury to seem the greatest, inciting one to revenge without any proportion. Lust and anger are the most evil counselors. To an angry man, even a crime seems like good advice <note>original: "Iratus etiam facinus, consilium putat"</note>.

<margin>Anger. Seneca, in *Proverbs*. His fury. Romans 12:19, Deuteronomy 35:32. Seneca: "Anger is always a liar, which is why one should never believe a grieving mind." <note>original: "Semper mendax iracundia, quare animo dolenti nihil oportet credere"</note> Virgil: "Fury provides the weapons." <note>original: "Furor arma ministrat"</note> His revenging rage. Numbers 24:1.</margin>
The angry man swells with pride, is hasty in resolution, is displeased with everything, and cannot tolerate an opponent <note>original: "gain-sayer"</note> or anyone who stands against him. In his face, he has the signs of fury, impatience, inconstancy, and impiety. He will not rest until he avenges himself; he refuses to yield to God’s anger or the authority of the magistrates. He spares no lies when he lies in wait for revenge. His fury provides him with great strength to carry out his revenge. His other passions lead, entice, dazzle, and incline him; but this passion draws, compels, blinds, and hurls him into the gulf of all wickedness. He seeks to be revenged upon everything; and when he lacks a suitable target, he will rage at any nearby, unworthy thing—as Balaam did at his donkey, or Xerxes at the rivers and hills. He spares nothing.

<margin>A dangerous case. Seneca, *On Anger*, Book 1, Chapter 1; Proverbs 19:19. Ensuing evils to a man's self. 1 Timothy 2:8; Plutarch; Stobaeus, Sermon 18; Aristotle, *Politics*, Book 5, Chapter 10.</margin>
# I
If the habit of this fury is not prevented, or if it is not addressed in its seedbed <note>original: "seminary"</note>, the cure will be most difficult. If it begins to carry us perversely <note>original: "overthwart"</note>, the return to health will be hard. "No plague has cost mankind more than this" <note>original: *Nulla pestis humano generi pluris stetit*</note>. There was never so dangerous a pestilence to mankind as this is. He who is possessed with this fury—even if you deliver him from it once—his anger will surely return.

It blinds the mind, deforms the body, and exposes it to contempt and danger. It makes the soul furious; it subverts men's estates, families, commonwealths, and kingdoms; and it causes one to lose his life with its own sting. It defaces God’s image, quenches grace, and stops prayer. Marcus Cato said that an angry man and a madman differ in nothing but the "duration of time" <note>original: *temporis mora*</note>. It is the "beginning of insanity" <note>original: *initium insaniæ*</note>, said Ennius, and the "beginning of repentance" <note>original: *initium pœnitentiæ*</note>, said Seneca. It begins with rashness and rage and ends with repentance and sorrow, which soon outweighs the delight of revenge. 

Anger is more irrational than hatred because hatred is separate from the physical pain <note>original: "dolour"</note> that always accompanies anger and keeps it fresh <note>original: "greene"</note>. And although anger contains a certain poisonous sweetness, yet it torments its owner and possessor with pangs, like vipers gnawing and gnashing within their mother’s belly <note>A common historical folk belief held that young vipers were born by eating their way out of the mother's body.</note>. It brings on deadly illnesses and often does more hurt to the person who feels it than the original injury itself did.

Anger is a cruel monster, from which spring all seditions, riots, battles, murders, and destructions. This abyss of all evil degenerates into hatred. All evils come from anger: such as the revealing of secrets, the betrayal of friendship, the destruction of piety, making men like the devil, and the violation of all the commandments. *Anger is cruel, and wrath is raging, but who can stand before envy?* <note>Proverbs 27:4</note>

Other vices move men's minds slowly, but anger drives them headlong into ruin <note>original: "precipitates"</note>. It transforms men into monsters, beasts, tigers, and devils. Saul, in his anger, killed Ahimelech <note>original: "Abimelech"</note> the Priest, burned the city of Nob, and slaughtered every man, woman, child, and beast, including eighty-five priests; and all this he did based on an imagined insult. For the fault and offense of one man, Simeon and Levi punished Hamor and Shechem; they killed the prince and the people, plundered the city, and led the people away captive. Pyrrhus, in his wrath, killed his trusted secretary Fabatus. The Emperor Vitellius <note>original: "Bitillion"</note> killed his greatest friend Cinnatus. Hadrian killed his once-favored Apronia <note>original: "Anpronia"</note>. Diocletian killed his friend Patritius, and Alexander the Great killed Cleitus <note>original: "Clitus"</note>. But *anger kills the foolish man, and envy slays the simpleton. A man of great anger shall suffer punishment.* 

Anger even in thought is subject to judgment. Expressing anger with the voice but without a specific word—for *Raca* <note>original: "Racha"</note> in Hebrew <note>Raca is generally considered Aramaic, meaning "empty-headed" or "worthless."</note> is not a word, but a sound of anger—is worthy of punishment by the Council. But whoever is angry in word, calling someone a "Fool," is worthy of hell. *As the degree of guilt increases, so does the severity of the sentence.* <note>original: "Per gradus culpæ, crescit ordo sententiæ."</note> It excludes one from the Kingdom of God.

->## TO THE READER.<-

You have here the *Soul’s Medicine* <note>original: "Soules Physicke"</note>: The *spiritual sicknesses* are fully described. The *faculties* <term>the powers of the mind or soul, such as reason, will, and emotion</term> (as the parts immediately affected) are briefly touched upon. The *causes* are distinctly set down, like so many fountains from which diseases spring. The *signs* and *symptoms* are particularly specified, like so many branches, leaves, blossoms, and bitter grapes that grow up and arise from any deep-rooted <note>original: "radicall"</note> sickness and impurity. The *prognoses* <note>original: "Prognosticks"</note> show the difficulties of the cure, along with the danger and all the evils that are likely to follow. The *remedies* are not gathered from among animals, plants, or minerals (a whole world of those are not able to ease the soul for one moment) but out of the clear streams of reason and the most pure and perfect fountain of Divine Scripture. The body and soul have their most fitting medicine from their own proper elements: the body from beneath, the soul from above.

May it please you to take some pains to read it thoroughly for your own necessary use, for your maladies—both those you already have and those that are threatening <note>original: "imminent"</note>.

The *physician* of the soul <note>Referring to a pastor or minister.</note> will find this treatise very suitable for his people when he looks upon them with a compassionate heart, as if they were many diseased patients—like those sick people, *blind, lame <note>original: "halt"</note>, and withered, waiting for the moving of the water at the pool of Bethesda*. By the preaching of the Word—having his doctrines, applications, exhortations, and consolations stocked with a variety of heavenly antidotes and specific remedies—he may draw their minds toward soundness and health. | <margin>Physicians and their patients.</margin> | The physician of the body will often find that his patient's passionate mind disturbs and upsets the humors <note>The four bodily fluids thought to determine health and temperament</note> and spirits of his body; beneath a frail <note>original: "crazie"; meaning physically broken or infirm</note> body lies an even more diseased soul. A heart full of comfort for the soul is better than a box full of drugs for the body. |
| <margin>A specific warning to the reader.</margin> | If you improve yourself through this treatise, it is the thing I seek. But if you look upon it with a disdainful eye and a mind careless of your soul's health, you are an object of pity. If you meet my hard work with malicious criticism, first do as much yourself as you find here. It is easier to complain than to create; to chatter than to paint; to blame than to build. Whatever you object to out of a diseased mind (in blindness or in passion) against this treatise or the author, I reject the judgment of such a mind. Just as the petitioning woman appealed from "drunken King *Philip*" to "sober King *Philip*" <note>A famous anecdote about Philip II of Macedon, where a woman refused to accept a judgment made while he was drunk, demanding he reconsider while sober</note>, so I appeal from my irrational critic to my healthy critic. However, whatever you find blameworthy here while in a sound mind, I am certain that in wisdom and love you will advise, excuse, or correct it. |

-> Yours in the Lord, <-
-> **Mr. John Abernethy.** <note>original: "Io. Abrenethy"</note> <-

# TO THE REVEREND PRELATE
# JOHN ABERNETHY, Doctor of Sacred
# Theology, Bishop of Caithness, etc.

->A man most richly furnished with a vast store of manifold learning, but especially most skilled in both kinds of medicine <note>Strang refers to Abernethy’s expertise in both physical health (medicine) and spiritual health (theology).</note>: upon the occasion of publishing anew his book on the **healing of the soul**, enriched with fresh care.<-

<insert>Woodcut initial Q</insert> **I**f we bestow wonderful praise upon those who heal the limbs of the body through the arts of Apollo <note>original: "Phœbæis... artibus." Apollo was the Greek god of healing and light.</note>;

And since a thousand troops of diseases infest the soul—evils that are both more numerous and more serious than those of the body—

How great an honor is rightfully yours, most worthy Prelate <term>prelate: a high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop</term>, who provides remedies for the diseases of the soul.

As much as the body is inferior to the soul, as the son of Leto <note>original: "Latonia proles," referring again to Apollo.</note> is inferior to Christ, and as fleeting things are inferior to eternal goods;

So much should Podalirius and Machaon <note>Legendary physicians of Greek mythology, said to be the sons of Asclepius.</note>, and the great schools of Galen and Hippocrates, yield to this work.

Could even the foremost of physicians have applied the methods of physical science so skillfully to sacred matters?

Well done! It is your special gift to excel in both kinds of medicine, so that a sound mind may exist in a sound body <note>A reference to the famous Latin maxim *mens sana in corpore sano*.</note>.

Our one salvation, physician, and medicine is Christ; you teach Him, and He has taught you.

->**John Strang, Doctor of**<-

-># THE MEDICINE<-
->## OF THE MIND.<-

->### CHAPTER 1.<-
->#### Of spiritual sicknesses in general.<-

---

->*Matthew 9:12. The healthy do not need a physician, but those who are sick.*<-

<margin>Job 4:19; 2 Corinthians 5:1; Proverbs 14:13.</margin>

**S**ince the body is only the soul’s earthly tabernacle <note>A biblical metaphor for the temporary nature of the human body</note>, and a sound heart is the *life of the body*, our chiefest care should be that a healthy mind be in a healthy body. This is so that, just as we enjoy the sweetness of this life through the health <note>original: "soundness"</note> of the body, so by the health of the mind, we may have the happy enjoyment <note>original: "fruition"</note> of both this life *here* and that endless life *hereafter*. 

<margin>The health of the soul is a great happiness.</margin>

<margin>"That there be a healthy mind in a healthy body" <note>original Latin: *Ut sit mens sana in corpore sano*</note>; Lucretius; Juvenal, Satire 10; Seneca, *On the Happy Life*.</margin>

Almost all philosophers have aimed at this health of mind (though darkly and confusedly) and thought there was no happiness without it. They believed that a happy life could not be attained unless the mind was first made whole and then kept in a state of perpetual health. 

<margin>Titus 1:9 and 2:1.</margin>

But *theologians* <note>original: "Divines"</note>, by *Scripture* (that healing and wholesome doctrine), aim <note>original: "level"</note> at this goal <note>original: "mark"</note> more clearly:

->clearly:<-

<summary>This page introduces the concept that spiritual health is as vital as physical health, noting that while ancient philosophers recognized the importance of a healthy mind, only Christian scripture provides a clear path to achieving it.</summary>
<keywords>spiritual health, soul, tabernacle, philosophers, theology, Scripture, happiness, wellness</keywords>

<meta>Continuation of Chapter I. This page continues the introduction to the nature of spiritual health and its decline into sickness.</meta>

[[page number: 2]]

->**C**HAPTER I. *Of Spiritual Sicknesses in General.*<-

...clearly: showing both the sores and the salve <note>salve: a medicinal ointment or remedy used for healing</note>, and demonstrating that there is no true life without this health. The diseases by which this health is plagued and destroyed are many, being both dangerous and deadly. For just as all impurities were spread through the body from that first divine curse <note>original: *Malediction*; referring to the Fall of Man and the resulting corruption of nature</note>—the seeds of all following diseases and death—so from that same fountain spring all the fundamental <margin>Romans 7:24</margin> impurities of *that body of death*. These cause all manner of spiritual diseases in the soul and carry everything toward that *Second Death*. 

The soul is most slavishly employed in repelling and repairing the ongoing ruins of this molded, muddy cottage <note>original: "moulded muddy cottage"; a metaphor for the human body made of dust or clay</note> in which it lives. It should instead make a far greater effort to look after itself, for the sake of correctly obtaining both soundness and safety. The majority of people are encumbered and troubled by many things <margin>Luke 10:40</margin> regarding the care and cure of the body. But few, like *Mary*, choose that good part (namely, the soul's health) which shall not be taken away. 

When Christ cured diseased bodies, he also cured sick souls. When he opened the <margin>John 9:6, 37, 38</margin> eyes of the body, he also opened the eyes of the soul. When he healed the lame body, he also healed the lame soul, so <margin>John 5:5, 14 and 7:23</margin> that the diseased person might be *made every bit whole*. 

We are sensitive enough to the smallest sicknesses of the flesh, and even the point of a tiny pin pricking the most distant part of the body. But as for spiritual diseases, they are both numerous and very easily contracted; they are difficult to avoid, harder to find and feel, and most difficult of all to help and heal. Both their diagnosis <note>original: *cognition*</note> and their cure must be considered. First, in general, they should be touched upon in their *nature, causes, signs, symptoms, prognoses, cures, and remedies.*

->*A thousand species of evil, and a thousand will be of health.*<-
<note>original: *Mille mali species, mille salutis erunt* (Ovid, *Remedia Amoris*)</note>

->*That*<-

<summary>This page establishes a parallel between physical and spiritual illness, arguing that while humans obsess over bodily health, they often ignore the more dangerous diseases of the soul caused by the Fall. The author notes that Christ's miracles were intended to heal both the body and the soul entirely.</summary>
<keywords>spiritual sickness, original sin, soul vs. body, healing of Christ, spiritual diagnosis, Mary and Martha</keywords>

[[margin: Ibid.]] [[margin: The same author, 3. Tusculan Disputations.]] |
| For diseased souls, there is no medicine more fitting than sickness <note>original Greek: "Νόσος ψυχῆς οὐδὲν φάρμακον πλὴν νόσος"</note>. *We are born into this condition, to be living creatures subject to no fewer sicknesses of the mind than of the body* <note>original Latin: "Hac conditione nati sumus, animalia obnoxia non paucioribus animi quàm corporis morbis."</note>. | [[margin: Isocrates, *On the Peace*.]] [[margin: Seneca, *On Anger*, Book 2, Chapter 9.]] |
