<meta>This page begins Chapter 1, detailing the various categories and characteristics of spiritual "sicknesses" or sins, drawing parallels between physical ailments and those of the soul.</meta>

->## CHAPTER 1. Of Spiritual Sicknesses,<-

The diseases of the soul differ among themselves. <margin>Some are idiopathic.</margin> Some are *idiopathic* <term>original: "idiopathicke"; a disease that arises spontaneously within the organ itself</term>, arising from a specific passion occurring directly in the soul and residing there—such as blindness of the mind, hardness of heart, and so on. Others are *sympathetic*, involving a more indirect passion. These either arise from the body and are passed to the soul—such as that kind of a wounded *spirit* which arises from melancholy—or they arise from the soul and are spread <note>original: "diffunded"</note> to specific organs of the body, such as the poisonous tongue, the deaf <margin>Some are sympathetic.</margin> ear, and the evil eye. In some respects, these may be called <margin>Mark 7:22–23.</margin> *symptomatic*.

<margin>No spiritual disease exists alone; they are neither simple nor solitary. (Latin: *Ut simplex intemperies*—as a simple lack of balance.)</margin> Furthermore, it is often seen that in the body there will be one single disease alone, without the company of another. But in the soul, there is always more than one; indeed, many and diverse sicknesses often exist at one time. In the body, there may be a simple and solitary disease that lacks an active cause <note>original: "efficient"</note> and exists without any great *symptom*. But in the soul, every sickness is accompanied and fueled by its own internal cause and has some harsh *symptom* following it—much like that *nephritic* <term>kidney-related</term> ailment in the kidneys that has both *obstruction* as the *cause* and *pain* <note>original: "dolour"</note> as the *symptom* at the same time.

<margin>Spiritual diseases are always accompanied by their own causes and by the company of other sicknesses (Acts 28:27). They are also intertwined.</margin> No disease of the soul can exist by itself but is always accompanied by others. For they are either *intertwined* <note>original: "implicate"</note>, remaining in their own affected parts but conspiring together to damage some common function—as blindness in the mind and hardness in the heart work together to stop repentance. This malady was present for a long time among the *Jews*: *For their hearts had grown calloused, and their ears were hard of hearing, and they closed their eyes, lest they should see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and return so that God might heale them.*

<margin>Or connected.</margin> Or else they are *connected*, fastened, and coupled together, where one is always the internal cause of the other. They are so similar in nature and such close neighbors in the parts they affect, and share such 

->## CHAPTER 1. and their differences,<-

acquaintance and communication, that the *latter* <note>original: "posterior"</note> (in nature, order, or time) cannot be cured unless the first is helped first. Thus, blindness of mind and the evil heart of unbelief <note>original: "incredulity"</note> were connected together in the *Apostle* Paul when he was a blasphemer; he did it *ignorantly through unbelief*. Blindness and hardness were coupled <margin>1 Timothy 1:13; 2 Corinthians 3:4; Ephesians 4:18; Romans 2:5. Or successive.</margin> together in the *Jews*. Hardness and a lack of repentance <note>original: "impenitency"</note> were fastened together in the *Gentiles*.

Or else they are *consequences* and *successive*, occurring when the first goes away and the other succeeds it in that place by a certain exchange and substitution. The former is not the immediate and joined cause (though it may be a prior cause) of the other; before the second comes in, the first must go away. For example, *Judas’s* despair followed his spirit of *slumber* <note>A state of spiritual stupor or apathy.</note>. The slumber went away entirely and left anguish of conscience behind it to keep him awake with endless torments. And in many, *impatience* <note>original: "impatency"</note> followed *intemperance* <note>lack of self-control or moderation</note>, once the pleasure of the one turned into the grief of the other.

<margin>2 Samuel 13:15, 19. Or disjunct.</margin> Or else they are *disjunct*, or disjointed, residing in separate parts and faculties. They have different strengths and have little or no coordination in harming any common function. They are like *blindness* in the eye and the *gout* in the foot, which have little or nothing to do with each other, except that they are in one body. Similarly, the *gangrene* of heresy and *intemperance* may both exist at once in one soul.

<margin>2 Peter 2:14; Revelation 2:14. Compound.</margin> Sometimes a number of diseases occurring in one part and coupled together will grow into one and become a *compound* sickness. For example, *unbelief, self-love, discontent, and anger* make up the grief of impatience under the *Cross* <note>The "Cross" refers to trials, suffering, or divine discipline.</note>.

<margin>They differ according to the person affected and in their timing and severity.</margin> Sicknesses of the soul exist in the regenerate <note>those spiritually reborn</note> as they do in the unregenerate. In infants and children, they are yet to manifest *in action* <note>original: "actu"</note>, but they currently exist in their *potential seeds* <note>original: "seminary potentia"</note>. Furthermore, they are not the same in all persons, nor are they the same in degree in any one person at all times. They have their own [periods and degrees].

<summary>This text categorizes spiritual ailments into types such as idiopathic, sympathetic, intertwined, and successive, arguing that unlike physical illness, the soul is rarely afflicted by only one "sickness" at a time. The author emphasizes that many spiritual vices are interconnected and must be treated in a specific order for a cure to be effective.</summary>
<keywords>spiritual sickness, soul, idiopathic, sympathetic, repentance, Judas, Apostle Paul, vice, regeneration, moral philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Chapter 1, detailing the progression and origins of "spiritual sicknesses" (sins and mental afflictions). It concludes a discussion on how these maladies surround the soul and begins a detailed analysis of their external and internal causes.</meta>

->## CHAPTER 1: Of Spiritual Sicknesses, <-

[[margin: Application.]] their own beginning, growth, peaks, remissions, pauses, returns, and declines. 
Thus we see how we are surrounded by such a strange conspiracy of ailments, and how strong they are in their combined attacks and invasions. We see how great our care should be to be cured and freed from these troops of more than mortal diseases.

->### The causes of spiritual diseases. <-

[[margin: The causes are either external.]]
[[margin: Objects.]]
[[margin: 1 John 2:16.]]
[[margin: Satan.]]
[[margin: Revelation 12:4.]]
[[margin: God.]] The causes are diverse: some are *external, evident*, and *primary* <note>original: "primitiue"</note>. These include all those external objects in the world that provoke us toward sin: the *lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life*. The devil in his malice works upon our corrupt affections by seducing and poisoning the heart. When he is near, he can seduce like a *serpent* and bite like a *viper*; when he is further off, he can inflict his *narcotic venom* with the *torpedo* <note>original: "Torpedo" — a type of electric ray fish believed in the Renaissance to be able to numb a fisherman through his rod and line</note> through any indirect touch. And even if he were ever so far off, he is that *dragon whose tail drew the third part of the stars out of heaven*. In this, God, in his justice, is a "deficient cause" <note>A theological term meaning God allows evil to happen by withdrawing his protective grace, rather than actively causing the evil himself</note>, deserting whom he will and handing them over to Satan’s hands and to their own wits and wills.

[[margin: Or internal.]]
[[margin: Internals are either antecedent or continent.]]
[[margin: Antecedents are either idiopathical or sympathetical.]]
[[margin: Continent or conjunct causes.]]
[[margin: Romans 6:16, 17.]] Some causes are *internal*, and of those, some are *antecedent* <note>those that come before</note> and some are *continent* <note>those that sustain the disease currently</note>. As for the *antecedents*: some of them are *idiopathic* <note>original: "Idiopatheticke" — a disease arising from within the soul itself</note> and work immediately upon the soul. For example, our native corruption is a most *universal, internal, antecedent* cause of all ailments. Others are *sympathetic*, such as melancholy in the body; through a *sympathy* with the soul, it works upon the mind, corrupts the imagination, deceives the heart, frightens the conscience, and perverts and disturbs the affections.

As for causes that are *continent* and *conjunct* <note>those directly joined to the sickness</note>, they are those most closely adjacent to the sickness itself. Such as that particular and special *giving of ourselves as servants to obey sin unto death*. This is an acquired and embraced corruption,

->## CHAPTER 1: ...and their causes. <-

and impurity joined with the sickness. This happens when (in every particular disease) the soul yields to the yoke, gives place to corruption, and allows wit, reason, and grace to be disordered. Just as bad humors <note>original: "humours" — the four fluids thought to control health and temperament</note> overrule the good in a fever, and the natural internal heat yields to unnatural and external heat, so here the heavenly spark gives place to diabolical flames. The flesh overcomes the Spirit. Just as that "gall of bitterness" and "bond of iniquity" causes disbelief, the vanity of the mind causes *blindness* and *hardness*. Here, one disease is the specific "continent" cause of another. For instance, hardness causes impenitence. Madness of opinion, self-love, and discontent cause the *gangrene of heresy*.

By this we may see that sicknesses are the causes of other sicknesses. This is because: 
1. Previous sicknesses lose the grace of the Holy Spirit and prepare the way for a second. 
2. God punishes the contempt shown to him in a former sickness by inflicting a new one, and by giving the diseased person over to himself and to Satan to be further infected. 
3. There is a short and easy passage from one sickness to another like it: *Sin is drawn by sin* <note>original Latin: "Peccatum peccato trahitur"</note>. Thus, prodigality is a cause of greed, and drunkenness <note>original: "Ebriety"</note> is a cause of lust. 
4. One sickness cannot be contracted without many more. *Avarice is the root of all evils. He that offends in one is guilty of all. Be not drunk with wine, in which is excess.* 
5. Often, to complete the symptom of one sickness, another must be contracted. As *Judas* and *Ahab* in their greed, and *David* in his lust, willingly became malicious: the first against *Christ*, the second against *Naboth*, and the third against *Uriah*.

By this also we are warned to always look to the causes of our evils; to be watchful, wise, and circumspect; as far as possible, to avoid all the occasions of our deadly maladies; to give place to none; and not to neglect the present remedy for any one, lest many more fall upon us, chained one to another.

## The Causes of Spiritual Diseases

The causes are diverse: some are *external, evident*, and *primary*. These include all those external objects in the world that provoke us to sin: the *lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life* <note>1 John 2:16</note>. The devil, in his malice, works upon corrupt affections by seducing and poisoning the heart. When he is near, he can seduce like a serpent and bite like a viper; when he is further off, he can—like the *torpedo fish* <note>original: "Torpedo"; the author refers to the electric ray, believed to numb through touch</note>—inflict his *numbing venom* <note>original: "narcoticke venome"</note> through any indirect touch. And even if he were ever so far off, he is that *dragon whose tail drew the third part of the stars out of heaven* <note>Revelation 12:4</note>. In this, God in His justice is a "deficient" cause, deserting whom He will and handing them over to Satan's hands and to their own wits and wills.

Some causes are *internal*, and of those, some are *antecedent* <note>term: antecedent: occurring before or leading up to the sickness</note> and some *continent* <note>term: continent: the immediate or containing cause of the sickness</note>. As for *antecedents*: some of them are *idiopathic* <note>term: idiopathic: a condition originating within the soul itself, rather than being triggered by something else</note> and work immediately upon the soul. For example, our native corruption is a most *universal, internal, antecedent* cause of all maladies. Others are *sympathetic*, such as melancholy in the body which, through a *sympathy* with the soul, works upon the mind, corrupts the imagination, deceives the heart, frightens the conscience, and perverts and disturbs the affections.

As for causes that are *continent* or *conjoined*, these are those most closely connected to the sickness itself. One such example is the *particular* and *special* act of *giving ourselves as servants to obey sin unto death* <note>Romans 6:16</note>. This is an acquired and embraced corruption...

<margin>Revelation 12:4. God.</margin>

->CHAPTER 1: and their causes.<-

...and impurity joined with the sickness. In every particular disease, the soul yields to the yoke and gives place to corruption; it suffers wit, reason, and grace to be disordered. Just as bad humors <note>term: humors: the fluids in the body—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—believed by early physicians to control health and temperament</note> overrule the good in a fever, and the natural heat of the body yields to unnatural and external heat, so here the heavenly spark gives place to diabolical flames. The flesh overcomes the Spirit. Just as the "gall of bitterness" and "bond of iniquity" cause unbelief, the vanity of the mind causes blindness and hardness of heart. Here, one disease is the specific "containing" cause of another. For instance, hardness of heart causes a lack of repentance. Madness of opinion, self-love, and discontent cause the *gangrene of heresy*.

From this, we can see that sicknesses are the causes of other sicknesses. This happens because:
1. Preceding sicknesses lose the grace of the Holy Spirit and prepare the way for a second illness.
2. God punishes the contempt shown toward Him in a previous sickness by inflicting a new one, giving the diseased person over to himself and to Satan to be further infected.
3. There is a short and easy passage from one sickness to another like it: *Peccatum peccato trahitur* <note>original Latin: "Sin is drawn by sin"</note>. Thus, prodigality <note>term: prodigality: reckless spending or wastefulness</note> is a cause of greed, and drunkenness is a cause of lust.
4. One sickness cannot be contracted without many others. *Avarice is the root of all evils* <note>1 Timothy 6:10</note>. *He who offends in one point is guilty of all* <note>James 2:10</note>. *Do not be drunk with wine, in which there is excess* <note>Ephesians 5:18</note>.
5. Often, to fulfill the symptoms of one sickness, another must be contracted. For example, Judas and Ahab in their greed, and David in his lust, willingly became malicious: the first against Christ, the second against Naboth, and the third against Uriah.

By this, we are also warned to always look to the causes of our evils; to be watchful, wise, and cautious. As much as possible, we should avoid all occasions for our deadly maladies. We should give no ground to them and not neglect the immediate remedy for any one of them, lest many more fall upon us, chained one to another.

-> ### Prognostics. <-

**P**rognostics are signs that declare the outcome of the disease, or what evils and miseries are likely to follow from it: whether it is curable, incurable, or doubtful. They are gathered, partly from the <term>deplorate</term> <note>original: "deplorate"; desperate, hopeless, or beyond remedy</note> essence of the disease; or from the causes, if they are great, malignant, deeply impressed, and strong; or from the lack, contempt, and rejecting of the right remedy; or from the most deadly and dangerous symptoms.

As for example: *The persecution of the godly, proceeding from the malice of the wicked, is a manifest token (as a prognostic) of the righteous judgment of God. Again, God shall send them strong delusions, so that they should believe lies: that all they might be damned who believe not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness. And you, after your hardness and heart that cannot repent, heap up for yourself wrath against the day of wrath and the declaration of the just judgment of God.* And, *“if you were to <term>bray</term> <note>original: "bray"; to crush or grind into powder using a mortar and pestle</note> a fool in a mortar, he will not amend.”* And many more shall be set down for every particular disease.

By this we are taught to see the danger we lie in, and the justly deserved miseries that are due to us for our voluntary sicknesses and contempt of such excellent remedies.

-> ### *That the Diseases of the Soul are Curable* <-

**We** must not think that there is no medicine for souls. *Moral Philosophy* <note>original: Morall Philosophy; the study of ethics and human behavior</note> provides clear testimony to the contrary. And *Divinity* <note>original: Diuinity; theology or the study of God</note> most plainly declares and brings about the fact that we are afflicted with curable illnesses. *David* says, "*Heal my soul.*"

And the Lord heard *Hezekiah* and cured the people. That is to say, by the power of His Spirit, He sanctified them. *A healthy heart is the life of the flesh* (Proverbs 14:30). And, *A joyful heart brings good health, but a sorrowful mind dries up the bones.*

*They have also healed the hurt of the daughter of my people with sweet words, saying, "Peace, peace," when there is no peace.*

*Behold, I will give it health and healing; for I will cure them, and will reveal to them an abundance of peace and truth. I will cleanse them from all their iniquities <term>sins or wrongdoings</term> by which they have sinned against me; yes, I will pardon all their iniquities by which they have sinned against me and by which they have rebelled against me. Christ was sent to heal the broken-hearted, to recover sight for the blind, and to set at liberty those who are bruised.* Our Physician <note>original: Mediciner</note>, coming to us from above and finding us oppressed with such great diseases, applied to us something similar and most like us, and yet something contrary. Being a man, He came to men; but to sinners, He came as a righteous one. He agreed with us in the truth of our nature, but disagreed in the perfection of His justice.

We may comfort ourselves in this: that our infirmities <term>physical or spiritual weaknesses</term> and sicknesses are curable. Therefore, we may be more justly blamed for neglecting, despising, or despairing of the remedy.

-> ### *How the sick soul is to be cured* <-
-> ### *and remedied.* <-

**T**he perfect curing of the diseased body requires both the outward and inward physician. The inward physician is commonly called *Nature*, but more properly, it is our natural liquid of life and the inbred balm of our firmamental spirit <note>original: "firmamentall Spirit," referring to the vital life force believed to connect the human body to the heavens</note>. This, in all men, is the best and greatest physician; without it, no medicine can be useful and no malady can be cured. This is what digests, concocts, matures, deobstructs <note>original: "deopilat," meaning to clear blockages in the body's channels</note>, purges, strengthens <note>original: "corroborat"</note>, expels, mitigates, restores, averts, and dispatches all sorts of bodily ailments—unless injury is done to it by some obstacle, or if it does not receive the proper and convenient service and employment of natural means. The *outward physician*, with all his art, methods, simples <note>medicines made from a single herb or plant</note>, compounds, antidotes, cathartics <note>purgatives</note>, minoratives <note>gentle laxatives</note>, diaphoretics <note>medicines that induce sweating</note>, corroboratives <note>strengthening medicines</note>, and anodynes <note>painkillers</note>, is but a servant; and all his actions are but service to the inward physician of the body.

Even so, the soul cannot be cured without two physicians: the internal and the external. The internal is God in his unity and Trinity, who ordinarily, through outward means, gives to his own the spirit of a sound mind. By this (as by an inward *balsam* of grace), he helps all the diseases of the soul and brings it to a healthy balance. He cures the *hardening of the heart* by taking away the stony heart and giving one of flesh. And he heals *impenitence* by giving repentance to those who were formerly of a contrary mind.

*Christ* is the great physician of our souls. The great physician came from heaven because the sick lay everywhere throughout the whole world. In *Christ* is that *fountain opened for sin and for uncleanness, even a fountain of living water. And by himself, he has made a cleansing <note>original: "purgation"</note> of our sins—and that by his blood, which cleanses us from all sin. In him we have both the bread of life,* and

...and the water of life: both for food <note>original: "meate"</note> and for medicine. He is that tree of Life, which bore twelve kinds of fruits and gives fruit every month; and the leaves of the tree served to heal the Nations. <note>A reference to Revelation 22:2, identifying Christ as the ultimate source of healing.</note>

The Holy Spirit also works <note>original: "concurreth"</note> by sanctification and washing <note>original: "ablution"</note>. *And such were some of you: but you are washed, but you are sanctified, but you are justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God (1 Peter 1:22; 1 Corinthians 6:11).*

The *external Physician* is everyone who has the skill and the calling for it. This might be a person themselves, through their own consideration, meditation, and right application of various remedies to their own heart. Or it may be any other person fit for the purpose. In ancient times, *Philosophers* filled this role; but now among Christians, the fittest man is a true <term>Theologian</term> <note>original: "Theologue"</note>, a "Messenger" or an "Interpreter"—one in a thousand—to declare to a person their righteousness <note>Job 33:23</note>. *But the servant of the Lord must not fight, but must be gentle toward all men, apt to teach, instructing evil men patiently (verse 24). Instructing them with meekness who are contrary-minded, proving if God at any time will give them repentance, so that they may know the truth (verse 25). And that they may come to amendment (or to a sound mind) out of the snare of the devil, who are taken by him at his will (verse 26).* In these words, it plainly appears:

I. The **Patients**, whose sicknesses are *Blindness, Unbelief <note>original: "Incredulity"</note>*, and *Lack of Repentance <note>original: "Impenitency"</note>*. (As follows from verse 25). The cause of their sickness is the *Devil*, by whom they are taken as prisoners. The signs are that they are *evil (verse 24)* and *contrary-minded (verse 25)*. They do the *Devil's will (verse 26)*. The bad outlook <note>original: "prognosticke"</note> is that they are in the *Devil’s snare (verse 26)*.

II. The **Internal Physician** is God, who cures those whom He will, and at whatever time He will (verse 25).

III. The **External Physician** is the servant of the Lord (verse 24). His qualities are his gifts: *Apt to teach.* His calling: the *servant of the Lord*. His wisdom is: *he must not fight, but be gentle toward all men, suffering the evil (verse 24).*

<term>Simples</term> <note>medicines made from a single natural ingredient, usually a herb or plant</note> that come out of the terrestrial ground are fit medicines for the body. But words and sentences which proceed from the grounds of grace or reason are the only best remedies for the soul. Physical simples come from the gross earth and alter the <term>humors</term> <note>the four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—once thought to determine a person's health and temperament</note> of the body. Spiritual simples come from a spiritual fountain, whether divine or human, and alter and cure the motions of the heart. <margin>Proverbs 12:25.</margin> *Heaviness in the heart of a man brings it down, but a good word makes it glad.*

<margin>The remedies are either universal or particular.</margin>
There are both *universal* and particular remedies to be used in the soul's sickness. The *universals* are but few; the particulars for every special malady are many. The particulars serve the *universals*, and when the particulars fail, the *universals* must provide the supply. The *universals* are those which serve to cure almost all diseases. # CHAPTER II.
## 1. Blindness of mind.

> *Revelation 3:17. You do not know that you are blind.*

### Description.

<margin>The mind’s beams, projecting toward all creatures.</margin>
<insert>T</insert>he mind’s speculative beams <note>Original: "speculative beams," referring to the rays of intellectual vision or thought.</note>, projecting and directed toward nature, were once so great, so sure, and so clear that they knew all creatures completely, truly, and distinctly—without exception, error, or confusion. However, in that first ruin <note>The "first ruin" refers to the Fall of Man in the Garden of Eden.</note> and ever since, they have become extremely dimmed. Yet, through research, study, instruction, science, and experience, they are much repaired. 

<margin>Remaining within ourselves.</margin>
But the internal <note>Original: "immanent," meaning inherent or staying within.</note> beams reflected upon ourselves, by which we should behold, contemplate, and study ourselves—which is both great philosophy and a beginning of theology—are far more darkened. 

<margin>Ascending unto God.</margin>
And most of all, those ascending beams that should penetrate toward *God* for humanity's final safety are not only wonderfully weakened so that they cannot reach their highest zenith, and strangely stopped by the interference of so many clouds, but are also so suffocated in the very crystalline humor <term>crystalline humor: traditionally the lens of the eye, used here to describe the essential clarity or "eye" of the mind.</term> of the mind that man has now become darkness itself.

<margin>Matthew 6:23.</margin>
*And if the light that is in the eye is darkness, how great is that darkness?*

<margin>Ignorance of ourselves and of God.</margin>
These two sorts of blindness are two sorts of the most dangerous and deadly forms of ignorance, which are most difficult to help. One is the ignorance of ourselves, which will be handled first; the other is the ignorance of *God*, which follows next.

For example, we do not need to know how many of the smallest branches of veins, nerves, or arteries are spread <note>original: "disseminate"</note> through the body, or how often we have breathed, eaten, or drunk. This type of self-ignorance is not a vice, nor a sin, nor evil; it is tolerable. |

This is an ignorance of mere and simple deprivation; it is a lack of that knowledge that we are born to have, or that should be inherent. Just as rest is a naked and simple deprivation of motion, so we do not know our noble parts nor their use. We do not know the temperament <note>original: "complexion"</note>, humors, and principles of our body. We do not know how the elements are turned into our food <note>original: "aliment"</note>, and how our food is turned into our substance. This type of self-ignorance is miserable; yet it is not a sin, but a part of our misery and a punishment for sin—which we should labor to see repaired in some measure, for our great good and God’s glory. |

This is not a simple and naked deprivation like the former, but a potential deprivation, including a power and disposition toward evil. It is like rot in an apple, which is not only a deprivation of its natural heat but also a tendency toward corruption. <margin>Description of our blindness.</margin>
This blindness of the mind is not only a simple deprivation <note>original: "privation"</note> of the knowledge of ourselves, but also a willful lack of meditation upon ourselves. It is a failure in the calling to employ our thoughts on ourselves so that we might become skillful and impartial judges of ourselves. Because of this, we are most unwilling to call to mind, to consider, to notice—even to feel—and to continually study ourselves.

<margin>Revelation 3:17.</margin>
And even when we are most blind, we still will not acknowledge our blindness. This is an ignorance of ourselves that is both *miserable and abominable*. It is a most fearful 

<margin>Deuteronomy 28:28.</margin>
plague. *The Lord strikes many with madness, and with blindness, and with astonishment of heart.*

->### *Part affected.*<-

<margin>The mind.</margin>
<insert>T</insert>he faculty of the mind is the part affected here; within it, reason, understanding, and judgment are eclipsed. They are both unable and unwilling to reflect their own light—as if by a mirror—so that a man might behold and contemplate himself.

->### *Causes.*<-

<margin>Diverse causes. Cornea. Pupil.</margin>
<insert>A</insert>s among the causes of physical blindness, some are more outward, occurring on the outermost membrane <note>original: "tunicle"</note>; some are more inward, such as those in the pupil <note>original: "sterne"</note> and in the *crystalline lens* <note>original: "crystalline humor"</note>; and some are the most inward of all, such as those in the *optic nerves*, in the *visual spirits*, and in the brain itself. Even so, the causes of our spiritual blindness are sometimes outward and sometimes inward.

<margin>Flattery. *Everyone is a flatterer to himself* <note>original Latin: "Sibi quisque adulator est"</note>: Thales.</margin>
That dangerous and deceiving poison, which enchants the spirit, feeds and entertains a man with his

<margin>Curiosity. <note>original Greek: Πολυπραγμοσυνη (Polypragmosyne) meaning meddlesomeness.</note> <note>original Greek: Αλλοτριοεπισκοπα (Allotrioepiskopa) meaning meddling in the affairs of others.</note> 1 Peter 4:15. <note>original Greek: Αργαι φλυαροι περιεργοι (Argai phlyaroi periergoi) meaning idle, gossiping busybodies.</note> 1 Timothy 5:13, 15. 2 Thessalonians 3:11. 1 Peter 4:15. *You are anxious about the world, and do not care for your own impurity.* <note>original Latin: "Vos de mundo solliciti estis, & vestram ipsorum immunditiem non curatis."</note></margin>
The mind wanders away from itself and loses itself in many external things—whereas only one thing is sufficient and should be done first—and so it falls into that vice of wandering. Many go to admire and know the height of mountains, the raging surges of the sea, the loftiness of hills, the most profound waterfalls, the circumference of the ocean, and the rotating motions of the stars. Yet they are too idle toward themselves: *they learn to go about from house to house; indeed, they are not only idle, but also gossips and busybodies, speaking things which are not proper.* These are those busybodies: busy abroad to know all things, but too idle at home to know themselves. It may be said to them, as Demonax <note>A Greek Cynic philosopher (c. 70–170 AD) who lived in Athens.</note> answered when asked if the world had a soul, or if it was round: *"You are curious about the world, and careless of your own uncleanness,"* bringing the two points together.

<margin>Cares. Matthew 13:22. Luke 21:34. *Gregory in Moralia.*</margin>
Tearing and dividing cares separate the mind from itself and from God: the distrusting and distracting cares of this world and of this life. Choking and oppressing the heart and tyrannizing over the mind, they claim all the thoughts; they permit none to be given to **God**, nor to ourselves. The mind is scattered among many things; it seeks a place where it may rest, and cannot find it. In the visible things that we see, our heart is scattered here and there away from itself; it forgets whatever (of itself and within itself) ought to be done. This happens while it is externally occupied with cares that are too great, too long-lasting, or too premature.

<margin>God. Deuteronomy 28:28. Romans 1:28. Isaiah 6:10. Satan. 2 Corinthians 4:4.</margin>
God in His anger (as a most just punisher, forsaking the sinner) inflicts this blindness as a punishment and causes the eyes to be shut so that they do not see.
Satan, that prince of darkness and god of this world, blinds the mind so that it can see neither itself nor **Christ**.

<margin>Corruption. Of the mind. Memory. Aristotle. Cicero, *Partitiones Oratoriae*. Jeremiah 44:9. James 1:23, 24. Conscience. Genesis 42:21. 1 Timothy 4:2. Heart and affections. Luke 19:14. Reasonings <note>original Greek: Λογισμος (Logismos)</note>. Romans 2:15. 2 Corinthians 10:14. Isaiah 57:20. 2 Peter 2:12. Jude 10.</margin>

That radical, first inbred venom (even the "law in our members" <note>original: "law of our members"; a reference to Romans 7:23 regarding the conflict between sin and God's law</note>), which is further acquired by the daily and habitual contagion of sin and, most of all, hourly spewed in by that tyrannizing Dragon <note>referring to Satan</note>, so perversely affects and infects the mind (being so deprived of light and so depraved with darkness) that it cannot reflect its own beams upon itself. We are so far gone—not only inclined toward sin but declined from good—that our minds can approve us in our worst actions and reprove us in our best.

The Memory (that inward scribe), which should retain, record, revolve, and furnish the mind with material for thought, is so perverted that it will spend itself on anything except ourselves. Because of this, we forget our own wickedness. And if we have considered ourselves for a moment, *we immediately forget what kind of men we were.* <note>A reference to James 1:24 regarding the man who looks in a mirror and forgets his face.</note>

When the conscience is either numbed or seared <note>original: "seared"; likely a reference to 1 Timothy 4:2, where a conscience is "seared with a hot iron," meaning it is insensitive to right and wrong</note>, neither accusing one of sin nor issuing judgment against oneself, a person cannot truly know or rightly judge themselves.

The heart and affections, through a violent *ataxie* <note>original: *Ataxie* (Greek: *ataxia*); meaning disorder, confusion, or a lack of discipline</note>, stage a seditious mutiny and a slavish insurrection against the more noble faculties of the soul, like an insolent people rising up against their sovereign. The mind, memory, conscience, will, and affections do not work together with reason to enable a man to know himself. (The mind does not show him the law; the memory does not show him the facts; the conscience does not show him his sentence; and the affections and will do not move him forward, nor do they cry out, "All this is more than true; and woe to us, we are like *a raging sea*.") Thus, blinded men become *like natural brute beasts, led by sensuality, and born to be captured and destroyed. And whatever things they know naturally as beasts—which are without reason—in those things they corrupt themselves.*

### ->Signs and Symptoms.<-

<margin>He is foolish. Matthew 23:17, 19. Luke 12:20. Titus 1:16. Arrogant. Vain. 2 Samuel 7:23. He forgets himself. Jeremiah 8:6. He foresees no danger. Ezekiel 16:43. His life is evil. James 1:23, 24. Revelation 3:17. Matthew 7:3.</margin>
**H**e who does not know himself is not truly wise; he makes himself a fool at his own expense. He either does not know God, or if he claims to know Him, he denies Him through his actions. He is persistently arrogant. He maintains no modesty, nor does he keep himself within his own station <note>original: "rank"</note>. He undertakes many things that exceed his strength. He never doubts himself, thinking he understands well enough when he actually understands nothing at all.

He forgets himself and loses himself in external matters. He always looks ahead of him; he scatters his wits on vanities and never gathers them back home to himself. He can put his house in order, but not his life or his soul, much like Ahithophel <note>original: "Achitophel," a biblical counselor to King David who famously set his house in order before committing suicide (2 Samuel 17:23).</note>. He does not remember his past passions or his perverse opinions. He is never wary of himself except in the most obvious ways, noticing only glaring and open faults. He deals with himself superficially, partially, and sparingly—either making excuses or never asking, "*What have I done?*" He never considers his natural temperament and leanings. He does not know his own weaknesses and needs. He cannot suppress <term>mortify</term> or control his passions, and he does not care to improve them.

He does not consider the evils he runs into or those that have threatened him. He neither feels nor fears his own troubles, and he seeks no remedies for his miseries. He does not prepare himself for future changes and challenges. He often falls to the ground and tumbles headfirst into the same mistake. He does not lead a disciplined life; all his actions are either bad or trivial. He is a creature of circumstance—a "weathercock" <note>original: "weather-cocke," a person who changes their mind or character frequently based on external conditions like a wind vane.</note>—and his goodness comes only from lucky timing rather than a virtuous character. He is a self-pleaser, saying to himself, "*I am rich and increased with goods, and have need of nothing,*" while in reality, he has nothing at all. He does not consider the beam <note>A metaphor for a large, obvious fault, referencing Matthew 7:3.</note> that is in his own eye.

### ->Prognostics<-
<note>original: "Prognostickes"; in a historical medical context, a prognosis is a forecast of the likely course of a disease. Here, the author uses it to describe the spiritual outlook for a person suffering from "blindness of mind."</note>

[[margin: A dangerous case. Genesis 6:5; Luke 8:14; Revelation 18:7. Resulting sins. John 9:41; 1 Corinthians 11:32; 1 Thessalonians 5:4. A less dangerous case. Grievous distress. Anselm in his Meditations: "No one tries to descend into themselves, no one." <note>original: "Nemo in sese tentat descendere, nemo."</note>]]
**I**f this blindness is long-standing, the hope for a cure is more unlikely. If a person is not freed from it before they die, they shall be harmed by the <term>second death</term> <note>a biblical reference to eternal damnation (Revelation 20:14).</note>. If this condition is constantly accompanied by distracting cares, the abuse of wealth, a lack of instruction, bad examples, <term>curiosity of brain</term> <note>an obsession with trivial or speculative intellectual matters rather than spiritual truth</note>, and daily flattery, the situation is even more desperate.

If it is not helped in time, it degenerates into a lack of repentance, hypocrisy, false security, and hardness of heart. It is a messenger for the "prince of darkness" (the Devil), who delights in dwelling in a dark cabinet where he hatches <term>cockatrice eggs</term> <note>a mythical serpent; here used to represent the hidden beginnings of deadly sins</note> and a nursery of many sins. It deprives a person of God's favor and brings about His judgments, always tending in the end toward desperation and destruction. Because of this, *the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night.*

But if the man who is thus blindfolded accepts a reproof gently and seriously; if he holds the word and servants of God in some reverence and regard; if he is not <term>opinionated</term> <note>original: "opiniotiative"</note> or a lover of himself; if he carries himself civilly and loves moral virtues; if he delights in better company than his own and does not despise others; if he listens to the Word of God when the occasion is offered—then there is some hope for that man. 

But, "Oh, what heavy distress!" said one. <note>referring to Saint Anselm of Canterbury (c. 1033–1109).</note> "If I look into myself, I cannot bear myself. If I do not look into myself, I do not know myself. If I look into myself, my own face terrifies me. If I do not consider myself, my own damnation deceives me. To see myself is an intolerable horror; not to see myself is an intolerable death." It is a rare thing indeed to find a man who sees himself truly.

### ->Curations and remedies.<-

<margin>Difficult to cure. Jeremiah 17:9 and 8:6. Ezekiel 16:2, 43. Avoid the causes, and fear the evil. To know ourselves is commanded. 1 Corinthians 11:31, 32. Know yourself <note>Greek: Γνωθι σεαυτον (Gnōthi seauton)</note>. It must be prayed for. Make a habit of it.</margin>
**T**o make the blinded mind able and willing to see and know itself through its own reflected beams is a task as difficult and rare as misjudging and deceiving ourselves is easy. *The heart is deceitful and wicked above all things: who can know it? No man says, "What have I done?"* Man is a little world <term>microcosm</term>, said the philosophers. Man is the greatest miracle, said Augustine (as he is God's creature). But, as a fallen man, he is the Devil's workmanship; and a man’s tongue is a world of wickedness. *If the tongue is such, what is the whole man?* <note>original Latin: "Si lingua, quid totus?"</note>. To know ourselves, therefore, is a great work and requires a thousand eyes. It is hard to know ourselves, yet it is a blessing.

Shun all the external causes of this blindness, and consider deeply the many great evils that follow it, as can be seen especially among the previously mentioned symptoms and prognostications.

Remember to turn your eyes back upon yourself; it is both God’s counsel and command to *judge yourselves.* The pagans <note>original: "Ethnickes"</note> acknowledged it as an oracle from heaven: *To know ourselves.* Through humble prayer, "buy" a portion of *that eye-salve from that True Light* <note>A reference to Revelation 3:18</note> so that the eyes of your mind may be anointed and you may see. The pagans labored much in this by the light of nature. You are bound to go beyond them by the light of grace.

Begin and acquaint yourself with yourself. Through practice and habit, learn to examine yourself, so that at length you may attain a perfect habit of seeing and knowing yourself thoroughly. Through frequent practice and habit, a child proceeds from creeping to walking, from babbling to speaking, and from messy blotting to perfect writing. Many things are learned through practice and skill <note>original: "Art"</note> that nature does not provide, as is seen in acrobats <note>original: "Tumblers"</note> who perform by walking upon a tightrope <note>original: "cord"</note>. So much more should you, who have the light of nature, and

## -> CHAPTER 2. 1. *Blindness of mind.* <-

...forms, transforming them into your nature to carry them lightly on your celestial wings. Your quickening power <note>original: "quickning"; meaning life-giving power</note> feeds the senses; the senses feed your intellect <note>original: "wit"</note>. Your quickening power would only *be*; the senses would *be*, and *be well*; but the intellect would *be, and be well, and endlessly well*. O <margin>Revelation 1:8</margin> *Soul, go to your highest sublimity and the farthest horizon of your sight*, and let that *Alpha and Omega* <note>The beginning and the end; a title for God</note> dwell within your dimensional limits. With your senses, see His works; with your intellect, know Him; and with your will, choose Him. Always behold His Trinity in the *trinity of your own powers: vegetative, sensitive, and rational.* <note>These refer to the three levels of the soul in Aristotelian philosophy: the vegetative (growth), sensitive (feeling), and rational (reasoning).</note>

The Spirit is a third part of man's person: just as the <margin>The Spirit. Luke 1:47, 1 Thessalonians 5:23, Genesis 2:7.</margin> body is of the earth, the Spirit is of the firmament <note>The "firmament" refers to the heavens or the celestial realm.</note>. This Spirit is <term>extraduce</term> <note>original: "extraduce"; a term from "traducianism," the belief that the soul or spirit is transmitted through biological generation from the parents rather than created anew.</note>, nourished by the subtlest spirits of nourishment and the world's elements. It is the immediate life of the body. It has been given many names among the learned: it is called the *link* <note>original: *vinculum*</note> <margin>*Sidereal spirit. Invisible body. Magnet of the microcosm. Garment of the soul. Magnetic spark of the soul of the world. Link and Vehicle of the soul.* <note>original Latin: *Spiritus sydereus. Corpus invisibile. Magnes micro-cosmi. Vestimentum animae. Animae mundi scintillula magnetica. Vinculum & Vehiculum animae.*</note></margin> because these two extremes—the elementary earthly body and the divine heavenly soul—could not be coupled except by a firmamental Spirit. It partakes of both to join both together. Just as *Christ* is both man and *God*, partaking of both to join God and man together, it is also called the *vehicle* <note>original: *Vehiculum*</note> because it carries all the Soul’s faculties so readily through all parts of the body to all the organs for the speedy discharge of all its functions and actions. For example, in a moment, the skill of a musician playing an instrument is quickly conveyed from the intellect of his brain to the farthest joints of his finger. It has many duties and effects in the body: it is born with the body, sympathizes with the body, and dies with the body; yet it differs from the body in substance and in power.

So, within yourself, observe an *elementary body, a firmamental spirit, and a divine soul—a shadow of the blessed Trinity.* <margin>Shadow of the Trinity.</margin> This is the difference: in us, there are three essences in one person, but with *God*, there are three Persons in one essence.

# C H A P. III.
## The other blindness of mind, *or* ignorance of God.

---

> ### Isaiah 42:19 & 56:10. *Who is blind but my servant?*

---

### Description.

<margin>How far God is to be known.</margin>

Our knowledge cannot comprehend *God* as he is; yet we ought to comprehend him as he has revealed himself to us: partly in his works, and partly in his Word. *Adam* could have known him this way perfectly. But we cannot do it, so great and so gross is our miserable blindness and ignorance of *God*, and of his will and ways in *Christ* for our salvation.

<margin>Holy ignorance. **Romans 11.** **Deuteronomy 29:29.** **Romans 12:3.** <gloss>Unspeakable words <note>original: Ἀρρὴ τα ρηματα (*arrheta rhemata*)</note></gloss> **2 Corinthians 12:4.**</margin>

The ignorance of *God*, in so far as he has obscured and hidden himself from us, is no sin. *As in: Who knows the mind of the Lord? Who knows the moment of Christ's second coming?* This ignorance is of the secrets of *God* and is a "holy ignorance." Secret things belong to *God*, and revealed things to *us*. It is of things that are above, *that which is appropriate to understand*. Such was *Paul's* experience: *his words which cannot be spoken*. We must know all that we need and all that we may; we should think ourselves happy if *God* makes us members of his Court, even if we are not of his counsel <note>A metaphor: being allowed into God's presence as a subject, even if we are not privy to his private plans or "cabinet."</note>.

<margin>Perverse ignorance.</margin>

But the ignorance of *God* (in so far as he has most clearly and carefully revealed himself in his works and Word) is not a simple *nescience* <note>original: "nescience"; meaning: a simple lack of knowledge or awareness</note>, and a general want

of knowledge: Nor a simple privation, or lack of that knowledge in particular, that we should have had. But it is an *ignorance with a perverse disposition*, whereby the mind is not only blinded against God and godliness, but also plainly rebels against the same. There are left since the Fall some notions of God, of good, of evil, of life, of right, of wrong, truth, and falsehood: but they are generally corrupted, maimed, and covered with dross—like carved stones in the heap of a ruined palace, serving only to make us inexcusable.

<margin>It is native and acquired.</margin>
<margin>It grows.</margin>

This perversely disposed ignorance of *God* (in which we are all born, and with which we are corrupted) soon takes to itself increase, strength, and degrees, spreading further like fire. It becomes a compound blindness, made up of the native and acquired; it continues increasing until it passes all bounds.

<margin>Ignorance excusable.</margin>

According to the degrees of this ignorance, so are its specific types. One kind is in part *excusable*; the rest are more *inexcusable. Excusable ignorance* is that which is witless <note>original: "witleffe"; meaning lacking in information or understanding rather than lacking in intelligence.</note>, but not willful; in which the will is deceived and errs only according to the mind's blindness.

<margin>**1 Tim. 1:13.** **Phil. 3:15.** **Acts 17:30.** **John 9:41.**</margin>

Thus *Paul* says: *God had mercy on me, because I did it ignorantly.* And, *If any be imperfect in the faith, they should be borne with.* <note>The author is paraphrasing the sentiment of being patient with those who lack full understanding.</note> *If you are otherwise minded, God will reveal the same to you.* And *the time of this ignorance, God overlooked*—meaning that of the Gentiles. And *If you were blind, you should not have sin.* But mark this: that this simple ignorance is not altogether excusable, since it is our duty to know that which we are ignorant of. But it is excusable in part when compared to willful ignorance, or to sins committed against knowledge. The servant that knows his master's will shall be beaten with many stripes, but he that knows it not shall be beaten with few.

<margin>It excuses not from the whole, but from so much. <note>original Latin: "Excusat non a toto, sed a tanto" — a legal and theological principle meaning it lessens the severity of the guilt rather than removing it entirely.</note> **Luke 12:47.**</margin>

<margin>Ignorance inexcusable and malicious. **Job 21:14.** **2 Pet. 3:5.** **Rom. 1:28.** **Ps. 14:1.** **John 12:4.** **Gen. 6:5.**</margin>

### Parts affected.

<margin>The mind.</margin>

**T**he mind is chiefly affected here, to a greater or lesser degree, and the rest of the <term>faculties</term> <note>original: "faculties"; the powers of the soul, such as the will and emotions</note> follow suit. Through the light of nature, the mind possesses some principles and <gloss>common notions</gloss> <note>original Greek: κοιναὶ έννοιαί (koinai ennoiai)</note> by which *God* may be known. But the *mind* is narrow and weak—like the eye of an owl before the *sun's beams*—and it can only know Him in general, but not in particular.

<margin><gloss>Common notions</gloss> <gloss>Apprehension</gloss> <note>original Greek: Καταληψις (Katalepsis)</note> **Aristotle in Metaphysics.** *Principles known through themselves and unmoving.* <note>original Latin: "Principia per se nota & immota"</note> *In general, but not in particular.* <note>original Latin: "In communi, sed non in particulari"</note> **Acts 14:14. Acts 17:24.**</margin>

For instance, the ideas that *there is a God* and *God is to be worshipped*, etc., are common, obscure, and imperfect principles. The men of Lystra knew there was a *God* by their natural light, but they erred in the specifics because they tried to sacrifice to *Paul* and *Barnabas*. Through reason, the blinded mind may attain this natural vision of *God*, but only with great effort and through many helps and remedies; it is achieved by few and takes a long time to acquire. Even when it is attained, it is mixed with many errors and the *“suppressing of the truth in unrighteousness.”* Thus, without the supernatural remedies of grace to strengthen and perfect it, the mind must remain in darkness.

Through these means, he offers grace to many but does not bestow <note>original: "conferre"</note> it, convicting <note>original: "Conuincing"</note> them because it pleases him; his will is just. God in his wrath not only withholds the light of his grace but also most justly withdraws <note>original: "detracting"</note> the light of nature. He blindfolds the eyes of the ungodly and hardens their hearts *so that they do not see with their eyes and understand with their hearts, which would allow him to convert and heal them.* And as it did not please the *Gentiles* to keep *God* in their knowledge, so God gave them over to a reprobate mind <gloss>original Greek: εἰς ἀδόκιμον νοῦν (eis adokimon noun)</gloss> **Romans 1:18**, so that they might commit things that are not fitting <note>original: "conuenient"</note>.

### ->CHAPTER 3. 2. Blindness of mind.<-

---

[[margin: Harmony of the world.]] ...together. And in the case of *Judas*, after he betrayed *Christ*. Behold the order, progress, and end of all causes: the whole harmony of the *Universe*, where there are so many contrary things, and yet such a harmony exists among them: *All things come from one, and all things lead to one* <note>original Latin: "Omnia ab uno, omnia ad unum"</note>.

[[margin: Predictions.]] Behold the prediction of future things; the strange signs and wonders that have occurred, along with their outcomes, which proclaim a higher power.

[[margin: This appears by the analogy of a ship.]] If you see a well-equipped <note>original: "well-apparelled"</note> ship at sea, coming into her harbor <note>original: "hauen port"</note> and sailing fair before the wind, would you not quickly conclude that there is a Captain <note>original: "Gouernour"</note> inside who guides it? In the same way, you may say, when you behold this beautiful *Universe* with all its decorations and continuous motions, that there is an internal and supreme Mover of it.

[[margin: A Clock.]] If you look into a clock, one wheel is moved by the next wheel; that one is moved by another, and that by yet another, until you reach the weight <note>original: "poize"</note>. Then you must conclude that a Craftsman designed <note>original: "formed"</note> it and made everything move, while he himself remains unmoved.

[[margin: Yourself.]] If you consider yourself, think how the veins from your liver provide nourishment. Your nerves from the brain provide movement. Your arteries from the heart provide your life. In these, you perceive a spirit, and by that, a pulse, which you cannot stop even to save your life. Observe the wonders of your brain, your heart, and your other vital <note>original: "noble"</note> organs—how wonderfully you are made <margin>Psalm 139:14</margin>.

[[margin: A tree.]] Does not the tree your eye sees lead your mind to the root hidden under the earth? Does not a river lead your thoughts to its head and its first springs? And should not *Creatures* lead your mind to the *Creator*?

[[margin: An Indian cottage.]] If you enter *India* and, in some newly discovered part <note>original: "new-found part"</note> there, see a cottage, would you not say, "Here are the footsteps of men"? And who does not see the footsteps of God throughout the whole world? *How excellent is His name throughout all the world!* <margin>Psalm 8:1</margin>.

### ->CHAPTER 3. 2. Blindness of mind.<- | 49

---

It is a fair and seemly thing when a man, by the *inward light* of his mind and the *outward sight* of the world, is drawn to God. But it is a backwards <note>original: "preposterous"</note> way to be led forward by the devil's hand. For example, that governor <note>original: "president"</note> in Sicily <note>original: "Cicilia"</note>, an atheist, believed there was a God only because there was a devil, after he asked his *idol* for an answer to a question he had delivered in a sealed envelope.
<margin>It is a wrong way to know God by the devil. Plutarch, in the treatise *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*.</margin>

Go through every corner of the world, search out all ages, and behold all kingdoms—even the very dens and caves of the most barbarous people, wherever man has lived. <margin>Consent of all.</margin> This universal consent was found among them: that there is a God. This is written and read in every climate; this is engraved and ingrained in man. People in the "New-found Lands" <note>The Americas</note>, though they may be without kings, laws, houses, or clothes, are never found to be without some knowledge of the Godhead. It is so natural for man to know the author of life and the cause of nature. All of antiquity agrees with <note>original: "applauds to"</note> this: the *Indian Brahmins* <note>original: "Brachmanes"</note>, the *Persian Magi*, *Pythagoras*, and *Plato*; and all the most ancient poets—*Orpheus, Homer, Hesiod, Pherecydes, Theognis,* etc.—always begin with *Jupiter* <note>The Roman name for the supreme deity, Zeus</note>.
<margin>The testimony of antiquity.</margin>

That ancient Egyptian, *Trismegistus* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom</note>, calls God the Father of the world, the Creator, the Beginning, the Glory, Nature, the End, Necessity, the Act of all powers, the Power of all acts, the only Holy One, the only Innate One <note>original: "Inbred"</note>, the only Eternal One, the Lord of Eternity, Eternity itself, and the only Author of the World. He is that only and universal "Unnamed One" <note>original: "Innominat"</note> who is above every name. To conclude: He alone is to be praised, He alone is to be called upon, and He alone is to be pleased by sacrifices. *Pythagoras* says God is one, all in all, the life of the *Universe*. *Plato* says, "When I write in earnest, I begin my letter with the one God; when otherwise, I begin with many gods." He calls God "The Being" <note>original Greek: *To on*</note>, and all other things "That which does not truly exist" <note>original Greek: *To me ontos*</note>. He also calls Him "Self-begotten" <note>original Greek: *autophyes*; Latin: *ex se se natum*</note>, as one who most truly exists of Himself and of no other.
<margin>Of Trismegistus. In *Poimandres* 6. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 13. Also in *Asclepius* chapters 1. 6, 7, 11. In *Ascu. sap.* chapters 1. 6 and 7. Of Pythagoras, cited by Cicero, Plutarch, Clement, and Cyril. Of Plato. Plato in Epistle 13 to Dionysius. One God acknowledged.</margin>

Whereas the *Pagans* had many gods, the learned

### ->CHAPTER 3. 2. Blindness of Mind.<-

---

<margin>Polytheism is atheism <note>original Greek: πολυθεοτης εστι αθεοτης (polytheotes esti atheotes)</note>.</margin> [They] did not in their hearts acknowledge them, but only to please the people and the King. To have many gods is to have no God; for the gods of the **Gentiles** were either nobles who were dead, or devils falsely taking on the names of Gods, or else they were stars.

<margin>The Gentiles did not have this knowledge from the Jews.</margin> Whereas it may be said that the **Gentiles** had the knowledge of God from the **Hebrews**, the answer is: 1. The **Jews** did not spread their mysteries of religion among the infidels <note>original: "Infidels," referring here to non-believers or those outside the Jewish faith</note>. 2. The **Ethnics** <note>original: "Ethnickes," meaning pagans or non-Christians</note> mocked the **Jewish** religion.

<margin>God is seen and blessed in his works. Psalm 103:22.</margin> Therefore, say with **Hermes** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom</note>: *Lord, shall I contemplate you in things above, or in things below? You have created all things, and this universal nature is nothing else but your image.* But rather say with **David**: *Bless the Lord, all you his works, and let my soul bless the Lord.*

<margin>The school of nature has three sorts of scholars: 1. Epicureans. 2. Philosophers. 3. Christians. Cicero <note>original: "Cic."</note></margin> The school of the creatures <note>meaning the school of the created world or nature</note> contains three sorts of scholars. 1. Carnal **Epicureans** <note>original: "Epicures"; followers of Epicurus, here used to mean those who pursue only physical pleasure</note>, wallowing sensually among the creatures, feeding themselves like beasts, and are filled with **vanity**. 2. Curious heads, busied in dark and troublesome questions, and are filled with **variety**. 3. Spiritual **Christians**, using the creatures as if they used them not, and are filled with **verity** <note>truth</note>. Be one of this third sort, who both sees God and enjoys him best in the creatures, and can more sensibly perceive what the Orator <note>referring to Cicero</note> could declaim, saying: *The benefits that we use, the light that we enjoy, and the spirit that we breathe, we see they are given and imparted to us by God.*

<margin>Nature teaches only that God exists, but not what he is. Acts 17:23 to 29.</margin> This natural knowledge of God teaches only in general that there is a God. But who he is, and how he should be worshipped, it does not explain. Yet this kind of knowledge is granted to men to draw them to a further and better search for God. As **Paul** said, *As I passed by and beheld your devotions, I found an altar whereon was written,* ***Unto the unknown God***, *whom you then ignorantly worship; him I show unto you: God that made the world, and all things that are therein, etc. That they should*
->*seek*<-

Many people shall come to seek the Lord in Jerusalem, and so on. And shall take hold of the hem of him who is a Jew, and say, We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.* So God always set his Church as a clear, burning, and shining lamp in some prominent and visible kingdom or monarchy.

2. *In his word*, by the lighting up and revealing of that mystery now made manifest. 3. *In his Christ*, the living character of God and the engraved form of his person <note>original: "ingraued forme of his person," referencing the "express image" mentioned in Hebrews 1:3.</note>, through our participation in him.

[[margin: The light of nature leads us toward God or leaves us without excuse. Romans 1:18, 21.]]
Again, this natural knowledge is granted to men so that whoever neglects and despises this guidance <note>original: "manuduction."</note> and instruction <note>original: "Pedagogie," referring to the world acting as a teacher.</note> of the world, and will not be moved to seek God, might be made inexcusable: *Because they did not seek him, and suppressed their light in unrighteousness, and did not glorify him as God.*

[[margin: Scriptural knowledge of God. Psalm 19:1–2.]]
By the light of nature alone, man could never dream of the scriptural knowledge of God, of which no trace <note>original: "liniament."</note> could be found among all created things. For although God is proclaimed to us as God through his creatures throughout the whole world, he is not only revealed that way. He is revealed far more clearly in the Scriptures and declared to be a God *in his Christ* for man's salvation. So both God’s *Works* and his *Word* are two books by which he is made manifest to man. This is the prerogative of the Scriptures: that whatever we know of God through his creatures, we know that same truth about him in the Scriptures—and we also have him clearly revealed and offered to us as a Father in Christ. *No one knows the Son but the Father; neither can any know the Father but the Son, and he to whom the Son will reveal him.* This Scriptural knowledge

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of knowledge, transitioning from knowledge gained strictly through the study of Scripture to a deeper "spiritual knowledge" granted by the Holy Spirit. It contrasts the "shining lamp" of intellectual understanding with the "burning coal" of spiritual fervor.</meta>

### ->CHAPTER 3. 2. Blindness of Mind<-

***

<margin>John 5:39; Acts 8:31; Romans 10:14; Acts 26:18; Romans 2:20. Scriptural knowledge is common even to the wicked.</margin> This knowledge is obtained by searching the Scriptures and by the help of a guide or preacher. It serves to open blinded eyes through a form of knowledge that is common even to the wicked. And when a person possesses nothing more than *natural* and *scriptural knowledge*, he may become a shining lamp but not a burning coal <note>original: "cole"</note>. He may enlighten others, but not inflame himself. He may reveal to others their inward slumber, deadness, darkness, and hardness. Meanwhile, he himself remains within the depths of his soul, which is *darkness* in the abstract—or darkness itself. He is one who cannot see far off <margin>Short-sighted <note>original Greek: μυωπάζων (myōpazōn)</note>. Ephesians 5:8; 2 Peter 1:9.</margin>. This knowledge is only very general; it is merely a form of training <term>pedagogy</term> and a helping hand <term>manuduction</term> toward a more holy and heavenly knowledge that follows.

<margin>Spiritual knowledge of God. Ephesians 1:17; Colossians 1:9; Job 34:32.</margin> Spiritual knowledge of God is that Spirit of revelation, wisdom, and spiritual understanding. Through it, although a person sees no more than what is already in the Scriptures, he sees those same things more clearly and deeply than the Scriptures alone can show him. His enlightened eyes see supernatural truth more deeply than the simple letter of the Scripture can direct him. This is accomplished by the secret illumination of the *Spirit*. And through that *anointing* <margin>1 John 2:27.</margin> which he has received—which dwells within him—the Spirit teaches him all things; this teaching is true and not a lie. He is made truly "taught by God" <margin>Taught by God <note>original Greek: θεοδίδακτοι (theodidaktoi)</note>. 1 Thessalonians 4:9; John 6:45.</margin> and is truly acquainted with the mysteries of salvation. He also knows its dimensions: the breadth, length, depth, and height. He has a glorious and comforting, transforming sight of God's face. His light makes him both <margin>Colossians 1:13; Psalm 4; 2 Corinthians 3:13; Philippians 1.</margin> a shining lamp and a burning coal: he is at once enlightened and inflamed. He decides judiciously and sincerely in all matters of conscience. He does everything with a gracious sense of singleness of mind and sincerity of heart, directing all circumstances toward God’s glory, his own well-being, and the good of others. In moments of perplexity, he holds the most courageous resolutions. In afflictions <margin>Psalm 119:99.</margin> he makes the best use of the greatest evils,

->## CHAPTER IV.<-
---
->## Madness of Mind.<-

<margin>Ecclesiastes 9:3.</margin>
*2 Timothy 3:9. Their madness shall be evident unto all men.*
*2 Peter 2:16. The beast forbade the Prophet’s madness.*
---
### Description.

<insert>(Decorative initial 'T')</insert>
The mind is like a vessel that can never be empty: if it is not filled with the heavenly knowledge of ourselves and of God (the two fountains of true wisdom and happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note>), it is full of strange mad <note>original: "made"</note> imaginations and notions <note>original: "conceits"</note>. From these flow the floods <note>original: "inundations"</note> of all wickedness and vice. For there is no evil that can be either thought or performed <note>original: "wrought"</note> that must not be ascribed to this disease of <margin>Romans 1:27, etc. Titus 3:3. Galatians 3:1. 2 Peter 2:16. 2 Timothy 3:1 and 9.</margin> madness and folly. Just as these high ranks <note>original: "troupes"</note> of impieties of the Gentiles <note>original: "Gentiles"; historically referring to non-Jewish or non-Christian people</note> against God and nature sprang from a mad and foolish heart, and from the fact that men are unwise, so the Galatians' fall flowed from their foolishness. *The dumb beast forbade the Prophet’s madness.* And all the wickedness of men in these *last days* and *perilous times* begins with their madness and is nothing else but its symptoms.

This is not like that madness that results from the body's imbalance <note>original: "distemper"</note> and is cured by natural medicine <note>original: "Phyſike"</note>. Nor is it like the rage of those who are *Tarantati* <note>original: "Tarantat"; those suffering from tarantism, a psychological impulse to dance uncontrollably, once thought to be caused by spider bites</note> and are cured by 

[[page number: 55]]
CHAPTER 4. Madness of Mind.
music. Nor is it like that *Corybantic* fury <note>original: "Corybanticke furie"; a wild, frenzied ritual dance associated with the priests of Cybele</note> of the Vestal Priests, as if they were in an ecstasy. Neither is it like the madness of those demoniacs whom Christ cured, <margin>Mark 5:2.</margin> *Mark 5:2.*

But it is that acquired, impure, and immediate calamity of the mind by which—*through the fabrication and imaginations of man's own heart, which are only evil and that continually*—he runs headlong in error to his endless ruin. If those who run into fires, waters, depths, and dangers to the hazard of their body are considered furious, much more are they to be considered mad who willfully throw themselves into endless dangers by their idle and foolish notions.
<margin>Genesis 6:5 and 8:21. Matthew 15:19.</margin>

The first and immediate work of this madness of mind is an imagined opinion proceeding from the mind, deluded <note>original: "illuded"</note> by the imagination, which the diseased person thinks to be both true and good, even though it is in itself both false and evil, and the vanity of the mind.
<margin>Vain Opinion</margin>

Opinion, as it is always weak and uncertain in its own nature, so in regard to the object it is true or false, and in respect to the effect and end, it is good or evil, wise or foolish. Although an opinion were false, if it tends to no evil, it is less foolish and less to be regarded. For a man to consider his black wife fair makes him loving; to consider himself worse than he is makes him humble; to account all things for the best procures peace for himself: his opinion may be false, but not very foolish. Such opinions and imaginations are not to be cured. But if an opinion is both false and tends toward ill effects and ends—to the offense of himself, of others, or of God—and are the imaginations of *wicked enterprises*, then it is foolish and to be cured, if it is possible.
<margin>Galatians 5:8. Ephesians 4:17. 1 Peter 1:28.</margin>
<margin>Opinion is either true or false, good or evil. True and good. False and good. False and evil.</margin>
<margin>Opinion false and evil, and is either, Proverbs 6:18.</margin>

Some are simply corrupted by themselves or deceived by others, having soft minds like wax that admits any stain <note>original: "stame"</note>, and are like a foolish dove. Some, again, are of a self-conceit, *wiser in their own conceit than seven men who can render a reason.*
<margin>Simple. 2 Peter 2:10. Hosea 7:11. Willful. 2 Peter 2:10.</margin>

The author distinguishes between harmless false opinions and dangerous, willful delusions that lead to sin and ruin.</summary>

->Description.<-

<insert>T</insert>he mind is like a vessel that can never be empty. From these flow the floods of all wickedness and vice. 

For there is no evil that can be either thought or performed that must not be ascribed to this disease of madness and folly. For example, the highest ranks of impieties committed by the Gentiles against God and nature sprang from a mad and foolish heart, and from the fact that men are unwise. <margin>Romans 1:27, etc.; Titus 3:3; Galatians 3:1; 2 Peter 2:16; 2 Timothy 3:1 and 9.</margin> The fall of the Galatians flowed from their foolishness. *The dumb beast forbade the Prophet’s madness.* All the wickedness of men in these last days and perilous times begins with their madness and is nothing else but the symptoms of it.

This is not like that madness which proceeds from the body's physical imbalance <note>original: "distemper"</note> and is cured by natural medicine <note>original: "Phyſike"</note>. Nor is it like the rage of those who are <term>Tarantat</term> <note>original: "Tarantat" - referring to Tarantism, a psychological phenomenon or "dancing mania" popularly believed to be caused by the bite of a tarantula spider.</note> and are cured by music. Nor is it like that <term>Corybantic fury</term> <note>original: "Corybanticke furie" - a wild, frenzied state associated with the Phrygian priests of the goddess Cybele.</note> of the Vestal Priests, as if they were in an ecstasy. Neither is it like the madness of those possessed by demons <note>original: "Demoniacks"</note> whom Christ cured, as seen in *Mark 5:2.* <margin>Mark 5:2.</margin>

But it is that acquired, impure, and immediate calamity of the mind whereby—through the <term>forgery</term> <note>original: "forgery" - in this context, the act of fabricating or creating something false within the mind.</note> and imaginations of man's own heart, which are only evil and that continually—he runs headlong into error to his endless ruin. <margin>Genesis 6:5 and 8:21; Matthew 15:19.</margin> If those who run into fires, waters, depths, and dangers to the hazard of their body are considered furious, how much more are they to be considered mad who willfully throw themselves into endless dangers by their idle and foolish conceits?

The first and immediate work of this madness of mind is an imagined <term>opinion</term>, proceeding from the mind when it is deceived <note>original: "illuded"</note> by the imagination. <margin>Opinion vain; Galatians 5:8; Ephesians 4:17; 1 Peter 1:28.</margin> The diseased person thinks this opinion to be both true and good, when in itself it is both false and evil, and is merely the vanity of the mind.

Opinion, as it is always weak and uncertain in its own nature, is true or false in regard to its object; <margin>Opinion is either true or false, good or evil.</margin> in respect of its effect and end, it is either good or evil, wise or foolish. Even if an opinion were completely false, if it leads to no evil, it is less foolish and less to be disregarded. <margin>True & good.</margin> For a man to consider his "black" wife <note>original: "blacke wife" - in this period, "black" often referred to having dark hair or a swarthy complexion, which was contrasted with the era's "fair" or pale-skinned beauty standard.</note> beautiful <note>original: "faire"</note> makes him content; <margin>False & good.</margin> to consider himself worse than he is makes him humble; to account all things for the best procures peace for himself. In these cases, his opinion may be false, but it is not very foolish. Such opinions and imaginations are not the kind that need to be "cured."

But if an opinion is both false and tends toward evil effects and ends—to the offense of himself, of others, or of God—and if they are the imaginations of *wicked enterprises*, then it is foolish and must be cured, if possible. <margin>False and evil. Opinion false and evil is madness; Proverbs 6:18.</margin>

Some people are simply corrupted by themselves or deceived by others. <margin>Simple; 2 Peter 2:10; Hosea 7:11.</margin> They have soft minds like wax, admitting any stamp, and are like a foolish dove. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Madness of Mind," specifically describing the various ways a stubborn or arrogant intellect can become "brain-sick" and detached from reality.</meta>

[[page number: 56]]
->CHAP. 4.<-
->*Madness of mind.*<-

Usually, men who can provide a reason [for their actions]. The heart flatters itself; the mouth kisses the hand <note>An archaic gesture of self-congratulation or self-worship; see Job 31:27</note>. Having their minds filled with a self-satisfied and arrogant <note>original: "over-weening"</note> opinion, they exclude all opportunity for better information. They are like a vessel full of bad liquid <note>original: "ill liquor"</note>, which admits no **[[margin: Prov. 3:7]]** **[[margin: Rom. 12:16]]** **[[margin: Prov. 26:16]]** **[[margin: Job 31:27]]** **[[margin: Malicious.]]** better. And some are so brain-sick that they go plain mad in their opinion; not only through a weakening of the mind (as the two former types) but through an alienation, corruption, and disturbance of it. With fury, rage, and beast-like irrationality, they will **[[margin: Eccles. 7:23]]** think, reason, debate, and conclude preposterously, falsely, and foolishly within themselves (no matter how great the evils that follow). Such was *Balaam’s madness, which was falsely attributed to Paul.* Those who are thus diseased are like **[[margin: 2 Pet. 2:16]]** *the raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame,* **[[margin: Acts 26:24]]** Jude 1:13.
**[[margin: Jer. 26:26]]** Some are subject to reckless boldness <note>original: "audacious temerity"</note> in defending their imagined opinions, condemning and rejecting everything as false that they do not understand or **[[margin: Pertinacious.]]** like. Of this sort are *Heretics, Sophists, and Pedants*, thinking to themselves that they have a special point of the spirit and know more than the common sort. And so they adopt a frantic folly, rejecting all opinions and sayings but their own.
**[[margin: Devilish.]]** Some are subject to a devilish subtlety, like *Elymas* **[[margin: Acts 13:10]]** *the Sorcerer*, who were inventors of evil. Of this sort are *Arch-* **[[margin: Rom. 1:30]]** *heretics*, devisers of new opinions and foolish, ungodly fashions; and *Schismatics*, from whose own brains come new, internal <note>original: "in-bred"</note> opinions which they most stubbornly <note>original: "pertinaciously"</note> keep as if they were oracles.
**[[margin: Persistent.]]** Some are subject to a poisonous <note>original: "pestilent"</note> mood <note>original: "humor"</note>, ever thirsting for a way and an outlet for their own invincible and obstinate opinion, infecting others so that they may err with them. They are so married to their own opinions (as positive **[[margin: Rev. 2:15, 20]]** and affirmative dogmatists) that they would have all the world ruled by their laws and would tyrannically have all subject to the scepter of their own sayings.
