### Part Affected
The part affected is chiefly the imagination, the immediate seat of opinion; and consequently, the mind is readily <note>original: "haustily," meaning hastily or quickly</note> subject to fantasy and deceived by its own imagination. *If any man seems to himself that he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself in his imagination.*

**[[margin: God deserts.]]**
**[[margin: Gal. 5:8]]**
### Causes
Many are left to themselves to follow the impulse <note>original: "swindge"</note> of their own corruption. God neither restrains nor renews them; indeed, on some, he so revenges himself that because they dishonored him, *he delivers them up to a reprobate mind, to do those things that are not proper.* And because they would not believe, **[[margin: Rom. 1:28]]** *God sends them strong delusions so that they might believe lies.* As the god of this world blinds the minds of the infidels, so he works effectively in the children of disobedience, enticing, helping, and furthering them to devise **[[margin: 2 Thess. 2:11, 12]]** their wickedness and to defend it.
He provoked *David* to his ambitious and arrogant <note>original: "presumptuous"</note> imaginations, to number the people, which afterward **[[margin: 2 Cor. 4:4]]** he confessed, saying, *I have done very foolishly.* He filled **[[margin: Isa. 44:24]]** the heart of *Ananias,* so that he conceived his lying and sacrilegious forgery. He entered into *Judas* and caused him to contrive treason against his Lord. The spirits **[[margin: Satan seduces.]]** of error teach the doctrine of *Devils* and *Satan’s* **[[margin: Eph. 2:2]]** deep secrets.
**[[margin: 1 Chron. 21:7, 8]]** Lack of instruction, and bad instruction, cause a **[[margin: Acts 5:3]]** sworn... <note>The text ends mid-sentence.</note>

| | ...a sworn, obstinate, and prejudiced <note>original: "preiudicate"</note> imagination by which the mind is driven mad. If learning is added (which inflates one's ego), it brings with it audacity, presumption, and sometimes the intellectual weapons to defend that preconceived opinion. *Learning* is a staff that not everyone can handle. If it is used poorly, it makes weak and sickly spirits even more foolish, though it polishes a natural, healthy, and good spirit. The weak spirit is like a weak stomach trying to digest tough meat, or a weak arm trying to wield a heavy staff; it results in *pedantry* <note>original: "Pedantisme"; an excessive or inappropriate display of learning</note> if learning is forced upon it. |
| <margin>Learning.</margin> | |

| <margin>Bad examples.</margin> | The imitation of public habits and customs, accepted superstitions, and bad examples make *the eyes of a fool wander to the ends of the earth* <note>Proverbs 17:24</note>. The well-trodden path easily deceives us; whatever is approved by everyone has a great appearance of being good. We follow examples out of a desire to emulate others because of our tendency to go along with the crowd and our common human weaknesses. Once the first impression is formed, it grows and fastens itself to the mind. Supported by a multitude of believers, witnesses, years of tradition, and authorities, the mind allows itself *to be carried about like a cloud by the wind or a storm* <note>2 Peter 2:17; Jude 12</note>. |

But if the imbalance is hot and dry, it causes a bold and wicked foolishness; one is like fire, the other like water. If, in addition, it is stained by any evil quality, the person's imaginations become even worse. |
| <margin>brain.</margin> | |
| <margin>Proverbs 26:16</margin> | |

He misinterprets everything and makes all things serve his own goals. He defends bad causes, follows his lusts, and flatters wicked people. He biasedly soothes his own mind—which is already tainted and preoccupied with specific prejudices—and lacks any impartiality in judgment. He makes himself prone to wild imaginations and stubborn opinions. |
| <margin>2 Peter 3:9</margin> | |

### ->Treatment and remedies.<-
<note>original: "Curation," meaning the process of curing or healing.</note>

**T**he sowing of the seeds of grace in the minds of youth—so that they may be nourished in the faith by careful instruction and a holy education—serves greatly to avoid this madness. Thus was *Timothy* prepared, <note>original: "preuented," which in this context means guided or anticipated by grace before error could take root.</note> having learned the Holy Scriptures from childhood. When they reach more maturity, they must be nurtured in religion and, if necessary, disciplined by correction. Folly is bound in the heart of a child, but the rod of teaching will drive it away from him. Teach a child the way he should go, and when he is old, he will not depart from it.

*If you have been foolish in lifting yourself up, and if you have thought wickedly, lay your hand upon your mouth.* <note>A reference to Proverbs 30:32, advising silence as a remedy for pride.</note> And hereafter, do not be carried away with the stream and swift river of general madness.

Suspect that which pleases the senses, for sensuality gives birth to many fantasies. Mistrust commonplace notions <term>vulgar conceits: ideas held by the general public or uneducated masses</term> that are protected by public applause and popular custom. Suspect a novelty of opinion as the untimely birth of an idle brain.

Search and examine all opinions that occur. And by a sharp and clear spirit, seek out the motives, causes, natures, effects, and ends—even down to the root. There may be a thousand opinions on one thing, of which only one is true. One truth may be overshadowed by a thousand lies. Truth, like a pearl, may be scattered and covered among heaps of many unnecessary ashes; and like gold, it may lie hidden in the deepest mines. Set your mind at liberty, therefore, and free it from all men's opinions. Let it expand itself in a stately universality to search for the truth in everything—a truth that is not obvious to everyone.

Sever your mind little by little from the world's opinion and (like the stars) walk in a contrary course. <note>An astronomical metaphor: in the early modern period, it was believed that while the heavens rotated one way, the planets ("wandering stars") moved in their own individual, contrary directions.</note> And like a wise traveler, do not choose the fairest path, but the safest.

**Unbelief** <note>original: Incredulity</note> is when a person either does not believe the *truth of the promises of grace in general*, or else does not believe that the *truth and grace belong to himself specifically* and particularly. Unbelief is either *general* or *special*.

<margin>General Unbelief.</margin> **General Unbelief** is when the unbeliever has neither the *cognition* (knowledge), nor *approbation* (approval), nor *appropriation* (personal application) of the truth of grace: that is, when neither his mind nor his heart yield to it, nor believe in it: as was *Paul's* unbelief before his conversion.

<margin>Or special.</margin> **Special Unbelief** is:

<margin>General Unbelief. 1 Timothy 2:3.</margin> 1. When the unbelieving have the knowledge of the truth, but do not approve of it. They *do not receive the love of the truth.* And this is the *historical faith*, or *dead faith*, which is nothing but mere unbelief because the known truth is disdained. It is common to devils, who *believe and tremble.*
<margin>Special Unbelief 1. *Knowledge* <note>original: gnōsis</note>. Romans 2:20 & 1 Corinthians 13:2. Luke 12:47. 2 Thessalonians 2:10. Luke 4:22, 28. James 2:19. John 10:38.</margin>

2. This is that *temporary faith*, which still remains unbelief because although they know and love the truth, they do not make true use of it by applying it to the heart. And this is found in many reprobates <note>reprobates: individuals rejected by God and destined for damnation</note>, who know the Word and account it sweet, like a *Love-song*. They hear it gladly, as *Herod* did, and *Simon Magus*. From this there often proceeds that *gust, or taste of the heavenly gift*: and that *power of the world to come*: without actually possessing it in the heart.

### -> *Cure and remedies.* <-

<margin>Cautions for various <term>infidels</term> <note>In this 17th-century context, "infidels" refers broadly to anyone lacking Christian faith, including Pagans, Jews, or "nominal" Christians.</note>. Acts 17:18, 22, 28; Acts 2:14.</margin>

**I**n the curing of <term>incredulity</term> <note>original: "incredulitie"; meaning a refusal to believe or a state of skepticism regarding religious doctrine.</note>, this caution should be observed: If it is like a *Pagan's* incredulity, you must begin your cure with natural principles, from philosophy and nature. If it is like a *Jew's* incredulity, deal with him at first with principles and grounds from the *Old Testament.* If it is like the incredulity of a *common Christian*, deal with him with grounds from the *Evangelists* <note>The authors of the four Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.</note>. A *Pagan* denies all Scripture. A *Jew* denies the *New Testament.* An *infidel-Christian* denies that the truth and grace of the *New Testament* belongs to himself in particular. A *Pagan* admits only the light of nature, reason, and <term>history</term> <note>original: "stories."</note>. A *Jew* admits only the *Old Testament.* A *Christian* admits the whole Scripture.

<margin>Remedies against general incredulity. Natural and supernatural truth.</margin>

Consider that <term>verity</term> <note>original: "veritie"; meaning truth.</note> is more extensive than nature, sense, and reason can reach. For just as there are natural truths, there are also supernatural truths that are invisible yet credible; reason is not capable of grasping these until they are revealed. But once revealed, reason understands and approves of them—like the eye that sees nothing in darkness, but when the sun has risen and shines, it reveals and manifests all visible things to the eye. Nature and sense are reason's servants, and reason is truth's handmaid. <term>Truth</term> <note>original: "Veritas" (transcribed as "Veritio" in OCR); Latin for truth.</note> enlightens reason, and reason strengthens truth. Reason will not reject faith; rather, reason declares that there are many things beyond reason's capacity and nature's limits, and therefore they are to be believed. You must not say, "This or that is not agreeable to nature, sense, or reason; therefore I will not believe it." For this is to imprison truth within nature, sense, and reason. Therefore, learn to submit...

<margin>Truth compared with sense, nature, and reason.</margin>

<margin>Submit reason to Divine truth. *To be mad with reason* <note>original: "Et cum ratione insanire." This implies the folly of trying to use human logic to explain away divine mysteries.</note>.</margin>

<meta>This page continues a discussion on the relationship between human reason and divine faith, specifically addressing how reason serves as a precursor to belief.</meta>

[[page number: 72]]

### -> CHAP. 5. *The evil heart of Unbelief.* <note>original: Incredulity</note> <-

...reason to truth <note>original: veritie</note>, and that is to believe. You shall find faith to be the end and the farthest horizon of reason.

<margin>Example.</margin>

-> For example. <-
1. *Nature says, nothing can be moved by itself.*
2. *Sense says, the heavens are moved.*
3. *Reason says, therefore they are moved by another.*
4. *Faith says, this "other" is God.* And I believe this just as it is written in the Scriptures, *Psalm 148:6.*

<margin>Romans 1:20.</margin>

The first three above are natural truths; the fourth is a supernatural truth. *For the invisible things of God—that is, his eternal power and divine nature—are seen through the creation of the world, being understood through his works.* <note>This is a paraphrase of Romans 1:20, suggesting that the physical world provides evidence of a Creator.</note>

<margin>Example.</margin>

-> Another example. <-
1. *Nature says, by nature's laws, nothing can be made from nothing.*
2. *History and our senses say that from nothing—and even from opposites—Christ made great things.*
3. *Reason says, he worked therefore by a virtue and power above nature: namely <note>original: viz.</note>, by his divine power or divinity.*
4. *Faith says, I believe he is both God and man, as it is written in Philippians 2:6–7.*

The first is a natural truth; the second is a historical and sensory truth; the third is a truth of reason; the fourth is above all these—a heavenly truth.

<margin>Reason is the unbeliever's <term>pedagogue</term>: as is testimony.</margin>

And consequently, because God cannot lie, it follows that the Scripture of God contains perfect truth. Therefore, all that is written there is to be believed. Against unbelievers <note>original: infidels</note>, reason is to be used as a <term>pedagogue</term> <note>pedagogue: a teacher or tutor who leads a student to a higher level of learning</note> to bring them to the school of faith. Reason, drawing from nature, kindles small sparks which contemplation <note>original: Theorie</note> turns into great flames to give light to faith. Reason and testimonies have great force in persuading unbelievers. Reason is a sufficient witness on its own; a large number of witnesses provides even more compelling reasons.

-> Here <-

Yes, a very strange voice. God shall take hold of you as His own more than you are able, through your desire, to take hold of Him as your own. You need only to will it, and God will come of His own accord.

It knits us to Christ. God will perfect it. It justifies. God will not bruise it, nor quench it <note>an allusion to the "bruised reed" and "smoldering wick" of Isaiah 42:3</note>. Let it proceed from a true certainty to much assurance; from a weak, simple <note>original: "silly"</note> beginning to a most solid, substantial ground of all things hoped for, and a sure defense against all assaults (Rom. 8:33). Let it grow until it overcomes all doubts and convinces all opposing sensuality, fantasy, imagination, worldly knowledge <note>original: "science"</note>, doubting, unbelief, and despair. But faith affirms with a convincing power: "God gives life to the dead; He calls those things that are not as if they were. God is willing, true, and able to perform His promises. I will give glory to God and believe." It is as if he were to say: "God’s Power is above nature; His Wisdom is above reason; His Truth is above my doubting. I am therefore fully assured." <br> In this way, the latter parts—the defects, poverty, and faintness in the race of faith—are completed <note>original: "accomplished"</note>. Even the truest faith (even that *effectual faith*) may be burdened by these faintings and delays until it is helped and cured. |

It grows hard through the drying up of internal moisture, leaving behind sticky and glue-like dregs. These block the passages and shut out the vital spirits <term>vital spirits <note>original: animall spirits; in early medicine, these were believed to be fluids or gases that moved through the nerves to facilitate sensation and movement</note></term>, causing that part of the body to become unfeeling. Likewise, in spiritual hardness, the essence <note>original: liquor</note> of grace, of light, and of reason is dried up. The poisonous dregs of sensuality remain and block every entrance for the heavenly graces of the Spirit, and so the heart remains unfeeling. If any bilious humor <term>bilious humor <note>one of the four "humors" or bodily fluids in ancient medicine, associated with bitterness and anger</note></term> is mixed with this physical hardness, it is called a painful and cancerous scirrhus. Similarly, when God mixes the terrors of conscience with hardness of heart, it is felt in a most horrible and painful way. <br><br> It is also called a stony hardness (referred to by physicians as a *tophos* <note>a gritty deposit, such as those found in gout</note> or a *callosity* <note>a callus</note>). It also signifies a tough, unfeeling hardness, like that white, hard, and dry substance that binds <note>original: conglutinates</note> broken bones back together. It may also be called a sort of abscessed discharge <note>original: apostumate Sanies; "sanies" refers to a thin, foul-smelling discharge from a wound or ulcer</note> and matter, clotted— |

## Chap. 25. ->*Insatiable Avarice.*<-

| [The poor lack] many things, but the avaricious lack everything: He is good to no one, and he is worst to himself. <br> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Gold is his bait for sin and a snare for his soul (1 Timothy 6:9). He has devoured wealth, and he shall vomit it up, for God shall draw it out of his belly. His riches are like a peacock's tail <note>original: "Pauonis cauda"; a traditional symbol of vanity—showy and beautiful to look at, but heavy and a hindrance to flight.</note>. He who trusts in his riches shall fall (Proverbs 11:28). He who oppresses the poor to make himself rich shall come to poverty; his wife and fields shall be given to others. There is a grievous sickness that I have seen under the sun: namely, riches kept by the owner to his own harm. God will strike his hands against his greed; He shall enter into judgment against him (Isaiah 3:14). Woe shall be to those who join house to house and field to field until there is no more room for the poor. Achan <note>A biblical figure executed for stealing forbidden spoils from the city of Jericho (Joshua 7).</note> was burned for a wedge of gold, and Gehazi <note>The servant of the prophet Elisha, cursed with leprosy for deceptively taking gifts from Naaman (2 Kings 5).</note> was made a leper for his sets of garments. What hope does the hypocrite have when he has heaped up riches, if God takes away his soul? <br> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; In his avarice (by which he is tossed to and fro), he seeks death. His money shall perish with him, as it did with Ananias and Sapphira <note>Early Christians who were struck dead for withholding money from the apostles and lying about it (Acts 5).</note>. Achan and Judas met miserable ends because of their greed. Moguntinus <note>A reference to the legend of Hatto, the Archbishop of Mainz (Mentz), who supposedly burned starving peasants in a barn during a famine; he was later chased and eaten by rats in the "Mouse Tower."</note>, that Bishop of Mainz, burned an innumerable company of poor people (who cried to him for help during a famine), calling them a "company of rats." Immediately thereafter, he was visibly plagued with rats for his cruel stinginess <term>original: "parsimony"; here meaning extreme or excessive frugality</term>. This was not because he gave a stone for bread, a serpent for a fish, or a scorpion for an egg—but because he gave fire instead of bread, death instead of life, and most merciless cruelty instead of human pity. Balaam's wages led him astray, and he was snared by the devil (1 Timothy 6:9). <br> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Hermon <note>A character from Greek epigrams noted for being so miserly that he died of grief after dreaming he spent money.</note>, when he merely dreamed that he lost some money, hanged himself out of grief of heart. Dinarcus Phidon, at a certain loss, sought death more cheaply <term>original: "better cheape"; meaning at a lower price or more easily</term> than by the cost of a rope. ### Chapter 26: The Tympany <term>A "tympany" is a medical condition causing swelling or bloating; here it is used metaphorically for the puffed-up nature of pride.</term> of Pride.
---

<margin>Glorious pride. Base pride. Pride under base clothing.</margin>
...is either called glorious, or base. *Socrates*, when he beheld *Antisthenes* the *Cynic* showing to everyone the rift that was in his cloak, said: "Through the cleft of your cloak I behold your vanity." By this, he declared that pride found in the shabbiness of clothes was more filthy than that which comes from more gorgeous apparel.

<margin>Diogenes Laertius, Book 6. Examples of both.</margin>
The pride that is under a sordid <note>original: "sordid habit," meaning filthy or wretched clothing</note> dress is viler than that which is covered with silks. *Plato* was fit and clean in his apparel, but *Diogenes* was filthy; he trampled upon *Plato's* carpets and cushions, saying, "I trample upon *Plato's* pride." To whom *Plato* quickly replied, saying, "You trample indeed upon my pride, but with another pride."

<margin>Pride under humility.</margin>
Marvelously, it happens that the mind of man is more proud of false humility than if he were more openly proud. And that is a most deformed pride that lurks under certain signs of humility. Strangely do filthy vices lurk under the show and shadow of virtue.

<margin>Other examples.</margin>
*Diogenes*, when he saw *Olympias* and her company gorgeously apparelled, said with laughter, "This is but pride." When he saw the *Lacedemonians* <note>The Spartans, known for their austerity.</note> again, sluttishly and basely arrayed, he said, "This is but another pride." *Salacon*, a poor man, was as proud as if he had been most wealthy. *Absalom*, in the midst of his greatest ambition, conspiring against his father and aspiring to his crown, was both humble and humane, and stole the hearts of the people.

<margin>Pride under poverty. *Salaconian pride.* <note>Refers to the proverb of Salacon, a poor man who acted wealthy.</note> Pride under humanity. 2 Samuel 15:5, 6.</margin>

<margin>Arrogancy. <gloss>vanity/emptiness; original: χαυνοτης</gloss> <gloss>vainglory; original: κενοδοξια</gloss> Philippians 2:3. Galatians 5:26.</margin>
Arrogancy is one of the worst sorts of pride, by which a man extols himself vaingloriously above his merit, to be reputed better than he is. It is rightly called a fungosity <note>A spongy, diseased swelling.</note> or a swelling up with wind. He thinks he has the thing that he has not; or if he has it, he thinks he has more of it than he has; or that he has it of himself, or by his own merits; or that he alone has it, or that he is to have it forever.

<margin>Pride against God.</margin>
The highest degree of pride is that which is against God, to oppose him with a high hand, as *Pharaoh* did.

### CHAP. 26. The Swelling of Pride.
<note>original: "Tympany," a medical term for a swelling or bloating of the abdomen, used here as a metaphor for the inflated nature of pride.</note>

---

<margin>a Exod.; Isa. 37:23; Job 15:25. b Isa. 14:13, 14; Dan. 3; Acts 12:12; 2 Thess. 2:4.</margin>
As Pharaoh and Sennacherib did, or to presume to be like God, as Nebuchadnezzar and Herod did. But the Antichrist exceeds all in pride: *Who exalts himself against all that is called God, or that is worshipped; so that he sits as God in the Temple of God, showing himself that he is God.*

Many cannot discern their own pride, much less the pride of others. For there are many who seem to be humble and yet are very proud; and there are many who appear to be proud and yet are truly humble. It shall be most appropriate, therefore, to set down the difference between pride and modesty, and stateliness; and from the contrary extreme, baseness. The chief question concerns honor and reputation <note>original: "estimation"</note>: how far may it be sought, or how far neglected? What is the golden mean, and what are the extremes?

<margin>Differences.</margin>

<margin><gloss>φιλοτιμια</gloss> <note>original Greek: "philōtimia," meaning love of honor.</note> Phil. 4:8. <gloss>Μεγαλοπρεπεια. Μεγαλοψυχια.</gloss> <note>original Greek: "megaloprepeia" (magnificence) and "megalopsychia" (magnanimiy or greatness of soul).</note> Arist. book 2, ch. 7.</margin>
There is a lawful desire for honor: if it is in smaller degrees of honor, it is called *modesty*. If it is in greater and higher degrees, it is called *Magnificence*, or *Magnanimity*, *Stateliness*, or *Nobleness*.

<margin>Pride differs from modesty and honesty. Rom. 12:16; Phil. 2:3; 1 Pet. 5:5.</margin>
*Modesty* is a virtue by which we desire, acquire, and maintain a good name, a competent reputation, or moderate honors—and that both lawfully, appropriately, contentedly, and decently. (Here we take the word *modesty* somewhat more strictly: for that virtue that moderates the appetite for honor.) *Humility* is modesty’s sister, by which we desire no greater honors or reputation than we either deserve or can conveniently have, and when we prefer ourselves to none, but rather make ourselves equal to those of the lower sort. Pride and ambition, as vices in excess, are opposed to modesty. And *Baseness*, or the neglect of fame and appropriate reputation, is likewise contrary to it, in deficiency.

<margin><gloss>Ἀφιλοτιμια.</gloss> <note>original Greek: "aphilotimia," meaning a lack of ambition or indifference to honor.</note> Pride differs from stateliness. Arist. Ethic. book 4, ch. 4. Magnitude animi <note>original Latin: "greatness of spirit."</note> Cic.</margin>
As for *Magnificence* or *Magnanimity*, it is a lawful desire for great honors due to our virtues, together with an honorable acceptance and preservation of them. This virtue requires a mind that is great, and a heart that <insert>is</insert>

<summary>This page defines the "swelling" nature of pride and distinguishes it from the virtues of modesty, humility, and magnanimity (lawful desire for honor). It argues that while pride and ambition are excessive, there is a "golden mean" of seeking appropriate honor based on one's virtues.</summary>

<keywords>pride, modesty, humility, magnanimity, honor, Aristotle, Cicero, Antichrist, vices and virtues</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on human character and virtues, specifically transitioning into a detailed analysis of magnanimity as a counterpoint to pride. It references Aristotle’s Ethics to define the ideal noble character.</meta>

[[page number: 395]]

### CHAPTER 26. *The Swelling <note>original: "Tympany," referring to a bloating or swelling of the body, here used metaphorically</note> of Pride.*
---

...is full of spirit. In this context, the word *Magnanimity* <note>meaning "greatness of soul"</note> is not used (as it sometimes is) to mean *liberality, patience,* or *fortitude*.

Nothing is more similar to pride than this virtue, and yet they are clearly distinguished. For he who is endowed with this virtue seeks honors—great honors, indeed, yet lawful ones. He seeks to be honored by men who are themselves great and, more importantly, good. He does not care about the slanders <note>original: "calumnies"</note> of the unworthy, and he regards being held in high esteem by them just as little. He endeavors to possess all virtues and to be a person of complete and perfected integrity <note>original: "probity"</note>. He is moderate, generous <note>original: "liberal"</note>, content, thankful, just, serious <note>original: "grave"</note>, and kind <note>original: "sweet"</note>. He is slow to begin an undertaking but deliberate <note>original: "flower," likely a transcription error for "slower"</note> in carrying it out. He is strong in both good and bad fortune, bold in dangers, and open in declaring both his love and his hatred.

<margin>The properties of true dignity <note>original: "stateliness"</note> and magnanimity.</margin>

<margin>[[gloss: Nobility and goodness <note>original Greek: Καλογαθια</note>]] [[gloss: One who faces great dangers <note>original Greek: Μεγαλοκινδυνος</note>]] Aristotle's *Ethics*.</margin>

He is neither vengeful <note>original: "vindictive"</note>, nor a hypocrite <note>original: "dissembler"</note>, nor irritable <note>original: "bilious"</note>, nor a flatterer. He is not overly meddlesome <note>original: "busy"</note>, nor an excessive admirer of others, and he envies no one. His pace is slow, and his voice is deep <note>original: "grave"</note>, steady, quiet, and consistent. His temperament is a perfect mixture of blood and melancholy <note>referring to the "humors," or bodily fluids thought to determine personality</note>, without any irritable or sluggish <note>original: "bilious or phlegmatic"</note> dominance. It is a very difficult virtue, which can easily degenerate into pride. It agrees very well with Christian humility; the very same man may be both politically dignified and Christianly humble. A man may magnificently uphold the dignity of his honorable position (especially in the office of a judge or official <note>original: "Magistrate"</note>), and yet before God and his own conscience, he may be lowly, cast down, and humbled, and may "lick the dust" in His presence. He may most humbly mourn <note>original: "deplore"</note> his sins and acknowledge himself to be nothing but earth and a most miserable worm, rather than a man. Opposed to this noble virtue, in excess, is ambition or pride—by which we judge ourselves more worthy of honor than we actually are. And opposed to it in deficiency is baseness and the neglect of one's reputation <note>original: "estimation"</note>, as has been said.

<margin>[[gloss: Vanity <note>original Greek: χαυνοτης</note>]] Pride <note>original Latin: *Fastus*</note> [[gloss: Meanness or pettiness <note>original Greek: Μικροπρεπεια</note>]] Baseness.</margin>

### CHAPTER 26. *The Swelling <term>original: "Tympany"; a medical term for a swelling or bloating of the body</term> of Pride.*

---

#### Part affected.

<margin>Desire. 1 John 2:16. Pride is composed of six other emotions <note>original: "affections"</note>.</margin>
**P**ride has the emotion of desire as its primary location. As the scripture says: *For all that is in this world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life.* But because pride is a complex evil, it also takes over other emotions. For a person who is proud and ambitious both hates and fears being seen as lowly. He is envious if others match his status, and he is jealous of everyone. Likewise, he rejoices in the focus and direction of his pride. He hopes and trusts confidently that he will reach his highest peak. To this goal, he has addicted both his heart and his mind like a slave: the heart to devise and approve of all he does or intends, and the mind to choose those actions.

#### Causes.

<margin>God. Satan.</margin>
**T**he two universal and external causes of pride (which are common to all other sicknesses of the soul) are God and Satan. God is a most just "deficient cause" <note>A theological term meaning God allows evil to happen by withdrawing His grace</note>, leaving many to themselves. The other cause is Satan, whose own first sin was pride; therefore, he never stops infecting everyone with that same poison.

<margin>Prosperity. Isaiah 9:9–10. Isaiah 28:1, 3. Hosea 13:6. Psalm 30:6–7. Augustine, Sermon 31. A vice common to prosperous times <note>original Latin: "Vitium rebus solemne secundis"</note>. Claudian, *On Stilicho's Consulship*, Book 2.</margin>
Prosperity advances pride, and pride feeds upon prosperity so that it may become even prouder. The people of *Ephraim* and *Samaria*, in the pride and arrogance of their hearts, said: *The bricks have fallen, but we will rebuild with cut stones.* The "drunkenness" of Ephraim in its prosperity gave birth to the crown of pride. *They were filled, and their hearts were exalted.* In my prosperity, David said, *I shall never be moved.* Pride is the worm that is born from riches; it is difficult for a rich man not to be proud, as pride is the natural vice of prosperity. When the heart is lifted up to its full height (Ezekiel 31:10), an arrogant hope that prosperity will last forever exalts that pride (Isaiah 47:7). If beauty, strength, or any gifts of nature or skill <note>original: "Arts"</note> coincide, pride raises itself even higher.

<insert>Many</insert>

<summary>This chapter defines pride as a "swelling" of the soul rooted in desire and identifies its primary causes as the withdrawal of divine grace, the influence of Satan, and the temptations of worldly prosperity.</summary>

### CHAP. 26. *The Swelling of Pride.*
<note>original: "Tympany," a medical term for a swelling or bloating of the abdomen, used here as a metaphor for vanity.</note>

---

<margin>Comparing with others.</margin>
Many people compare themselves with others whom they consider worse than themselves, just as the proud Pharisee did with the humble Publican <note>A reference to the parable in Luke 18:9–14, where a religious leader looks down on a tax collector.</note>. He thinks himself superior to another, whereas the other may be superior to him in many ways. He is not careful to notice what he lacks, but only what he has, and he triumphs over it as if no one else could match him. He is ignorant of his neighbor, but far more ignorant of himself.

<margin>Madness of mind and opinion. <gloss>Thinking oneself to be something, when one is nothing. <note>original: Δοκεῖν εἶναί τι, μηδὲν ὤν</note></gloss> Galatians 6:3; 1 Timothy 3:6; 1 Corinthians 8:1.</margin>
Opinion brings forth pride; great ambition proceeds from the opinion of an evil man. To appear to yourself to be "somebody" is the foundation of pride. Self-love and complacency deceive many, making them imagine <note>original: "conceit"</note> more and better of themselves than they truly are, and to be greater in their own eyes than in the eyes of God or man. A young scholar is easily puffed up. The spring of all pride is a lie, gilded over with the appearance of truth. Ambition, like a crafty serpent, creeps into the mind through a small hole; its mother is presumption. We imagine we have the virtues we lack, or we think we have them in a greater measure than they actually are. From this are born Pride’s two daughters: **Ostentation** before others (through writing, gestures, clothing, and when we speak too much good of ourselves) and **Vainglory** <note>original: "gloriation"</note> within ourselves.

<margin><gloss>Boastfulness. <note>original: Ἀλαζονεια (Alazoneia)</note></gloss> <gloss>Evil boasting. <note>original: Καυχησις πονηρα (Kauchesis ponera)</note></gloss> James 4:16.</margin>

<margin>Native corruption. Erasmus, *Apophthegmatum*. Mark 7:21, 22; 2 Corinthians 12:7; Psalm 30:6, 7.</margin>
Native corruption <note>The inherent human tendency toward sin.</note> is the most immediate and connected cause of pride. It was the first sin in heaven <note>The fall of Lucifer.</note>, and the first sin in Paradise <note>The Fall of Man.</note>, and the first sin that springs up within us. Even the greatest moral philosopher cannot be free from it. Socrates, disdaining to receive the magnificent gifts of the proud Alcibiades, said, "He sends these gifts ambitiously, and it is our own ambition to refuse them." Thus, everyone has their own inbred pride. Christ said, *From within, even out of the heart, proceeds pride.* Even the Saints are hardly free of it; from this comes the pride in doing good things, which blots the face of innocence and stains it with secret hypocrisy.

CHAPTER 26. The <term>Tympany</term> <note>original: "Tympany," meaning a morbid swelling or inflation of the body; here used metaphorically for the "swelling" of pride.</note> of Pride. 403

...find there his lands in the territory of Athens. He answered that they were not recorded there. "How is it then," said he, "that you are proud of that which is in no part of the world?" <margin>Psalm 62:10</margin> If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them, nor let your heart be exalted. <margin>Cicero, *De Oratore*</margin> In the gifts of Fortune, it is a great praise not to be puffed up. In your flourishing youth, the flower is withering even while you are speaking.

Do not say that you are wise; if you were wise, you would never say that you are wise. <margin>Psalm 73:20 and 102:11. Seneca, *Thyestes*: "A short hour changes the highest things for the lowest. The man whom the morning saw proud, the evening saw lying low." 1 Corinthians 4:7. Psalm 75:5. Job 11:12. 1 John 2:17.</margin> If you are in a position of honor, remember you are but the dream of a shadow.

A short hour will make the highest things the lowest. The man that the day saw rising up so proud, that same day shall see him lying down as low. You have nothing of yourself, but all from Him who has as much power to take as to give. The best and wisest person is like a wild donkey's colt, without wit, until it is taught. If you have received <note>The author references 1 Corinthians 4:7: "What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast...?"</note> [your gifts], why do you boast? All those things are common even to the most unworthy, and they are ebbing and flowing, easily lost. They are given not to be boasted of, but to provoke you to a better life, not a worse one.

Keep your death and misery in perfect remembrance. <margin>Remember death. "After man comes the worm; after the worm, stench and horror. Thus every man is turned into a non-man." Where are all those things? Where are all those people? Chrysostom. Isaiah 66:24.</margin> While we are living, we are but so many images or shadows. The earth nourishes nothing more miserable than man. Behold the graves of those who are dead, and see if you can see their ornaments, honors, joys, or banqueting pleasures. &nbsp;

# CHAP. XXVII.
# The passion of Joy.

&nbsp;

Proverbs 14:13. *Even in laughing the heart is sorrowful, and the end of that mirth is heaviness.*

&nbsp;

### Description.

&nbsp;

<margin>Etymology: *Chara* [joy] because of the diffusion and flowing of the soul; it comes from the words "to pour" and "to flow." <note>original: $\chi\alpha\rho\alpha$ $ob$ $\tau\eta\nu$ $\delta\iota\alpha\chi\upsilon\sigma\iota\nu$ $\kappa\alpha\iota$ $\rho\upsilon\sigma\iota\nu$ $\tau\eta\varsigma$ $\psi\upsilon\chi\eta\varsigma.$ $fit$ $ex$ $\chi\epsilon\omega$ & $\rho\epsilon\omega.$</note></margin> In joy, the heart, in a sense, runs out; and through the enlarged passages, the vital spirits <term>original: "cordial spirits," referring to the "spirits" or vapors believed to reside in the heart and animate the body</term> are poured out. Because of this, a sudden stunned shock and even death often follow. <note>In the medical theory of the time, it was believed that sudden, intense joy could cause the heart's heat and spirits to rush outward too quickly, leaving the heart cold and potentially causing fatal heart failure.</note>

<margin>Description. 2 Cor. 6:11. Psalm 89:16.</margin> Joy is an emotion of the heart, arising from the belief that some good is either present or coming in the future. In all joy, the heart is enlarged and lifted up.

<margin>Joy internal and external. <gloss>chara</gloss> <gloss>epichairekakia</gloss> <gloss>epichairekakia</gloss> Job 31:29.</margin> Joy is either internal and hidden, which does not show; or else it is external, appearing in one's gestures, expression, laughter, or in some other way. Furthermore, joy is distinguished according to the variety of its object. It is either for some good happening to ourselves, or for some good happening to our friends, or for some evil happening to our enemies <term>original Greek: $\epsilon\pi\iota\chi\alpha\iota\rho\epsilon\kappa\alpha\kappa\iota\alpha$ (epichairekakia), often translated as schadenfreude.</term>

<margin>Joy natural and spiritual. Psalm 4:6, 7. 1 Cor. 3:21. Luke 10:20.</margin> Joy, regarding those who rejoice and their manner of rejoicing, is either natural or spiritual. Natural joy is common and is either lawful or unlawful. Unlawful joys are either those that arise only from the pleasure of God's gifts, or from the pleasure of sin. Joy arising from God's gifts—such as food and drink, men or women, the subjection of spirits, the destruction of our enemies, or pleasures—

->### Cure and Remedies.<-

**T**here is nothing so fitting to banish sinful joy, and to [[margin: Spiritual joy,]] temper all immoderate, natural, and sensual joys, as is that *spiritual joy* which comes from God (Rom. 15:13; 2 Cor. [[margin: Which is of God.]] 1:3; Isa. 9:3), worked in the heart by the Spirit (Rom. 14:17; 1 Thess. 5:16 & 1:6; John 15:26). It is belonging <note>original: 'Proper'</note> to those who seek the Lord (Psal. 105:3) and are upright in heart (Psal. 32:11), who rejoice with trembling (Psal. 2:11), and whose joy is furthered by the help of the ministry (2 Cor. 1:24). It is joined with peace in believing (Rom. 15:13). The Kingdom of God consists not of food or drink, but of righteousness, peace, and in this joy of the Holy Spirit (Rom. 14:17), in those who rejoice in serving God (Coloss. 1:11).

This spiritual joy must be centered on those things that pertain [[margin: In godly things]] to God (Rom. 15:17). Such as in God's holy name (Psal. 105:3; Isa. 61:10; Phil. 4:4). In His mercy (Psal. 32:10, 11 & 31:7 & 89:16). Through Christ, for the receiving of the [[margin: In Christ.]] ->reconciliation<- <note>original: 'atonement'</note>

-># CHAPTER XXVIII.<-
->## The Passion of Gluttony.<-

->*Philippians 3:19. Whose God is their belly.*<-

---

->### Description.<-

**H**uman appetite is threefold. 1. Natural: <margin>Appetite is threefold: Natural and Animal.</margin> shared with plants, through which it unconsciously draws nourishment. 2. Animal: shared with brute beasts, centered in the brain and spread to other parts; it feels a conscious desire for what it needs. 3. Rational: <margin>Rational.</margin> and unique to humans, desiring those things that are agreeable to reason; this is properly called *Voluntas* <note>Latin: "the Will"</note>, whereas the others may be called *concupiscence* <note>original: "concupiscence" (strong physical desire)</note> or *voluptas* <note>Latin: "pleasure"</note>.

The desire for food is either more natural and common—in which few fail except by eating too much—or the desire for food is more specific and acquired <note>original: "ascititious" (supplemental or not inherent)</note>, <margin><gloss>Natural desire.</gloss> Common desire. Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book 3, Chapter 11. <gloss>Gluttons.</gloss> Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book 3, Chapter 11. Specific desire. <gloss>Lovers of specific things.</gloss></margin> and more strangely provoked. For example, some are lovers of very specific things which they seek out and delight in, even though they are not necessary, or they desire them more than others do, or not in the way they should, or not for the right purpose. In this case, there is an excess—not so much in the quantity of the food, but an excess in the quality, or rather the perversity, of an empty appetite.

Gluttony is an unrestrained desire for food that goes <margin>Description of gluttony.</margin> beyond the limits of nature, whether it is for too great a quantity—"banquets sought without end" <note>Latin: *Epulae sine fine petitae*</note>—or for a vain variety. <margin>Horace, *Satires* (Sermonum), Book 2, Satire 7.</margin>

->[Continued] under<-

| If the physical <note>original: "mechanicke"</note> spirits of the stomach are too plentiful, they help create this passion. All our spirits—natural, vital, and animal (whether they are fixed or wandering and running at random)—eat up and consume our natural bodily heat <note>original: "firmamentall heate"</note>. This heat, in turn, wastes our innate moisture <note>original: "primogeniall humidity"</note>, and this moisture feeds upon the whole body. From this exhaustion <note>original: "exinanition"</note> and emptiness comes natural hunger and the desire for food. The lamp of life consumes the best sap and finest oil of our body. Just as a burning flame consumes a candle, life soon comes to an end if it is not supplied with more fuel. Through this natural and unnoticed <note>original: "insensible"</note> hunger, the veins suck from the stomach until it is empty; from emptiness comes a physical sensation, and from that sensation comes a desire to be filled <note>original: "repletion"</note>, which gives rise to animal and conscious <note>original: "sensible"</note> hunger. To make this hunger more noticeable—nature goads humans to nourish and preserve themselves—the stomach is supplied with a natural, sharp, and acidic <note>original: "vitriolate"</note> fluid (which some call melancholic). This fluid pricks, pinches, and, as it were, nips at the opening of the stomach <note>original: "ventricle"</note>, which creates a stronger sense of hungry appetite. If these two kinds of hunger, along with this fluid, are excessive or become too distorted, and if the imagination is strong while the wit is weak and the heart lacks reason and grace, then the entire soul is affected by this animalistic <note>original: "brutish"</note> passion. As for those cases where the stomach's function is impaired by excessive draining <note>original: "exfuction"</note> due to some unhealthy fluid (which leads to disease), they are to be excused because they are involuntary. In such cases, the soul is not enslaved by the passion, and they should be treated medically <note>original: "physically"</note>. | <margin>Natural hunger. Animal hunger. -> ## *Healing and Remedies.* <-

| <margin>Follow nature.</margin> | Nature teaches moderation. It has given man a small mouth and a narrow throat; it is a shame to him that neither earth, nor sea, nor heaven can satisfy it. And although the belly listens to no instructions—being like an unthankful beast that always craves and seeks—it is not a demanding creditor. It will be content with little if you give it what you should, rather than all that you could. Satisfy nature, but do not overfeed it. As *Socrates* said to his friends at his modest supper: "If you are virtuous, this will be enough; if not, you are unworthy of it." You should eat only enough so that your strength is refreshed, not overwhelmed. You must eat to live, not live to eat. Satisfy your body only as far as is necessary for health. |
| :--- | :--- |
| <margin>Seneca.</margin> | |
| <margin>One must eat to live, not live to eat. <note>original: "Esse oportet ut vivas: non vivere ut edas." Cicero, Rhetorica ad Herennium, Book 4.</note></margin> | |
| <margin>Christian abstinence and the motives for it. He who eats that bread is not concerned with how expensive the meat is that he eventually turns into waste. Yet, just as eating should be moderate, so should abstinence. It is necessary to restrain your flesh, not to destroy it; to repress it, not to crush it—so that it may serve you and not be wild, and that it may be humbled rather than being the commander. Let the flesh be subject to the soul, and the soul to God. Let God command your reason; let reason command your soul; and let your soul command your body. Treat your soul like a King and your body like a donkey: give it enough food so that it does not faint, and give it a burden <margin>Isaiah 58:8.</margin> <margin>Jerome in his Letter to Paulinus. <note>original: "Hieron. in Epist. ad Paulinum."</note></margin> |

### CHAPTER 29. *The Passion of Drunkenness.*
---

[[margin: A graceless heart.]] A graceless heart, turning the grace of God into wantonness <note>original: "wantonneſſe"; meaning lack of restraint or lewdness</note> and having a feeble and weak mind, allows sensuality to reign over reason and grace (Galatians 5:23; Jude 19, compared with verses 12, 16, 18). Such a person has a corrupt and unsettled mind (1 Peter 4:2, 3 and 2:10, 12), filled with a false idea of pleasure (2 Peter 2:13), and with foolishness (Ephesians 5:15, 17, 18; 1 Thessalonians 5:7). They suffer from a brutish and senseless blindness, like swine fed for the slaughterhouse <term>original: "shambles"; a place where animals are slaughtered or meat is sold</term>.

[[margin: Excuses.]] Drunkards—insane in their foolish vanity—invent imaginary excuses for themselves, thinking it is lawful to drink as much as they please, provided they are not "overcome" by it. They do not consider that those who are "strong" at consuming [[margin: Isaiah 5:22; Ecclesiastes 10:17; Plutarch.]] strong drink are cursed, or those who drink simply for the sake of drinking, or who are too frequent at drinking sessions. As Demosthenes said to King Philip, these people are "sponges" who desire only a belly as large as their unrestrained will so they might exceed the capacity of a barrel; in "overcoming" others in drinking, they are themselves overcome. Some, again, think that drink is given by God not only for necessity but also for delight, and believe they may therefore exceed moderation as they please. They do not consider that strong [[margin: Hosea 2:15. Drunkenness is not medicinal.]] drink was given to man to cheer the heart, not to oppress it—and to praise God for, not to offend Him. Some even pretend that drunkenness is medicinal <note>original: "phyſicall"; in this era, "physical" often referred to the practice of medicine or "physic"</note>. In this they err foolishly, believing the cause of a hundred sicknesses to be the cure for one, and the poison of [[margin: When the medicine is shameful, one should be ashamed to be cured. <note>original: "cùm turpis est medicina, ſanari pudeat"</note>]] the soul to be good medicine for the body. No physician of the body will recommend it, and no physician of the spirit will allow it.

-> #### Signs and Symptoms. <-

[[margin: The character of a drunkard.]] **A** drunkard is like a leech that continues to suck and cannot be satisfied. His delight is in that wine which best satisfies all five senses, according to the word *Costa* <note>The word "Costa" was likely used here as a mnemonic for the sensory qualities of wine (such as Color, Odor, Sapor/Taste, etc.).</note>. When his natural appetite fails, he resorts to artificial tricks and skills to continue.

### CHAPTER 29. *The Passion of Drunkenness.* [[page number: 429]]
---

To natural corruption, he joins artificial impiety; when necessity is satisfied, insolence <note>original: "insolency"</note> salts his appetite.

Anger is a madness, brief and involuntary; but this <note>drunkenness</note> is both customary and voluntary, and an insatiable evil. <margin>Seneca, Epistle 82. Aulus Gellius, book 19, chapter 20.</margin> *Philoxenus* wished for a crane's neck <note>original: "crag"</note>, and *Melanthius* for a swan's neck three cubits long <note>A cubit is approximately 18 inches; three cubits is roughly four and a half feet.</note>, so that they might, by <margin>Erasmus in his *Similes*. The life of frogs. He lives by sucking. Bruschius, book 1, chapter 19, from Vopiscus.</margin> the longer passage, enjoy the pleasure of their drink more. Frogs love to live in marshy <note>original: "moorish"</note> places, but the drunkard lives in pots; like flies, he lives by sucking, and wine is the mirror of his mind. He is like *Bonosus*, of whom *Aurelianus* said he was born not to live, but to drink.

He drinks for delight, for company, for bravado <note>original: "bravery," meaning a display of boldness</note>, for competition, and out of a burning affection <note>original: "inflamed charity"</note> for absent friends. His belly is his god (Philippians 3:19), making him unfit for the service of the High God. He abuses God's creatures <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to created things like food and drink.</note>, <margin>1 Thessalonians 5:7.</margin> shames himself, and makes himself capable of sinning. When he should mourn, he is merry, saying, "Tomorrow we shall die." <margin>Isaiah 22:12-13.</margin> He drinks wine from bowls when he should be sorrowful for the <margin>Amos 6:6.</margin> affliction of *Joseph* <note>A biblical reference to those who live in luxury while remaining indifferent to the suffering of others.</note>.

He can rule neither himself nor others, for wine so completely banishes his wit. A poor woman once appealed from the judgment of a drunken King *Philip* to that of a sober King *Philip*. <margin>Plutarch, *Apothegms* (sayings).</margin> Just as drink makes his body feel lighter, it also makes his mind and his tongue more loose <note>original: "voluble"</note>. Like that drunken critic who spoke against King *Pyrrhus* and said, "We said all that we are accused of, and we intended to say much more, if only our wine had not run out."

He is a disturber of peace, a devourer of good things, a corrupter of morals, and a pest to the granaries <note>original: "vermine to Garners"</note>.

His wit, foot, and hand shake as if with the palsy. His belly buries his drink, and his drink buries his wit. He is swallowed <margin>Augustine, *Book on Penance*. Isaiah 28:7.</margin> up by wine. Even his weakest enemy may overtake him; he is like a drunken Trojan <note>A reference to the fall of Troy while the inhabitants were sleeping and drunk.</note>. He disgraces his profession and <margin>"They invade the city [buried in sleep and wine]..." original: *Inuadunt urbem, etc.* Virgil, *Aeneid*, book 2. Isaiah 28:7.</margin> disqualifies himself from his calling; he stumbles in judgment; nothing is left of a man but his physical shape. He is like a beast because his understanding is gone, and he is worse than a beast because he can no longer stand.

### CHAPTER 29. *The Passion of Drunkenness.*
---

<margin>A mad secret, etc. Virgil, *On Wine and Love*. Drinking much, etc. Isaiah 28:7, 8.</margin> He is proud, furious, passionate, vain, foolish, quarrelsome, offensive, a ranter, and a revealer of secrets. And as it was written of the drunken *Timocreon* <note>original: Timocreon of Rhodes, a Greek poet known for his gluttony and drinking</note>, so the same may be said of him: he scowls and scolds; he plays the tyrant or the fool, the lion or the ape. His table is full of vomit, no place is clean; what can be more filthy? He stumbles, being swallowed up by wine.

He is dizzy and palsied, with a bright red nose <note>original: brazell nose; likely referring to the red color of brazilwood dye</note>, an inflamed face, and reeling eyes. He has stinking breath, staggering legs, and a stammering tongue set loose, resembling *Bacchus* <note>The Roman god of wine</note> in his role as *Liber Pater* <note>Latin: "Free Father," an epithet for Bacchus, here punning on the "liberty" or lack of restraint wine gives the tongue</note>. His tongue goes like the sail of a windmill. He swears, curses, and is shameless; he even makes songs mocking the godly (Psalm 69:12).

-> #### Prognostics <note>Signs or predictions regarding the course of a condition</note>. <-

<margin>The drunkard’s case. Isaiah 5:11, 12.</margin> **T**HE drunkard is cured with difficulty; he finds his disease so pleasant and allows his malady to become a habit. He disregards the work of the Lord and does not consider the works of His hands. He despises all correction. <margin>Proverbs 23:35.</margin> *“They have struck me,” he shall say, “but I was not sick; they have beaten me, but I did not know it. When I awake, I will seek it yet again.”*

<margin>Augustine, *To Sacred Virgins*. A seductive demon, a sweet poison, etc.</margin> Drunkenness is the mother of all vices. It is a deceptive fiend, a sweet poison, a pleasant sin. He who has it does not possess himself; he who commits it does not just sin, but is altogether sin itself. In a state of drunkenness, *Alexander the Great* killed his friend *Clitus*; for which deed, when he was sober again, he at- <margin>Proverbs 23:29, 31, 32.</margin> tempted to kill himself. *To whom is woe? To whom is sorrow? To whom is strife? To whom is complaining? To whom are wounds without cause? And to whom is redness of the eyes? Although wine goes down pleasantly at first, in the end it will bite like a serpent and sting like a cockatrice <note>A mythical serpent-like creature with a deadly glance</note>.* <margin>Jerome: Wine prepares the mind for Venus (lust). The fuel of lust. Genesis 19:32. 2 Samuel 11:13.</margin> *It brings forth venery <note>Sexual indulgence</note>. Never consider a drunken man to be chaste.* Examples of this are the Sodomites, and how *David* planned to use the same tactic with *Uriah* <note>Referring to King David making Uriah drunk to hide the fact that he had impregnated Uriah's wife, Bathsheba</note>.

### CHAPTER 29. *The Passion of Drunkenness.* [[page number: 431]]
---

*Uriah*. Drunkenness is the nourishment of lust.

<margin>Diogenes Laertius, Book 1, Chapter 8; Patrizi, *De Regno* (On the Kingdom), Book 6, Title 26, from Laertius; Alexander ab Alexandro, Book 3, Chapter 11.</margin> He is to be punished because he willingly serves evil. By *Pittacus’s* law <note>Pittacus was one of the Seven Sages of Greece; he enacted a law that crimes committed while drunk should receive a double penalty.</note>, he that does evil in his drunkenness should be twice punished. By *Solon’s* law, a drunken Prince should die. The Indians allowed a woman to kill a drunken King, and for her reward, she was given his successor as her husband. The drunkard, by *Moses’* Law, is to be stoned to death (Deuteronomy 21:20).

Drunkenness befools the wit; as young *Cyrus* gave as his answer to his grandfather *Astyages* regarding why he <margin>Origen, Homily 5 on Genesis; "The deceitful wrestler" <note>original: "Luctator dolosus"</note>; Augustine.</margin> refused to drink wine: "Because," he said, "I took it to be poison, for I have seen it spoil men of both wit and sense." As it is said of *Lot*, drunkenness deceived him whom all of *Sodom* could not deceive. Wine is a wily wrestler. *Alexander* the Great, the victor over all, was overcome by wine.

<margin>Seneca, Epistle 59; Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book 7; Proverbs 23:20 and 21:17.</margin> It turns strength to weakness and health to sickness. Drunkenness compensates the merry madness of one hour with long weariness; drunkards grow old quickly and shall come to poverty.

He deprives himself of regeneration (Galatians 5:21, Romans 6:16) and of Christ (Romans 13:13). The Spirit is quenched (Ephesians 5:18). The flesh and the body of sin are <margin>Proverbs 25:28; Habakkuk 2:15.</margin> strengthened (1 Peter 2:11), and the soul is made like a city, broken down and without walls. He incurs shame, of which the examples are *Lot* and *Nabal*. And famine (Joel 1:5). Wine in youth turns to water in old age <note>Likely referring to the loss of physical vigor or the "thinning" of the blood and spirit.</note>.

<margin>Proverbs 23:34, 35.</margin> He is exposed to all danger and has no skill to prevent any, for he shall be as one who sleeps in the middle of the sea, and as he who sleeps on the top of the <margin>Genesis 19:35.</margin> mast. *Lot* was surprised by drunkenness. It brings on sudden death; it sows the seeds of deadly and hereditary <note>original: "heritable"</note> illnesses. More perish by surfeit <term>surfeit</term> <note>Overindulgence in food or drink; gluttony.</note> than by the sword.

<margin>a. 1 Kings 16:9. b. Daniel 5:2, 30. 1 Corinthians 6:10. Galatians 5:21.</margin> $^a$*Elah* and $^b$*Belshazzar* were killed in their drunkenness. In the end, just as *Esau* sold his birthright for a bowl of pottage <term>pottage</term> <note>A thick soup or stew.</note>, so the drunkard sells his right to grace and glory for a full belly.

### CHAPTER 29. *The Passion of Drunkenness.*
---

[[margin: Plutarch, in *Moralia*.]] full of drink, for which he is excluded from heaven. So that, when that shall be fearfully accomplished, he may miserably say with Lysimachus <note>original: "Lysinia"; the author likely refers to Lysimachus, a general under Alexander the Great</note> (who was forced by thirst to yield himself to the Scythians; and when he had drunk his cold water, he said), "O God, for how short a pleasure have I given up such great happiness?" This is like the rich glutton <note>A reference to the biblical story of Dives and Lazarus in Luke 16</note> in his fiery torments, who shall not be pitied with even one drop of cold water to quench his endless and unquenchable thirst. He shall drink no more wine with a song; strong drink shall be bitter to him (Isaiah 24:9).

-> #### Curation and remedies. <-

[[margin: Caution. Plutarch in *Cato the Elder*. 1 Samuel 25:36. 1 Samuel 25:37. Avoid occasions.]] **I**t is hard to cure a man who is given to drunkenness. It is difficult to speak to the belly, which has no ears <note>A proverb meaning it is hard to reason with someone's physical appetites</note>. It is folly to rebuke a drunken man. The most fitting time to cure a drunkard is when the drink has left him.

The occasions <term>occasions: circumstances or triggers</term> for drunkenness should be avoided. Lycurgus, to cure the people's drunkenness, caused all the vines to be cut down; but he would have done better to have ordered a well to be made in every vineyard, and in every cup to have "married" a watery nymph to fiery Bacchus <note>original: "married a watry nimph vpon fiery Bacchus"—an allegorical way of saying wine should be diluted with water</note>. Diogenes, when he was urged to drink beyond measure, poured the drink onto the ground, saying, "If I drank all of this, I would ruin myself rather than the liquor." The company of those who are thus diseased should also be avoided.

[[margin: Consider the deformity of drunkards. Erasmus, Book 7, *Apophthegms*.]] The Lacedaemonians <note>the Spartans</note> scared their children away from drunkenness by showing them the deformity <term>deformity: the physical and moral ugliness</term> of their drunken slaves. The consideration of the filthy manners of drunkards is a great preservative to an honest heart. This was the remedy that Anacharsis <note>A Scythian philosopher</note> used, having ever before his eyes the most filthy and unseemly manners of those who were intemperate. ->### *Treatment and Remedies*<-

[[margin: Bad remedies.]]
[[margin: *Saran in the life of Perdiccas.*]]
[[margin: *Plutarch.*]]
The heathen physicians skillfully investigated this hidden disease, which they never noticed until they found it made the body waste away. *Hippocrates* observed *King Perdiccas* in a chronic sickness; after long inquiry, he perceived his wasting away flowed from a disease of the spirit: the love he had for *Phila*, his father’s concubine. He prescribed a cure by causing *Phila* to meet with *Perdiccas*. *Erasistratus* the physician did the same with *Antiochus*, curing his lingering fever caused by lust for *Stratonice*. And *Saluchus* <note>Likely Seleucus I Nicator</note> did so by causing the father to give his wife to the son to cure him. These two physicians cured the body but killed the soul—a bad kind of curing. They would have done better to have cured the lust first, so that the body might become whole on its own. Evil should not have been done so that good might come of it. A Christian has many better ways to cure this passion.

[[margin: It wounds the conscience to hell.]]
Consider that it is directly prohibited: *Deuteronomy 23:17, 1 Corinthians 6:18, Hebrews 12:16.* It should not even be named among Christians: *Ephesians 5:3.* Committing it wounds the conscience and brings on God's wrath and all manner of evils. The price of repentance is too high for the pleasure. That wound is to be avoided that cannot be cured except with an ointment of sorrow and grief. *Aristotle’s* counsel was to behold pleasures not as they arrive with delight, but as they depart with pain. A thousand pleasures are not as perfect as one of those torments. But how much further do the torments of hell exceed them? There, for every one pleasure, there shall be a thousand torments—perfect, total, and final. Value this animalistic pleasure, therefore, at its true high rate, and avoid the goods that are so dearly bought. The remembrance of the burning in hell quenches the burning lust of <term>luxury</term> <note>original: "luxurie"; in this context, it refers specifically to lechery or lust</note>.

[[margin: *"I do not buy repentance at such a high price," said Diogenes.* <note>original: "Non emo tanti Pœnitere"</note>]]
[[margin: *"Not as they come, but as they go."* <note>original: "Non venientes, sed abeuntes"</note>]]
[[margin: *"Pleasure bought with pain is harmful."* <note>original: "Nocet empta dolore voluptas"</note>]]

Some are born that way, some are made so by men, and some have "made themselves eunuchs" <note>original: "gelded themselves"</note> for the Kingdom of Heaven. There are other physical remedies thought to bridle lust, such as *chasteberry* <note>original: "Agnus Castus"</note>, *rue* <note>original: "Ruta"</note>, narcotics, *purslane* <note>original: "portualaca"</note>, *water lily* <note>original: "nymphea"</note>, *houseleek* <note>original: "Semper vivum"</note>, *lettuce* <note>original: "lactuca"</note>, *camphor* <note>original: "camphora"</note>, *hemlock plasters* <note>original: "cituta emplastrata"</note>, and *the application of lead plates* <note>original: "lamina plumbra adhibita" — lead was thought to have cooling properties</note>. All of these either dry out, numb, or drain the "spermatic spirits." <note>In Early Modern medicine, lust was thought to be driven by an excess of "spirits" or fluids in the body.</note> But what of it? They do not cure the mind; it remains festering <note>original: "apostumat"</note> in its own impurity, merely lacking a new opportunity and a fresh, fertile breeding ground <note>original: "recent pregnant seminary"</note>. 

However, the surest and most infallible remedy for this malady is true <term>mortification</term> <note>the spiritual practice of subduing physical desires through self-discipline</note> (Job 33; Romans 8:1, 13; 1 Peter 2:11 & 4:1). Considering that our bodies are the members of Christ, always set yourself in the presence of God as the searcher of hearts. *Beat down your body and bring it into subjection.* Ictis of Tarentum, Asbylus of Croton, and Cleitomachus <note>original: "Chitomachus"</note>—all three most worthy wrestlers—led a most con-

-># CHAP. XXXI.<-
-># The Leprosy of Ingratitude.<-

*2 Tim. 3:2. Men shall be unthankful.*
*Luke 17:17. Were there not ten lepers cleansed, but where are the nine?*

->### *Description.*<-

**A**S leprosy is a universal <term>canker</term> <note>original: "Cancer"; here meaning a spreading, destructive sore</note> of the whole body, full of venom and contagion, arising from the putrid, blackest <term>humor</term> <note>According to the medical theory of the time, the body was governed by four "humors" or fluids; an imbalance of "black bile" was thought to cause various diseases.</note> of the body; so *ingratitude* is a universal sickness of the soul, proceeding from an inbred and acquired corruption and vicious constitution of the heart.
That it may be the better known, the opposite virtue of gratitude and thankfulness must be briefly touched upon.
*Benevolence* is the parent of beneficence, and beneficence provokes another to gratitude. *Ungratefulness* receives the benefit but disregards the beneficence of the benefactor.
The benefit is the object of our desires. It may depart from us, while the benefactor's beneficence remains. Accidents may rob us of the use of the gift, while the affection of goodwill still has a relative existence in the mind. The benefit is but the print and <term>character</term> <note>A mark, impression, or outward sign.</note>

[[margin: Benevolence. Goodwill <note>original Greek: Εὐνοια (Eunoia). Aristotle.</note> Good pleasure <note>original Greek: Εὐδοκία (Eudokia). Paul.</note>]]
[[margin: Beneficence. Good-doing <note>original Greek: Εὐεργεσία (Euergesia).</note>]]
[[margin: The benefit. A good deed <note>original Greek: Εὐεργέτημα (Euergetema).</note>]]

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; character

character of the action of beneficence; and both these are the streams from the fountain of benevolence.

<margin>Beneficence described.</margin> **Beneficence** is a willing endeavor in giving gifts to others for their benefit <note>original: "commoditie"</note>. Every provision of a benefit is not an act of beneficence unless it comes from a willing mind. A stone, a beast, the earth, the sea, or an enemy may provide benefits through chance; but they cannot be said to possess or practice beneficence. One may profit another through ignorance or against their will; that is to be esteemed as neither a benefit nor an act of beneficence. It is not enough to have profited someone unless it be done willingly.

<margin>Worthy beneficence requires 5 things.</margin> **Beneficence** is either *worthy* or *unworthy*. A worthy beneficence requires:
1. A cheerful giver. 
2. The choosing of a fit receiver, who is either worthy or in need. 
3. A convenient time: the timelier the better. Swift benefits are sweet; he gives twice who gives quickly <note>A translation of the common Latin proverb "Bis dat qui cito dat."</note>. 
4. A convenient place: public places are for an honorable beneficence; a private place is fittest when one's necessity or poverty is to be helped. 
5. A fit matter, appropriate for the giver. A princely gift fits the hand of a Prince, not the hand of a poor man; the mite <term>a very small coin or humble contribution</term> befits the hand of the poor widow, not the hand of a King. The matter must also be fit in regard to the receiver, for his good and for his use. A benefit may be of little worth in itself, but great in its use and consequence. Often the thing that is given is small, but the good which follows from it is great.

<margin>Swift favors are the sweeter. <note>original: Ωκεῖαι χάριτες γλυκερώτεραι.</note></margin>
<margin>*Often what is given is small; what follows from it is great. Seneca.* <note>original: Sæpe quod datur, exiguum : quod sequitur ex eo, magnum est.</note></margin>

<margin>*Psalm 119:71.*</margin>
<margin>*To cut and burn so that you may heal. Seneca, On Benefits, book 5, chapter 20.* <note>original: Secare, urere, ut sanes.</note></margin>
<margin>Beneficence may be unworthy in 6 ways.</margin> **Beneficence** must always aim at its own proper end, which is the utility of the receiver, even if the entrance and beginning of the benefit be painful. As *David* says, **It is good for me, O Lord, that thou hast afflicted me, that I may learn thy statutes.** A surgeon <note>original: "Chirurgeon"</note> may cut and burn so that he may heal.

An *unworthy beneficence* and benefit is that which is either: 
1. *Naked*, without any good deed or endeavor to do the same, having only a professed benevolence and nothing—

It emphasizes that the ultimate goal of beneficence is the receiver's benefit, even if the act itself (like surgery or divine affliction) is initially painful.</summary>

2. Or a **Worthless** gift, being bad for the giver to give and for the receiver to have. Like the dish full of bones that Alexander the Great sent to Diogenes the Cynic, who said: "It is fitting indeed for you to send this, but it is not a princely gift for me to receive."
<margin><note>Antonius and Maximus, *Sermons on Benefits*.</note></margin>

3. Or **Accidental**, as when someone does good to another more by good luck, chance, and opportunity, or by some secret providence, rather than by any deliberate purpose to be helpful.
<margin><note>Genesis 45:5, 7, 8 and 50:20. These verses refer to Joseph telling his brothers that although they intended him harm, God used their actions for a greater good.</note></margin>

4. Or **Corrupt**, as when the giver is forced to give by persistent begging, or gives out of ambition, anger, disdain, or stubbornness, after making the receiver wait through a long and wearying expectation and petitioning. This is done more for the giver's own sake than for the receiver's, bestowing the benefit in a way that brings the receiver dishonor and disgrace; or doing it for his own praise, giving publicly what should be given privately, and giving privately what should be given publicly.

5. Or **Harmful** to the receiver: although the receiver may desire the benefit for the present and accept it with gratitude, if the giver knows it will harm him, his generosity is worth nothing. It is rather a cruel kindness, a "charming and polite hatred," <note>original Latin: Sæua bonitas, blandum & affabile odium.</note> which it would be a greater benefit to withhold than to bestow.
<margin>*Cruel kindness, a charming and polite hatred.* <note>Seneca, *De Beneficiis*, book 2, chapter 14.</note></margin>
For what could an enemy do more than to trap someone with a gift while his heart hates them?
<margin>*I fear the Greeks even when they bring gifts.* <note>original Latin: Timeo Danaos et dona ferentes.</note></margin>
<margin>*The gifts of enemies are no gifts.* <note>original Greek: Εχθρῶν άδωρα δῶρα.</note></margin>

6. Or **Malicious**, as when the giver is a true enemy but, under the cover of deception, gives a gift to harm the person he hates. Examples include making someone drink so they may be more easily killed, or the Trojan Horse. Or, if someone intends to kill a person they hate by secretly administering poison, but because the poison is weak, it instead purges his system and accidentally cures some hidden sickness which was otherwise incurable. In this case, the poison became a medicine, and the hatred became a remedy. This is not to be considered true generosity or a benefit, because he healed while intending to injure.
<margin>*He healed by hurting.* <note>original Latin: Nocendo sanavit. Seneca, *De Beneficiis*, book 2, chapter 19.</note></margin>
Similarly, if someone intends to kill another and wounds his body, but accidentally opens an abscess <term>apostume: a localized collection of pus or a swelling, often internal</term> and so heals him. This should not be esteemed as a benefit, for many may profit others against their will. It is not the outcome, but the intention that makes a benefit different...
<margin>*They do good while unwilling.* <note>original Latin: Prosunt dum nolunt. Seneca, book 6, chapter 8.</note></margin>

All these sorts of doing good are unworthy of the name of beneficence and of the name of a benefit; but just as a dead man may be called a man improperly, so they may be called *unworthy beneficence* and an *unworthy benefit*, because they lack the willing intention of the giver regarding the good and utility of the receiver.

<margin>The foundations of gratitude are truth and fairness.</margin> **Gratitude** is provoked by the worthy beneficence and worthy benefit of another, and these are the sparks that kindle that flame: it is grounded on *truth* <note>original: "verity"</note> and *fairness* <note>original: "equity"</note>. *Truth* acknowledges and professes the benefit by giving thanks to the benefactor, by making the benefit known before others also, and by the promise and purpose to repay according to one's power. *Fairness* <note>original: "Equitie"</note> studies how to make compensation as far and as soon as is possible: both oblige the heart to thankfulness. *Gratitude* has three degrees: 1. In heart. 2. In word. 3. In deed: as shall be specified more amply hereafter in the remedies.

<margin>Gratitude: feigned, forced, or restrained.</margin> As for *unthankfulness*: some are ungrateful only in part; some are merely and altogether unthankful. Feigned, restrained, and forced thankfulness is a kind of ungratefulness. Some pretend to be thankful while they have no such thing in their heart. Some are ashamed to publish their thankfulness; and if they utter it, it is done privately in a corner and whispered in the ear: they blush that anyone should know that they are obliged debtors.

<margin>"They give thanks stealthily, in a corner, and in the ear." <note>original Latin: "Furtiuè agunt gratias, in angulo, & in aurem." Seneca, *De Beneficiis*, book 2, chapter 23.</note></margin>

<margin>"He who owes unwillingly is ungrateful." <note>original Latin: "Qui inuitus debet, ingratus est." Seneca, *De Beneficiis*, book 5, chapter 39.</note></margin>
Some are forced by shame, by fear, by necessity, by imitation, or by occasion to be thankful: these are not truly thankful in heart. They find themselves bound to a duty which is against their will, and so they willingly remain ungrateful. Some, again, are merely unthankful: such as, 1. He who does not acknowledge within himself the benefit and the greatness of it. 2. He who does not profess it before others, or who dissembles or denies it.

### -> *Part affected.* <-

The whole faculties of the soul are affected and infected by this malady; none of them are found to be healthy. The ungrateful man's mind does not acknowledge the giver's generosity <note>original: "beneficence"</note>, nor the greatness and goodness of his gift. His memory forgets what kindness has been shown to him. His heart is in a turmoil of secret passions; rejoicing in the gift, but sorrowing to be obligated; fearing to be detected, and fretting when he is mocked <note>original: "twitted"</note>. His conscience is unjust, for it allows him to falsely deny what he has received and to refuse what fair repayment <note>original: "requiting equity"</note> demands.

<margin>If you call someone ungrateful, you have said everything. <note>original: *Ingratum dixeris, omnia dixeris.* A Latin proverb meaning that ingratitude is the sum of all vices.</note></margin>

### -> *Causes.* <-

<margin>An unworthy benefit.</margin> When either the benefit is unworthy, or when a worthy benefit is given unworthily, the receiver of the gift is moved to become ungrateful. For instance, the receiver may have obtained the benefit: 1. By wringing it out of the giver by persistent begging <term>importunity</term>; in this case, he thinks he has bought it at a high price, paid for by the cost of his prayers. 2. Or if the receiver has obtained it through irritation, with long delays and wearying hopes. 3. If the giver gave it with anger, with ill will, or with hesitation; or out of ambition or disdain (his gift being like "stony bread," which is hard for a hungry man to go without, and just as hard to take and eat). 4. Or with scolding, shaming, and throwing it back in his face <note>original: "up-casting"</note>, or only by chance. 5. Or if he knows the
