The forgetting of the giver and of his kindness makes many become unthankful; the benefit lives in their hands, but dies in their memory. As Joash did not remember the kindness of Jehoiada, and the chief butler did not remember Joseph, so the people of Israel forgot God their Savior, who had done great things for them in Egypt. The ox knows his owner, and the donkey <note>original: "Asse"</note> its master's manger <note>original: "crib"</note>; but Israel did not know God. "What more could I have done," says the Lord, "for my vineyard? I looked for grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes." Israel did not say, "Where is the Lord?" They did not remember his hand (Psalm 78:42) because they forgot him who was so kind to them. Israel was filled, and they forgot God. Nothing grows old sooner than a kindness; old kindness sleeps, and men are forgetful.

There are many sorts of unthankful men: some deny they have received the benefit, some hide it <note>original: "dissemble"</note>, some do not repay it; but the most ungrateful are those who forget. Shame, honesty, and opportunity <note>original: "occasion"</note> may correct the first three; but what can correct the last sort, when they forget so willingly?

The receiver—whether looking within himself, at the gift, or at the giver—can subtly devise <note>original: "excogitare"</note> an abundance of excuses <note>original: "extenuations"</note> to minimize the gift. Gifts may easily be misconstrued if they are viewed only where we think them deficient, rather than where they profit us or where we do not deserve them. We shall never lack causes for complaining if we look only at the worst and weakest side of benefits. Some can never be content; they are always quarrelsome murmurers against God and man. They will think the benefit is common <note>original: "vulgar"</note> and not rare; that the giver might have given much more and much better; that he has given more and better to those who are worse; and that he did not give it heartily or in a timely manner, etc.

Many are so hard and stiff-hearted that no benefit <margin>Hardening of the heart <term>induration</term>.</margin> can soften <note>original: "mollify"</note> and win them over; they are so inflexible that nothing can make them kind, as God complained of the Jews: "What more could I have done for <margin>Isa. 5:4</margin> my vineyard? I looked for grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes." From this arises that despising of the bountifulness of God, which should instead lead men to <margin>Rom. 2:4</margin> repentance.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the moral failings that lead to ingratitude, following previous sections on the nature of benefits.</meta>

[[page number: 454]]

| | **Cʜᴀᴘ. 31.** | *The Leprosy <note>original: "Leprosie"; used here metaphorically to describe a spreading moral decay</note> of Ingratitude.* |
| :--- | :---: | :--- |

---

<margin>An evil conscience.</margin> Just as nothing is more powerful in making a man both speak the truth and do what is most just than a good conscience, so there is nothing more able to make him unmindful of his duty—so ready to disguise the giver's generosity and so unrighteous as to never repay—than an evil conscience that is either blinded, sleeping, dead, or <term>cauterized</term> <note>meaning: insensitive or hardened, like skin that has been seared</note>.

<margin>Self-love.</margin> When men are too favorable judges of themselves, admiring their own merit too much, they think they have deserved more at the giver’s hand. They believe the giver has valued them at too low a price. The receiver thinks he might have gained more if his pains and labors had been bestowed upon someone else. 
<margin>2 Timothy 3:2. <note>The original text cites 2 Tim 7:2, likely a typo for 2 Tim 3:2, which describes men as "lovers of their own selves."</note></margin> The self-lover, just as he loves no one as much as himself, cannot love his benefactor as he should.

<margin>Avarice (Greed).</margin> Avarice makes a man ungrateful. There is no satisfaction for his greedy appetite. The more he gets (unless he gets even more), the more discontented he becomes. And if he gets no more, he thinks all he has obtained is nothing. He forgets what he has and considers it an injury if anything he craves is withheld. Greed for things desired makes us forget what we have received, and avarice is always ungrateful.

<margin>Envy.</margin> Envy arrives with her comparisons, feeling indignant that others should have been treated as equals or preferred over the receiver in the distribution of gifts. Envy disturbs the receiver's heart with comparisons. 
<margin>No one can both envy and give thanks. <note>original: "Non potest quisquam, & inuidere, & gratias agere." Seneca, *De Beneficiis*, Book 3, Chapter 3.</note></margin> He who envies, sorrows; but the grateful person rejoices. No man can both envy a person and give him thanks.

<margin>Pride.</margin> Ambition and pride allow no one to be thankful. The proud man does not remember his own lowliness; he does not consider his current state—now receiving a benefit—which he once desired most. He does not look back to where...

### Signs and Symptoms.

The ungrateful person considers a benefit to be only a light thing, <margin>A benefit lightly esteemed or forgotten.</margin> and regards gratitude as a burden. The benefit delights him no longer than it lasts; if he is unthankful to God, he forsakes the fountain of living waters and digs for himself broken pits <term>cisterns</term> that can hold no water. <margin>Jeremiah 2:13, 5, 6, 8.</margin> He can say, "Here is the benefit," but will not once say, "Where is the Lord?" He casts God away and rebels against Him. <margin>1 Samuel 10:18, 19.</margin> He despises the bountifulness of God <margin>Isaiah 1:2.</margin> like the Gentiles <note>The non-believing nations of the ancient world</note> who knew God and yet were not thankful. <margin>Romans 2:4, Romans 1:21.</margin> He never thinks of God except in times of trouble. He has a trained memory for wrongs and can name them all as easily as Cyrus could name his soldiers. <note>Cyrus the Great was famously said to know the name of every soldier in his army.</note>

There is no worse thing than an ungrateful man. He is always either devising evil or doing evil. He flatters himself and disparages others. Just as he hates all men, he regards his benefactor only for the sake of the benefit received. The worse he becomes, the more bold he is to commit any vice. Ingratitude is a monstrous sin and the breeding ground <note>original: "seminary"</note> of many vices. There is no virtue that is not blamed and criticized by some, except only gratitude; and there is no vice that some will not commend, except only ungratefulness. There is no vice so condemned by all, and yet so widely embraced by many. Serpents carry venom within themselves, which they release to the hurt of others; but the ungrateful man is tormented by his own venom. There is nothing so great an enemy to harmony and human society as ungratefulness. It is the summary <note>original: "epitome"</note> of all vices. It is a vice that increases daily. For in the last days, perilous times shall come, and men shall be unthankful <margin>You have said everything when you have said "ungrateful." <note>original Latin: "Omnia dixeris, si ingratum dixeris."</note> 2 Timothy 3:2.</margin>. God will be to those who forget Him through unthankfulness like a lion, a leopard, and a bear robbed of her cubs <margin>Hosea 13:6, 7, 8.</margin>. Jerusalem, for her unthankfulness, had great destruction <note>original: "discretion," likely a printer's error for "destruction" or "distress"</note> threatened and executed against her <margin>Luke 13:34; 1 Samuel 12:7.</margin>. When Israel forgot the Lord, He sold them into the hand of Sisera. And God complains <note>original: "quereleth"</note> against His people for their great ingratitude <margin>Micah 6:2.</margin>. Ingratitude provokes revenge by constant habit, both with God and with man.

<margin>Endeavor to be thankful, either in:</margin>

*Answer:* Thankfulness consists of *affection*, *profession*, or *action*. Thankfulness in *affection* is when we heartily accept the benefit, heartily consider ourselves indebted for it, and heartily endeavor to make <term>recompense</term> <note>original: "recompence"; repayment or compensation for a favor</note>, even if power, opportunity, and the chance to perform the act fail. One may be a skilled craftsman <note>original: "cunning Artificer"</note> and yet can do nothing for lack of tools, or for want of fit material and a subject to work upon. So he is thankful who can do no more but is willing to be thankful. He is thankful in his conscience; he has no other witness but himself. We must not think that an idle wish is thankfulness, but rather he who wills and endeavors. An endeavor is often better than a larger recompense. The will must be accepted for the deed, and the affection for the action, in one who has sought every opportunity for repayment and could not find it.

<margin>Affection. "He who wills and endeavors." Seneca, *De Beneficiis*, Book 7, Chapter 18. "The disposition for the deed." Seneca, Book 7, Chapter 13.</margin>

Thankfulness in *profession* is when we are not only thankful in affection but also make the benefit known <note>original: "make publication of the benefit"</note> and offer commendation and praise for the giver, promising and vowing to repay him according to our power.

<margin>Profession.</margin>

Thankfulness in *action* is when any suitable recompense is made for the benefit (whether the recompense is more, less, or equal to the benefit). If we repay...

If the treasure of the heart is filled with true and mutual benevolence, the hand shall not be empty of real, requiting kindness <note>original: "beneficence"</note>.

It should therefore be the care of one who would be truly thankful to be the same in all these three ways. To be so in *action* only, or in *profession* <note>original: "profession," here meaning an outward declaration or claim</note>, without the affection of the heart, is mere hypocrisy. To be so in *affection* only, when no more is in our power, is true thankfulness; this has always a care to profess and perform as far as we can.

The ancients have set forth thanks, *thankfulness, and mutual favors* symbolically <note>original: "hieroglyphically"</note> under the figures of three sisters fathered by Jupiter, to show that it is a divine virtue, and from God, to be thankful and bountiful. They are called the *Graces* <note>original: "Charites, Gratiæ"</note>, because giving, receiving, and repaying should be done with mutual joy. There are three of them to represent those three actions of giving, receiving, and repaying. One of them has her face turned away from us: showing the giver, who should forget his gift. But the other two have their faces toward us, to show that the receiver should remember what he has received and remember to repay it. They are naked, declaring that in generosity and thankfulness there should be no hypocrisy, but simplicity and sincerity. They are coupled together, because between the giver and receiver there should be a reciprocal love and concord. They are merry and smiling, because there should be cheerfulness <note>original: "hilarity"</note> among them. And they are young virgins, because the memory of a kindness should never grow old.

# CHAPTER XXXII.
## The Poisonous Tongue.

> *James 3:8. The tongue is full of deadly poison.*

---

### Description.

<margin>Epiglottis</margin>
<margin>A description of the tongue.</margin>
<margin>James 3:5</margin>

**T**he top of the throat and its cover <note>original: "couer"; referring to the epiglottis</note> make and modulate the voice. But the instrument used to frame and articulate words is the *tongue*. It is the messenger of the mind, the character of a man, the pantry <note>original: "buttery"; a room where provisions and liquors were stored and dispensed; here used metaphorically as the place where reason is stored and distributed</note> of reason, the shaper of words, and the discerner of tastes. And though it is a small fire, it can kindle a great matter and boast of great things.

In substance, it is of a small size; yet it consists of almost as many parts as there are letters in the alphabet. It has a bony root, with glands <note>original: "kernels"</note> on both sides and a large amount of fatness. In its lower part, it is tied with a bond, as if with a rein, to bridle its <term>volubility</term> <note>The quality of speaking fluently, quickly, or incessantly.</note>. It has two large veins to give it nourishment, with two arteries to give it life. It has two nerves spread throughout it; one serving for motion, the other for tasting. It consists of nine muscles: four on either side, serving to move it in every direction. The ninth muscle is in the midst of the other eight, serving to extend the tongue in length and to draw it in again (two contrary motions, a function unique to this muscle alone among all the other muscles of the body).

->The<-

[[margin: <note>original: "Νοσ' αχαλινος. Morbus effrenis."</note> An unbridled disease. Theodorides. The disease of talking. Cato.]]
[[margin: Exodus 6:11, 12.]]
[[margin: Isaiah 6:5.]]
[[margin: James 3:8, 6.]]
[[margin: It is a fire, a world of iniquity. Ibid. <note>referring to James 3</note>]]
[[margin: The tongue's poison.]]
[[margin: Psalm 140:3.]]
[[margin: Romans 3:13.]]
[[margin: Job 20:16.]]

The substance of the tongue is a muscular and fibrous flesh, entirely covered on the outside with a membrane and a skin. *It is like the pen of a ready writer*; and, like an eel, it can turn and return itself into all forms, and revolve itself into all sorts of motions. It is one of the smallest members, yet the most mobile and the least easily tired; by which a man naturally pours out in language the image of his life.

*Anacharsis* <note>Anacharsis was a Scythian philosopher of the 6th century BCE, famous for his blunt wisdom.</note> being asked what was both the worst and the best thing in a man, answered: "The Tongue." If it is not ruled, it is the worst; if well-ruled, it is the best. *Death and life are in the power of the tongue.* One is the result if it is sound and used rightly; the other, if it is infected and abused. *A wholesome tongue is like the tree of life.* And, *the tongue of the wise is health*, both to himself and to others. Speech (if the tongue is wholesome and well-governed) is a remedy for sorrow, anger, and for a sick soul.

The disease of the tongue is a fierce malady, and he who is affected by it either can never keep silent or else never speaks well. It is the devil's coach if it is not bridled—and a most filthy channel, says *Chrysostom* <note>St. John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father known for his powerful preaching.</note>. Naturally, it is (as the lips are) <term>uncircumcised</term><note>In this biblical context, "uncircumcised" refers to being spiritually impure or resistant to God's word.</note>, polluted, and unclean, and becomes at last *an unruly evil, full of deadly poison*. It is so inflamed by this that *it is set on fire by hell, and sets on fire the course of nature.* 

This poison makes the tongue so venomous that it is both poisoned in itself and a poisoner of others. It is both *passive* and *active*: it is inflamed, and it inflames others. It is paralyzed toward everything good, and furious toward everything evil. It defiles the whole body and harms those who hear it, or those of whom it speaks—spouting out <note>original: "Adders poyson"</note> *vipers' poison from under their lips.* This is a disease as loathsome to others as it is dangerous to the speaker himself, as if he had sucked the poison of <term>asps</term><note>A type of venomous snake, often used in the Bible as a metaphor for malicious speech.</note>.

->Part<-

| CHAPTER 32. *The Poisonous Tongue.* | | [[page number: 465]] |
| :--- | :---: | ---: |

### The Part Affected.

<margin>Matthew 12:34</margin>
<margin>Matthew 15:19, 20</margin>

**T**his poison of the tongue is not physical, but spiritual. The tongue itself is not naturally affected by this poison as if it were fixed or inherent within the organ. This disease is not *idiopathic* <note>original: *Idiopatheticke*; a medical term for a disease that arises spontaneously or from within the organ itself, rather than being caused by another condition</note> or unique to the tongue alone. Instead, it is *sympathetic* <note>original: *Sympatheticke*; in older medicine, this referred to a condition occurring in one part of the body as a result of a disease in another part</note> and arises through its connection to the evil-disposed and poisonous soul. For, *“out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.”* And, *“out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, false witness, blasphemies, etc.”* The wicked heart sends no holy tasks to the tongue; instead, many foolish imaginations and godless passions are released.

### The Causes.

<margin>A corrupt and poisoned heart.</margin>
<margin>Romans 6:6</margin>
<margin>Ephesians 4:22</margin>
<margin>Psalm 41:6</margin>
<margin>Deuteronomy 32:32</margin>
<margin>Acts 8:23</margin>
<margin>Joel 3:13</margin>

**T**he most general cause of this poison of the tongue is a poisonous and poisoned heart, full of the venom of reigning corruption and the power of the *“body of sin.”* This is that raving and frantic "old man" <note>A biblical reference to the unregenerate human nature or the sinful self (see Ephesians 4:22)</note> who can speak nothing but evil. It is a heart that is wicked above all things and gathers iniquity to itself, filled *“with grapes of gall and the gall of bitterness.”* It is a heart burdened with sin (Isaiah 1:4). Just as *“a full winepress and an overflowing vat”* <note>original: *fat*; an archaic word for a large vessel or vat used in wine or oil production</note> spill over, this heart sends up an excess of many poisonous and corrupting thoughts to the tongue to be proclaimed to the world. Through this, the tongue becomes full of deadly poison, both to itself and to others.

<margin>Ignorance and vanity of mind.</margin>

The vanity and ignorance of the mind prevent the right consideration and weighing <note>original: *ponderation*</note> of the subject matter and the necessity of speaking. The greatness, goodness, evil, secrecy, and ultimate purpose of things to be spoken of are not balanced. The tongue is ready to harmonize <note>original: *sympathize*; here meaning to act in accordance with the mind's state</note> with the careless and inconsiderate mind. From this proceed blasphemy, swearing, cursing, verbal abuse <note>original: *railing*</note>, and the revealing...

Using biblical metaphors of winepresses and "the old man," the author explains that the tongue merely vents the sinful passions and lack of foresight found within the soul.</summary>

<margin>Carelessness for the good reputation of others.</margin>
<margin>Proverbs 22:1</margin>
<margin>Ecclesiastes 7:1</margin>

There are many who, out of self-love and pride and lacking all charity, have no care for the good name of others (which is better to them than riches <note>original: Proverbs 22:1</note> and precious ointment <note>original: Ecclesiastes 7:1</note>). From this contempt for the good reputation of others proceed <term>railing</term> <note>insulting or abusive speech</note>, reviling, gossip, and false testimony, etc.

<margin>Malice.</margin>
<margin>Ephesians 4:31</margin>
<margin>Psalm 64:3, 4</margin>

When the heart is irritated with anger, accustomed to hatred, and set in malice, then the tongue utters bitterness and is bent like a bow to shoot the arrows of bitter words. It is fiery, with lips of burning fire, chattering with malicious words and striking with the tongue.

<margin>Dissimulation.</margin>
<margin>1 Timothy 3:8</margin>
<margin>Psalm 55:21</margin>
<margin>Psalm 64:6</margin>
<margin>Psalm 55:20, 21</margin>

<term>Dissimulation</term> <note>deceit or hypocrisy</note> in the heart makes a person double-tongued; they have a mouth smooth as butter but a heart ready for war. Out of a deep heart, they use words softer than oil, yet sharpened like swords. Burning lips and a wicked heart produce the crafty, hypocritical, deceitful, flattering, and lying tongue.

<margin>Contention.</margin>
<margin>Proverbs 15:1</margin>
<margin>1 Timothy 6:4</margin>
<margin>Galatians 5:20</margin>

Those who are of a turbulent and contentious spirit utter harsh words which stir up anger: insults and suspicious guesses about disputed matters, shouting and quarreling, which are the works of the flesh and prevent men from inheriting the Kingdom of God.

<margin>Filthiness.</margin>
<margin>Ephesians 4:29 and 5:3</margin>
<margin>Ephesians 5:4</margin>

When filthiness reigns in the heart, rotten speech buds forth from the tongue: vulgar communication, filthy and profane songs and ballads, and all other such improper speech and foolish talking that is not appropriate.

<margin>Lightness of mind.</margin>

There are many whose minds are hasty, shallow, and of small capacity; this makes them subject to the vice of <term>loquacity</term> <note>excessive talkativeness</note>, by which they are so "pregnant" with their own ideas that they must either be delivered of them or else burst in the middle. From this proceed all rash judgment, thoughtless and idle speeches, a multitude of words, and empty, boastful speeches.

<margin>Impatience.</margin>
<margin>Exodus 11:7</margin>
<margin>Exodus 16:7, 22</margin>

The impatient heart makes a person like a mad dog, sparing no one but biting everyone with their tongue, whether they are absent or present. Such a person curses, murmurs, and complains.

-> ### *Signs and Symptoms.* <-

The poisoned tongue accuses the servant to the master (Proverbs 30:10; 1 Samuel 22:9; 2 Timothy 3:4) with false accusations (Titus 2:3). It is set against God (Isaiah 3:8) and against man, like an arrow shot out (Jeremiah 9:8). In a bad servant, it talks back (Titus 2:9), but in a rich man, it answers roughly (Proverbs 18:23).

It babbles (Proverbs 9:13; Matthew 6:5, 7; Ecclesiastes 5:3, 7; Judges 5:28, 29, 30; Acts 17:18) about vain and profane things (1 Timothy 6:20), which lead to more ungodliness (2 Timothy 2:16; Acts 17:18). It backbites (2 Corinthians 12:20) and kills from further away than the <term>basilisk</term> <note>A mythical serpent said to be able to kill with its gaze; here used to describe the range and lethality of slander.</note> does with its eyes (Proverbs 30:14). It barks at people's persons but is silent <note>original: "dumbe"</note> regarding their sins. <margin>Psalm 15:3; Isaiah 56:10.</margin> It is bent like a bow to shoot the arrows of bitter words (Psalm 64:3–4, 57:4, and 122:4; Jeremiah 9:4, 8). It bites like a serpent (Ecclesiastes 10:11). It is bitter (Ephesians 4:31; Romans 3:14). It blasphemes God and man (Ephesians 4:31; Colossians 3:8; 2 Timothy 3:2, 4; Titus 3:2; Revelation 13:6; Leviticus 24:15–16). It blesses God, but hypocritically; and it blesses a friend with a loud voice—an act which is turned into a curse for itself (Proverbs 27:14). It boasts of mischief (Psalm 52:1) and of great things (James 3:5; 2 Timothy 3:2; Romans 1:30). It bubbles or belches out foolishness (Proverbs 15:2).

It scolds (Ephesians 4:31), condemns others (James 5:9), and argues with others (Proverbs 18:6; Galatians 5:20; 1 Timothy 6:4). It is full of cursing (Romans 3:14; James 3:10). It curses itself and wishes a curse upon the soul of another (Job 31:30). It curses father and mother (Proverbs 20:20 and 30:11) and even curses God (Leviticus 24:15, 16). It is crafty (Job 15:5). It is loud and heard everywhere (Ephesians 4:31; Proverbs 9:13). It is always complaining and never content (Jude 16).

It deceives (Romans 3:13; 2 Samuel 16:4; Psalm 36:3) and is deceitful (Psalm 120:2 and 52:4). It devises mischief and, like a sharp razor, cuts deceitfully and devours others (Psalm 52:2, 4). It sows discord (Proverbs 6:14; 15:18; 16:28; 26:21; and 29:22). It disguises itself with burning lips and a wicked heart, like a <term>potsherd</term> <note>original: "potshard"; a piece of broken ceramic or pottery</note> covered with silver <term>dross</term> <note>original: "drosse"; the scum or impurities formed on the surface of molten metal</note> (Proverbs 26:23, 24, 25). 

Like the ***Crocodile***, when he smiles, he poisons; and when he weeps, he devours. It resembles the ***Panther***, which with the sweetness of his breath and the beauty of his skin lures animals to approach so that he may kill them. And like the ***Hyena***, it has the voice of a man, acting as a friend, but the mind of a wolf, devouring like a fiend. It makes a noise like a dog around the city (Psalm 59:6, 7, 14). But the greatest barkers are not always the <note>original: "shrewdest"; here meaning the most dangerous or malicious</note> biters. 

It argues where there is no doubt or question (1 Timothy 6:5). It is double-tongued and <note>original: "winnoweth"; figuratively shifting or blowing with every change in opinion</note> with every wind (Ecclesiastes 5:9). It is drawn out—in insults against God and man (Isaiah 57:4). Like a dreamer, it utters a multitude of idle words (Ecclesiastes 5:3). It detracts from and disgraces others, and it is dumb where it should bark (Isaiah 56:10). It defends evil causes and attacks those that are good. It drips like a honeycomb, but in the end, it is as bitter as <term>wormwood</term> <note>a plant known for its extreme bitterness, often used in the Bible as a metaphor for bitter suffering or herbal medicine</note> (Proverbs 5:3). It is a deep pit into which those whom the Lord abhors fall (Proverbs 22:14).

It utters much evil talk, which corrupts good manners (1 Corinthians 15:33 <note>original: "15. 31."</note>). It entices sinners (Proverbs 1:11).

It is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison (James 3:8, etc. <note>Original text cites James 3:5, but the "deadly poison" description appears in James 3:8.</note>).

->### *Cure and remedies.*<- <note>original: "Curation and remedies"</note>

<margin>A purified heart.</margin>
**T**he healing of the tongue is a tree of life (Proverbs 15:4). A tongue that is healed and speaks wholesome words is most profitable and comforting, both for the speaker and for others. Because the impure and poisoned heart—due to natural and <term>inherent corruption</term> <note>the theological concept that humans are born with a tendency toward sin</note>—is full of secret venom, it produces both poisoned deeds (Deuteronomy 32:33) and poisoned, corrupt talk (Romans 3:13; Ephesians 4:29). Therefore, the heart must first be purged.

<margin>By faith.</margin>
And nothing is more suitable for this than faith, for faith purifies the heart (Acts 15:9 <note>Original text cites Acts 19:15, but Acts 15:9 is the traditional reference for faith purifying the heart.</note>). By faith, we apply the power of Christ crucified to our hearts to bring about the <term>mortification</term> <note>original: "mortification," the spiritual practice of subduing sinful desires or bodily appetites</note> of sin and of all our earthly members (Colossians 3:5). Of these members, the tongue is one of the most important in terms of its use and its role in the quickening of the *inner man*. Those who belong to Christ crucify the lusts and affections that bud forth in those members, and especially in the tongue (Galatians 5:24).

<margin>Prayer.</margin>
Prayer is an appropriate remedy to cure the poison of the tongue. If it is fervent, constant, and effective, it avails much (James 5:16). This is true in two respects:

1. It creates an acquaintance with God (Job 22:21) and accustoms a person to choose their words carefully when turning to God (Hosea 14:2). This is that holy, secret speech mentioned in scripture (Isaiah 26:16; Job 15:4). Through this, a person eventually becomes so circumspect and holy in his talking with God that he is taught over time to be wise and <term>grave</term> <note>serious, solemn, or dignified</note> in his speech with other people.

2. Through prayer, he becomes a humble petitioner, because God is best able to cure and rule the tongue. As the scriptures say, "the preparation of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the Lord" (Proverbs 16:1), and "the Lord God has given me the tongue of the learned, that I should know how to speak a word in season" (Isaiah 50:4). He entreats God through prayer that He would set a watch before his mouth, and—

Reverence depends upon true fear. We should learn to serve God with reverence (Hebrews 12:28) and religiously and reverently regard in our speech all those things which belong to God directly. <margin>And men.</margin>

In our speaking, we should preserve the reputation and good name of others, which is "better than precious ointment" (Ecclesiastes 7:1) and "better than great riches" (Proverbs 22:1); "a good report makes the bones healthy" <note>original: "fat"</note> (Proverbs 15:30). In honor, we ought to prefer one another (Romans 12:10) and by no means hurt the reputation <note>original: "fame"</note> of another (Titus 3:2). This right reverencing of God and man cures and corrects in the tongue all blasphemy, taking God's Name in vain, joking about the Scriptures, cursing, slandering, backbiting, railing, reviling, and such like.

[[margin: Silence and restraint in speech.]]
*silence* <note>original: "taciturnity"</note>, nor reveal the secret depths and mysteries of wise silence. Therefore, we do not need to speak things that are trivial, irrelevant, unnecessary, filthy, hateful, harmful to God’s glory or to our neighbors, scandalous, offensive, secret, tedious, or the like, even if they are entirely true. We should not speak every truth before everyone indiscriminately; we must not "cast pearls before swine" <note>Matthew 7:6; a metaphor for sharing valuable truths with those who will not appreciate them</note> nor give what is holy to dogs (Matthew 7:6; 27:14), nor answer a fool according to his folly unless it is to prevent him from being wise in his own conceit (Proverbs 26:4-5; 23:9). We should be slow to speak before the elderly (Job 32:6), before magistrates and honorable men, or those in authority (Titus 2:9; Acts 20:10), or in the presence of angry, malicious, and deceitful <note>original: "dissembled"</note> people. This virtue of truthfulness cures all lying, deceit, flattering <note>original: "glozing"</note>, excessive pleasing <note>original: "smoothing"</note>, cheating <note>original: "cogging"</note>, and so on.

[[margin: Peaceableness]]
Learn to have a meek and quiet spirit, which is of great value in God’s sight (1 Peter 3:4). This consists in striving to be quiet and for a person to attend to their own business (1 Thessalonians 4:11); to live in peace with all people as far as it depends on you (Romans 12:18); to bear with others in love (Ephesians 4:2); and tolerating <note>original: "suffering"</note> the behaviors of men which you cannot change (as a consequence of Acts 13:18). It involves covering sins with love (Proverbs 10:12) and—being both prudent and peaceable—covering the shame of others (Proverbs 12:16). One should avoid all strictness and rigor, use moderation toward everyone (Philippians 4:5), and shun all occasions of discord and strife (Genesis 13:7). The habit and practice of this virtue cures all bickering, clashing, false rumors, blasphemy, cursing, and all evil words that arise from discord and debate.

Ii *Study*

<summary>This page outlines truthfulness and peaceableness as moral antidotes to a "poisonous tongue," emphasizing that while truth is a virtue, it must be used with discretion and silence.</summary>
<keywords>veracity, taciturnity, peaceableness, biblical ethics, speech, prudence, social conduct</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on controlling the tongue, specifically focusing on the virtue of silence and the importance of moderation when judging the actions and character of others.</meta>

| 482 | ### CHAPTER 32. ->*The Poisonous Tongue.*<- |
|---|---|

[[margin: <margin>Taciturnity</margin> <note>original: "Taciturnity" — the habit of remaining silent or being reserved in speech.</note>]]
Study the virtue of silence and wise restraint, through which those things that should be kept secret, and those things that are not necessary to be spoken, are not said. In this virtue, necessary things are spoken sparingly, and only as much as may serve for the good of others. This virtue cures garrulity <note>original: "garrulitie" — excessive talkativeness, especially on trivial matters.</note>, lack of self-control in speech, futility <note>original: "futilitie" — here meaning the inability to keep a secret or "leaky" speech.</note>, the revealing of secrets, flattery, slander, contumelies <note>original: "contumelies" — insulting or humiliating treatment.</note>, insults, and similar vices.

[[margin: <margin>Moderation of judgment.</margin>]]
Our judgment of others and of their actions should neither be too high nor too harsh. We should not admire people’s persons for the sake of personal advantage (Jude 1:16). Neither should we condemn others too hastily or too severely when we think they have offended. Do not be suspicious where there is no ground for it, and do not judge things to be worse than they are. Do not interpret things in the worst possible light by giving them a wrong construction (Matthew 7:1). 

Judge those you respect truly, according to what you certainly know. As for those you dislike (whose actions or sayings you do not approve of), either suspend your judgment of them or, where a matter is doubtful, interpret it for the best. When you know of and dislike something in another, excuse it—either by their intent (which may be good), or by their ignorance and weakness (which is to be pitied), or by their natural inclination (which is common to many), or by their temptation (which may have been great), or by their necessity (which was unavoidable), or by the circumstances of their action (which may lessen the fault), or by the hope of their repentance (which may happen tomorrow), or by reflecting on yourself—knowing that you may be in the same position at some other time as they are now. 

This is the right sobriety and moderation of our judgment of others. It corrects the words of flattery and does not allow men to "bless with a loud voice" (Proverbs 27:14) or to give flattering titles (Job 32:21-22). But much more, it corrects all backbiting, upbraiding <note>original: "vpbraiding" — criticizing or scolding severely.</note>, blasphemy, and all such words that suggest rash judgment.

*Meekness—* <note>This is a "catchword," indicating the first word of the following page.</note>

<summary>This page advises readers to practice "taciturnity" (wise silence) to avoid social vices and encourages a charitable, moderate approach to judging others' actions by considering their intentions and circumstances.</summary>
<keywords>silence, taciturnity, judgment, charity, flattery, slander, ethics, biblical citations</keywords>

-># CHAPTER VII.<-
->## The Spirit of Slumber.<-
---
> *Isaiah 29:10. The Lord has covered you with a spirit of slumber.*

### ->Description.<-

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **A**s bodily sleep binds up all the senses and vital spirits <note>original: "animall spirits"; in the 17th century, these were believed to be fluids or gases that moved through the nerves to produce sensation and movement.</note>: this *spirit of slumber* binds up the soul from all sense of sin and feeling of grace. It is a most profound drowsiness, depriving one of all sense and feeling. And Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), a prominent Early Church Father known for his powerful preaching.</note> says that it is such a habit of the soul whereby it is so given to sin that it cannot be brought back to a better state. And as there are various sorts and degrees of sleep-inducing <note>original: "soporiferous"</note> diseases in the body, so there are different types of this *slumber*. The godly, because of their remaining corruption, sleep to some extent, yet *their heart is awake* <note>A reference to Song of Solomon 5:2.</note>. Some are (like the ungodly) in a deeper sleep, indeed a dead sleep, to whom it is said, *Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead* <note>Ephesians 5:14.</note>. They cannot be woken from their sleep, like those who are oppressed with sleep-inducing diseases: such as lethargies, *carus* <term>a state of deep stupor or complete loss of consciousness</term>, *catalepsies* <term>a condition of muscular rigidity and fixed posture</term>, *cataphoras* <term>a state of semi-coma or heavy sleep</term>, or *typhomania* <term>a state of lethargic delirium common in cases of typhus</term>; all of which are deadly unless they are quickly cured. And just as all these deadly sleeps result from a cold humor <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids thought to govern health; "cold" humors were associated with sluggishness and death.</note> or a vapor filling the brain and oppressing the vital spirits and senses, so this deadly *spirit of slumber* occurs when men have their | [[margin: What it is.]] [[margin: *Pneuma katanyxeos* <note>Greek: "spirit of stupor" or "spirit of slumber".</note> Romans 11:7, 8.]] [[margin: Types and degrees of slumber. Song of Solomon 5:2.]] [[margin: Ephesians 5:14.]] |

<summary>This page introduces the concept of the "spirit of slumber," comparing it to physical medical conditions like comas or lethargy that dull the senses. It describes this spiritual state as a profound numbness toward sin and grace, affecting both the godly (mildly) and the ungodly (fatally).</summary>
<keywords>spirit of slumber, Isaiah 29:10, Chrysostom, lethargy, medical metaphors, spiritual apathy, vital spirits, humors</keywords>

| They are at their merriest in this state, constantly blessing themselves. *The harp and the viol, the tambourine, and pipe, and wine are in their feasts; but they do not regard the work of the Lord.* <note>Isaiah 5:12</note> They also say to God, "Depart from us, for we do not desire the knowledge of your ways." <note>Job 21:14</note> Sometimes they are like *Gallio* <note>original: "Gallio"; a Roman proconsul who famously refused to involve himself in religious disputes, often used as a symbol of indifference.</note>, treating religion as merely a question of names. ### ->*Curation and remedies.*<-

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| [[margin: Meditate on the shortness of your life.]] <br> [[margin: Job 4:19.]] <br> [[margin: Isa. 37:27.]] <br> <br> [[margin: Job 14:1, 2.]] <br> <br> <br> [[margin: <gloss>Stinking seed, a sack of dung, food for worms. Bernard.</gloss> <note>original: Sperma foetidum, saccus stercorum, cibus vermium.</note>]] <br> <br> [[margin: <gloss>This is the moment upon which eternity depends.</gloss> <note>original: Hoc momentum unde pendet eternitas.</note>]] <br> <br> [[margin: Prov. 6:9.]] <br> [[margin: Jer. 8:7.]] <br> <br> <br> [[margin: Matt. 25.]] | **A**bsorb into your heart the brevity of your life: and remember solemnly <note>original: grauely</note> that your body is but a tabernacle of clay and flourishing grass. What is man that is born of a woman? He is of short duration and full of trouble: he blossoms <note>original: shooteth out</note> like a flower and is cut down; he also vanishes as a shadow and does not continue. As soon as he is conceived, he is condemned to die. The building is hardly finished before it is ready to fall; each moment threatens our departure. <br> The feeble <note>original: silly</note> spark of our uncertain and dying life is but a shadow, a dream, a night-watch, a smoke. Accidents <note>original: Casuality</note>, sickness, and age are always the messengers <note>original: summoners</note> attending us. We are always rushing toward an uncertain end. ...that they be neither unlawful nor immoderate. <margin>Mental sobriety.</margin> **Mental sobriety** is a moderation of all our joys, confidence, desires, designs, delights, hopes, and inquiries; it ensures they are bounded by honesty, reason, and religion. Do not let your heart swell with pride, nor your mind with curiosity; do not presume too much on mercy, nor confide in your own perfection. Do not think your religion is great, and suspect your conscience even in its best moments of self-approval. <margin>1 Peter 1:13; Luke 12:35; 1 Thessalonians 5:7; Isaiah 29:9 & 19:14.</margin> *Gird up the loins (or the affections <note>original: "affections," referring to the emotions or desires</note>) of your mind; be sober. Let your loins be girded about, and your lights burning.* Contrary to this is spiritual drunkenness (Isaiah 29:9).

<margin>Light. 1 Thessalonians 5:5.</margin> Be a child of the light and of the day: endeavor always to keep light in your mind by using every diligent means for common light out of the Word <note>The Bible</note>, and for special light out of the application of the Word to your heart. This should be accompanied by regular meditation and the lively exercise of holy feeling.

<margin>Prayer.</margin> Be diligent in prayer and strive within it. Watchmen watch best when they are talking; acquaint yourself with the Lord and keep yourself awake by conferring with Him. Let the body stir up the spirit, and the spirit the body; give no rest to your soul, and let your soul give no rest to that *Holy One of Israel*. Incessantly petition <note>original: "importune"</note> Him, like the persistent widow; do not leave Him until, like *Jacob*, you receive a blessing.

<margin>Suspect Satan. 2 Corinthians 2:11; 1 Timothy 3:6 & 6:7.</margin> Carefully recognize and always remember Satan’s deceptions <note>original: "circumventions"</note>; do not be ignorant of his machinations. On every occasion, suspect his "pageants" <note>original: "pageants," meaning deceptive shows or spectacles</note> and snares. The tempter has a thousand ways to tempt; he desires nothing so much as that we take some grains of his *laudanum* <note>an opium-based sedative used here as a metaphor for spiritual lethargy</note> and fall asleep, so that he may sow his tares and spread his traps. There is not one whom he does not assault, whether to bait a *Judas* or buffet a *Paul*. <margin>2 Corinthians 2:17; 1 Peter 5:8.</margin> Let us watch, therefore, because our adversary goes about continually, *like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour.*

These aforementioned remedies one may use by himself; but

# -> CHAPTER VIII. <-
## -> A cauterized conscience. <-

---

*1 Timothy 4:2. Whose conscience is cauterized (or burned) with a hot iron.*

### -> Description. <-

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **C**onscience does not concern itself with generalities, as the mind does; but only with all particular thoughts of the mind, desires of the heart, words of the mouth, and actions of the body. It has a *witness in heaven* <note>original: Job 16:19</note>, with whom we are said to *conscire* <note>Latin: "to know with," the root of the word conscience</note>. For this reason, it is called "conscience": a private knowledge shared with another besides ourselves. This "other" is only God. It combines two "secretaries" <note>individuals who share a secret</note> to one thing, and two knowledges to one matter, so that we can know nothing by ourselves alone. It is also called a preservation of the light of nature, or the light of the law, meant to convict us in all our actions. God has appointed it to give sentence before Him and with Him—either for us or against us—to help His chosen people to be converted and to leave the wicked convicted. In the end, it shall testify against them, showing how often it warned them, though they would not listen; God, in His own time, will ratify this sentence against them. | <margin>Conscience deals only with specific details.</margin> <br><br> <margin>Job 16:19.</margin> <br><br> <margin>Why it is called *syneidesis* <note>Greek: συνειδησις, joint-knowledge</note> or conscience.</margin> <br><br> <margin>1 John 3:20, 21.</margin> <br><br> <margin>Why it is called *synteresis* <note>Greek: συντηρησις, the innate preservation of moral principles</note>.</margin> <br><br> <margin>It is God's deputy.</margin> |
| It gives testimony of all our thoughts, words, and deeds. It is that Notary <term>a clerk or official recorder</term> who always has a pen in his hand to note what is done. From it, nothing can be hidden, and no one can be freed. | <margin>It gives testimony. Romans 12:15.</margin> |

| -> CHAPTER 8. *A cauterized conscience.* <- | |
| :--- | :--- |
| ...the heart, stirring up shame, sadness, sorrow, fear, and our own thoughts, to trouble and frighten us: making our joints loose and our knees knock together, as happened to *Belshazzar* <note>Belshazzar: A Babylonian king in the Bible (Daniel 5) whose knees knocked in fear when he saw a supernatural hand writing on a wall.</note>: terrors of conscience and desperation are like the raging of the sea. No beauty of face, no hypocrisy in speech, no cleverness in wit, nor pleasure on earth can stop its convicting power. <br> It excuses and absolves: making the righteous bold as a lion <note>Proverbs 28:1</note>; rejoicing in godly purity as if in a continual feast; indeed, it is a confident defense against all the slanders <note>original: "calumnies"</note> in the world. <br> In the wicked, it becomes cauterized, or seared <note>original: "feared" — likely a printing variant of "seared"</note> with a hot iron. In this word, the Apostle alludes to medical cauterization <note>original: "physicall cauterization"</note>, which serves for: 1. Stigmatizing or marking any part of the body (with a hot iron). 2. For cutting away any rotten and gangrenous <note>original: "gangrenate"</note> part. 3. To make any putrefied part turn into a dead, senseless scab <term>escarre: a dry slough or crust caused by a burn (modern: eschar)</term>, which shortly thereafter falls away. 4. It is also fit for venomous bites, carbuncles <note>carbuncles: severe skin infections or boils</note>, venereal and plague-related sores <note>original: "pestilent botches"</note>, and for stubborn <note>original: "contumatious"</note> tumors that otherwise refuse all help. So, when any diseased part cannot be helped by softening <term>emollition: the act of softening or relaxing</term>, maturation, digestion, incision, etc., then the place is only fit for cauterizing—either by heat or chemicals <note>original: "actually or potentially"</note>—as the occasion requires. <br> Therefore, a cauterized conscience is: 1. A conscience blotted and stigmatized with inseparable past, unrepented marks and badges of guilt and corruption. 2. Having all its former <note>original: "bygane"</note> light, feeling, and life (of both reason and grace) turned into a hard, calloused, putrid, dead, and crusty senselessness. 3. A conscience that is rotten, venomous, ulcerated, plague-ridden, filthy, and gangrenous, whereby one most boldly dares to fall away and commit any sin with greediness. 4. ***

<margin>The case is dangerous.</margin> If this disease is long neglected, it becomes almost incurable; and it is in vain to say, after many years, "God is merciful, I have sinned." Pharaoh, Saul, and Judas all cried, *Peccavi* <note>Latin: "I have sinned"</note>. Yet Pharaoh is hardened and perishes. Saul consults with a witch <note>Referring to the "Witch of Endor" in 1 Samuel 28</note> and is cast away. Judas despaired and laid hands on himself. And most difficult is it helped; almost no one escapes: for he who is thus affected runs (so strongly) either to a reprobate mind <term>reprobate mind: a mind rejected by God and incapable of moral judgment</term> or (so hastily) to a desperate end. He had no desire to improve himself, but shall have a raging mind to end himself. His hardened <note>original: "indured"</note> heart can endure the hardest rebukes and corrections of others, but he is most impatient with himself.

<margin>A reprobate sense. Desperation. *Occultum quatiente animo tortore flagellum: Juvenal* <note>Latin: "The torturer shaking the hidden whip in the mind." A quote from the Roman satirist Juvenal regarding the internal sting of a guilty conscience.</note></margin>

<margin>The manifold evils of a seared <note>original: "feared" - likely a transcription of "seared" (cauterized)</note> conscience.</margin> The cauterized conscience, as it can never prove a friend, so it is always a man's greatest enemy. It is the Lord's Sergeant <term>Sergeant: an officer responsible for arresting offenders and bringing them to court</term>, constantly arresting and bringing the owner before God. It is his Jailer, keeping him in heavy irons and ensuring he appears against that great day. It is a thousand witnesses to accuse him; the Judge to condemn him; the executioner <note>original: "hang-man"</note> to punish him; and flashing fire-brands to torment him. It remains a forerunner and executioner of God’s most righteous judgment. When He shall rouse it, it shall become most cruel and fierce, like a ravenous beast.

<margin>False peace. True terror.</margin> The conscience's judgment (by God’s permission) may (for a time, and in some great measure) be smothered down, and its definitive sentence not heard. But in the end, it rages and is invincible, and cannot be fully and finally extinguished. At last, it shall lift up its voice like a trumpet and thunder with a most authentic, divine, condemning echo from God’s tribunal. Although it is in this life a *closed book*, yet (after the body’s death, and much more after the body’s resurrection) it shall be a *book opened* <margin>A book opened. Revelation 20:11, 12.</margin>. God shall enlighten it and stir it up by His mighty power; it shall disclose plainly the most ancient and hidden abominations, with ten thousand millions of endless woes. And in this life, it shall make...

<summary>This page warns that a neglected or "cauterized" conscience becomes an inescapable enemy that acts as accuser, judge, and executioner. Though it may stay silent for a time, it will eventually be "opened" like a book at the final judgment to reveal every hidden sin.</summary>

## ->CHAPTER IX<-
## ->*A Wounded Spirit*<-

| **Proverbs 18:14** | *But who can bear a wounded spirit?* <note>original: "But a wounded spirit who can beare it?"</note> |
| :--- | :--- |

### ->*Description*<-

[[margin: What it is]] **T**he deepest wound of the spirit is caused by trouble of conscience or distress of mind: when a person's conscience is unsettled before God; where the power of the conscience to excuse <note>original: "excusing power"</note> is too weak, and its power to accuse <note>original: "accusing power"</note> is too great.
[[margin: How it is]]
[[margin: The lowest degree]]
The lowest degree of this wound is when a person is in suspense and doubts their spiritual standing <note>original: "good estate"</note> before God, and experiences a simple fear and grief regarding their own condemnation (a common condition among the regenerate <term>regenerate: those who have experienced a spiritual rebirth or conversion</term>).
[[margin: The highest degree]]
The highest degree of this is when a person feels (in their own perception and understanding) entirely without hope of salvation. This is more than a simple fear; it is a kind of terrifying desperation.
[[margin: Three types of this wound]]
There are three types of this wound: 1. It either arises directly from the soul. 2. Or it arises directly from a melancholic body <term>melancholic body: a physical condition believed in the 17th century to be caused by an imbalance of "black bile," leading to depression and irrational fear</term>. 3. Or it is a mixture, arising from both.

| | *Part* |
| :--- | ---: |

<summary>This page defines a "wounded spirit" as a crisis of conscience where a person's sense of guilt outweighs their sense of peace with God, ranging from mild doubt to total desperation. The author identifies three possible origins for this distress: the soul, the physical body (melancholy), or a combination of both.</summary>

<margin>Symptoms of blasphemous temptations <note>original: "tentations"</note> suggested by Satan.</margin> When the devil wounds the conscience with filthy, suggested thoughts, they enter the mind quickly and are forced upon it violently. They are unavoidable, occurring again and again, entering perhaps a thousand times a day. They are conveyed to the mind from the outside. The memory is weakened, the senses are dulled, and the brain is confounded. These vile thoughts are directly against the light of nature, and even more against the light of grace, as they involve thinking unreverently of God. They are conceived with fear, and trouble and fainting follow. They are cast into the mind, not bred there. They will befall both the bad and the good: the most moral citizen <note>original: "Ciuilian," referring to one who lives by civil law or outward morality.</note> and the most sincere believer <note>original: "fairest professor"</note> may be in the depths of depression <note>original: "the dumps"</note> because of them. The godly cannot promise themselves freedom from these; but when they have them, they abhor them.

<margin>Symptoms of blasphemous temptations proceeding from ourselves.</margin> There is another sort of impure thoughts, most vile and filthy, that are not so much inserted and suggested by Satan; rather, they come more directly from a person’s own heart. They come with greater leisure, less violence, and more moderation. They are not so far against the light of nature. They do not cause fear, fainting, or sickness. People are not amazed by them. They come more orderly, even from the hearts of degenerate minds. They do not distress the conscience because the mind approves of them; they belong more to madness of the mind, or to a seared conscience <note>original: "cauterized conscience," a biblical term for a conscience that has become insensitive to sin</note>, than to a wounded conscience.

<margin>Symptoms of common trouble befalling the godly.</margin> When the godly and born-again <note>original: "regenerate"</note> have their trouble of conscience in a more common and less violent way: they are sorry for not sorrowing as they should; they are grieved by their hardness of heart and vexed with doubts. They complain of infirmities, wants, weaknesses, imperfections, omissions, lapses, and backsliding. They lament that God’s graces are not as sweet to them, and their own sins are not as bitter as they should be.

<margin>Symptoms of a melancholy trouble.</margin> If trouble of conscience seems to come from melancholy <note>original: "melancholyous," referring to the medical theory of the four humors where an excess of "black bile" caused depression and anxiety</note>, the imagination will be monstrous in its perceptions, thinking...

The sufferer often thinks himself to be a beast (such a one was Nebuchadnezzar <note>The Babylonian King who, according to the Book of Daniel, lost his mind and lived like a wild animal.</note>). Sometimes he thinks he is a pitcher, a pig, a dog, or a dead body. He may imagine his nose to be monstrously large, his buttocks to be made of glass, or his belly to be full of small cats, and so on. A person affected in this way will apply every evil thing he hears to himself. He will suffer many horrors, fears, and despairs, even concerning his own salvation. He fears every man, every creature, and even himself; indeed, he fears most when there is the least cause for fear. He is displeased with himself and with his own actions. 

This specific trouble is not weighed down by a sense of sin and divine wrath in particular (as true trouble of conscience is). It lacks courage in everything, whereas true trouble of conscience will remain most courageous in many godly matters. This condition may be cured with medicine <note>original: "Physicke"</note>, but true trouble of conscience scorns all medical remedies. This passion is long in developing and comes on more slowly than true spiritual trouble does.

->### *Prognostics.*<-
<note>Predictions or likely outcomes of a condition.</note>
---

<margin>Dangerous cases.</margin> **If** the trouble and wounding of the conscience come from a capital crime (which wastes and wounds the conscience), it becomes almost incurable. It causes many—like Cain, Judas, and Saul—to perish in the temptation.

<margin>Less dangerous.</margin> If it comes purely from the will of God (as was the case with Job’s trouble), it is then more curable.

<margin>More dangerous.</margin> If anyone is troubled with that filthy temptation of blasphemy and consents to it, it is then most dangerous—especially in those who have begun to choose the way of truth. It brings forth strange evils and horrors of the mind, great astonishment, and desperation. It leads people to kill themselves <note>original: "dispatching themselues"</note> and judge themselves to be the firebrands of hell, rejecting all holy means and spiritual exercises for recovery. Nevertheless, just as Christ escaped this temptation without sin, so many of his members <note>Followers or believers.</note> are delivered from it.

-> ### Chapter 9. *A wounded spirit.* <-

[[margin: The patient should be patiently supported.]] He will greatly respect your disposition: he will bear patiently with your shortcomings, stubbornness <note>original: "frowardnesse"</note>, irritability, rashness, and your disordered feelings and actions. He will accommodate you and sympathize with you in various things; he will be grieved when you are grieved, and weep when you weep. He will not give up on you quickly. He knows that God has the greatest influence <note>original: "stroke"</note> in this matter, and he will wait for God's own timing <note>original: "leasure"</note>; so that after all means are used, you may at length find him, *in whom your soul delights*. He will not deal as harshly with a woman as [[margin: Song of Solomon 3:4. Making a distinction. Jude 23.]] with a man; nor with a person suffering from melancholy as with someone whose trouble is simpler; nor with one who is troubled by a lack of grace, as with someone who lies wounded under the guilt of sin and the terror of God's wrath.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;He must not apply false remedies, nor begin with words of compassion and consolation, nor with untimely, sweet, sugary comforts before the conscience [[margin: Cautions: Do not begin with comforts. Do not comfort too soon. Do not comfort too much. Do not comfort externally, such as with merry-making.]] has been opened up <note>original: "ripped vp"</note> by specific repentance. He must not comfort you too soon, before you are humbled, nor too much, lest you later become worse; iron that is heated and cooled too much and too often becomes harder. You must not begin with drinking, pastimes, merry-making, company, purging, and so on, which may mitigate the pain for a while, but will bite more deeply afterward, when the violent fit returns with a second remorse more dangerous than the first. If the trouble is not mixed with melancholy, [[margin: Do not comfort with medicine.]] medicine <note>original: "physicke"</note> is merely folly. If the trouble comes entirely from <term>melancholy</term> <note>In this period, "melancholy" was seen as a physical ailment caused by an imbalance of fluids (humors) as well as a mental or spiritual state.</note>, then using theology alone will prove to be idle labor. Some are so driven to madness by the fury of this disease [[margin: Danger of false remedies.]] that when they can get no ease from common false remedies, nor obtain the true and most specific helps, they run to a violent death to end their grief: like the foolish fish that leaps out of the boiling <note>original: "seething"</note> water into the burning fire.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;When this wound comes from a sense of wrath for [[margin: If the wound proceeds from the sharp sense of wrath for sin:]] sin: First, you must be purged and brought low by the bitter "Aloes of the Law" <note>Aloes were used as a powerful, bitter purgative medicine; the author uses this as a metaphor for the harsh but necessary realization of one's sins through God's Law.</note>, before you are soothed with the oil...

[[margin: Purge before you restore, and cast down before you raise. A caution.]] Before applying the healing oil of the Gospel <note>The "oil of the Gospel" refers to the soothing and healing message of God's grace and forgiveness.</note>, one must first use the "purgatives." Purgatives <note>original: "purgatiues"; medicines used to clear the body of impurities.</note> must come before restoratives. Your sores should be gently examined, and from them, a sense of specific and secret sins should be drawn out. It is not appropriate to press the conscience too harshly, nor to release it from its guilt too thoughtlessly.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;[[margin: Lamentations 3:39. Convert sorrow into a sorrow for sin.]] Begin with your current sorrow and convert it into a sorrow for sin, remembering that man suffers for his own sins. It is a very effective cure for a nosebleed <note>original: "hemorage of the nose"</note> to redirect the flow of blood by bloodletting <term>phlebotomy</term> in the arm. Similarly, when you are brought to feel sorrow for sin, let not this [[margin: And reduce general and vague griefs to specific ones.]] sorrow be general or vague, but distinct and specific—focusing on particular great sins. In this way, let your abscessed <term>apostumate</term> wound ripen; let the infection drain out. Reduce vague griefs to specific ones. Say to yourself, "He that violates one commandment is guilty of all." If I am disciplined and wounded for one sin, what might God justly do to me for the millions and mountains of my other sins?

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;[[margin: Do not wander in the vagueness of sins. Be convinced of your greatest and specific sins. Begin repentance, or else renew it.]] Do not look at general sins too superficially, nor at particular sins too obsessively. Bind some specific great sin upon your conscience by the clearly convincing power of the Law; notice the most frequent warnings of your conscience. This shall be to your advantage: when you are truly and sincerely grieved for any one sin, you shall be easily led to be proportionately grieved for all sins known to yourself. You shall be brought humbly to repentance if you have not repented before; and if you have already repented, this will help to renew your repentance. This allows [[margin: Psalm 32:5.]] you to confess with David: *I acknowledge my sin to you, and I do not hide my iniquity; for I thought, I will confess my wickedness against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the punishment of my sin.* And you may say with Job: [[margin: Job 39:37.]] *Behold, I am vile; what shall I answer you? I will lay my hand over my mouth.*

Let your heart soar high: be heavenly-minded rather than earthly-minded. Live your life as a citizen of the heavens <note>original: "Have thy conversation in the heavens," referring to Philippians 3:20 where "conversation" means citizenship or conduct</note>, and practice all the means of grace.

Rejoice exceedingly when you have glorious feelings, yet do not rely on them; rely only upon the unchangeable promises that are all "Yes and Amen" in *Christ*.

<margin>Comfort others. Luke 22:32. 2 Corinthians 1:4.</margin>
Accustom yourself to comforting others: when you have been converted and comforted, *strengthen your brothers*. God has comforted you so that you may be able to comfort those who are in a similar affliction with the same comfort you yourself have received from God. This comfort will reflect back from the person you comfort to your own heart, confirming and preserving your own peace.

-> ### Description. <-

<margin>Romans 2:5. Repentance has 2 parts. Contrition must have a threefold sorrow: first from the heart, secondly for sin, thirdly toward God. 2 Corinthians 7:9, 10. Contrition must be accompanied with four things. Jeremiah 3:13. 1 Corinthians 11:31. 1 John 1:9. Jeremiah 15:20. Job 42:6. Repentance gets the names of contrition. ª Jeremiah 4:4 and Hosea 10:12. ᵇ Joel 2:13. ᶜ Acts 3:37. ᵈ Psalm 51:17. ᵉ Jeremiah 31:18, 19. ᶠ Ezekiel 36:32. ᵍ Job 42:6. 1 Samuel 7:3.</margin>

**I**mpenitency, and a heart that cannot repent, will be better known if true repentance is first rightly understood. True repentance has two most essential parts: *Contrition* and *Conversion*.

*Contrition* is a sorrow of heart toward God for sin: that is, for the offense against God, and that draws the heart to God. It is not a worldly sorrow, which is conceived for the punishment and harm <note>original: "skathe"</note> of sin. Contrition must be accompanied with:
1. The knowledge of sin.
2. The hatred of sin.
3. The judging and condemning of ourselves for sin.
4. An humiliation and confession of sin.
5. A love for God.
6. A hope of mercy in Him.

This is ª the ***breaking up of the fallow ground*** <note>term: "fallow ground" refers to land that has been plowed but left unseeded; metaphorically, a heart prepared for spiritual growth</note> of our hearts; the ᵇ ***renting of the heart***; the ᶜ ***pricking of the heart***; a ᵈ ***contrite spirit***; the ᵉ ***lamentation of Ephraim***; a ᶠ ***shaming and confounding***; the ᵍ ***abhorring of ourselves***; and a ***lamenting after the Lord.***

In regard to this sorrow, the Latins give repentance a name...

### **CHAPTER 10.**
-> *Dedolent <term>dedolent: feeling no pain or grief; calloused or insensitive.</term> impenitence.* <- [[page number: 139]]

<margin>Repentance derived from punishment. <note>original Latin: *Pœnitentia a pœna*</note> Regret or remorse. <note>original Greek: *Μεταμελεῖα*</note> Matthew 27:3. Conversion consists of three things. ª Ephesians 4:23. ᵇ Colossians 3:6. ᶜ Romans 6:4. Names of repentance taken from contrition. ᵈ Jeremiah 4:4. ᵉ Isaiah 55:7. ᶠ Acts 26:18. ᵍ 1 Thessalonians 1:9. ʰ Acts 26:20. ⁱ Isaiah 1:16, 17. Jeremiah 4:1. Change of mind. <note>original Greek: *Μετανοια*</note></margin>
Repentance is a name derived from that grief <note>original: dolour</note> with which the heart is punished. The Greeks derive the term from the care, solicitude, and anxiety that accompany contrition.

As for **conversion**, it must be: 
1. A changing and turning of the heart to God by ª **regeneration**. 
2. A turning from all sin by ᵇ <term>mortification: the spiritual practice of "killing off" sinful desires or the old self.</term> 
3. A constant turning to God in that grace of ᶜ <term>vivification: the process of being "made alive" or quickened by the Spirit.</term> and a rising up to a new life.

This is the ᵈ **circumcision of the heart**, that ᵉ **turning to God**, a ᶠ **turning from darkness to light**, and from the power of Satan to God. It is a turning from sin to serve the ᵍ living God, and the ceasing to do evil while learning to do well. Regarding this turning, repentance is called by the Hebrews *Teshuvah* <note>original: *Thefchubah*</note> (Jeremiah 4:1), a word borrowed from those who have gone long astray and are now returning to the King’s highway after receiving a warning. The Greeks call it an amendment of former foolishness, or a changing of the mind from worse to better.

<margin>What repentance is. The seven effects of it. 2 Corinthians 7:11.</margin>
So, repentance is a constant sorrow in the heart for offending God through sin, combined with a sincere turning from all sins toward God. This is accompanied by seven effects and signs: **care for amendment**; **clearing** oneself from the guilt of others; **indignation** against yourself; **fear** of offending God; a **great desire** to prove yourself to Him; **zeal** for His glory; and **revenge** against your own corruption.

<margin>What impenitence is. Romans 2:5. An unrepentant heart. <note>original Greek: *Ἀμετανοητος καρδια*</note> Romans 2:5. How it is said that the impenitent cannot repent. Jeremiah 18:11, 12. Ephesians 4:18.</margin>
By contrast, **impenitence**—or a heart that cannot repent—is a lack of either this sorrow, this turning, or both. It is not only a simple lack of repentance but also a perverse disposition through which the heart neither can nor will repent. Thus, a heart that cannot repent is one that both lacks repentance and can hardly be moved to it; indeed, it has a malicious quality within itself that is directly opposed and contrary to repentance.

It is called **dedolent** <note>original: *Dedolent*</note> because those who are impenitent lack true sorrow...

<summary>This page defines repentance (metanoia/teshuvah) as a sincere turning toward God involving regeneration and mortification, contrasting it with 'dedolent' impenitence, which is a calloused and malicious refusal to feel sorrow for sin.</summary>

[[page number: 140]] **CHAPTER 10.** -> *Unfeeling Impenitence* <note>original: "Dedolent impenitency," referring to a state of being unable to feel sorrow or remorse.</note> <-

<margin>Insensitive <note>original Greek: Ἀνάλγητος (*analgetos*).</note> Impenitence is either obvious or else covered with false repentance. Matthew 26:3. Various types of false repentance. Hebrews 12:17. Exodus 8:8, 15; 9:27; 10:16. Joel 2:13. Isaiah 58:5, 6.</margin>
...sorrow for sin and are past feeling; they have ceased from all grief and have no sense of pain. Under *Impenitence* is included not only common and open refusal to repent, but also every kind of delayed and false repentance. Examples include the desperate repentance of **Judas**, who felt remorse but did not convert <note>Judas's "repentance" led to despair rather than a return to God.</note>; the feigned repentance of **Ahab**, who repented hypocritically; the temporary grief and tears of **Esau**; and the fake humility of **Pharaoh**. It is the tearing of the clothes but not of the heart. It is the act of punishing ourselves and afflicting our souls for a day—bowing down the head like a bulrush and lying down in sackcloth and ashes—without inward remorse or a true turning toward God.

Thus, anyone who is grieved (no matter how intensely) for sin and yet does not turn to God, or he who turns from one sin to another, or he who stops sinning only because of impotency <note>being physically or practically unable to commit the sin any longer.</note>, or he who turns from many sins but not from all (as **Herod** did), or he who turns from all outward sins (as the <term>Civilian</term> <note>one who follows social and civil laws rather than divine grace.</note> or **Moralists** do), cannot be said to truly repent. Furthermore, anyone who turns from sin because they are weary of it, or through the light of reason, or for fear of punishment, or for the love of virtue—rather than through the special grace of true contrition and regeneration—still remains under that heavy calamity and disease of impenitence.

---
-> ### Part affected. <-

<margin>The Heart.</margin>
**T**he part affected is chiefly the heart, which will not be contrite or broken with sorrow, but instead continues to take pleasure in unrighteousness and refuses to return to God. The rest of the soul's faculties sympathize: the mind does not acknowledge sin, the conscience is in a state of senseless stupidity, and all the affections follow their own sway and momentum.

**CHAPTER 10.** -> *Callous Impenitence.* <- <note>original: "Dedolent Impenitency." From the Latin "dedolere," meaning to stop feeling pain; it refers to a state where the conscience is seared or numbed to sin.</note> [[page number: 141]]

-> ### Causes. <-

[[margin: Prosperity abused. Proverbs 1:32. Jeremiah 48:11. Nehemiah 9:28. Jeremiah 22:21. Amos 4:11.]]
**W**hen the spleen <note>original: "milt." In early medicine, an enlarged spleen was thought to cause the rest of the body to waste away.</note> swells, the rest of the body decays. The person who swells with prosperity (if he is left to himself) wastes away into impenitence. Concerning this, it is said: ***Ease kills the foolish, and the prosperity of fools destroys them.*** The heart that enjoys too much prosperity is deprived of grace and is loosened toward all impiety. ***Moab has been at rest from his youth, and he has settled on his dregs, and has not been poured from vessel to vessel, neither has he gone into captivity; therefore his taste remained in him, and his scent is not changed.*** <note>Jeremiah 48:11. This metaphor compares a person's character to wine that becomes harsh if it sits too long on its sediment (lees/dregs) without being disturbed.</note> The Levites complained about the people of Israel: *When they had rest, they returned to doing evil before the Lord.* And the Lord complained of the same, saying: ***I spoke to you when you were in prosperity, but you said, "I will not hear." This has been your manner from your youth. And you were as a firebrand plucked out of the burning; yet you have not returned to me.***

[[margin: Habitual sin. Isaiah 31:6. Jeremiah 13:23. Romans 2:4. Ezekiel 23:43.]]
The habit of sinning makes a man sink deep into rebellion and take on a habit of impenitence. Of such a person it is said: ***Can the Ethiopian <note>original: "Blacke-Moore."</note> change his skin? Or the leopard his spots? Then may you also do good, who are accustomed to doing evil.*** Combined with this is a habitual despising of those things that lead him to repentance—namely, the riches of God's bounty and patience—and so he grows old in sin.

[[margin: God in justice. Because of contempt, He does not give His Word, or else He gives it in wrath. To convince. To harden. To astonish. To dull. To irritate.]]
In His most righteous justice, God gives many people over to themselves and to a senseless impenitence. This is because of their former contempt. Sometimes He deprives them of the benefit of His Word; sometimes He gives them His Word (as an aroma of death <note>original: "savour of death," referencing 2 Corinthians 2:16.</note>) with a convicting and killing effectiveness, constantly drumming in their ears. Sometimes He astonishes them, other times He numbs them, and sometimes He irritates them, by which they are more and more confirmed in their impenitence. As it is said:
Go...

**CHAPTER 10.** -> *Callous Impenitence.* <- <note>original: "Dedolent Impenitency"—a state of being "past feeling" or insensitive to the guilt and pain of sin.</note>

[[margin: Isaiah 6:9–10. Satan's deceit. 2 Timothy 2:26.]]
***Go and say to this people, "You shall hear indeed, but you shall not understand; you shall plainly see, and not perceive. Make the heart of this people fat, make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their hearts, and convert, and I heal them."***

The devil is both diligent and cunning here, and—now with almost six thousand years <note>According to the standard biblical chronology used in the 17th century, the world was approximately 5,600 years old.</note> of experience—is highly skilled in making the snares of impenitence and trapping men within them. There they lie as prisoners to do his will. He covers the misery and poison of sin with his sweet-sugared, deceitful, and alluring baits. He makes sins delightful both to attempt and to welcome, and causes a person to sleep long in them until at last, under some grievous calamity, he begins to show his horns and terrifies the poor impenitent soul so that it may be swallowed up in the gulf of final despair.

[[margin: Blindness. Revelation 3:17. James 1:24. Jeremiah 8:6. Ephesians 4:18–19.]]
When a man never reflects the beams of his mind upon his miserable self, but instead measures himself by his own standards, he remains impenitent. He thinks he is rich and increased with goods and has "need of nothing," and does not know that he is "wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked." He has a Pharisaic conceit <note>Pharisaic: self-righteous or hypocritical, referring to the Pharisees described in the New Testament.</note> of himself; he does not truly consider his own state and never asks, "What have I done?" Along with this coincides an ignorance of God and His will—a darkened way of thinking.

[[margin: Incredulity <note>Unbelief.</note>. Acts 8:13, 21–22. Induration <note>Hardening of the heart.</note>.]]
Just as faith is the cause of repentance, so unbelief is the cause of impenitence, as it is said: *Take heed, brethren, lest at any time there be in any of you an evil and unfaithful heart, departing from the living God.* Simon Magus <note>A practitioner of magic who attempted to buy the power of the Holy Spirit from the Apostles (Acts 8).</note> had a hypocritical and temporary faith; but because he lacked true saving faith, his heart remained unbelieving, "in the gall of bitterness, and in the bond of iniquity." He could not repent, for his heart was not right in the sight of God. Hardness of heart is a specific cause of this, as it is said:

...all the other Galileans, because they have suffered such things? *I tell you no; but unless you amend your lives, you shall all likewise perish. And the Lord is not slow concerning his promise (as some men count slowness) but is patient toward us, and would have no man to perish, but would have all men to come to repentance.*

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; When you are frightened and humbled for your <term>impenitency</term>, you must know the good and benefit you are to obtain if you will repent. [[margin: Consideration of the profit of repentance. It diverts judgments before they come. Jeremiah 26:3. Jonah 3:9, 10. Matthew 10. Revelation 1:19.]] Repentance diverts imminent judgments (which a refusal to repent otherwise brings about). *God relents from the evil that he had said he would do: and quenches the fire in the house of Joseph and Bethel.* He *withdraws the axe from the root of the trees and holds back his wrath.* It likewise delivers us out of present judgments, if only we will *search and examine our ways, and turn again to the Lord: and acknowledge our faults, and seek him diligently in our affliction.* [[margin: It relieves us from present judgments. Lamentations 3:40. Hosea 5:15. Luke 15.]] The <term>Prodigal Son's</term> <note>Referring to the parable in Luke 15:11-32.</note> only refuge was repentance, to run home to his father and obtain favor.

Jeremiah 3:12 and 4:14.]] Christ said, *The sick have need of the physician.* And, *I am come to call sinners to repentance.* And, *Come unto me all you that are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. [[margin: Acts 3:19. Amos 5:4. 2 Samuel 12:13. Luke 18:13. Luke 23:42.]] *and have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities and cast all our sins into the bottom of the sea.
