The humbled tax collector <note>original: Publicane</note> departed justified; the penitent thief received his sweet response: *Today you shall be with me in Paradise.*

[[margin: Promises of things temporal and spiritual. Job 22:22. Jeremiah 3:22.]] &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Many are the specific promises of easing <note>original: mitigating</note> and removing worldly <note>original: temporall</note> calamities, of excellent deliverances, and of spiritual and worldly blessings, as the Lord in his wisdom finds them suitable for you. So God says to you, *“You disobedient child, return, and I will heal your rebellions.”* Answer him in return, *“Look, I come to you, for you are the Lord my God.” See Job 22.*

[[margin: Consideration of God's patience. Romans 2:4. Genesis 39:9. 1 Peter 4:3. Romans 2:5.]] &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Consider the bounty, patience, and long-suffering of God, so that you may be led to repentance. Think of God's goodness, as Joseph says of his master's kindness: *“He has kept nothing from me; how then can I do this great wickedness and so sin against God?” It is more than enough for us that we have spent the past time of our lives according to the lusts of the pagans <note>original: Gentiles</note>.* If his patience and bounty are abused through a lack of remorse <note>original: impenitency</note>, it will *heap up for yourself wrath against the day of wrath.*

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Set your eyes upon that wondrous <note>original: admirable</note> Cross of Christ, with which you must arm yourself against a lack of remorse. [[margin: Meditation on Christ's death. 1 Peter 4:2. Augustine, Book on Virginity.]] *“That you henceforth should live (for as much time as remains in the flesh) not after the lusts of men, but according to the will of God.”* Immediately <note>original: Incontinent</note> at the presence of Christ's Cross, the whole armies of sin and the flesh are put to flight. Look into the wounds of him who hangs there, upon the blood of him who is dying, upon the price paid by him who redeems, and upon the print of the wounds of him who rises. He has his head bowed down to kiss, his heart opened to love, his arms stretched out to embrace, and his whole body displayed to redeem. Consider how great these things are; weigh them in the balance of your heart, so that he may be entirely fixed within your heart.

-> ## **Chapter 10. &nbsp;&nbsp; *<term>Dedolent</term> Impenitence.*** <-
<note>original: "Dedolent"; a term meaning callous, unfeeling, or insensitive to pain—in this context, being numb to the guilt of sin.</note>

[[margin: Heb. 12:17; Matt. 25:11; Rev. 3:20; Rev. 2:21.]] This puts them out of all hope for the time to come, by giving them over to desperation, or else to a reprobate mind. Thus **Esau**, when he would have inherited the blessing, was rejected; for he found no place for repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears. The **foolish virgins** neglected their time and were excluded, though they cried out, "Lord, Lord, open to us." If Christ’s long standing at the door of our hearts and his knocking are despised, he will depart without returning. The Lord gave **Jezebel** time to repent of her sexual immorality, and she did not repent; therefore, she is threatened with final destruction to fall upon her and her children.

[[margin: Speedy repentance is most profitable. Phil. 1:23; 2 Cor. 5:1; August.]] &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The great benefit of speedy and timely repentance should be highly regarded. For it takes deeper root in us; it makes holiness far more pleasant and easy; it breeds more joy, peace, and comfort in the heart; it causes more time to be spent in God’s service, leading to a greater reward. It makes life sweet and joyful, and death calmly expected, saying: *I desire to be dissolved <note>original: "dissolved"; meaning to die or be released from the body</note>, that I may be with Christ, which is best of all.* And, *We know that if our earthly house of this tent <note>original: "tabernacle"</note> be destroyed, we have a building given by God—that is, a house not made with hands, but eternal in the heavens.* Neither can he die poorly who has lived well.

[[margin: Consider the shortness of life. Jer. 8:7; Eccles. 9:12; Job 17:16 and 34:20; Luke 12:46; Luke 12:20.]] &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Consider the momentary shortness of your life: It is but the passing of a weaver’s shuttle, a shadow, a span, a story, a dream, a vapor, a smoke, a flower, a cloud, and vanity itself. Consider the extreme uncertainty of this short life; we are tenants at will <note>a legal term for residents who can be evicted at any time by the owner</note>—here tonight and gone in the morning. Many who thought they would live longest died soonest. *So man does not know his time; suddenly he goes down to the grave. The evil and foolish servant said, "My master delays his coming."* And, *O fool, this night they may fetch your soul from you.*

[[margin: Remedies against the delay of repentance until the hour of death.]] &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The hour of death is (of all the times of our life) the most unfit time for repentance: when the body is full of pain, the mind full of fear, and one is loath to leave the world.

| CHAP. 10. | Callous Impenitence <note>original: "Dedolent Impenitency" — 'Dedolent' means being past feeling, callous, or insensitive to pain and guilt.</note> |
| :--- | :---: | ---: |

Satan is busy with dangerous temptations. At one time, the poor impenitent person is entangled with so many disturbances: an angry God, an accusing conscience, a tempting *Devil*, a snaring world, a panting heart, a pained body, and a distressed soul. What leisure can an old impenitent person have to gather his wits to examine <note>original: "fanne himſelfe" — to winnow or sort through one's thoughts, like separating grain from chaff.</note> himself and turn to God? <margin>Zephaniah 2:1</margin> Would it not be a thousand times better to repent in time, so that when death comes, we have nothing more to do but to die and to say: <margin>2 Timothy 4:6, 7, 8</margin> *“I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, and I have finished my course; I have kept the faith. From now on, there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness,” etc.*

Delayed repentance allows sin to gain strength, and <margin>Remedies against delayed repentance until old age.</margin> every entertained sin makes a way for more sins, worse than itself. Just as *David’s* idleness overcame him and brought on adultery, and adultery brought on murder. <margin>One sin brings on another.</margin> *Herod’s* incest opened a door to his murder, and both of these led to his devilish impiety. *Judas’s* greed <note>original: "couetouſneſſe"</note> brought on treason, and treason made a way for desperation. Sin is a poison that spreads itself and converts every fluid <note>original: "iuyce" (juice)</note> into its own nature: *“Like a piece of leaven that leavens the whole lump.”* <margin>1 Corinthians 5:6; Galatians 5:9</margin>

If we do not turn to God before we are old, when sin <margin>Repentance is best learned in youth and worst in age. Proverbs 22:6.</margin> has become old within us, we shall be too weak to cast it off. All other trades are best learned in youth; for those who learn young, learn well. *“Train a child in the way he should go, and when he is old, he shall not depart from it.”* Age is unfit for learning and more prone to forgetfulness. It is full of distractions, infirmities, sickness, griefs <note>original: "dolours"</note>, troubles, and cares of the mind. It is most fitting, therefore, to turn to God in youth, when the mind <note>original: "wit"</note> is quickest, memory strongest, and the prime and best fruits of our life should be dedicated to God.

By all these considerations, stop the delay of your <margin>Avoid partial repentance. Repentance must be true. John 4:8.</margin> repentance. Repent through practice and not just by intention; do not give to God a blind or lame offering <note>original: "blind or lame offering" — a reference to Malachi 1:8, where God rejects defective animal sacrifices.</note> of partial penitence. Both feel sorrow and sin no more; let your repentance...

<summary>The author argues that delaying repentance until old age is dangerous because sin gains momentum over time and the physical and mental burdens of aging make spiritual focus difficult. He urges the reader to dedicate their youth to God rather than offering a "lame" or partial repentance at the end of life.</summary>

Stripes and wounds (of God’s corrections) are a purging medicine against the evil (of human impenitence).

-> # CHAPTER XI. <-
-> ## Pestilent Self-love. <-
---

[[margin: 2 Timothy 3:1, 2.]] *Perilous times, for men shall be lovers of their own selves.*

-> ### Description. <-

[[margin: 2 Samuel 13:2.]] **A**S Amnon was severely distressed <note>original: "fore vexed"</note> and fell sick for the love of his sister Tamar: so does the self-lover for the love of himself. He pines away; all his vital spirits are exhausted with that pestilent venom. There [[margin: 2 Samuel 24:1.]] die more by this plague than the seventy thousand who died in Israel in the days of the pestilence <note>original: "pest"</note>.

[[margin: The lawful love of ourselves. Ephesians 5:29. 1 Corinthians 10:31, 33. & 8:13. Romans 14:15. Cicero, *On Moral Ends* <note>original: "de finib."</note>. Scholastic rule. Aristotle, *Ethics* book 9, chapter 4.]] There is one lawful and tolerable love of ourselves: one that is not harmful to God, nor to our neighbors; nor to our own reputation <note>original: "valuation"</note>, conscience, health, estate, and integrity <note>original: "honesty"</note>. It is subordinate to God’s will and to sanctified reason, and is ruled by those. Every man is a lover of himself by nature. All naturally do love themselves. *Charity begins with itself.* For a man to be a lover of himself is natural; to love himself with integrity, it is a virtuous thing; to love himself with piety, it is a matter of grace <note>original: "gracious"</note>. This lawful self-love is the director of moral virtues and a host <note>original: "entertainer"</note> of divine graces; the end of which is that it may be well with those who love themselves in this way.

[[margin: Who best and most lawfully love themselves.]] This is only suited <note>original: "competent"</note> to him who is truly good and truly wise; because he loves himself according to...

<summary>This page defines the difference between a "pestilent" obsession with oneself and a healthy, "lawful" self-love that is guided by reason, piety, and integrity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on self-love, contrasting virtuous self-care with destructive selfishness, citing classical philosophers and biblical figures.</meta>

| 156 | CHAPTER 11 | Destructive <note>original: "Pestilent"</note> Self-Love. |
| :--- | :---: | ---: |

<margin>Only the wise man is satisfied with all he has. Seneca, Epistle 9.</margin> ...to his own most noble part: namely, his mind: to endow it with virtue and grace. His appetite follows reason, and his reason follows grace. He dwells with himself most willingly, peaceably, and pleasantly. His good conscience regarding things already done, his hope of future happiness <note>original: "hap"</note>, and his contemplation and affection for the best and most perfect good make him happy and content with himself. He only wishes and does the best for himself; he alone agrees and sympathizes best with himself, both in prosperity and in sorrow. He does not senselessly <note>original: "stupidly"</note> neglect himself like a fool, nor does he hate himself like a cruel, desperate person, nor does he love himself in any shameful way. <margin>Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book 9, Chapters 4 & 12.</margin> He is helpful both to himself and to others. This true self-love is true self-friendship and the fountain of all true friendship toward others; he is the best friend who loves himself best.

<margin>The unlawful love of ourselves.</margin> There is another love of ourselves that is unlawful, intolerable, and vicious—prejudicial to God, to others, or to ourselves. The self-lover loves himself and does all things for his own sake; in all his actions, he always considers himself. He is his own primary goal that he aims at. <margin>Augustine, *Sermon on the Times* 239.</margin> This is a disease that destroys a man's self and others also. *If you love yourself so that you destroy yourself,* <margin>Self-love is self-hatred.</margin> *you will also destroy the person whom you love as yourself.* This self-love is self-hatred. To love sin is to hate the soul. Indeed, self-love is self-murder, as shown by Saul, Ahithophel <note>original: "Achitophel"</note>, and Judas, whose self-love within their own hearts led to self-murder by their own hands. Just as a drunkard, through love for his belly, inflames and hardens his liver, causing a wasting disease or dropsy <note>original: "atrophy or hydropisie" (edema/swelling)</note>, and so kills himself; so Esau, for the love of a bowl of stew <note>original: "messe of pottage"</note>, <margin>Hebrews 12:16, 2 Timothy 3:4.</margin> sold his birthright and his spiritual inheritance <note>original: "grace-right"</note>. And many who are lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God make their self-love become their self-ruin.

-> *Part* <-

<summary>This page distinguishes between "true self-love," which is rooted in reason and virtue, and "unlawful self-love," which leads to spiritual and physical destruction, as exemplified by figures like Judas and Esau.</summary>

-> ### Part affected. <-

<margin>Heart.</margin> **T**he part affected is chiefly the heart, which draws all the rest of the faculties into its own disorder <note>original: "ataxie"; a Greek-derived term for lack of order or functional imbalance.</note>. By this, it is so destructively <note>original: "pestilently"</note> infected that it prefers its own appetites and desires above all things.

-> ### Causes. <-

<margin>Blindness. Psalm 10:3, 4; Job 21:14, 15.</margin> **T**he less a man knows God, the more he loves himself; and the more he comes into His presence, the more he hates himself. *The wicked has boasted of his own heart’s desire, and the greedy man blesses himself; he despises the Lord. The wicked is so proud that he does not seek God; he always thinks that there is no God.*

<margin>Luke 18:11; Revelation 3:17. Blindness.</margin> That lukewarm <note>original: "Laodicean"; referring to the church in Revelation 3:14–22 criticized for being neither hot nor cold.</note> and self-righteous <note>original: "Pharisaical"</note> blindness regarding ourselves makes us fall into a foolish delusion <note>original: "fond fantasy"</note> with ourselves. When we do not recognize our weakness, vileness, wickedness, and insignificance—and not only our general infirmities and miseries common to all mankind, but also when we do not know our own specific and personal faults and imperfections—we cannot help but foolishly <note>original: "fondly"</note> love ourselves. Furthermore, we do not know ourselves entirely; we do not realize that the soul, the mind, and its happiness are far more precious than the body. Thus, our affections are set more on the one than on the other.

<margin>Lack of regeneration. Philippians 3:19; Romans 13:14.</margin> He misplaces his own *identity* (the basis of self-love) and thinks of himself more as a *body* than as a *soul*. This makes him love his body more than his soul. Because he is entirely focused on physical nature <note>original: "flesh"</note> and is as yet unregenerate <note>spiritually unrenewed or not yet "born again."</note>—not being part physical and part spiritual—*he minds only earthly things and takes care only to fulfill the lusts of the flesh.* He is in too great...

<summary>This page identifies the heart as the primary site of "pestilent self-love" and argues that this condition arises from a lack of self-knowledge and a failure to know God. The author explains that when people prioritize their physical bodies over their souls, they fall into a spiritual blindness that fuels their vanity.</summary>

# C H A P T E R XII.
## *Putrid Hypocrisy.*

> Matthew 23:27. *Whitewashed tombs, which are within full of all filthiness.*

-> ### Description. <-

[[margin:
What hypocrisy is.

**H**ypocrisy signifies a simulation <note>pretending to be what one is not</note>, or dissimulation <note>hiding what one actually is</note>. We feign <note>original: "faine"</note> those things to be that are not; we disguise those things that are, pretending they are not. Or, hypocrisy is the faking of another person. The word "hypocrite" properly signifies a *stage-player*, who takes upon himself another man's person; such as a slave playing the king, or someone pretending to be more holy than he is, or one who puts on another's face or another's clothing.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; In the path of religion and godliness, and in the profession of it, hypocrisy is a most filthy consumption <term>consumption: a wasting disease, similar to tuberculosis, that eats away at the body</term>. It is like a painted tomb, inside of which there is nothing but rottenness. It is a decay, and the same thing in the soul that a consumption is in the body, which is a universal wasting of the *balsam of life* <note>original: "Bal-same of life"; a contemporary medical term for the vital fluids or "radical moisture" thought to sustain life</note>. So hypocrisy is a universal consumption of the soul's lamp of light and life, of reason and of grace.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Hypocrisy exists either in worldly matters or in religion.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Hypocrisy in worldly matters is forbidden, and we are commanded to *lay aside all maliciousness, all guile, and hypocrisy.* David did feign <note>original: "faine"</note> himself to be mad because he distrusted

God's promised help. Simeon and Levi talked deceitfully with the Shechemites and caused them to be circumcised so that they might kill them. But when God gave Samuel two errands at once and allowed him to show one to Saul, to cover and keep secret the other, this was no hypocrisy, but secrecy; wherein, being simple as a dove, God made him wise as a serpent. The wisdom of the serpent instructed the simplicity of the dove. Wisdom without simplicity is maliciousness; and simplicity without reason and wisdom is foolishness. That imperial speech, "He who does not know how to dissemble, does not know how to reign," <note>original: *Nescit regnare, qui nescit dissimulare*</note> is to be understood of a King's clemency, who towards some small offenses must use connivance <note>original: "connivance" here refers to the act of deliberately overlooking or ignoring something</note>. This was the wisest King’s counsel: *Do not take to heart all the words that men speak, lest you hear your servant cursing you. For often your own heart knows that you yourself have likewise cursed others.* Neither are the stratagems and warlike policy of Joshua, nor the threatening trials and sagacity of Solomon, hypocrisy. We pass by this kind of hypocrisy, as it is not to be insisted upon in this place.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Hypocrisy in religion has a forged union of diverse and contrary things: of two parties, of two actions, and of a twofold relation.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The two things are: 1. One in appearance—conceived, represented, signified, and professed—and that by some show, form, or representation, without a competent subject matter or meaning. (According to which all hypocrisy may be called a show or form, consisting more or less in a powerless formality.) 2. There is another thing, in effect diverse or contrary to the former, lurking and secretly couched under the false show; whereby all hypocrisy may be called private or hidden.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The two parties are: one, the actor in his act, playing the part of the stage-player and deceiving with his mask <note>original: "vizard"</note>. The other is the deceived beholder. Sometimes one and the same person may play both these parts.

these parties, deceiving himself in his own imagination: playing the hypocrite to himself first, and then to the world.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The two actions are: either a conceiving <note>original: "conceiting"; the act of forming an idea or opinion in the mind</note> and representing within oneself; or else an external profession of some secret thing that either is not so, or is not as great as it seems. It either does not exist at all as it is conceived, or it is not expressed in the same way it is conceived in the mind.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The twofold relation is false; when the thought represents and argues for something other than the truth, and the truth does not match the thought, there is a simple falsity and error. And when the words, writing, facial expression, or action do not resemble or reflect the thought, there is a manifest lie. Hypocrisy always involves a contradiction: either between the truth and the thought, or between the thought and its outward expression. In contrast, within veracity <note>truthfulness</note>, integrity, and sincerity (the opposites of hypocrisy), there is a constant uniformity in truth, thought, word, and deed: their "yes" is "yes," and their "no" is "no."
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; There are three degrees and specific types of hypocrisy. Sometimes there is more grace and godliness imagined to be in the heart than there truly is. This type is specific to the regenerate <note>those who have been spiritually reborn or converted</note>; the other two types are more common. Sometimes the true saving graces of God are imagined to be in the heart when they are not there at all; by this, the hypocrite seems to himself—and to others as well—to be a member of the true Church. He does indeed possess the common graces of the Spirit, but he mistakes them and counts them as special and saving graces. His form of godliness is Satan's *middle ground* <note>original: *Mediocrity*; here meaning a moderate or lukewarm state</note> between the two extremes of careless impiety and hopeless desperation. And sometimes that grace and godliness, which is neither truly within nor even imagined in the heart, is professed.

It may be called *hidden, private, or secret*: both because of the hidden thing falsely imagined in the mind in this hypocrisy, and also because this kind is hardest to discern, as the error is only in the quantity, not in the substance.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The second sort may be called **double hypocrisy**, because in it, grace is both imagined to be in the heart when it is not there at all—neither in quantity nor in substance—and it is also professed before others. It may also be called **Temporizing**, because the "temporary believer" <note>A term based on the Parable of the Sower (Matthew 13), referring to those who receive the word with joy but have no root and soon fall away.</note> is affected by this kind and is called a **Temporary**. Similarly, it may be termed **Lukewarm**—the devil’s middle ground—or **A form of godliness**.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The third sort may be called **Triple hypocrisy** because he who is thus diseased: first conceives mischief; secondly brings forth a lie; and thirdly causes others to believe <note>original: "conceiue"</note> a lie. It may also be called the *highest, the grand, grossest*, and most lying kind of hypocrisy. This is when men "speak lies through hypocrisy." <note>See 1 Timothy 4:2.</note>

-> ### *Part affected.* <-

**A**S out of the heart come false testimonies, so there is no greater falsehood than hypocrisy. For the hypocrite lies to himself in a false <note>original: "safe"</note> persuasion, or lies to the world under dissimulation. Or else he gives a false testimony both ways: pride and deceit are always his designs.

## CHAPTER 12. Putrid Hypocrisy.
### Causes.

<margin>Causes of secret hypocrisy: Satan’s seduction.</margin>
When *Satan* cannot tempt the *regenerate* <note>original: "regenerate"; those who have been spiritually reborn or converted</note> toward reigning sins or higher degrees of hypocrisy, he goes about to stain the face of innocence with a conceit <note>original: "conceit"; meaning a false or overly favorable opinion</note> of more grace than the heart actually has. He makes the remnants of his proud nature rise up in his own opinion and esteem himself and the worth of his own graces too highly. He dazzles his eyes so that for a long time he cannot recognize his own hypocrisy. <margin>God's desertion.</margin> God deserts his own for a time and permits Satan to test them.

<margin>Spiritual pride. Proverbs 28:26. 2 Peter 1:4.</margin>
When the *godly* person finds himself more *excellent than his neighbor* and that he is a *partaker of the divine nature*, and beholds his own reformed shadow in a fair fountain of godliness, he is joyfully amazed and admires his own happiness. He begins to conceive a better opinion of himself than he truly is. He becomes proud of his humility—and proud because he is not proud! Other sins spring from pestilent roots; this one is drawn from the purest streams of grace. It is specific to God’s child, whereas other sins are universal. *Paul* was overtaken by this, as he says: <margin>2 Corinthians 12:7.</margin> *“And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure.”*

<margin>Causes of temporizing hypocrisy: Satan's policy; he bribes them.</margin>
As for "temporizing" <note>acting to suit the time or current circumstances for personal gain</note> hypocrisy: God permits *Satan* to bestow worldly trifles upon man. These are to him like golden fetters, a sleeping potion, *Naboth’s* vineyard, an honorable servitude, a golden wedge, a glorious misery—and his only *Diana* <note>a reference to the idol of Ephesus, meaning his primary obsession or object of worship</note>. The *Devil* is wise, willing, and cunning; he reigns and rules in their hearts. If he cannot lead men to open impiety and the rejection of religion, he labors to make them subject religion and subordinate it to their idol. He also makes him

[[page number: 169]]

<margin>He grants them an imaginary persuasion of mercy.</margin>
## CHAPTER 12. Putrid Hypocrisy.
to have an imaginary persuasion of mercy, grounded upon outward shows and general, confused impulses—like morning dews and clouds of common graces, natural light, civil behavior, and external restraint from open sins. He causes the man to think these are sufficient *religion*.

<margin>Ignorance of self.</margin>
He is so busy and delighted with the world that he is loath to see the vileness within himself. He never descends into himself to examine the lowest depths of his heart. He can never rightly see nor admit his own inherent darkness, deadness, disorder, and slumber. This does not make his sins better known to himself, but rather more conspicuous and sinful before God; it makes his damnation more just and himself more inexcusable.

<margin>By comparing himself with those who are worse, he thinks himself good enough. Luke 18:11. Proverbs 30:12.</margin>
He compares himself with those worse than himself and says with the *Pharisee: "O God, I thank you that I am not like other men—extortioners, unjust, adulterers—or even like this tax collector."* He thinks himself far beyond adulterers, murderers, and oppressors. He keeps the external forms of *Religion* and belongs to *the generation of those who are pure in their own conceit, and yet are not washed from their filthiness*. He also notices that the end and death of others (who are worse than himself) seem godly and happy (as he perceives it), while seeing in their death some show of penitence and forced, brief cries for mercy. Thus, he contents himself with his current model of imaginary confidence in his own "sufficient" perfection in grace.

<margin>A misconstruction of true godliness. Psalm 38:20. Proverbs 28:1. Isaiah 8:13.</margin>
He has a prejudiced opinion of true *godliness* and of those who are truly *godly*. He thinks that the *godly* have many adversaries and are poorly thought of. Their boldness (like a *lion*) is called pride; their zeal is counted as "preciseness" <note>original: "preciseness"; excessive or fussy religious strictness</note>; their sorrow is esteemed as melancholy; their austerity is seen as mere misery; their minds are considered weak; their spirits low; and they themselves are viewed as base, unfit for the world, and "wonders in *Israel*" <note>objects of astonishment or ridicule</note>. And if he himself should follow their course, he thinks there is a *lion* <note>a proverbial danger or obstacle</note> in the way; the way...

It details how people avoid self-examination by comparing themselves to worse sinners or mischaracterizing true religious zeal as a mental or social defect.</summary>

[[page number: 170]]
->## CHAP. 12.<- ->## Putrid Hypocrisy.<-

<margin>He fears the inconveniences of true godliness. Isaiah 59:15.</margin>
He fears the inconveniences of true godliness. His way is too strait <note>original: "straite"; here meaning narrow or difficult.</note>, too narrow, and full of thorns. He will not fight with his own corruptions, the devil’s temptations, and the world’s vexations, claiming that *he who refrains from evil makes himself a prey.*

For these reasons, he thinks the safest and best course is not to be "precise" <note>original: "preciſe"; in this period, "precise" often referred to "Precisians" or Puritans who were extremely strict in their religious observance.</note> or too absolute in piety. Instead, he maintains a mediocrity <note>original: "mediocrity"; here meaning a middle way or a moderate, lukewarm path.</note> fit for his worldly mood and the common customs of the time, and troubles his mind no further. Upon this foolish notion, and with misplaced hope, he ventures his soul for the best.

<margin>A misconstruing of sin, justice, and mercy; and false testimonies of them.</margin>
He is replete <note>OCR: "repeat"; likely "replete," meaning full of.</note> with a foolish misconstruing of sin, of judgment, and of mercy. Sin is seen as small and pardonable; justice is minor and avoidable. Mercy is placed above all of God’s works, His truth, and His promises, and is expected to be had at the first call. He presumes upon mercy; he thinks prosperity, outward peace, and a superficial, powerless taste of *godliness* are the assured testimonies of mercy. He thinks to himself that he is holy enough because he is happy enough and secure enough, making no further progress in piety but contenting himself with common graces.

<margin>An ill conscience.</margin>
His conscience is too wide and unlimited, strong enough to digest any sin; he most favorably minimizes, excuses, interprets, and distinguishes it. He has reconciled the accusing and excusing power of conscience so that one shall not much disadvantage the other. He thinks that a little grace may be gained while much sin may be committed, based on certain good intentions and hopes. He does not lack theoretical principles of divine truth, but in practicing them, he has his own reservations, exceptions, and limitations. He follows them only as far as they are compatible with his worldly welfare; when they cross his path, he stops or else falls away. Hence, he is a temporizer <note>original: "temporizer"; one who changes their behavior or opinions to suit the current circumstances or to gain worldly advantage.</note>. The guides of this broad conscience are examples, customs, opinions, worldly wisdom, and the common natural notions of right and wrong. He will not subject his conscience to the full yoke...
<margin>Matthew 13:21.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 13:31.</margin>

[[page number: 171]]
->## CHAP. 12.<- ->## Putrid Hypocrisy.<-
...of God’s will, nor will he walk according to that rule.

<margin>Ignorance of God.</margin>
He may have a natural and scriptural knowledge of God, but he lacks spiritual and sanctifying knowledge. He is a shining lamp, but not a burning coal; he may enlighten others, but he does not set himself on fire with zeal. His light shines outwardly, but not within. He is enlightened like the moon (which has a borrowed light to give others, but darkness within its own body, which makes its spots more conspicuous); he remains in his own heart as darkness itself. He thinks honey is sweeter than his life, and gold more precious; pleasure is better, profit more relevant, and honor more delightful. He subordinates godliness to his wealth, his honor, his pleasures, and to the light of nature.

<margin>Ephesians 5:8.</margin>
Although he goes beyond the open atheist and the blatant hypocrite, and is more moderate and civil than they are—abhorring the infamous sins of adultery, drunkenness, heresy, and the like—yet he always lodges within himself some sweet, secret "bosom sin" <note>original: "boſome ſinne"; a favorite, hidden sin that a person is most attached to and reluctant to give up.</note>. This is what his mind mostly runs upon, where his best thoughts are spent, and for which all light and grace within are resolutely made to serve.

<margin>He harbors some secret bosom sin that keeps him back from true piety.</margin>
As for the grossest hypocrisy, *Satan, by God’s special permission, fills the heart.* Like a *spirit of error to make a man* believe through hypocrisy. He causes him to lean too much on bare knowledge and the ceremonies <note>original: "ceremonies"; external religious rituals or formal observances.</note> of religion more than the substance of it, having the *form of knowledge* but no practice of it. At once glorying in the law while simultaneously breaking it, he relies more upon the "circumcision of the flesh" <note>A reference to external religious rituals versus internal spiritual change.</note> than upon the "circumcision of the heart." *And he will come and stand before the Lord in His House and say, "We are delivered," though we have done all these abominations.*

<margin>Causes of grossest hypocrisy: Satan, etc. Leaning to ceremonies. Acts 5:3; 1 Timothy 4:1-2; Proverbs 7:14; Romans 2:27; Isaiah 1:13-15; Jeremiah 7:10, 4.</margin>
He is skillful at discerning the appearance of heaven and earth, but as *Christ says, "And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?"* This self-ignorance made the Laodicean Church...
<margin>Blindness. 1. Luke 12:56-57.</margin>

The author warns that such individuals rely on external rituals and selective obedience while harboring secret sins and misinterpreting God's mercy.</summary>

## ->CHAPTER 12. *Rotten Hypocrisy.*<-

[[margin: He fears the inconveniences of true godliness. Isaiah 59:15.]]
The way is too narrow <note>original: "straite"</note> and full of thorns. He will not fight against his own corruptions, the devil’s temptations, and the world’s frustrations <note>original: "vexations"</note>; claiming that *he who refrains from evil makes himself a prey*. 

For this reason, he thinks the safest and best course is not to be too precise or too firm <note>original: "peremptory"</note> in piety. Instead, he maintains a middle ground <note>original: "mediocrity"</note> that fits his worldly mood and the current customs of the time, troubling his mind no further. Based on this foolish idea, and under a false hope, he risks his soul for what he thinks is best.

[[margin: A misunderstanding of sin, justice, and mercy; and false proofs thereof.]]
He is filled <note>original: "replete"</note> with a foolish misunderstanding of sin, judgment, and mercy. To him, sin is small and pardonable; justice is minor and avoidable; and mercy is above all of God’s works, His truth, and His promises—and can be had at the first call. He presumes upon mercy. He thinks that prosperity, outward peace, and a shallow <note>original: "powerless"</note> taste of godliness are certain proofs <note>original: "testimonies"</note> of mercy. He thinks to himself that he is holy enough because he is happy and secure enough. He makes no further progress in piety but contents himself with common graces.

[[margin: An evil conscience.]]
His conscience is too broad and unrestricted, strong enough to stomach <note>original: "digest"</note> any sin. He favorably minimizes <note>original: "mincing"</note>, excuses, interprets, and justifies it. He has negotiated the accusing and excusing power of conscience so that one hardly interferes with the other. He thinks that a little grace can win much, and much sin can be committed for the sake of some "good" reasons and hopes. He is not lacking in the theoretical principles of divine truth, but in practicing them, he has his own reservations, exceptions, and limitations. He follows them only as far as they are compatible with his worldly welfare. When they cross his path, he stops or else falls away. Therefore, he is a "temporizer" <note>one who changes their views or behaviors to suit the current time or circumstances</note>. The sources of information <note>original: "intelligencers"</note> for this broad conscience of his are examples, customs, opinions, worldly wisdom, and common natural notions of right and wrong. He will not subject his conscience to the full yoke

### ### Chap. 12. ->Putrid Hypocrisy.<- [[page number: 173]]

---

...deceive the eye of man to make his unworthy self glorious; he makes himself a whited tomb <note>original: "whited tombe"; a biblical reference to Matthew 23:27, describing something that looks beautiful on the outside but is full of decay within</note> and justifies himself before men.

<margin>**Fear**</margin> Fear constrains him (for the safety of his person and to avoid greater inconveniences) to play the hypocrite in some details. For example, *Peter* did this when the mere breath of a servant girl caused fear for his life to overcome his faith; <margin>**Matt. 26:74**</margin> he cursed *himself* and *swore, "I do not know the man."* Similarly, he, <margin>**Gal. 2:12, 13**</margin> *Barnabas*, and some other *Jews* played the hypocrite by withdrawing and separating themselves from the *Gentiles* <note>Non-Jewish people</note>, *fearing those who were of the circumcision* <note>The Jewish faction that insisted on following Mosaic Law</note>. Peter did not do this with his whole heart, yet he was condemned for not walking in the right way. <margin>To walk uprightly <note>original Greek: **Orthopodein** (ὀρθοποδεῖν), meaning to walk straight or act sincerely</note></margin> However, the ungodly, to aid their fear, will adopt the craftiest forms of filthy hypocrisy and will continue in them until the end.

<margin>**A cauterized conscience**</margin> A seared conscience, insensitive to all sin, will make a man put on the fairest masking visor <note>A mask or disguise</note> of the most deceitful hypocrisy so that he may speak all the lies he can devise. He becomes a literal stage-player and laughs to himself when he is clever enough to make the world believe what he himself does not believe. <margin>**1 Tim. 4:2**</margin> *Speaking lies through hypocrisy, having their conscience seared with a hot iron.*

<margin>**The heart turning away from God**</margin> The heart that is distanced from God—and is not content to be ruled by the straightforward form of His truth—is satisfied to be entangled with an easier form of piety taught by the rules of men and the "doctrines of devils." As it is said: *“Because these people draw near to me* <margin>**Isa. 29:13, 1 Tim. 4:1** <note>The original margin cites 1 Tim 4:12, but the context refers to the "doctrines of devils" mentioned in 1 Tim 4:1</note></margin> *with their mouths and honor me with their lips, but have removed their hearts far from me; and their fear of me consists of rules taught by men.”*

<summary>This page explores the psychological and spiritual causes of hypocrisy, including fear of man, a "cauterized" or numb conscience, and a heart that prefers human traditions over God's truth.</summary>
<keywords>hypocrisy, Apostle Peter, Barnabas, conscience, legalism, Isaiah 29:13, 1 Timothy 4:2, orthopodein, religious pretense</keywords>

## ->Signs and Symptoms.<-

[[margin: **Signs and symptoms of secret hypocrisy: his blindness.**]] He who is subject to secret hypocrisy fixes his eyes too much upon his own worthiness and graces; he admires himself above his fellows.

He looks too little and too seldom at his own wants and weaknesses. He is not thoroughly acquainted with the slowness of his race and the smallness of his progress toward so high a prize.

[[margin: **His carelessness.**]] He strives coldly against his most secret pride; he does not take as much pains as he ought in humbling <note>original: "deiecting"</note> himself so that he may sensibly feel the depth <note>original: "bottome"</note> of the secret mystery of his hidden corruption, and cry out with a [[margin: **Rom. 7. 24.**]] wounded spirit: *O wretched <note>original: "miserable"</note> man that I am! Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?*

[[margin: **Signs and symptoms of temporizing <term>temporizing</term> hypocrisy.**]] <term>temporizing</term> — The act of adapting one's behavior or beliefs to suit the current time or circumstances, typically for personal gain or safety rather than out of true conviction.

The temporizing hypocrite's light is only general and confused; it puffs him up but does not sanctify him. His calling is ineffectual; he gives no response <note>original: "eccho"</note> to it. $^a$ In [[margin: $^a$ **Luk. 8. 13.** **Heb. 6. 4.**]] his faith, he has both illumination by the truth and approval of the truth, but no application or adoption <note>original: "appropriation"</note> of the same to his heart. $^b$ In place of true mortification <term>mortification</term>, he has nothing but the restraint of some sins and a [[margin: $^b$ **Mark. 6. 20.**]] conformity of external manners with Christians. <term>mortification</term> — A spiritual practice of "killing off" or subduing sinful desires and worldly passions.

$^c$ He is careful to stop the more obvious <note>original: "groffer"</note> sins; [[margin: $^c$ **Rom. 7. 24.**]] he amends some things, but the idol of the heart is still preserved, and the very root of sin remains unkilled <note>original: "vnmortified"</note>. $^d$ He works [[margin: $^d$ **Phil. 2. 12.** **and 3. 13.**]] out his salvation securely, coldly, and without fear. He makes all heavenly matters secondary <note>original: "subordinate"</note> to his worldly business; his care for heaven (*"that one only necessary thing"*) is set aside for the future <note>original: "vnder reuerfion" — a legal term meaning a right to property that only begins after a certain event or time</note>. $^a$ His feeling of sin is confused; $^b$ his terror of conscience is only a servile fear <term>servile fear</term>: [[margin: $^a$ **1. Sam. 29. 21.** **Gen. 4. 13.** $^b$ **Mat. 27. 19, 24.** $^c$ **Heb. 12. 17.** $^d$ **Numb. 23. 10.** $^e$ **Exod. 9. 27.** **Act. 8. 24.** **Rom. 8, 16, 26.**]] <term>servile fear</term> — A fear of punishment, like that of a slave for a master, rather than a "filial fear" based on love and respect for God.

He is sorry for the sin that he does not actually dislike, $^c$ and is more grieved for the punishment than for the fault. $^d$ And because he fears hell, he would gladly be happy. $^e$ His love for God is mercenary <note>original: "mercenary" (motivated only by reward or pay)</note>; he would rather be prayed for than pray himself. He confides much in his

He is $^a$ a well without water and a cloud carried about by the winds. ## ->Prognostics. <note>Prognostics: predictions of the likely course or outcome of a condition</note><-

<margin>**The danger of secret hypocrisy.**</margin> **I**f secret hypocrisy is not cured in time, the egg will grow into a cockatrice <note>Cockatrice: a mythical serpent-like creature hatched from a cock's egg that could kill with a single glance</note>. It will eventually make even the best man embrace some groundless eccentricity <note>original: "singularity"</note> and degenerate into the madness of unjustifiable opinions; rooting deeply, spreading dangerously, and causing harm under the guise of truth <note>original: "hurting plausibly"</note>. This happens because of his secret pride, as he regards his own virtues <note>original: "graces"</note> with too much admiration. Yet, because this only happens to the person of a chosen child <note>Chosen child: in Reformed theology, one of the "elect" predestined by God for salvation</note>, he still remains under the hope of recovery and final mercy.

And as for the double-minded or temporizing <note>Temporizing: changing one's behavior or opinions to suit the current time or circumstances</note> hypocrite; if <margin>**The case of temporizing hypocrisy in a reprobate.**</margin> he is a reprobate <note>Reprobate: a person predestined to damnation</note>, he will never amend his ways. However, his pains in that "second death" <note>Second death: eternal damnation in the afterlife</note> will be mitigated because of his great restraint from outward sin.

A chosen child, before they are born again <note>original: "regenerate"</note>, might <margin>**In a chosen child.**</margin> be an open atheist—just like the thief who became penitent <note>The "Good Thief" crucified alongside Jesus</note>, or the fierce persecutor Saul, who became a preacher <note>The Apostle Paul</note>. In the same way, he may first be either a blatant or a merely formal hypocrite. God, in His own time, may use that hypocritical form of godliness as a tutor <note>original: "pedagogue"</note> leading toward true grace. There is some hope of reformation for such a person, especially if he is willing to take advice <note>original: "counselable"</note> and is manageable <note>original: "tractable"</note> in using all the means of grace <note>Means of grace: religious practices like prayer and scripture reading</note>.

He who accustometh himself to formal hypocrisy will eventually, <margin>**Dangers.**</margin> at the slightest temptation, become a more blatant hypocrite or an open atheist. And he who continues in that state—having a reputation for being alive, but in truth being dead <note>A reference to Revelation 3:1</note>—must <margin>**Rev. 2.** <note>The margin cites Revelation 2, though the quote regarding a "name that he is alive" is found in Revelation 3:1</note></margin> either

The dangerous case of a grosser hypocrite.

If God blesses his worldly estate, it is either to convert him or else to convict <note>original: "conuince"</note> him: when he calls for temporal things, God may grant his desires, but in wrath.

As for the grosser and grand hypocrite, he is of less hope and more miserable than the open atheist; he possesses the Christian name for his condemnation, and not for his remedy. He is an oilless, shining lamp, by which men's eyes are dazzled and wholesome admonitions are barred, so that he cannot amend. Open atheism provokes others to give admonitions, but hypocrisy bars all opportunity for good counsel.

He who is thus infected and affected sins against the light of conscience, which makes him incapable of saving graces. To his natural hardness, he joins his acquired <term>obfirmation</term> <note>original: "obfirmation"; a stubborn persistence in one's own way or a hardening of the heart.</note> and willfully shuts the windows of his soul. Because he is unknown, he thinks public admonitions do not belong to him, nor are they directed to him. He transfers them onto open sinners and cheats himself of that benefit.

His Christian name shall never make him a Christian. His judgment is likely to be extraordinary, and most great and certain. Feigned righteousness is not righteousness, but double iniquity <note>original: "Simulata equitas est duplex iniquitas."</note>. While he goes about to deceive men, he makes God as a mediator of his wickedness.

Though Isaac was deceived through ignorance <note>Referring to the biblical story where Isaac was tricked into blessing Jacob instead of Esau.</note>, yet God will not be mocked: He perfectly knows both the true Nathanael and the false-hearted Simon Magus. What hope has the hypocrite? His hypocrisy must at last break out and be detected. No man can long maintain a feigned persona: feigned things soon return to their own nature; his confidence is vain. (a) He shall not come into God's presence. (b) He cannot pray; and if he does it, God does not hear him: (c) and his prayer is turned to sin. *Will God hear his cry when trouble comes upon him?*

Remedies for secret hypocrisy.
Know yourself.

Closely observe the complacency you have in your own gifts; rip up new matters to renew repentance; beat down pride to increase humility, and to double your zeal.

If you are polluted with the grossest and <term>triple hypocrisy</term> <note>Likely referring to hypocrisy in heart, word, and deed, or toward God, oneself, and others.</note>, consider your thrice-miserable state: how you are not only of that "generation of vipers," and of that evil sort of "children of the adulteress and the sorcerer," but also of the Devil your father, who is a liar and the father of lies. The Lord Jesus perceives your wickedness, and many fearful woes are threatened against you. Nineveh and the Queen of Sheba <note>original: "Saba"</note> shall rise in judgment and shall condemn you. You are a fool and blind; how can you escape the damnation of hell? This consideration, deeply felt in your heart, should awake you who sleep, so that you may stand up from among the number of dead hypocrites and Christ may give you life.

Remember that just as the Searcher of all hearts knows your hypocrisy, so all your most hidden sins are most conspicuously registered—by the hand of God, with the <term>point of a diamond</term> <note>A reference to Jeremiah 17:1, meaning an indelible or permanent record.</note>—both in your slumbering conscience and before His tribunal. He is coming against you as a most hateful object of His revenging justice, with armies of plagues. Why, therefore, should you continue any longer in such base and unnatural enmity against so pure a Majesty?

<margin>
Romans 2:8–9.

And God’s mercy if you repent.
James 4:8.
</margin>

...[Are you] still a most notorious instrument of Satan’s deepest malice? What can you expect but indignation and wrath, tribulation and anguish? Your soul is immortal, your body must rise again, and you shall be presented before that Tribunal; you must give an account of everything. Eternal life and endless death are both set before you; you are rushing toward an uncertain end, and every moment threatens your departure.

Therefore, cast off your hypocrisy and mourn for your bygone iniquities. The Lord still calls for you and waits for you: *Draw near to him (with sincerity) and he shall draw near to you; cleanse your hands, you sinner, and purge your heart, you double-minded* (James 4:8). If you do this, you shall live here with a blessed contentment, die with unspeakable and glorious joy, shine thereafter like the firmament <note>The heavens or the sky.</note>, and dwell forever most blessedly in God’s presence.

<margin>
Remedies for temporizing hypocrisy.

The form and power of godliness are two different things.
</margin>

If you are subject to temporizing <term>hypocrisy that adapts to the current times or social climate for personal gain</term> and the false belief that you have saving grace and the power of godliness while you only have the *show* of it, it is best to enlighten your mind so you can distinguish between things that are different. For a temporizing hypocrite has nothing but the *show*, and has nothing at all of the true sanctifying and saving power of godliness. You must clearly see that all your godliness is but a *show*, and you must be put quite out of all hope of obtaining mercy and life through it.

<margin>
The form and show of godliness consist of the following particulars:
Natural and moral gifts.
2 Peter 2:20.

Supernatural and common gifts.
</margin>

The show of godliness consists of the following things: natural and moral gifts; science <note>original: "science"; here meaning general knowledge or learning rather than the modern scientific method</note>; experience; arts; and political skill; moral virtues; and civil honesty. It includes being more respectable than an open atheist or a triple hypocrite <note>A term likely referring to a specific classification used by the author for those who deceive God, others, and themselves</note>. It involves a heart frightened by the suggestion of infamous sins, the amendment of life in many things, respectful works of charity, and the suppressing of many evil actions and grosser sins—but not mortifying <term>to subdue or put to death sinful desires at their root</term> them at the root.

It includes an outward progress in one's religious profession and the external exercise of religion: acknowledging the truth, professing, con-

Examine your imaginary godliness.
</margin>

...professing, preaching, and defending the same. These are the general graces of the Spirit and a shadow of <term>regeneration</term> <note>original: "regeneration"; the process of spiritual rebirth or being "born again"</note>; the gifts of important callings, the working of miracles, an outward and ineffective calling, a general confused arrogance, and an unsanctified light. It is a dead faith without works; an <term>historical faith</term> <note>original: "hiſtoricall faith"; a belief that the facts of the Bible are true without a personal, saving trust in Christ</note> without any real approval of the truth; and a temporary faith without true application or personal adoption of that truth into the heart.

It includes good intentions, good inclinations, and holy longings for happiness more than for holiness: mere wishes, desiring to be happy in heaven while only fearing torment in hell. It consists of earthly prayers for worldly trash—desiring to be prayed for by others more than praying for oneself. It is a stinging terror and a slave-like fear of sin; a frightening sorrow and a reluctance to commit sin only for fear of punishment. It is sorrow for a sin already committed without a true hatred of it; mourning more for the pain it causes than for the sin itself. This is external humiliation: confession made only in extreme circumstances or in the agony of body or soul.

It is a <term>mercenary love</term> <note>original: "mercenary loue"; loving God only for the sake of rewards or personal gain</note> of God, superficial joys in the Word, and flashes of fleeting and passing comforts that die as soon as they are born, their life vanishing in a moment. It shows respect for ministers, a reluctance to displease them, and a desire for their company. It is a frivolous, simple, and weak taste of the powers of the world to come. It is ignorant zeal; such a person is a member of the visible Church and esteemed as such (though not part of the <term>Catholic Church</term> <note>original: "Catholike"; here meaning the universal, invisible church of all true believers across time, rather than the Roman Catholic denomination</note>), being externally within the <term>Covenant</term> <note>original: "Couenant"; the spiritual agreement between God and His people</note> and a participant in the symbols of spiritual privilege.

Therefore, examine your supposed and imaginary godliness. You have not reached its *true power*. You shall find it lacking in many points of the common outward display. You will find that you, with your formal religion, are far inferior to many <term>Ethnics</term> <note>original: "Ethnicks"; pagans or non-Christians</note> and outcasts who have run far ahead of you. Your former worldly conviction has been like a hungry man dreaming of food, or a poor man dreaming of gold.
